cases.question: Is the citation beginning 'האמר' part of Rav Oshaya's objection or an anonymous reply? What does the wider passage (Sanhedrin 59a-59b) support about people and relations, keeping R. Yosi bar Avin and R. Yosi bar Hanina as alternative attributions?

findings.claim: The subject is circumcision. The wider passage (59a-59b) asks why circumcision is not one of the Noahide commandments. One answer says circumcision was commanded only to Abraham and his offspring. The Ishmael, Esau and Keturah exchanges test that answer.

evidence.exact_quote: אי בעית אימא מילה מעיקר' לאברהם הוא דקא מזהר ליה רחמנא ואתה את בריתי תשמור אתה וזרעך אחריך לדורותם אתה וזרעך אין איניש אחרינא לא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: If you wish, say: circumcision was from the outset commanded by the Merciful One to Abraham, 'and you shall keep My covenant, you and your offspring after you' - you and your offspring, yes; another person, no.

evidence.exact_quote: והרי מילה שנאמרה לבני נח דכתיב (בראשית יז, ט) ואתה את בריתי תשמור ונשנית בסיני (ויקרא יב, ג) וביום השמיני ימול לישראל נאמרה ולא לבני נח
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: But what of circumcision, which was said to the descendants of Noah ... and repeated at Sinai ... it was said to Israel and not to the descendants of Noah.

findings.reasoning: This settles the first reading's needed_context: the obligation is circumcision. Rav Oshaya's 'אלא מעתה' ('if so, then') builds on the offspring answer at 59b:9-11.
findings.graph_effect: Close the episode's needed_context. Abraham is named at 59b:9, which was outside the first reading's window, so add him as a biblical figure in the wider passage.

findings.claim: The printed text reads 'האמר' before the two attributed teachers. The form is a rhetorical question ('but did he not say?'). Grammatically, it can close Rav Oshaya's objection or open an anonymous reply. The Hebrew itself does not mark the change of speaker.

evidence.exact_quote: מתקיף לה רב אושעיא אלא מעתה בני קטורה לא לחייבו האמר ר' יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא ר' יוסי בר חנינא (בראשית יז, יד) את בריתי הפר לרבות בני קטורה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rav Oshaya objected: If so, the sons of Keturah should not be obligated? Did not R. Yosi bar Avin, and some say R. Yosi bar Hanina, say: 'he has broken My covenant' - to include the sons of Keturah.

evidence.exact_quote: הָאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר אָבִין, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא

findings.reasoning: In Talmudic Aramaic, 'הא אמר' / 'והאמר' often introduces a counter-citation inside a question. That supports reading the citation as the end of the objection: 'your rule exempts them, but a known teaching includes them'. It can also be heard as 'but surely X said'. That is a reply: the sons of Keturah are covered by a separate inclusion, so the offspring rule still stands. The general usage point is this dossier's reasoning, not something a fetched source says.
findings.graph_effect: Do not fix the citation's voice to Rav Oshaya. Add a reading group, 'citation_frame', with two branches: 'objection_continuation' (Rav Oshaya or the objection cites the teaching) and 'anonymous_reply' (the anonymous Talmud answers with the teaching).

findings.claim: Three published translations or explanations read the citation as the reply, not as part of Rav Oshaya's objection: the William Davidson English, the Steinsaltz Hebrew and the Soncino English.

evidence.exact_quote: Rav Oshaya objects to this: If that is so, the descendants of Keturah, Abraham’s second wife, should not be obligated to observe circumcision. The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin says, and some say that it is Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina who says
ומשיבים: האמר [הרי אמר] ר' יוסי בר אבין, ואיתימא [ויש אומרים] שהיה זה ר' יוסי בר חנינא:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: And they reply: 'behold, R. Yosi bar Avin said, and some say it was R. Yosi bar Hanina'

evidence.exact_quote: R. Oshaia objected: If so, the children of Keturah should have been exempt!
Did not R. Jose b. Abin, or as others say, R. Jose b. Hanina, state:
This is the reply. The verse teaches the inclusion of the immediate sons of Keturah, but not of their descendants.

findings.reasoning: All three end Rav Oshaya's words at 'לא לחייבו' and give the citation to the anonymous discussion: 'The Gemara answers', 'ומשיבים' and 'This is the reply'. These are modern editorial judgements. They are not manuscript evidence, and they may depend on one another.
findings.graph_effect: Make 'anonymous_reply' the preferred branch of 'citation_frame', with provenance: the three translations. Keep 'objection_continuation' open (see F4, F5).

findings.claim: Older authors do not settle who says the citation. The Minchat Chinukh summarises the whole line, including 'האמר', as the Talmud's own question and does not name Rav Oshaya. The Yad Ramah wonders what Rav Hoshaya based his objection on. He says that if the basis were the verse 'את בריתי הפר', there would be no objection.

evidence.exact_quote: דמקשה הש"ס אלא מעתה בני קטורה לא לחייבי האמר ריב"א ואיתימא ריב"ח את בריתי הפר לרבות בני קטורה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: that the Talmud asks: if so, the sons of Keturah should not be obligated - but did not R. Y. b. A., and some say R. Y. b. H., say ...

evidence.exact_quote: ולא ידענא מהיכא פשיטא ליה לרב הושעיא דבני קטורה חייבין דקא מקשי ליה אלא מעתה בני קטורה לא ליחייבו דמשמע דפשיטא לן דחייבין ואי משום דמשמע ליה את בריתי הפר לרבות בני קטורה א"כ מאי קושיא דקא מקשי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: I do not know from where it is obvious to Rav Hoshaya that the sons of Keturah are obligated, that he objects 'if so, the sons of Keturah should not be obligated', which implies it is obvious to us that they are obligated; and if it is because he understands 'he has broken My covenant' as including the sons of Keturah, then what objection is he raising?

findings.reasoning: The Minchat Chinukh's summary joins the citation to the question (the 'objection_continuation' branch), but gives it to the Talmud, not to a named sage. The Yad Ramah does not treat the verse as Rav Hoshaya's stated ground. He raises it as a possible ground and rejects it because it makes the objection empty. That fits the view that Rav Hoshaya's own words end at 'לא ליחייבו'. From the saved text alone, it cannot be known whether the Yad Ramah's copy contained the R. Yosi clause.
findings.graph_effect: Record that commentators disagree about how the citation relates to the objection. Even under 'objection_continuation', the speaker may be the anonymous Talmud expanding the objection, not Rav Oshaya himself.

findings.claim: Sefer HeArukh quotes this line with two differences from the printed text. It has 'אמר' ('said'), not 'האמר', and its alternative teacher is 'בר זבידא' (bar Zevida), not 'ר' יוסי בר חנינא'.

evidence.exact_quote: כדגרסינן (סנהדרין נט) אלא מעתה בני קטורה לא ליחייבו אמר רבי יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא בר זבידא את בריתי הפר לרבות בני קטורה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: as we read (Sanhedrin 59): 'If so, the sons of Keturah should not be obligated. Said R. Yosi bar Avin, and some say bar Zevida: he has broken My covenant - to include the sons of Keturah.'

findings.reasoning: 'כדגרסינן' ('as we read') presents this as the Arukh's text of Sanhedrin 59. A plain 'אמר' reads more easily as a reply or a separate statement than as a rhetorical counter-question. The saved file is the Lublin 1883 printing. Whether this was the medieval author's reading or came in during transmission of the Arukh is not checked here.
findings.graph_effect: Treat the name of the second teacher as a textual variant: 'yosi_bar_hanina' in the printed Bavli, 'yosi_bar_zevida' in the Arukh. This variant sits inside the 'ואיתימא' alternative, so it is nested. Keep the two printed teachers as alternative attributions, and flag the second with the variant.

findings.claim: J. N. Epstein says the Bavli regularly writes 'ר' יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא ר' יוסי בר זבידא'. He lists Sanhedrin 59b among places that should be corrected to that form ('וכצ"ל', 'and so one should read').

evidence.exact_quote: ונחלף להם לבבלים ר' יוסי בר זבידא (= ר' יוסי סתם בירוש') בר' יוסי בר אבין, כרגיל בבבלי בכ"מ
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: The Babylonians confused R. Yosi bar Zevida (= plain R. Yosi in the Yerushalmi) with R. Yosi bar Avin, as is usual in the Bavli in many places

evidence.exact_quote: ר' יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא ר' יוסי בר זבידא
ברכות יג א, שבת סח א, יבמות מה ב, כתובות מד ב, הוריות ד ע"א וחולין נה א, וכצ"ל בסוכה לז ב וסנהד' נט ב.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Berakhot 13a, Shabbat 68a, Yevamot 45b, Ketubot 44b, Horayot 4a and Chullin 55a; and so one should read in Sukkah 37b and Sanhedrin 59b.

evidence.exact_quote: בכ"י פ' ורי"ף: בר חנינא, וזו טעות.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: [about the Taanit case] in manuscript P and the Rif: bar Hanina, and this is an error.

findings.reasoning: This is a scholar's emendation. The note does not say which manuscripts support it at Sanhedrin 59b, but it agrees with the Arukh (F5). Epstein's note on Taanit shows he regards 'bar Hanina' in this slot as a known scribal error elsewhere. Epstein's historical claim, that the Babylonians confused the two names, is his interpretation and is kept separate from the textual finding.
findings.graph_effect: Lower confidence in the printed 'ר' יוסי בר חנינא' as the second attribution. Do not delete it: the instruction is to keep both printed teachers as alternatives. Add 'yosi_bar_zevida' as a proposed variant, backed by the Arukh and Epstein.

findings.claim: In the Sefaria search results checked here, R. Yosi bar Avin is paired with R. Yosi bar Zevida in several Bavli passages. The pairing 'R. Yosi bar Avin, and some say R. Yosi bar Hanina' appears only at Sanhedrin 59b:12. In Yevamot 45b, the Talmud itself reports that a story told of R. Yosi bar Avin was really about R. Yosi b. R. Zevida.

evidence.exact_quote: מֵתִיב רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר אָבִין, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר זְבִידָא
אמר ר' יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא רבי יוסי בר זבידא משל דסומכוס
א"ר יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא ר' יוסי בר זבילא זאת אומרת
מתקיף לה רב אושעיא אלא מעתה בני קטורה לא לחייבו האמר ר' יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא ר' יוסי בר חנינא
איקלע ר' יוסי בר אבין לאתרין והוה עובדא בפנויה ואכשר באשת איש ופסיל א"ר ששת לדידי אמר לי רב גזא לא ר' יוסי בר אבין הוה אלא רבי יוסי ברבי זבידא הוה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: R. Yosi bar Avin came to our place and there was a case ... Rav Sheshet said: to me Rav Geza said, it was not R. Yosi bar Avin but R. Yosi b. R. Zevida.

findings.reasoning: The search results show Avin/Zevida pairs at Berakhot 13a, Ketubot 44b, Chullin 55a, Horayot 4a and Sukkah 37b. At Sukkah 37b the Wikisource text reads 'זבילא' and the Davidson text reads 'זבידא'. Both searches for 'ואיתימא ... יוסי בר חנינא' returned no other Bavli passage paired with bar Avin. This is limited to what Sefaria's search returned for the exact phrases. Spelling variants could be missed. Yevamot 45b is a story about one event, and the same two names are confused in it. That is transmission evidence only and does not make them one person.
findings.graph_effect: This supports F5 and F6. Record a corpus-level finding that bar Avin and bar Zevida often alternate. Do not merge R. Yosi bar Avin, R. Yosi bar Zevida and R. Yosi bar Hanina; different names are not evidence of one person or of two.

findings.claim: The wider sugya is built on a principle of R. Yosi b. R. Hanina, stated at 59a. That name is written 'ר' יוסי בר' חנינא' at 59a and 'ר' יוסי בר חנינא' in the focal line.

evidence.exact_quote: כדר' יוסי בר' חנינא דא"ר יוסי בר' חנינא כל מצוה שנאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני לזה ולזה נאמרה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: In accordance with R. Yosi b. R. Hanina, for R. Yosi b. R. Hanina said: every commandment stated to the descendants of Noah and repeated at Sinai was stated to both.

findings.reasoning: This dossier's own hypothesis, not stated by any fetched source: the nearby name may have influenced a scribe to write 'בר חנינא' at 59b:12 where the Arukh has 'בר זבידא'. It is weak and unproven. Separately, the shared name 'Yosi' plus 'Hanina' does not show that the 59a sage and the second teacher at 59b:12 are the same person.
findings.graph_effect: Add the two only as a coreference candidate for review, not a merge. Also record R. Yosi b. R. Hanina as the author of the principle discussed at 59a, which is outside the focal line.

findings.claim: The Yad Ramah names the objector 'רב הושעיא' (Rav Hoshaya). The printed text has 'רב אושעיא'. The Soncino English has 'R. Oshaia'.

evidence.exact_quote: מתקיף לה רב הושעיא אלא מעתה דלא פקדיה רחמנא אלא איצחק בני קטורה הילודים לאברהם לא ליחייבו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rav Hoshaya objected: if so, since the Merciful One commanded only regarding Isaac, the sons of Keturah born to Abraham should not be obligated.

evidence.exact_quote: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אוֹשַׁעְיָא

findings.reasoning: Aleph/he spelling variation is common in this name. It is a spelling variant of the same mention, not evidence of a different person. The Yad Ramah also says the objection targets the 'only Isaac' rule.
findings.graph_effect: Add 'רב הושעיא' as a variant spelling on the Oshaya mention. Make no global identity claim.

findings.claim: Commentators disagree about who 'בני קטורה' ('sons of Keturah') are. Rashi, Ritva, the Soncino note, and most commentators as reported by the Meiri say the six sons themselves, not their descendants. Rambam, as read by the Kessef Mishneh, the Maharsha and the Ran (quoted in Reshimot Shiurim), includes their descendants.

evidence.exact_quote: לרבות בני קטורה - אותם ששה לבדם ולא זרעם אבל אברהם נצטוה לכל הנולדים לו:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: To include the sons of Keturah: those six alone and not their offspring; but Abraham was commanded regarding all born to him.

evidence.exact_quote: בני קטורה - אותן ששה שנולדו לאברהם הן עצמן לא לחייבו ונימא השתא דלא מל אברהם כל בניו שהיו לו בחייו:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: The sons of Keturah: those six born to Abraham, they themselves should not be obligated, and shall we now say Abraham did not circumcise all the sons he had in his lifetime?

evidence.exact_quote: ויש לומר דההיא על בני קטורה לבדם ומדין יליד בית אבל זרעם אינם בני מילה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: One may say that it refers to the sons of Keturah alone, by the law of one born in the household, but their offspring are not subject to circumcision.

evidence.exact_quote: ומ"מ רוב מפרשים פירשו לרבות בני קטורה הם עצמם ולא זרעם
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: In any case, most commentators explained 'to include the sons of Keturah' as themselves and not their offspring.

evidence.exact_quote: אמרו חכמים שבני קטורה שהם זרעו של אברהם שבא אחר ישמעאל ויצחק חייבין במילה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: The Sages said that the sons of Keturah, who are the offspring of Abraham that came after Ishmael and Isaac, are obligated in circumcision.

evidence.exact_quote: האמר ר' יוסי בר אבין ואי תימא ר"י בר חנינא את בריתי הפר לרבות בני קטורה ומפרש דהיינו בני קטורה וזרעם
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: ... and he [Rambam] explains that this means the sons of Keturah and their offspring.

evidence.exact_quote: ופי' אלא מעתה בני קטורה כו' לרבות בני קטורה כו' על זרעם של בני קטורה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and he [Rambam] explained 'if so, the sons of Keturah' ... 'to include the sons of Keturah' as referring to the offspring of the sons of Keturah

evidence.exact_quote: רש"י ז"ל מפרש אותן בנים שילדה קטורה לאברהם בלבד שהיה אברהם חייב בהן. ולא מחוור
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: [Ran, as quoted:] Rashi explains: only those sons whom Keturah bore to Abraham, for whom Abraham was obligated. And this is not clear.

evidence.exact_quote: ובעיקר מחלוקת רש"י ורמב"ם אם בני קטורה נצטוו גם לדורות או לא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: On the basic dispute between Rashi and Rambam whether the sons of Keturah were commanded for later generations too, or not.

findings.reasoning: The Talmud text only says 'בני קטורה'. Whether that means six sons or a lineage is a commentary dispute. The father-son link between Abraham and Keturah's sons comes from Rashi ('שנולדו לאברהם') and the Rambam ('זרעו של אברהם'), with Genesis 25 in the background. The focal line does not state it. The Ran's words are known here only as quoted in Reshimot Shiurim.
findings.graph_effect: Give the 'k_desc' group a scope reading group: 'six_sons' (Rashi, Ritva, Soncino note, most commentators per the Meiri) versus 'lineage' (Rambam per the Kessef Mishneh and the Maharsha; the Ran as quoted). A father-child edge from Abraham to Keturah's sons is commentary or biblical background with that provenance, not a claim of the focal line.

findings.claim: The Maharsha, explaining Rambam's view, grounds the objection in what can be observed: many nations descended from Keturah practise circumcision, which shows they were obligated. On that account, the objection does not rest on R. Yosi's teaching.

evidence.exact_quote: ופריך הכי בפשיטות דלא ליחייבו לפי מה שאנו רואים דהרבה אומות מבני קטורה שקבלו עליהם מצות מילה דמוכח דנתחייבו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and he asks this simply, 'they should not be obligated?', according to what we see, that many nations from the sons of Keturah took upon themselves circumcision, which shows that they were obligated

evidence.exact_quote: לפי מה שכ' הר"ן דודאי דאבני קטורה ל"ק דהא הוצרך אברהם למול אותם משום יליד בית ולכן לא פריך רק אזרע דב"ק
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: according to what the Ran wrote, about the sons of Keturah themselves there is no difficulty, since Abraham had to circumcise them as household-born; therefore he asks only about the offspring of the sons of Keturah

findings.reasoning: If the ground is observation, the citation of R. Yosi does the answering, which fits the 'anonymous_reply' branch. This is the Maharsha's reconstruction of the argument, not something the text says.
findings.graph_effect: This supports the 'anonymous_reply' branch as a commentary reading. Save it as interpretation with the Maharsha's name on it.

findings.claim: No reading checked makes Rav Oshaya hear, meet or study with either R. Yosi, and there is no chain of transmission. The two R. Yosis are alternative answers to one question, 'who said this teaching?'. They are not two people who both said it, and they are not linked to each other.

evidence.exact_quote: האמר ר' יוסי בר אבין ואיתימא ר' יוסי בר חנינא
ואיתימא [ויש אומרים] שהיה זה ר' יוסי בר חנינא:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and some say it was R. Yosi bar Hanina

findings.reasoning: Under 'anonymous_reply', the Talmud's editors set a teaching against Rav Oshaya's challenge. The link is between statements, and neither person speaks to the other. Under 'objection_continuation', the objection cites a known teaching. That is a literary citation, which may be the editors' elaboration, not evidence that Rav Oshaya heard it from either sage. 'ואיתימא' signals uncertainty about whose teaching it is.
findings.graph_effect: Create no edges between Oshaya and Yosi bar Avin or Yosi bar Hanina, such as heard_from, met or student_of, and no edge between the two Yosis. At most, record a statement-level 'answered_by' or 'cites' relation, with the speaker left branch-dependent.

findings.claim: The Davidson English adds family information that the Aramaic does not contain: 'Abraham’s second wife' for Keturah and 'Isaac’s son' for Esau.

evidence.exact_quote: the descendants of Keturah, Abraham’s second wife, should not be obligated
the descendants of Esau, Isaac’s son, should be obligated
בני עשו לחייבו ביצחק ולא כל יצחק

findings.reasoning: In that edition, bold marks the literal translation and plain text marks the translator's explanation. These phrases are unbolded glosses. The Talmud does imply that Esau's line belongs to 'Isaac', because 'ביצחק ולא כל יצחק' ('in Isaac, but not all of Isaac') is the reason given for excluding Esau's descendants.
findings.graph_effect: Family edges such as Keturah wife_of Abraham should carry provenance 'translator gloss / biblical background', not 'Talmud text'. An Esau-Isaac descent link is at most implied by the argument.

findings.claim: The Meiri gives the teaching with no name at all ('והוא שאמרו', 'and this is what they said'), and the Arukh drops the title and first name of the second teacher ('ואיתימא בר זבידא'). Later authors cite this line in different ways.

evidence.exact_quote: אבל בני קטורה שנולדו אחרי יצחק וישמעאל חייבים והוא שאמרו את בריתי הפר לרבות בני קטורה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: but the sons of Keturah, born after Isaac and Ishmael, are obligated, and this is what they said: 'he has broken My covenant' to include the sons of Keturah

evidence.exact_quote: ואיתימא בר זבידא

findings.reasoning: When a later author paraphrases a line and leaves out a name, that is not evidence that the name was absent from the author's Talmud text.
findings.graph_effect: Do not treat the Meiri's missing names as a textual variant.

lessons: A quoted teaching introduced by 'האמר' / 'והאמר' needs a speaker branch. The same words can end an objection or begin an anonymous reply. A reader should not give it the objector's voice without evidence.

An 'ואיתימא' alternative can itself carry a textual variant. Here the second teacher is bar Hanina in print and bar Zevida in the Arukh. The contract needs nested variants inside a branch; the pilot README already flags nested dependencies.

Recurring name-pair formulas across the corpus ('X ואיתימא Y') are useful evidence for textual criticism. A one-off pairing is a signal to check manuscripts and medieval quotations before building any edge on it.
Unbolded glosses in a translation (such as 'Abraham’s second wife') are not the text. Family edges need provenance: Talmud text, commentary, translator or biblical background.
Group membership ('בני קטורה') can be disputed by commentators. Model its scope as a reading group with named holders.
A patronymic parent should not become a person node by default.
When a later author paraphrases without a name (the Meiri's 'שאמרו'), that is not evidence the name was absent from the text they read.

The user explicitly requested these name-internal relations.

findings.target: F12; reading.md The two attributed teachers
findings.reason: The passage reports alternative attributions. It does not establish that both teachers historically said the teaching, but neither does it establish that only one did. Replace categorical wording that they are not two people who both taught it with that narrower statement.

The English Davidson translation and the Steinsaltz Hebrew explanation share an editorial basis. They show how that edition reads the speaker boundary; they are not two independent witnesses voting for it. Soncino supplies a separate published explanation, not proof of historical speech.

Keep the Arukh quotation as a textual witness and Epstein's proposed correction as a scholarly emendation. Neither replaces the saved printed text. Bar Zevida in the Arukh lacks the full first name at that position; the expanded identification depends on additional interpretation.
Search results document the examples actually returned and checked. They do not establish an exhaustive count across all textual witnesses.

The saved Hebrew lacks an explicit new speaker, while the checked published explanations supply an anonymous reply. Keep the named objector separate from the citation voice and preserve the remaining interpretive branch. None of this proves a meeting or direct hearing.

cases.question: Preserve expressly unsaid speech: ולא אמר מי בדיל מר. Separate a formal question not asked from the exchange that actually occurs. Research student-colleague claims and their limits.

findings.claim: The segment holds three different speech items. Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba asks Rav a question. Someone, Rav by context, answers. Then the anonymous Talmud remarks that he did not say the formal wording 'has the Master separated'. Only the first two are reported utterances. The third reports a wording that was not used.

evidence.exact_quote: והיינו דקאמר ליה רבי ירמיה בר אבא לרב מי בדלת
אמר ליה אין בדילנא
ולא אמר מי בדיל מר
And Rabbi Yirmeya did not say to him: Did the Master distance himself, as would have been appropriate had he merely been Rav’s student.
and he did not say to him, Has the Master laid aside

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'And this is what Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba said to Rav: Have you separated? He said to him: Yes, I have separated. And he did not say: Has the Master separated?' The question uses the second person (בדלת). The reply is first person (בדילנא). The third clause is negative and introduces a counterfactual wording in the third-person form of address (מר). All the checked witnesses share this three-part shape: the Wikisource Bavli, the Davidson Aramaic and English, the Cohen English and the Soncino English. The unsaid wording is content inside a negative report, not an event.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the asks claim (Yirmiya to Rav, content 'have you separated') and the answer claim (Rav to Yirmiya, content 'yes, I have separated'). Add a third, separate record for the remark that the formal wording was not said. Mark it negative, give it the anonymous Talmud as voice, and make the counterfactual wording its content. Never turn the formal wording into an asks edge or into an 'addressed as Master' edge.

findings.claim: The student-colleague status comes from the anonymous Talmud, not from a narrator. It answers a difficulty ('Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba is different'). The Talmud supports it by citing the exchange ('and this is why he said to him'). Rashi reads the missing formal wording as the proof.

evidence.exact_quote: שאני רבי ירמיה בר אבא דתלמיד חבר הוה
ורבי ירמיה היכי עביד הכי והא אמר רב יהודה אמר רב לעולם אל יתפלל אדם
ולא אמר ליה מי בדיל מר – שמע מינה תלמיד חבר הוי ליה
he was not a mere student of Rav. Rather, he was a disciple-colleague

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba is different, for he was a student-colleague.' The word שאני marks an answer to the difficulty raised at 27a:17-27b:2. Rashi's translation (mine): 'And he did not say to him, has the Master separated: learn from this that he was a student-colleague to him.' So in the text the relation is a claim with its evidence attached. The narrator of the prayer story does not report it.
findings.graph_effect: Change the voice of the student-colleague claim (earlier c14) from narrator to the anonymous Talmud's resolution. Record its basis as explicit statement plus a proof from the form of address. Link it to the negative speech record from f1 with a 'supported by' link. The inverse display (Rav as teacher-colleague of Yirmiya) is not a second observation.

findings.claim: In the printed Talmud the other party is not named in the status sentence. Context supplies Rav. The Halakhot Gedolot quotation names Rav explicitly ('in relation to Rav'). Some later authors quote the sentence with Rav added.

evidence.exact_quote: והוה מצלי רבי ירמיה בר אבא לאחוריה דרב
שאני רב ירמיה בר אבא דתלמיד חבר הוה לגבי רב
דקמשני תלמודא שאני ר' ירמיה בר אבא דתלמיד חבר דרב הוה
who was a fellow (under Rab)

findings.reasoning: The difficulty is about praying behind one's teacher, and the only teacher in the scene is Rav, so the object is clear from context. Halakhot Gedolot is an early quotation carried in a printed code. It is a different kind of evidence from the Talmud editions. It is not a manuscript. The Bach and Taz quotations may be paraphrases. Jastrow's parenthesis is a lexicographer's gloss.
findings.graph_effect: Keep Rav as the object. Mark it as supplied by context in the printed text, and as explicit in the Halakhot Gedolot quotation (a separate evidence type). Do not count the later quotations as more witnesses.

findings.claim: The Talmud uses the status only to explain why Yirmiya could pray behind Rav. The later authorities who give its scope do not agree. Tosafot extends it to everything in Rabbi Eliezer's list. Maimonides defines it as someone who did not learn most of his wisdom from that teacher; such a person still stands up for him and tears his garment when he dies. The Shulchan Arukh codifies only the prayer permission. The Taz and the Bach draw a rule of speech from it: a student-colleague need not call the teacher 'Master'.

evidence.exact_quote: ובתלמיד חבר דשרי ככל הני דלקמן
אבל אם לא למד ממנו רוב חכמתו הרי זה תלמיד חבר ואינו חייב בכבודו בכל אלו הדברים
תלמיד חבר מותר להתפלל אחורי רבו
ובתלמיד חבר אין מוטל עליו להזכירו בשם מר כשמדבר עמו
והיינו משום דמסתמא תלמיד חבר רשאי לחלוק על רבו

findings.reasoning: These are later readings in their authors' own voices. Maimonides' definition, 'did not learn most of his wisdom from him', is not stated in Berakhot 27b. The relation still keeps a teacher side: the codes go on calling the other party רבו, 'his teacher'. Hyamson renders Maimonides as 'a junior to a senior fellow-student'. That is a translator's phrasing.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the subtype student_colleague with fixed roles: Yirmiya is the student-colleague and Rav is the teacher. Do not flatten it to plain colleague or plain student. Do not add 'learned most of his wisdom from' or 'did not learn most of his wisdom from' as textual facts. Attach the Tosafot and Maimonides scopes as commentary notes, each under its own author.

findings.claim: One commentator gives a further reason why the formal wording was not used. The Tziyyun LeNefesh Chayyah says Yirmiya cut his words short because he wanted to know at once whether Rav had accepted the Sabbath. It also says that addressing a full student's teacher this way would be real disrespect, so the proof still holds.

evidence.exact_quote: ור' ירמי' שלא אמר מר היינו משום שרצה לידע אם קיבל רב שבת בתפלתו
אבל בתלמיד גמור הוא אפקרותא ממש אם אומר לנוכח מי בדלת ושפיר הוכיח דר' ירמי' תלמיד חבר הוה

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'Rabbi Yirmiya did not say Master because he wanted to know whether Rav had accepted the Sabbath in his prayer'; 'but for a full student it is real disrespect to say to his face: have you separated; so the proof that Rabbi Yirmiya was a student-colleague is sound.' The same commentator says a student-colleague should still ideally say 'rabbi' when greeting. This softens how much the omission shows. It does not remove the proof.
findings.graph_effect: Attach this as a commentary note on the negative speech record. It does not change any edge.

findings.claim: Midrash Sekhel Tov quotes the question with the formal wording: 'Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba said to Rav: Has the Master separated from work?' That is the opposite of the printed Talmud. Its quotation also places the exchange at Rav's visit to Geniva and does not mention the student-colleague point.

evidence.exact_quote: תא שמע דרב איקלע לגבי גניבא צלי של שבת בערב שבת. אמר ליה ר' ירמי' בר אבא לרב מי בדיל מר ממלאכה אמר ליה בדילנא
ולא קאמר ליה מי בדיל מר
ולא אמר מי בדיל מר

findings.reasoning: Sekhel Tov quotes the story for a different legal point (whether one may make havdala early when the Ninth of Av falls on Sunday). It may paraphrase. The printed Talmud and the older Halakhot Gedolot quotation both have the negative remark. One later quotation cannot overturn them. Still, it is a real, different wording and should be kept as a separate evidence type.
findings.graph_effect: No change to the Bavli reading. Record a quotation variant on the asks claim: 'Sekhel Tov quotes the question with the formal address.' Do not create a 'Yirmiya addressed Rav as Master' edge from it.

findings.claim: The questioner's title varies between Rabbi and Rav. The printed Berakhot has Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba. The parallel citation in Eruvin 40b and the Halakhot Gedolot quotation have Rav Yirmiya bar Abba. Tosafot reports that most copies of Berakhot read Rav Yirmiya.

evidence.exact_quote: שאני רבי ירמיה בר אבא דתלמיד חבר הוה
דהאמר ליה רב ירמיה בר אבא לרב מי בדלת ואמר ליה אין בדילנא
דא"ל רב ירמיה בר אבא לרב מי בדלת וא"ל אין בדילנא
בברכות גרסינן ברוב ספרים רב ירמיה ובקדושין רבי ירמיה

findings.reasoning: Tosafot's remark reports the manuscripts it knew. It is not a manuscript itself. Eruvin 40b is a parallel inside the Talmud that cites the same exchange for a different point. It lacks the negative remark about the formal wording, which says nothing about the Berakhot text.
findings.graph_effect: Add 'רב ירמיה בר אבא' as an attested name form (alias) of the local Yirmiya entity. Keep the patronymic child_of claim and the local Abba placeholder unchanged. The title variant does not settle his historical identity.

findings.claim: Medieval authors did not agree on who this Yirmiya was, or on who his teacher was. In Kiddushin 46a a Rav Yirmiya bar Abba is called 'the student' next to Rav Huna. Tosafot raises the clash with Berakhot and suggests there were two sages called Rav Yirmiya. On Pesachim 106b Rashi takes 'his teacher' as Rav, while Tosafot considers Rav Huna. The Rivash calls Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba a student of Rabbi Yochanan and says Rav was not his main teacher.

evidence.exact_quote: נראין דברי תלמיד
רב הונא אמר אינה אוכלת רב ירמיה בר אבא אמר אוכלת
ונראה דתרי רב ירמיה הוו
לאו היינו רבי ירמיה דאמרי' בברכות
שם דתלמיד חבר הוה. עיין קדושין ד' מ"ו ע"א תוס' ד"ה נראין
שבקיה כרביה סבירא ליה
כרב דרב הונא משמיה דרב הוה אמר שמעתתיה
דרבי ירמיה בר אבא תלמיד של רבי יוחנן
אלא שלא היה רבו מובהק של רבי ירמיה בר אבא

findings.reasoning: These are identification hypotheses in their authors' voices. The Ritva on Kiddushin also says the Kiddushin figure is not the Yirmiya of Berakhot. His wording, as printed, is partly unclear. The Gilyon HaShas on Berakhot sends the reader to the Tosafot on Kiddushin. The Rivash's claim about Rabbi Yochanan is a later historical statement. I did not check it against the passage he cites. The Davidson English of Kiddushin 46a ('was like a student compared with Rav Huna') and of Pesachim 106b ('was a student of Rav') adds interpretations to the translation.
findings.graph_effect: Do not merge the Berakhot Yirmiya bar Abba with the Kiddushin or Pesachim figure on the name alone. List these as provisional identity candidates with their proposers. Do not add a 'student of Rabbi Yochanan' or 'student of Rav Huna' edge from this passage.

findings.claim: The Talmud does not say when the exchange happened. It only cites it ('and this is what he said to him'). Rashi on Berakhot puts it on the day Rav prayed the Sabbath prayer early. Rashi on Eruvin 40b puts it on a day when the sky was clouded over. The Rashash objects to that, because Rav's early prayer was deliberate. Sekhel Tov ties the exchange to the Geniva visit.

evidence.exact_quote: אותו היום שהתפלל רב של שבת בערב שבת אמר ליה רבי ירמיה מי בדלת מן המלאכה
פעם אחת נתקשרו שמים בעבים והתפלל רב של שבת מבעוד יום
ומעשה דרב הוה במתכוון
on one occasion, when Rav prayed the Shabbat prayer early

findings.reasoning: My translation of Rashi on Berakhot: 'that day on which Rav prayed the Sabbath prayer on Friday, Rabbi Yirmiya said to him...'. Rashi does not say explicitly that 'that day' is the Geniva visit. Soon after (27b), Rav Chiya bar Avin reports that Rav used to pray the Sabbath prayer early, so there may have been more than one such day. The Davidson English adds its framing without brackets.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the exchange as its own event, separate from 'Rav arrives at Geniva's house' and from the prayer event. At most, add a provisional 'possibly same occasion' link, citing Sekhel Tov and possibly Rashi. Do not place the exchange at Geniva's house as a text fact.

findings.claim: The earlier inference 'a student may pray behind his teacher' (27a:15) is later narrowed. The objection from Rav's own rule, as taught by Rav Yehuda, is answered by making Yirmiya a special case. The codes forbid a student to pray behind his teacher but allow a student-colleague to do so.

evidence.exact_quote: ושמע מינה מתפלל תלמיד אחורי רבו
לא כנגד רבו ולא אחורי רבו
ולא יתפלל לא לפני רבו ולא לאחר רבו ולא בצד רבו
תלמיד חבר מותר להתפלל אחורי רבו

findings.reasoning: The Talmud does not withdraw the inference outright, but the answer at 27b:3 limits it to a student-colleague. The earlier review noted that the three inferences were not tied to Rav's conduct. This is the link that ties the 'behind' inference to its qualification.
findings.graph_effect: Link the 'a student may pray behind his teacher' statement to the scene as an inference, and mark it as qualified by the student-colleague resolution. Do not show it as a standing general rule in the Talmud's final voice.

findings.claim: Inferring student-colleague status from a form of address happens elsewhere too. In Bava Batra 158b Rabbi Shamlai infers that ben Azzai was Rabbi Akiva's student-colleague because he spoke to him in the second person. Later authors link that passage to ours. The Maadaney Yom Tov uses the same method to propose that Abaye was Rav Yosef's student-colleague. In Eruvin 63a Ravina claims the status for himself.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר רבי שמלאי עדא אמרה בן עזאי תלמיד חבר דרבי עקיבא הוה דקאמר ליה שבאת
וכי האי גוונא אמרו פרק תפלת השחר
ודייקינן התם מדלא א"ל מי בדיל מר ש"מ תלמיד חבר הוה
יש לי להוכיח מכאן דאביי תלמיד חבר דרב יוסף הוה
ואורי בשני דרב חסדא דתלמיד חבר דיליה הוה ואנא נמי תלמיד חבר דמר אנא

findings.reasoning: In Bava Batra a named sage makes the inference. In Berakhot the anonymous Talmud makes it. In Eruvin a party claims the status for himself. These are three different kinds of evidence for the same relation type. The Maadaney Yom Tov extension is a later author's inference about other people. Those relations belong to other passages.
findings.graph_effect: For ontology only: treat 'status inferred from form of address' as a recognised basis. Add no edges for ben Azzai, Abaye or Ravina from this case.

findings.claim: Halakhot Gedolot also quotes an extra detail: Yirmiya prayed a weekday prayer behind Rav. The Rif's digest leaves out the Geniva story and the exchange. It moves straight from the rule against praying behind one's teacher to Rav Chiya bar Avin's report.

evidence.exact_quote: וצלי רב ירמיה בר אבא אחוריה תפלה של חול
אמר רב יהודה אמר רב לעולם אל יתפלל תלמיד לא לפני רבו ולא אחורי רבו ולא כנגד רבו
אמר רב חייא בר אבין רב צלי של שבת בערב שבת

findings.reasoning: The Rif abridges for legal purposes, so leaving the story out is not evidence that his text lacked it. The 'weekday prayer' detail in Halakhot Gedolot belongs to the quotation, not to the printed Talmud.
findings.graph_effect: Optional: add a note on Yirmiya's prayer event that one early quotation calls it a weekday prayer. The Rif's silence has no graph effect.

findings.claim: Ramban's novellae on Pesachim 54b quote the exchange with different people: 'Rav said to Rabbi Chanina, who prayed the Sabbath prayer on Friday: Have you separated?'

evidence.exact_quote: אמר ליה רב לר' חנינא דצלי של שבת בערב שבת אמר מי בדלת אמר ליה אין בדילנא

findings.reasoning: This does not match any other witness I checked. It is probably a garbled quotation or a printing problem in that edition, but I cannot show that. It is a quotation variant, not a Talmud witness.
findings.graph_effect: None. Keep only as a recorded quotation variant. Do not create a Rav and Chanina edge.

findings.claim: The modern vocalized edition and the Steinsaltz Hebrew both end 'and he did not say: has the Master separated' with a question mark, which may make it a rhetorical question. The Davidson English turns it into a plain statement. On either reading the formal wording was not said.

evidence.exact_quote: וְלָא אֲמַר ״מִי בְּדֵיל מָר״?
ולא אמר אליו בלשון "מי בדיל מר" ["האם בדל אדוני"]? כדרך שהיה צריך לומר אם היה תלמידו.

findings.reasoning: The punctuation is a modern editorial choice, and all three renderings come from one editorial project. The unvocalized text has no punctuation.
findings.graph_effect: None beyond f1. The negative polarity holds either way.

findings.claim: In the surrounding text the names vary between witnesses and translations. At 27b:2 the teacher of the warning is Rabbi Eliezer (printed), Rabbi Elazar ben Chisma (Rif, Halakhot Gedolot), Rabbi Eliezer ben Chisma (Rosh) or R. Eleazar (Soncino). At 27b:4 the printed text has Rabbi Avin reporting about Rabbi (Rabbi Judah the Prince), with Rava answering. The Rosh quotes Rabbi Abbahu. The Soncino English has 'Rab' where the text has Rabbi. lessons: Model an expressly unsaid utterance ('X did not say W') as its own speech record with negative polarity and counterfactual content. It is neither an utterance nor mere silence. Its usual job in the Talmud is to serve as proof.

A relation can be claimed with its proof attached. Store the resolving voice (here the anonymous Talmud) separately from the voice of the story. Store 'basis: proof from the form of address' separately from 'basis: narrated'.

Student-colleague is a relation of its own, with fixed roles: the student-colleague and the teacher. It keeps a teaching side, since the codes still call the other party 'his teacher'. Collapsing it into plain student or plain colleague loses exactly what the passage turns on.

Later scopes of a relation belong to the authors who give them, not to the passage. Examples: Tosafot's 'all the items in the list', Maimonides' 'did not learn most of his wisdom', the Taz's 'need not say Master'.
An exchange that the Talmud cites as proof is not automatically the same occasion as the nearby story. Keep separate event nodes and let 'same occasion' be a sourced, provisional link.

Quotations in later works (Halakhot Gedolot, Sekhel Tov, Ramban, Bach) are their own evidence type. They are neither manuscripts nor extra witnesses to the printed text. They can preserve a real variant, or they can paraphrase.
Translations from one editorial project (Davidson Aramaic, vocalized text, English and Steinsaltz Hebrew) count as one witness to the edition, not three.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

findings.reason: The negative wording is itself evidence for the stated student-colleague relationship. Store its content, negative polarity and anonymous explanatory voice. Do not create an utterance event for words the text says were not spoken.

The passage states this status in its argument about prayer behind a teacher. Later definitions and extensions of the status should be attributed separately, without making every possible teacher obligation part of this passage.

findings.claim: In the base text, the servant is the speaker and 'that man' (the father) is the target of her ban formula. The base text names no addressee: it has 'אמרה' ('she said'), with no 'ליה' ('to him'), and it refers to the man in the third person.

שפחה של בית רבי מאי היא דאמתא דבי רבי חזיתיה לההוא גברא דהוה מחי לבנו גדול אמרה ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא דקעבר משום (ויקרא יט, יד) ולפני עור לא תתן מכשול
אמתיה דבי רבי חזיתיה לההוא גברא דמחי לבנו גדול אמרה ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא
אמתא דבי רבי חזיתיה לההוא גברא דהוה קמחי לבנו הגדול אמרה להוי ההוא גברא בשמתא

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: 'The maidservant of Rabbi's house saw a certain man who was striking his grown son. She said: Let that man be under a ban.'
findings.reasoning: Speaker: the feminine verb אמרה goes back to אמתא דבי רבי. Target: ההוא גברא in the ban formula is the same phrase used for the man she saw striking his son. Addressee: none is stated in the William Davidson or Wikisource text on Sefaria, the Rif, or the Rosh. Using the third person for the target does not rule out that he heard it; see F3.
findings.graph_effect: Record a ban-declaration event: speaker = servant, target = father, addressee = unknown in the base text. Do not record addresses(servant, father) as asserted.

findings.claim: Some later witnesses read 'אמרה ליה' ('she said to him'). This gives an explicit masculine-singular addressee, most naturally the man himself. These are citation or anthology witnesses, not the base text.

evidence.exact_quote: אָמְרָה לֵיהּ: לֶיהֱוֵי הַהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּשַׁמְתָּא
ואמרה ליה ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא
דקאמרה [ליה] ליהוי האי גברא בשמתא

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: Ein Yaakov: 'she said to him: let that man be under a ban'. Ran: 'and she said to him ...'. Teshuvot Rashi (1943 edition): 'that she said [to him]', where the brackets are that edition's.
findings.reasoning: Three witnesses of different kinds. Ein Yaakov is an anthology of the Talmud's stories with its own wording: it also has 'לבריה רבה' and a baraita attribution. The Ran cites the story inside another discussion. In the Teshuvot Rashi edition, 'ליה' is in square brackets. That marks it as an editor's supplement, so it is weaker evidence than an unbracketed reading. No manuscript of Bavli Moed Katan was checked. So this dossier cannot say which reading is older. With 'ליה', the addressee is grammatically 'him'. The father is the only male participant present who could be meant (the son is the other male in the scene). That reading is still an interpretation of the pronoun.
findings.graph_effect: Add a variant branch. In the Ein Yaakov / Ran reading, addressee = 'him' (most plausibly the father). Keep this as a source-variant branch, separate from the base-text claim. The Teshuvot Rashi bracket is an editorial supplement, not an independent reading.

findings.claim: The third-person ban formula 'ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא' is used in the next story about someone present who replies, and 'ההוא גברא' can refer to the addressee or the speaker. So in this sugya the formula does not tell you whether the target was present or addressed.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא אמר ליה אדרבה ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא אם ממון נתחייבתי לך נידוי מי נתחייבתי לך
אמר ליה לא מסתייך דשמתיה לההוא גברא אלא אחוכי נמי חייך בי

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: 17a:14: 'He [Reish Lakish] said: Let that man be under a ban. He said to him: On the contrary, let that man be under a ban ...' 17a:7: 'Was it not enough for you that you banned that man [= me] ...'
findings.reasoning: In 17a:14 the fig-eater answers at once, so he heard a formula that referred to him as 'that man'. His reply turns the same words back on Reish Lakish, who is its target and its addressee. In 17a:7 the banned scholar calls himself 'that man'. So the formula is idiomatic and fits a declaration made to the target's face, but it does not require one.
findings.graph_effect: Do not treat the third person as evidence against presence, or as evidence for an addressee. Keep the addressee unknown in the base text.

findings.claim: The narrated legal force comes from the wider sugya, not from 17a:13. At 17a:9, R. Shmuel bar Nachmani cites the servant's ban as a precedent: the Sages did not treat her ban lightly for three years. 17a:13 then tells the story as the answer to 'what is it?'.

evidence.exact_quote: עמד רבי שמואל בר נחמני על רגליו ואמר ומה שפחה של בית רבי לא נהגו חכמים קלות ראש בנידויה שלש שנים יהודה חבירינו על אחת כמה וכמה
עיין רבי אמי בדיניה סבר למישרא ליה
ולא נהגו חכמים קלות ראש בנדויה שלש שנים

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: 'R. Shmuel bar Nachmani stood up and said: If the Sages did not treat lightly the ban of the maidservant of Rabbi's house for three years, how much more so [the ban of] Yehuda our colleague.'
findings.reasoning: This settles the 'needed_context' that the pilot flagged: 'מאי היא' ('what is it?') points back to 17a:9. The three-year respect for the ban is R. Shmuel bar Nachmani's statement, given as an argument in the case of the scholar banned by Rav Yehuda (17a:4-10). The narrator of 17a:13 does not state it. The Rif (and the Rosh, S9) place the three-year line straight after the story. That is a codifier's arrangement, not a separate event.
findings.graph_effect: Add: R. Shmuel bar Nachmani cites the precedent (voice = R. Shmuel bar Nachmani, reported, in the setting of R. Ami's review). Add: the Sages treated her ban as binding for three years (discourse_status = reported by R. Shmuel bar Nachmani). This does not make Rabbi a participant or show that he approved.

findings.claim: It is unclear where the servant's words end. The reason 'דקעבר משום ולפני עור' may be part of her speech or a gloss by the Gemara. The following 'דתניא' baraita is the Gemara's supporting source, not the servant's words.

evidence.exact_quote: אֲמַרָה: לֶיהֱוֵי הָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּשַׁמְתָּא, דְּקָעָבֵר מִשּׁוּם ״וְלִפְנֵי עִוֵּר לֹא תִתֵּן מִכְשׁוֹל״. דְּתַנְיָא
She said: Let that man be excommunicated, due to the fact that he has transgressed the injunction
אמרה: ליהוי ההוא גברא בשמתא [שיהא אדם זה המכה בנידוי], דקעבר [שהרי הוא עובר] משום

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: '... because he transgresses “Do not put a stumbling block before the blind”. As it is taught: ... the verse speaks of one who strikes his grown son.'
findings.reasoning: Unpunctuated Aramaic does not mark where a quotation ends. The William Davidson English reads the reason as her words. The vocalized edition's punctuation and Steinsaltz both leave it inside the same sentence. Neither settles who is speaking. The pilot's c5 (holds_view servant → reason, basis explicit) takes one reading as explicit.
findings.graph_effect: Lower c5 to basis = interpretation. Give it two readings: (a) the servant's stated reason, (b) the Gemara's explanation. Attach the baraita to the narrator or Gemara voice.

findings.claim: The baraita is anonymous in the Vilna-based text. The Rosh attributes it to R. Yishmael. Ein Yaakov (Daat edition) prints 'דתנא דברי רבי ישמעאל' in parentheses and replaces it with '[דְּתַנְיָא]'.

evidence.exact_quote: דתניא ר' ישמעאל אומר לפני עור לא תתן מכשול במכה לבנו גדול הכתוב מדבר
(דתנא דברי רבי ישמעאל) [דְּתַנְיָא]
דתניא ולפני עור לא תתן מכשול במכה לבנו גדול הכתוב מדבר

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: Rosh: 'As it is taught: R. Yishmael says: “Do not put a stumbling block before the blind” — the verse speaks of one who strikes his grown son.'
findings.reasoning: This is a variant attribution in secondary witnesses. It shows that some text tradition named a tanna for the baraita. It does not show that R. Yishmael historically taught it, and it does not identify which R. Yishmael. The parenthesis-and-bracket markup in the Daat edition reflects that edition's corrections. This dossier did not check the edition's apparatus to confirm what the markup means.
findings.graph_effect: Optional variant branch: baraita attributed to 'R. Yishmael' in the Rosh (and in the uncorrected Ein Yaakov wording). Keep it separate from the base text. No identity resolution.

findings.claim: The kinship is explicit: the man is striking 'his son' (לבנו). 'גדול' describes the son's stage of life. Commentators disagree on what 'גדול' means.

evidence.exact_quote: דכיון דגדול הוא שמא מבעט באביו והוה ליה איהו מכשילו
ונראי' דברים דלא גדול גדול ממש אלא הכל לפי טבעו שיש לחוש שיתריס כנגדו בדבור או במעשיו
פירש רבינו פרץ עד כ"ב שנה
וְלא מִקְרֵי גָּדוֹל לְדָבָר זֶה, רַק אַחַר כ"ב שָׁנָה אוֹ כ"ד שָׁנָה

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'since he is grown, he may kick back at his father, and so [the father] makes him stumble.' Ritva: 'not literally grown, but according to his nature, if there is reason to fear he will rebel against him in word or deed.' Shulchan Arukh: 'for this matter he is called grown only after 22 or 24 years.'
findings.reasoning: The father–son relation stands on the possessive suffix in the text. Its age scope is commentary: Rashi gives the mechanism, Ritva reads it by the son's nature, and Rabbeinu Peretz and the Shulchan Arukh give age limits. These interpretations do not affect who the people are.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 child_of(son, father), basis explicit. Put 'גדול' in a note or subtype, with the interpretations attributed to their authors.

findings.claim: Later authorities explain why the ban lasted three years. The Raavad (cited by the Rosh) says no one would weigh himself against a known and worthy declarer. The Ritva says something similar. These are commentary inferences. The Talmud does not say how the ban ended.

evidence.exact_quote: תמה הראב"ד ז"ל למה שהה זה בנידויה ג' שנים אם היתה היא קיימת למה לא התירה לו ואם מתה למה לא התיר לו רבי
והשפחה היה בה חכמה יתירה ויראת חטא ולא רצו לשקול עצמם כנגדה עד שנזקקו לו גדולי הדור והתירו לו
שפחה של בית ר' לא נהגו קלות בנדוייה ג' שנים שלא היה א' שירצה לשקול עצמו כמותה

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: Rosh citing Raavad: 'Why did this man remain in her ban three years? If she was alive, why did she not release him; if she died, why did Rabbi not release him? ... The maidservant had great wisdom and fear of sin, and they did not want to weigh themselves against her, until the great ones of the generation took it up and released him.' Ritva: '... for there was no one who wished to weigh himself as her equal.'
findings.reasoning: The statement that the man stayed banned and that 'the great ones of the generation' eventually released him is the Raavad's reconstruction, reported by the Rosh. Tosafot Yom Tov (S22) repeats it. The rest of the Ritva's sentence (about Rabbi not being alive and the Nasi) is hard to construe; this dossier does not translate it with confidence.
findings.graph_effect: Do not add a release event, or 'the great ones of the generation' as participants. At most, attach these as commentary-voice notes to the ban event.

findings.claim: The codifiers turn the story into law. Rambam and the Shulchan Arukh rule that one who strikes a grown son is banned. Rambam's list of 24 offences includes 'one who trips the blind'. The Raavad's gloss, as reported by the Kessef Mishneh, gives this case as its example. Rashi's responsum uses the story to show that a spoken declaration was enough, with no shofar.

evidence.exact_quote: וְהַמַּכֶּה בְּנוֹ גָּדוֹל מְנַדִּין אוֹתוֹ שֶׁהֲרֵי הוּא עוֹבֵר עַל וְלִפְנֵי עִוֵּר לֹא תִתֵּן מִכְשׁל
המכשיל את העור. כתב הראב"ד כגון המכה את בנו הגדול
אֲפִלּוּ נִדָּהוּ קָטָן שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל חַיָּב הַנָּשִׂיא וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל לִנְהֹג בּוֹ נִדּוּי

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: Rambam Rebels 6:9: 'One who strikes his grown son is banned, for he transgresses “Do not put a stumbling block before the blind”.' Torah Study 6:14: 'even if the least in Israel banned him, the Nasi and all Israel must observe the ban.' Teshuvot Rashi: 'the maidservant of Rabbi's house did not sound [shofars]; she [only] said ...'
findings.reasoning: These sources describe the legal force the tradition gave the declaration. They do not add people to the episode. The Touger translation note on Torah Study 6:14 says 'the entire Jewish people observed that ban for three years'. That is a translator's gloss, and it overstates the Talmud's 'חכמים' ('Sages').
findings.graph_effect: None for people. Legal-force metadata on the ban event: declarative ban by a non-sage household servant, later treated as binding by the Sages (per R. Shmuel bar Nachmani), and codified as a ground for a ban.

findings.claim: The Yerushalmi has a structurally similar story with different people. In it the addressee is explicit ('אמרה ליה'), and the target is shown to have heard, because he goes to consult R. Acha. This is a parallel, not the same event.

evidence.exact_quote: חדא אמהא מן דבר פטא הוות עברה קומי חדא כנישא חמת חד ספר מחי לחד מיינוק יתיר מן צורכיה אמרה ליה יהוי ההוא גוברא מחרם אתא שאל לרבי אחא אמר ליה צריך את חשש על נפשך

findings.translation_by_this_dossier: 'A maidservant of Bar Pata's household was passing in front of a synagogue. She saw a Scripture teacher striking a child more than necessary. She said to him: Let that man be banned. He came and asked R. Acha, who told him: You must be concerned for yourself.' (The Guggenheimer English on Sefaria has 'He said to him'. The Aramaic verb is feminine.)
findings.reasoning: The household (Bar Pata's, not Rabbi's), the target (a teacher, not a father), the victim (a child, not a grown son) and the legal outcome all differ. So the Yerushalmi does not identify the Bavli's servant or man. It shows that the same formula can be spoken directly to its target. That supports F3, not a merge.
findings.graph_effect: No coreference between the Bavli and Yerushalmi servants or targets. At most, link the two episodes as a thematic or literary parallel.

findings.claim: 'רבי' appears only as the head of the household. The William Davidson English names him Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The Aramaic does not, and no source checked puts him at the scene.

evidence.exact_quote: the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s house saw a certain man
דאמתא דבי רבי חזיתיה

findings.reasoning: Reading the bare 'רבי' as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is the usual convention, and the translation makes it. That is an identification step, kept separate from the text. The Raavad's question (S9) about why 'Rabbi' did not release the man assumes Rabbi was a possible releaser. It does not place Rabbi in the event.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the household-affiliation link servant → Rabbi's household (the contract has no predicate for it). Identifying Rabbi as Yehuda HaNasi is a separate, provisional step. No participation claim for Rabbi.
