readings.label: base text
readings.text: Addressee unstated (אמרה with no ליה). Target = father.

readings.label: variant 'אמרה ליה'
readings.text: She said it to 'him', most naturally the father, who would then be target and addressee.
readings.note: S12 (Teshuvot Rashi) has [ליה] in editorial brackets.

readings.label: servant
readings.text: Part of her declaration, as the William Davidson English renders it.

readings.label: Gemara
readings.text: The Gemara's explanation, with the baraita as its source.

unresolved: No manuscript of Bavli Moed Katan 17a was checked (no manuscript database was accessed), so this dossier cannot say whether 'אמרה ליה' is an old reading or an addition made during citation.
The meaning of the Daat edition's parenthesis-and-bracket markup in Ein Yaakov was not checked against that edition's introduction.
The second half of the Ritva's comment (S6, item 10) about Rabbi and the Nasi is not construed with confidence.
Neither the Talmud nor the commentaries checked say whether the father was present, repented, or was released. The release is the Raavad's reconstruction only.
Whether the servant here is the same person as 'Rabbi's maidservant' elsewhere (e.g. Ketubot 104a, Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1) was not decided. A shared description does not establish identity.

corrections.change: Replace addresses(servant, father) with a ban-declaration claim or event: speaker = servant, target = father, addressee = unknown, basis = explicit for speaker and target. Add a variant branch (Ein Yaakov, Ran) with addressee = 'him', plausibly the father.
corrections.why: The base text has no 'ליה' and refers to the target in the third person (F1). The explicit addressee appears only in secondary witnesses (F2).

corrections.change: Change basis from explicit to interpretation. Add a reading group: servant's stated reason vs the Gemara's explanation.
corrections.why: The text does not mark where her quotation ends (F5).

corrections.change: Keep, with voice = narrator/Gemara. Optionally add a variant attribution of the baraita to R. Yishmael (the Rosh; Ein Yaakov's uncorrected wording) as a source-variant branch.

Add a reported claim: the Sages did not treat her ban lightly for three years (voice = R. Shmuel bar Nachmani, 17a:9). Also add R. Shmuel bar Nachmani citing the precedent during R. Ami's review. Change episode coverage from needs_context to resolved, because 17a:9 is what prompts מאי היא.
corrections.why: F4. The legal force is stated in the wider sugya, not in 17a:13.

corrections.change: Relabel mentions m6-m10 from kind 'name' to event or statement anchors.
corrections.why: They anchor actions and statements, not names.

lessons: The target of a sanction and the addressee of speech are separate roles. A ban formula in the third person ('let that man be banned') gives a target. It gives an addressee only if the text says 'to him' or the target responds.

Legal force belongs to a different voice and segment from the act: the act is narrated (17a:13), its binding force is asserted by a named sage (17a:9), and later codifiers generalise it. Model these as separate claims with their own voices.

A reading such as 'אמרה ליה' that is found only in anthologies or citations (Ein Yaakov, Ran) is a source variant. It is not a correction of the base text, and a bracketed editorial supplement (Teshuvot Rashi) is weaker still.
Structurally similar stories in the Yerushalmi (Bar Pata's maidservant) are literary parallels. Different households and targets mean no coreference.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

findings.reason: The saved base wording אמרה leaves the addressee unstated. The separate אמרה ליה witnesses support a branch with an addressee. The same father can remain the target across both readings.

The duration comes from a precedent cited in the wider discussion. Preserve its attributed voice and relation to the later retelling. It is not an independent observation just because the same story is quoted twice.

Do not accept a merge of the differently described people. Also do not turn that into a claim that the stories cannot be related. Preserve a possible relationship between the tellings for a later evidence pack.
The claimed later release must stay attributed to the commentator or quoted commentator. Do not add it as a directly narrated Talmud event.

cases.question: Collect every named and pronominal mention. Preserve legal roles and the target of each objection, including repeated references.

findings.claim: The two positions that 43a:9 calls 'the one who says במותם' and 'the one who says מלהחלו' are set up at 43a:5. An anonymous baraita voice (ת"ר, 'the Sages taught') derives the rule from להחלו (Lev 21:4, said of a priest). Rebbi derives it from במותם, said of a nazirite. So in this sugya, 'the one who says במותם' in 43a:9 is Rebbi's position, and 'the one who says מלהחלו' is the anonymous first tanna.

evidence.exact_quote: ת"ר (ויקרא כא, ד) להחלו עד שעה שימות רבי אומר (ויקרא יא, לב) במותם יטמא עד שימות
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: The Rabbis taught: 'to profane himself' - until the time he dies. Rebbi says: 'when they die ... he becomes impure' - until he dies.

evidence.exact_quote: למאן דאמר מלהחלו אפילו גוסס למ"ד במותם עד שימות אין גוסס לא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: According to the one who says [it is derived] from 'to profane himself', even a dying person; according to the one who says 'when they die', until he dies yes, a dying person no.

evidence.exact_quote: ת"ר לא יטמא בעל בעמיו להחלו עד שעה שימות - מותר לעסוק בו ואינו עובר עליו משום לא יחלל עד שעה שימות והאי קרא קאי בכהן והוא הדין לנזיר
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'the Rabbis taught ... to profane himself, until he dies' - he may attend to him and does not transgress 'he shall not profane' until he dies; this verse is about a priest, and the same applies to a nazirite.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי אומר לא יטמא להם במותם עד שימות - והאי קרא בנזיר קאי והוא הדין בכהן
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'Rebbi says: he shall not become impure for them when they die' - this verse is about a nazirite, and the same applies to a priest.

evidence.exact_quote: פליגי בה רבי ורבנן דרבנן אמרי בההיא שעתא דקבעיא מימת אסור לכהן למיקרב ליה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Halakhot Gedolot: Rebbi and the Rabbis disagree about it; the Rabbis say that at the time he is about to die a priest may not come near him.

findings.reasoning: The segment labels 'למאן דאמר X' first occur at 43a:6, where they sort the two sides of the 43a:5 baraita by their proof word. 43a:7-11 keep the same labels. Rashi on 43a:5 matches each proof word to its speaker. Halakhot Gedolot names the two sides 'Rebbi and the Rabbis'. That name for the anonymous side is a later authority's label. The baraita itself says only ת"ר.
findings.graph_effect: Link the 43a:9 mention 'ולמ"ד במותם' to the local person Rebbi as a role reference (a position label resolved by the sugya), not as a new unnamed person. Link 'ולמ"ד מלהחלו' (43a:7, 43a:10, 43a:11) to a local group voice: the anonymous first tanna of the 43a:5 baraita. Keep the position node, since 43a:7-11 are argued on the Gemara's construction of each position (F3). This closes the earlier needed_context.

findings.claim: In 43a:9 no one is named. An unmarked anonymous Gemara voice asks the question and gives the answer. The question targets Rebbi's במותם position: 'isn't להחלו written?' The answer gives that position a use for the verse: להחלו applies to one who is not profaned, and excludes one who is profaned and remains so. The Gemara constructs this use on the position's behalf. The text does not quote Rebbi as saying it.

evidence.exact_quote: ולמ"ד במותם הכתיב להחלו להחלו להכי הוא דאתא במי שאינו מחולל יצא זה שמחולל ועומד
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: And according to the one who says 'when they die' - isn't 'to profane himself' written? 'To profane himself' comes for this: [the prohibition applies] to one who is not profaned, excluding this one who is profaned and remains so.

evidence.exact_quote: The Gemara asks the reverse question: And according to the one who says that the source for the earliest time of the impurity of a corpse is the verse “when they die,” isn’t it written: “To profane himself”? What does he derive from that verse?
ושואלים מצד אחר: ולמאן דאמר [ולדעת מי שאומר] שהמקור הוא ממה שנאמר "במותם", הכתיב [הרי נאמר] "להחלו" ומה עושה הוא בכתוב זה?
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Steinsaltz: They ask from the other side: according to the one who says the source is 'when they die' - isn't 'to profane himself' written, and what does he do with this verse?

findings.reasoning: There is no attribution formula (אמר, תניא, מיתיבי) in 43a:9. The frame 'ולמ"ד X הכתיב Y' is the anonymous Gemara's question. The same voice answers. The Koren English and Steinsaltz Hebrew both frame it as a question and answer about 'the one who says'. They come from the same editorial project and are not independent witnesses.
findings.graph_effect: Add one speech/challenge claim: anonymous Gemara voice -> challenges -> Rebbi's במותם position. The content is the verse להחלו (Lev 21:4). Add one views claim: that position, as constructed by the anonymous Gemara voice, uses להחלו to exclude one who is 'מחולל ועומד'. Record the basis as the Gemara's construction, not Rebbi's speech. Create no new person nodes for 43a:9.

findings.claim: The editors and Rashi read the questions in 43a:7-11 as working inside Reish Lakish's account of the dispute. On that account the two sides differ over a dying person. Rashi says the objection at 43a:11 is difficult 'for Reish Lakish, who derives from להחלו that even a dying person is forbidden'. So the target of the 43a:11 objection includes Reish Lakish's construction of the anonymous tanna's position, and not only that tanna.

evidence.exact_quote: The Gemara asks with regard to Reish Lakish’s opinion: And according to the one who says that it is derived from “to profane himself,” isn’t it written: “When they die”?
ושואלים לשיטת ריש לקיש: ולמאן דאמר [ולדעת מי שאומר] מ"להחלו", הכתיב [הרי נאמר] "במותם"!
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Steinsaltz: They ask according to Reish Lakish's approach: according to the one who says 'from to profane himself', isn't 'when they die' written?

evidence.exact_quote: מגוייד - חתוך לאיבריו ואפילו הכי אינו מטמא וקשיא לר"ל דמשמע ליה מלהחלו דאפילו לגוסס אסור
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'mutilated' - cut into limbs, and even so he does not transmit impurity; and this is difficult for Reish Lakish, who understands from 'to profane himself' that even for a dying person it is forbidden.

evidence.exact_quote: ריש לקיש אמר גוסס איכא בינייהו

findings.reasoning: Rashi's 'קשיא לר"ל' names whom the difficulty is for. The Koren English and Steinsaltz Hebrew name Reish Lakish as the frame for 43a:7. Rashi is a separate commentary tradition from the Koren/Steinsaltz editorial layer. The Gemara text itself does not name Reish Lakish after 43a:6. This is therefore commentary interpretation, not a textual statement.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the local person Reish Lakish (43a:6) in the episode. Record that 43a:7-11 argue within his account. Give the 43a:11 objection (earlier claim c5) a second, interpretive target role: Reish Lakish's construction, citing Rashi. Mark it basis=commentary. Leave Rabbi Yochanan's account (43a:6) as the alternative framing, in which the two sides differ only in their proof verse.

findings.claim: Rebbi is referred to repeatedly across 43a:5-10: by name at 43a:5 and twice at 43a:7 ('לכדרבי', 'רבי אומר'), and by the position label 'למאן דאמר במותם' at 43a:6, 43a:8 and 43a:9. At 43a:7 the anonymous tanna's side needs במותם for a second teaching of Rebbi: death, not lesions or discharges. At 43a:8 the Gemara treats that same teaching as one Rebbi's own במותם position also needs. So the sugya reads the two Rebbi baraitot as one person's teachings within the argument.

evidence.exact_quote: ולמ"ד מלהחלו הכתיב במותם מיבעי ליה לכדרבי דתניא רבי אומר במותם אינו מטמא אבל מטמא בנגעתם ובזיבתם
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: And according to the one who says 'from to profane himself', isn't 'when they die' written? He needs it for Rebbi's [teaching], as it was taught: Rebbi says: 'when they die' - he does not become impure, but he does become impure through their lesions and their discharges.

evidence.exact_quote: ולמאן דאמר במותם הא מיבעי ליה להאי סברא א"כ לימא קרא במות מאי במותם שמעת מינה תרתי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: And according to the one who says 'when they die' - he needs it for this reasoning! If so, let the verse say 'when [one] dies'; why 'when they die'? Learn two things from it.

evidence.exact_quote: הא מיבעי ליה להאי סברא - במותם אין מטמאין אבל מטמאין בנגעם ובזיבתם
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'he needs it for this reasoning' - when they die they may not become impure, but they may become impure through their lesions and discharges.

findings.reasoning: Rashi on 43a:8 names 'this reasoning' as the lesion/discharge teaching of 43a:7. So the במותם position (Rebbi at 43a:5) is said to need Rebbi's other baraita. 'לכדרבי' and 'רבי אומר' in 43a:7 are two mentions in one attribution: an anticipatory reference and the baraita's own attribution. The earlier review already flagged the missing 'לכדרבי' mention.
findings.graph_effect: Add mention records for 'לכדרבי' (43a:7), 'למאן דאמר במותם' (43a:6), 'ולמאן דאמר במותם' (43a:8, with the pronoun 'ליה') and 'ולמ"ד במותם' (43a:9). Link them all to the one local Rebbi, with the position-label mentions marked as role references. Add a teaching/views relation: the anonymous tanna's position is construed as adopting Rebbi's lesion/discharge teaching (43a:7). It is not a transmission or a meeting. 'Rebbi' in both baraitot is one local person in this sugya. Koren's expansion to 'Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi' is an editorial identification, recorded separately.

findings.claim: The pronominal mentions in and around 43a:9 point to biblical or generic legal figures, not to sages. In להחלו the suffix 'him(self)' is the priest of Lev 21:4 (Rashi: 'this verse is about a priest'). The 'them' in במותם, נגעתם and זיבתם are the nazirite's dead relatives in Num 6:7. The Rosh reads the discharge case as 'if his father was a zav or a metzora'. 'One who is not profaned' and 'this one who is profaned and remains so' are generic priest roles. 'הוא' in 'להכי הוא דאתא' refers to the verse.

evidence.exact_quote: והאי קרא קאי בכהן והוא הדין לנזיר
רבי אומר במותם - בנזיר כתיב לאביו ולאמו לא יטמא להם במותם
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Tosafot: 'Rebbi says: when they die' - it is written of a nazirite: for his father and his mother he shall not become impure for them when they die.

evidence.exact_quote: אבל מטמא הוא בזיבה ובנגעים אם היה אביו זב או מצורע
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rosh: but he may become impure through discharge and lesions, if his father was a zav or a metzora.

evidence.exact_quote: א"כ - דלא נדרוש ליה אלא חד טעמא נימא קרא להחל דמשמע לענין מי שאינו מחולל ומדקאמר להחלו שמע מינה תרתי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'if so' - if we were to derive only one reason from it, let the verse say 'to profane', which would mean [only] about one who is not profaned; since it says 'to profane himself', learn two things.

findings.reasoning: The pronoun suffixes come from the quoted verses. Rashi and Tosafot name the verse contexts. These are legal-example figures, not people in the narrative.
findings.graph_effect: Keep 'מי שאינו מחולל' and 'זה שמחולל ועומד' as generic legal roles (a priest), not as local persons. Relabel the earlier 'Generic person not yet defiled/already defiled' (m6/m7) as legal roles of a priest. Save the relatives of Num 6:7 as biblical generic roles only if the ontology keeps verse referents. Draw no family edges from 'his father' in the verse. It is a legal category, not a relation between Talmudic people.

findings.claim: The 43a:9 formula 'במי שאינו מחולל יצא זה שמחולל ועומד' also appears one page earlier, in a baraita that Abaye brings as an objection (Nazir 42b:3). There it is attached to 'ולא יחלל', in the case of a priest who has a corpse on his shoulder and is handed another. In 43a:9 the Gemara attaches the same exclusion to להחלו.

evidence.exact_quote: איתיביה אביי כהן שהיה לו מת מונח על כתיפו והושיטו לו מתו ומת אחר ונגע בו יכול יהא חייב ת"ל (ויקרא כא, ו) ולא יחלל במי שאינו מחולל יצא זה שהוא מחולל ועומד
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Abaye objected to him: a priest who had a corpse lying on his shoulder, and they handed him his [relative's] corpse and another corpse and he touched it - one might think he is liable; the verse says 'and he shall not profane' - [this applies] to one who is not profaned, excluding this one who is profaned and remains so.

evidence.exact_quote: Abaye raised an objection to Rav Yosef from a baraita

findings.reasoning: The wording is nearly identical. The verse behind 'ולא יחלל' is marked differently by the editors: Wikisource brackets say (ויקרא כא, ו) and the Koren English says Leviticus 21:12. That is an editorial verse identification. 'איתיביה' has a pronoun target. The Koren English supplies Rav Yosef, and Rav Yosef answers at 42b:4 ('א"ל').
findings.graph_effect: No person edge for 43a:9. Save a cross-reference: the exclusion used for the במותם position at 43a:9 matches baraita wording that Abaye cites at 42b:3. This does not make Abaye a participant in 43a:9. The objection target at 42b:3 (Rav Yosef) belongs to the 42b episode and should not be copied into 43a.

findings.claim: Commentators and translators disagree about what 'זה שמחולל ועומד' excludes. The Koren English and Steinsaltz render it broadly: a priest who is already impure is not forbidden to become impure again. Sifra, Malbim, Torah Temimah and Tosafot limit it to the time a priest is still in contact with, or busy with, the first corpse. Once he separates, the prohibition applies again. Mishpetei Uziel reports that the Ra'avad drew a broad rule from the related exegesis: priests today are already impure from the dead and carry no liability. Mishpetei Uziel then rejects that rule.

evidence.exact_quote: “To profane himself” comes for this purpose, that the prohibition against becoming impure apply only to one who is not profaned, excluding one who is already profaned. There is no prohibition against a ritually impure priest becoming impure from a corpse.
הן שאסור להיטמא לגוסס, והן שאין איסור למי שכבר טמא לחזור ולהיטמא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Steinsaltz on 43a:10: both that it is forbidden to become impure for a dying person, and that there is no prohibition for one already impure to become impure again.

evidence.exact_quote: "להחלו" – נהג מנהג כזה הרי הוא חולין. יכול יהא חולין לעולם? תלמוד לומר "להחלו" – בזמן שהוא מתעסק עמו הרי הוא חולין. פירש, הרי הוא בקדושתו.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Sifra: 'to profane himself' - if he acted so, he is profane. Might he be profane forever? The verse says 'to profane himself': while he is occupied with him he is profane; once he has separated, he is in his holiness.

evidence.exact_quote: ורמז גם כן הדרוש שדרשו בנזיר (דף מג) "להחלו" – במי שאינו מחולל. יצא זה שמחולל ועומד דהיינו בזמן שמתעסק במת מותר ליגע במת אחר באותו שעה. והאזהרה הוא רק אם פירש מן המת שאז אינו מחולל והוא בקדושתו.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Malbim: it also alludes to the exegesis in Nazir 43: 'to profane himself' - one who is not profaned, excluding one profaned and remaining so, i.e. while he is occupied with a corpse he may touch another corpse at that time; the warning applies only once he has separated from the corpse, when he is not profaned and is in his holiness.

evidence.exact_quote: מי שאינו מחולל, יצא מי שמחולל ועומד
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Torah Temimah (main text on 'to profane himself'): one not profaned, excluding one profaned and remaining so.

evidence.exact_quote: ר"ל אם בעת שנטמא לקרובו המת נטמא למת אחר אינו חייב מלקות, כיון דמחולל הוא מטומאת מתו, אבל לאחר שפירש ממתו חייב
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Torah Temimah (his footnote ל): that is to say, if at the time he became impure for his dead relative he became impure for another corpse, he is not liable to lashes, since he is profaned by the impurity of his dead; but after he has separated from his dead he is liable.

evidence.exact_quote: מהכא משמע דכהן אסור [ליטמא לאחרים אף כשהוא מטומא כבר] לקרוביו ואף כי מחולל ועומד הוא דאף לפי דברי רבה אם פירש אסור ליטמא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Tosafot: from here it follows that a priest is forbidden [to become impure for others even when he is already impure] for his relatives, even though he is profaned and remains so, for even according to Rabbah, if he separated he is forbidden to become impure.

evidence.exact_quote: הראב"ד ז"ל חדש הלכה זו דכהנים בזמן הזה טמאי מת הן ועוד אין עליהן חיוב טומאה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Mishpetei Uziel: the Ra'avad introduced this ruling, that priests nowadays are impure from the dead and there is no further liability of impurity upon them.

evidence.exact_quote: אולם הלכה מחודשת זו היא תמוהה לע"ד
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Mishpetei Uziel: but this novel ruling is, in my humble opinion, puzzling.

findings.reasoning: Every position here is a commentator's or translator's reading. The Gemara text of 43a:9 says only 'מחולל ועומד'. The narrow reading fits the 42b:3 baraita, which is about a corpse still on the priest's shoulder, and the concurrent-contact distinction at 42b:5. Koren English and Steinsaltz Hebrew come from one editorial project, so they count as one reading.
findings.graph_effect: Replace the earlier statement label 'להחלו excludes one already defiled' with a neutral wording: 'להחלו excludes one who is profaned and remains so'. Record two interpretation branches: (a) already impure in general (Koren/Steinsaltz rendering); (b) only while still in contact with or occupied by the first corpse (Sifra, Malbim, Torah Temimah, Tosafot). Attribute the Ra'avad's broad halakhic use to him as reported by Mishpetei Uziel, which disputes it. None of these commentators becomes a participant in the 43a:9 episode.

findings.claim: Halakhot Gedolot has a different text of 43a:6. It gives the two explanations of the Rebbi/Rabbis dispute to Abaye ('interpretation of the verses') and Rava ('a dying person'), not to Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Tosafot, Sefer Yereim and Haamek Sheilah report the reading as Abaye and Rava. The printed Rosh reports it as Abaye and 'רבה' (Rabbah).

evidence.exact_quote: מאי בינייהו אמר אביי משמעות דורשין איכא בינייהו רבא אמר גוסס איכא בינייהו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Halakhot Gedolot: what is between them? Abaye said: the interpretation of the verses is between them; Rava said: a dying person is between them.

evidence.exact_quote: מאי בינייהו אמר ר' יוחנן משמעות דורשין איכא בינייהו ר"ל אמר גוסס איכא בינייהו
ומיהו בה"ג גריס אביי במקום רבי יוחנן ורבא במקום ר"ל
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Tosafot: however, Halakhot Gedolot reads Abaye in place of Rabbi Yochanan and Rava in place of Reish Lakish.

evidence.exact_quote: ומיהו בה"ג גורס אביי במקום ר' יוחנן ורבה במקום ר"ל
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rosh: however, Halakhot Gedolot reads Abaye in place of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbah in place of Reish Lakish.

evidence.exact_quote: ועוד  בהלכות גדולות אמר אביי משמעות דורשין איכא בינייהו רבא אמר גוסס איכא בינייהו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Sefer Yereim: and further, in Halakhot Gedolot: Abaye said: the interpretation of the verses is between them; Rava said: a dying person is between them.

evidence.exact_quote: וקאמר אביי דמשמעות דורשין איכא בינייהו ורבא אמר גוסס א"ב. וכך היה נוסחת בה"ג.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Haamek Sheilah: and Abaye says that the interpretation of the verses is between them, and Rava said a dying person is between them. And that was the text of Halakhot Gedolot.

findings.reasoning: This is a source variant that a later work preserves. Tosafot, the Rosh, Yereim and Haamek Sheilah report it, and the Warsaw 1874 Halakhot Gedolot confirms it directly. The Rosh's 'רבה' disagrees with the other reports of 'רבא'. I did not check whether this is a print difference in the Rosh. The variant says which pair the two explanations are attributed to. It does not establish who historically said them. 'ר"ל' here is Reish Lakish: Tosafot and the Rosh set it against 'רבי יוחנן'.
findings.graph_effect: Put the 43a:6 speakers on a reading-group branch. Branch A (Sefaria editions, Tosafot/Rosh base text): Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Branch B (Halakhot Gedolot): Abaye and Rava. Branch B' (the Rosh's report of Halakhot Gedolot): Abaye and Rabbah. Do not merge Reish Lakish with Rava or Rabbah, or Rabbi Yochanan with Abaye. Because 43a:7-11 are framed by the 'dying person' explanation (F3), that framing voice carries the same branches.

findings.claim: The commentators who draw a ruling from this sugya disagree about what follows for a priest and a dying person. Tosafot and the Rosh say that on the standard text the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan, so a priest is not warned about a dying person, but on the Halakhot Gedolot text a priest is warned. Haamek Sheilah says Halakhot Gedolot itself ruled that a priest is not warned, 'the exact opposite' of what Tosafot reports in its name. Yereim argues for a prohibition.

evidence.exact_quote: ומהכא שמעינן דכהן אינו מוזהר על הגוסס דקי"ל כר"י לגבי ר"ל דאמר משמעות דורשים איכא בינייהו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rosh: from here we learn that a priest is not warned about a dying person, since we hold like Rabbi Yochanan against Reish Lakish; [Rabbi Yochanan] said the difference is the interpretation of the verses.

evidence.exact_quote: ולפ"ז הלכה כרבה לגבי אביי ולרבה פליגי ר' ורבנן בגוסס ואין הלכה כר' מחביריו נמצא כהן מוזהר על הגוסס
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rosh: accordingly the halakha follows Rabbah against Abaye, and according to Rabbah, Rebbi and the Rabbis disagree about a dying person, and the halakha does not follow Rebbi against his colleagues; it turns out a priest is warned about a dying person.

evidence.exact_quote: והוא להיפך ממש"כ התוס' נזיר ד"ה ומהכא בשם בה"ג דכהן מוזהר על הגוסס
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Haamek Sheilah: and this is the opposite of what Tosafot wrote in Nazir, s.v. u-mehakha, in the name of Halakhot Gedolot, that a priest is warned about a dying person.

evidence.exact_quote: לכן נראה לי איסור בגוסס כאשר פירשתי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Sefer Yereim: therefore it seems to me there is a prohibition regarding a dying person, as I explained.

findings.reasoning: This is later halakhic reasoning, not a relationship between Talmudic people. It shows that Rebbi and the Rabbis are treated as holding opposed practical positions only on the Reish Lakish (or Rava) account. Here 'ר"י' is set against 'ר"ל' and is Rabbi Yochanan.
findings.graph_effect: No Talmudic person edges. Record the practical-disagreement flag between Rebbi and the anonymous tanna as dependent on the framing branch. On Rabbi Yochanan's account they differ only in exegesis, so no 'disagrees_on_ruling' edge. On the Reish Lakish/Rava account they disagree about a dying person. Save it as conditional, not as a plain dispute edge.

findings.claim: The 43a:11 objection ('מיתיבי') cites a text that matches Mishnah Oholot 1:6. The Koren English calls it a mishna, citing Oholot 1:6. Rashi says it is 'the opening of the baraita in [the chapter] העור והרוטב'. The Koren English itself later calls it 'this baraita'. The answer is the anonymous Gemara's. The objection targets the להחלו position as Reish Lakish construes it (F3).

evidence.exact_quote: מיתיבי אדם אינו מטמא אלא עד שתצא נפשו ואפילו מגוייד ואפילו גוסס ולמ"ד מלהחלו הא קתני דאינו מטמא לענין טמויי עד דנפקא נפשיה לענין אתחולי הא איתחיל:
אדם אינו מטמא עד שתצא נפשו. ואפילו מגוייד. ואפילו גוסס.
The Gemara raises an objection from a mishna (Oholot 1:6)
מיתיבי אדם - הכי הויא רישא דברייתא בהעור והרוטב
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rashi: 'they objected: a person' - this is the opening of the baraita in [the chapter] Ha-Or ve-ha-Rotev.

findings.reasoning: Wikisource and the Davidson Aramaic read 'אלא עד'. The Davidson vocalized text puts '(אלא)' in parentheses. The Vilna Mishnah has 'עד' without 'אלא'. Halakhot Gedolot quotes the Mishnah with 'ואפילו צלוב' in place of 'ואפילו גוסס'; Toafot Re'em 322:9 discusses this. These wording differences do not change a person reference.
findings.graph_effect: Keep earlier claims c5 and c6. Identify the objection's source text as matching Mishnah Oholot 1:6, noting Rashi's 'baraita' label as an alternative description. Add the interpretive second target (Reish Lakish's construction) per F3. The 'אדם' of the Mishnah is a generic legal subject, not a person node.

findings.claim: Abbreviations in the sources can be misread as sage names. In Torah Temimah, 'ר"ל' opening footnote ל means 'that is to say', not Reish Lakish. In the Talmud text and in Tosafot and the Rosh, 'ר"ל' is Reish Lakish, set against Rabbi Yochanan. Sefer Yereim spells him out as 'ר"ש בן לקיש'. At 43a:2, Wikisource 'ר"א' is expanded by the Davidson edition to 'רבי אלעזר'.

evidence.exact_quote: ר"ל אם בעת שנטמא לקרובו המת
י"ל שאינו חולק על ר"ש בן לקיש
אלא אמר ר"א צירף ידו
אלא אמר רבי אלעזר צירף ידו

findings.reasoning: Syntax shows the Torah Temimah case: 'ר"ל אם בעת...' opens an explanatory clause. The Yereim expansion is a later author's usage. It supports but does not prove the historical identity behind the nickname.
findings.graph_effect: Do not create a Reish Lakish mention from Torah Temimah. Expand abbreviations for graph mentions only from the Talmud text, where the context sets a name against its pair.

findings.claim: Editors disagree about which verse Rebbi's 'במותם יטמא' (43a:5) comes from. The Wikisource brackets cite Leviticus 11:32, about creeping things. The Koren English, Rashi and Tosafot place it in the nazirite verse, Numbers 6:7. Sefaria's links list both.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי אומר (ויקרא יא, לב) במותם יטמא עד שימות

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that the verse stated with regard to a nazirite: “He shall not become impure for his father, or for his mother, for his brother, or for his sister, when they die” (Numbers 6:7)
רבי אומר במותם - בנזיר כתיב לאביו ולאמו לא יטמא להם במותם
Leviticus 11:32
Numbers 6:7

findings.reasoning: The words 'במותם יטמא' match Lev 11:31-32, while the Gemara's argument (nazirite, 'לאביו ולאמו') follows Num 6:7. The bracket in Wikisource is editorial. Rashi's and Tosafot's placement is commentary. This affects what 'them' refers to (creeping things or relatives), not which person holds the view.
findings.graph_effect: Record the verse identification as an editorial note on Rebbi's 43a:5 statement. Do not use the Wikisource bracket as evidence about the referent of 'them'. The Rebbi attribution itself is unaffected.

findings.claim: Koren expands the bare 'רבי' in 43a:5 and 43a:7 to 'Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi'. That is an editorial historical identification. The Hebrew says only 'רבי', and the dossier found no source in the checked passage that ties it to a biography.

evidence.exact_quote: He requires that verse for that which was taught by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. As it is taught in a baraita that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says
מיבעי ליה לכדרבי דתניא רבי אומר

findings.reasoning: Bare 'רבי' is conventionally read as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The graph treats that as a separate historical decision.
findings.graph_effect: Keep one local person 'Rebbi' for 43a:5-9. Store the identification with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as a provisional candidate, citing the Koren English expansion as an editorial source, not as text evidence.

unresolved: I did not check manuscript witnesses of Nazir 43a (for example Munich 95 or the Vatican manuscripts) for 43a:6 or 43a:9. The Abaye/Rava reading is known here only through Halakhot Gedolot and the later works that report it.
The Rosh prints 'רבה' where Tosafot, Yereim, Haamek Sheilah and the Halakhot Gedolot print 'רבא'. I did not check other editions of the Rosh.

Toafot Re'em 322:8 mentions a Yerushalmi Nazir passage (ch. 3) about a שמעון בר ווא and a dying person, tied to Reish Lakish. I did not fetch or read that Yerushalmi passage, and this dossier draws nothing from it.
The Sefaria links also list Sifrei Zuta and Yevamot 120b for these segments. I did not read them. Tosafot at 43a says there is a tannaitic dispute about a mutilated person at Yevamot 120b.

It is unresolved whether the 43a:7-10 questions are meant only within Reish Lakish's account. Rashi says nothing explicit on 43a:7-10, and no commentator I checked addresses 43a:9 directly on this point.

Resolve the needed context. The two proponents are the anonymous first tanna and Rebbi (43a:5). Reish Lakish or Rabbi Yochanan (43a:6) frame the analysis, with the Halakhot Gedolot variant Abaye/Rava.

lessons: A 'למאן דאמר X' label is a role reference to a position. Resolve it to the speaker who first set up X in the wider sugya. Do not create a new unnamed person for it. Keep the position node, because the Gemara argues about its construction of the position.

An objection in a 'dying person' (goses) framework can have two targets: the tanna whose position is challenged, and the amora whose account of that position creates the difficulty. Store the second as commentary-based unless the text names it.
A later work that quotes a different attribution (here Halakhot Gedolot: Abaye/Rava for R. Yochanan/Reish Lakish) is a source variant. Save it as a reading branch, never as a merge of the two people.
Reports of one variant can disagree (Rava vs Rabbah). Store each report with its own source rather than harmonising.
Pronoun suffixes in quoted verses (להחלו 'himself', במותם 'them') refer to biblical legal figures. Keep them as legal roles, and draw no family edges from 'his father' in a verse.
Abbreviation expansion needs context: 'ר"ל' is Reish Lakish in the Talmud text and 'that is to say' in Torah Temimah.
Translations and commentary from one editorial project (Koren English and Steinsaltz Hebrew) count as one reading, not two.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications and quoted evidence. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

An unnamed first opinion should not become a historical group merely because the introduction says the Rabbis taught. A later authority calls the side the Rabbis. Save that attribution separately and leave its actual membership unknown.

Keep the printed cross-reference as data about that edition and the different identification supported by the commentaries. Do not silently rewrite the saved source.

שצפו עומרין לתוך שדה חבירו - שנשבה הרוח והרימה את העומרין מן הארץ והציפתן לתוך שדה חבירו ושכחן כסבור שאינן שלו נפקא מבשדך ולא בשדה חבירך דלא הוו שכחה:

findings.reasoning: In 45a:14 the Rabbis derive standing grain from 'כי תקצור קצירך בשדך'. 45a:15 then asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with that verse. The answer, 'he needs it for the teaching of Rabbi Abahu from Rabbi Elazar', is the unnamed voice assigning a use of the verse to Rabbi Yehuda. Rashi takes the source word as בשדך ('your field, not your fellow's'). Rabbi Yehuda is not quoted citing either man. The link is the anonymous voice's reconstruction, which pairs a Tannaitic reading with a teaching carried by later named sages.

findings.claim: Transmission: Rabbi Abahu reports the floated-sheaves exclusion in Rabbi Elazar's name. The one chain is named twice in 45a:15 (a back-reference and then the full quotation) and again in 45a:17. These are three mentions of one transmission, not three observations.

findings.claim: The one legal disagreement behind the focal line comes from the baraita just before it (45a:10). Rabbi Yehuda excludes a hidden forgotten sheaf, and the Sages (חכמים) include it. The first reading's input began at 45a:11 and never saw this dispute. The Gemara's רבנן in 45a:11-15 refers back to these חכמים.

findings.reasoning: 45a:10 cites the baraita to test whether the anonymous mishnah (44b:11, a corpse hidden in a heap) follows only Rabbi Yehuda. Sifrei Devarim 283 has the same dispute in a plural form (טמונים). Mishnah Peah 6:10 has a related dispute under the same names about produce stored in the ground, which is a different case. These are parallel formulations in other works. They do not show that the dispute was held more than once. 'חכמים' in the baraita and 'רבנן' in the Gemara are two labels for the same anonymous majority, not for individuals.

findings.claim: In the focal line (45a:13) the unnamed voice asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not derive the hidden-sheaf exclusion from 'forgetting is like harvest', and concedes that he does. Rabbi Yehuda's legal ruling is unchanged. What moves is the source the baraita gave for it (בשדה).

evidence.exact_quote: לרבי יהודה נמי תיפוק ליה משכחה דומיא דקציר אין הכי נמי
evidence.translation: For Rabbi Yehuda too, let him derive it from 'forgetting is like harvest'. Yes, indeed so.

evidence.exact_quote: The Gemara answers: Yes, it is indeed so, he does not derive that halakha from the phrase “in the field.”
ההלכה שאמר שאין הטמון בכלל
בשדה - ושכחת עומר בשדה לרבי יהודה משמע בשדה על פני השדה ולרבנן משמע בתוך השדה:
evidence.translation: 'In the field': for Rabbi Yehuda it means on the surface of the field; for the Rabbis, inside the field.

evidence.exact_quote: ור"י בשדה על פני השדה לרבות שכחת קמה
evidence.ref: Tosefot Yom Tov on Mishnah Peah 6:10:1

findings.reasoning: The baraita (45a:10) has Rabbi Yehuda read בשדה as excluding the hidden sheaf. 45a:13 gets the same exclusion from the harvest comparison Rav used in 45a:12 and answers 'yes indeed'. 45a:14 then moves Rabbi Yehuda's בשדה to standing grain. The Davidson English adds a gloss that he does not derive it from 'in the field'. Steinsaltz keeps the ruling ('the halakha he stated, that the hidden is not included'). Rashi and Tosefot Yom Tov read Rabbi Yehuda's בשדה as 'on the surface of the field', which fits including standing grain. Two layers are kept apart: the baraita attributes a reading to Rabbi Yehuda, and the Gemara reconstructs his sources. The Davidson English and Steinsaltz come from one editorial project and are not independent witnesses.
findings.graph_effect: Replace earlier c3 (anon 'explains' yehuda_derive). New shape: the unnamed voice poses a question and concedes. No person edge.

findings.claim: Standing grain (45a:14) and floated sheaves (45a:15) are not legal disagreements. The Gemara presents Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis as reaching the same rule from different words. Their disagreement there is about which verse teaches it.

evidence.exact_quote: ורבנן שכחת קמה מנא להו נפקא להו מכי תקצור קצירך בשדך
evidence.translation: And the Rabbis, forgotten standing grain, from where do they [have it]? They derive it from 'when you reap your harvest in your field'.

evidence.exact_quote: ורבנן מבשדה בשדך ור' יהודה בשדה בשדך לא משמע ליה
evidence.translation: And the Rabbis: from 'in the field' / 'in your field'. And Rabbi Yehuda: 'in the field' / 'in your field' does not imply [anything] to him.

evidence.exact_quote: ורבנן - מיעוטא דשדה חבירו נפקא להו מדהוה ליה למכתב כי תקצור קצירך בשדה ושכחת וכתיב בשדך:
evidence.translation: 'And the Rabbis': they derive the exclusion of the fellow's field from the fact that it could have written 'when you reap your harvest in the field and forget' and wrote 'in your field'.

evidence.exact_quote: בַּשָּׂדֶה, לְרַבּוֹת אֶת הַקָּמָה

findings.reasoning: 'מנא להו' asks for the Rabbis' source for a rule the question takes for granted they hold. 'ורבנן מבשדה בשדך' gives them a source for the floated-sheaves exclusion. 'לא משמע ליה' rejects an inference, not a ruling. So c9 (yehuda opposes distinction) is right only as a disagreement about method. In Sifrei Devarim 283, 'בשדה to include standing grain' is anonymous. It matches the verse the Gemara assigns to Rabbi Yehuda but is not attributed to him.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c4 and c5 (both include standing grain), marked 'agreement on outcome, different source'. Relabel c9 from a bare 'opposes' to a disagreement about derivation (whether the בשדה/בשדך contrast teaches anything). Do not add a legal-disagreement edge for standing grain or floated sheaves. The only legal-disagreement edge here is F07's.

findings.claim: Rav (45a:11) answers an attribution question: must the anonymous mishnah follow Rabbi Yehuda? He says it can follow even the Rabbis, because each verse is read in its own context. Rav explains the Rabbis' position. He does not disagree with Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis. 'Here' is the slain person (Deut. 21:1) and 'there' is the forgotten sheaf (Deut. 24:19).

evidence.exact_quote: אמר רב אפי' תימא רבנן הכא מענייניה דקרא התם מענייניה דקרא
evidence.translation: Rav said: you may even say [it is] the Rabbis; here [it is read] from the context of the verse, there from the context of the verse.

evidence.exact_quote: נמצא טמון בגל או תלוי באילן או צף על פני המים לא היו עורפין שנאמר באדמה ולא טמון בגל
evidence.translation: If found hidden in a heap, or hanging on a tree, or floating on the water, they would not break [the heifer's neck], as it says 'in the ground' and not hidden in a heap.

evidence.exact_quote: התם מענייניה דקרא - צריכין למידרשיה והכא מענייניה דקרא תדרוש ליה גבי חלל כתיב כי ימצא חלל כל היכא דמשתכח ואפי' טמון

This is an attribution and harmonisation move. The first reading's needed_context note was right: the antecedents are 44b:11 and 45a:10.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 but make its target the question 'does the anonymous mishnah 44b:11 follow the Rabbis?', with the Rabbis as the group whose view Rav interprets (predicate interprets_view_of / harmonises). In this case, as it is written: “If one be found slain” (Deuteronomy 21:1), the default assumption is that the halakha applies no matter where it is found.

The earlier c2 (rav explains, basis local_coreference) is plausible, but its speaker boundary should be marked as not explicit.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c2 as a branch: branch A has Rav speaking through 45a:12, and branch B has the Gemara elaborating Rav. Either way there is no new person relation.

findings.claim: Wider text (45a:16-17): Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma. Rav Kahana resolves it with Rabbi Abahu's teaching from Rabbi Elazar, speaking to Rav Pappi or, as 'some say' (ואמרי לה), to Rav Zevid. Rav Kahana is not told to be answering Rabbi Yirmeya, and he is not reported as receiving the teaching from Rabbi Abahu.

evidence.exact_quote: בעי ר' ירמיה צפו עומרין לתוך שדהו מהו אויר שדה כשדה דמי או לאו כשדה דמי

findings.graph_effect: Outside the input segments, but it belongs to the same teaching. lessons: 'X מיבעי ליה לכדרבי A אמר רבי B' is the unnamed voice assigning a verse's use to X for a teaching carried by A from B. It links teaching to teaching. It is not transmission, contact or agreement between X and A or B.

Keep three kinds of disagreement apart. (1) A legal disagreement differs on the ruling (hidden sheaf, 45a:10). (2) A disagreement about the source reaches the same ruling from different verses (standing grain, floated sheaves). (3) An attribution question asks whose view an anonymous text follows (mishnah 44b:11, Rav 45a:11). Only (1) should be drawn as a legal-dispute edge.
'לכדרבי A... דאמר רבי A' names one teaching and then quotes it. It is one attribution with two mentions. Later citations such as 'תפשוט ליה מדרבי A' re-use the teaching and add no edge weight.
Pronoun and zero-subject mentions (ליה, להו, מיבעי ליה) carry who holds a claim in Gemara back-and-forth. Inventory them as mentions, so that claims like c4 have an anchored subject.
Group labels in different layers (חכמים in a baraita, רבנן in the Gemara) can point to the same anonymous majority. That is a group coreference, not a set of individuals.
The same name in one sugya can belong to different figures in different layers (the Amoraic source of Rabbi Abahu at 45a:15 against the baraita disputant at 45b:5). Keep separate local placeholders.
An abbreviation (ר"א) resolved from the same sentence and from a second edition is an edition spelling difference. Store it apart from true attribution variants.
'ואמרי לה' addressee alternatives belong in one branch group on one speech event.
When two works give the same scene different protagonists (Yerushalmi: Rav; Bavli: Abaye), record the literary difference. It is not identity or biography evidence.
A patronymic in the wider text ('Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda') still yields a local father placeholder. Do not merge it with a same-named sage elsewhere in the sugya.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications and quoted evidence. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

findings.reason: Separate every mention and connect repeated citations to the same teaching occurrence where context supports it. Repetition inside an argument must not automatically multiply the strength of an independent witness.

A view can use another teaching, or share a ruling while deriving it differently. These are connections between claims. They do not establish a personal encounter.

The differing Rav and Abaye attributions are evidence about the two textual accounts. They do not establish historical identity, but retain them for later narrative and identity comparison rather than declaring them no evidence about either person.

findings.claim: Reported scenes in the flood discussion are narrated inside a rabbi's interpretation. The characters who speak in them are God, the Flood generation as a collective, Noah, a raven, a dove, personified robbery, Shem and Eliezer. Noah's rebuke scene belongs to Rabbi Yosei of Caesarea (108a:22 to 108b:1) and to Rava (108b:2-3). Methuselah's seven days of mourning belong to Rav. The raven's argument with Noah belongs to Reish Lakish. The dove's plea belongs to Rabbi Elazar. The baraita says the dog, the raven and Ham were punished. The Shem and Eliezer dialogues belong to Rav Chana bar Bizna and Rav Chana bar Leva'ei.

lessons: When an unnamed reply answers a view about several targets, scope the 'opposes' edge to the sub-claim it answers. Record whether that scope is explicit or rests on commentary.
Editorial markers (מתני׳, גמ׳) mark sections. They are not speakers and should not anchor mentions of persons or groups.
Verse terms mapped by exegesis (רשעים → Flood generation) are interprets-as edges attributed to the interpreter, not new groups.
A parallel in another work that gives the same formula to a named sage is an alternative attribution. It is not an identity for the unnamed voice, and it does not prove who said it.
Scenes with biblical characters speaking are narrated inside a named rabbi's exegesis. Nest them as reported scenes under that rabbi instead of treating them as direct observations.
Personifications (robbery), animals (raven, dove) and parable figures are not persons.

Kinship stated in a character's speech ('אבא') is textual evidence within the story. Translation glosses ('son of Noah') from the same editorial work as another gloss are one source, not corroboration.
When witnesses disagree on a patronymic (יוסף/יוסי), keep one parent placeholder with variant labels, or two branches. Do not drop the parent.
Source variants (the Kaufmann text lacks the dispersion clause) and later proposed reorderings (the Vilna Gaon, reported by Rashash) are different evidence types.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

findings.target: F2/F3 anonymous reply and Sodom scope
findings.reason: Keep the unnamed plural respondents and their singular addressee. Attribute the identification as Sages to its editions and commentators. The Sodom-only scope is an interpretation supported by context and commentary, not an explicit noun in the reply.
Two voices agreeing does not make them the same speaker. The named parallel respondent remains in that work; it does not fill the Bavli’s unnamed group.

findings.target: F11–F15 nested stories and legal or verse categories
findings.reason: Keep narrated people, collective groups, verse categories, personified robbery and speaking animals distinguishable. The framing sage reports an exegesis; that does not place the sage inside Noah’s story. Kinship inside the story remains textual evidence.

findings.target: F5/F6 source variants and translation discrepancy
findings.reason: Keep each version’s list of generations. A translation that interprets both differently must not overwrite the adjacent Hebrew or be counted as independent confirmation.

cases.question: Investigate remembered encounter and pronouns, brother versus חביבך, and later unnamed speaker. Capture the competing rain date third of Marheshvan and narrated precedent. Use translations and commentaries to distinguish certainty from conjecture.

findings.claim: The halakhah opens with an unnamed plural group asking a question 'before him', and 'he' answers 'them': practice is that where one mentions rain one also asks for it. The text names neither the askers nor the one who answers.

evidence.exact_quote: בעון קומוי או נימר כאן להזכיר כאן לשאלה אמר לון הלכה מקום שמזכירין שואלין
They asked before him

findings.reasoning: בעון is a 3rd-person plural verb ('they asked'). קומוי is 'before him'. אמר לון is 'he said to them'. None of these has a named antecedent in the segment. (My translation: 'They asked before him: or should we say, here it is about mentioning and there about asking? He said to them: the practice is that where one mentions, one asks.')
findings.graph_effect: Keep the askers as an unnamed group node. Keep the answerer as a pronoun mention until coreference is resolved (see F2).

findings.claim: Every consulted commentary that comments on this phrase (Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah, Ohr LaYesharim), and both translations, take 'him' (the one asked, who then answers) to be R. Yohanan. The text also supports this: two lines later, R. Hiyya bar Ba brings the same formula from Tyre in R. Yohanan's name.

evidence.exact_quote: דר' יוחנן או דילמא נימר דכאן ברישא דהמתני' להזכיר
הקשו לפני רבי יוחנן
שאלו לפניו (לפני רבי יוחנן)
R. Joḥanan.
fut-il demandé à R. Yohanan
רבי חייה בר בא אתא מן צור ואמר מן שמיה דרבי יוחנן הלכה מקום שמזכירין שואלין

findings.reasoning: R. Yohanan is the last named authority in 1:2:2-1:2:3. The same halakhic formula is later brought explicitly in his name, so the commentators' identification fits the text. It is still a coreference reading, not an explicit naming.
findings.graph_effect: Link the opening answerer to R. Yohanan, with basis = commentary consensus plus internal support (not 'explicit'). The askers stay unnamed. Do not identify them with R. Yose and R. Hananya, whose remembered scene is a separate report.

findings.claim: As printed, R. Yose addresses 'R. Hananya the brother of Rav Hoshaya' (אחוי דרב הושעיה). In the same sentence he calls the shop owner 'Rav Hoshaya חביבך'.

evidence.exact_quote: א"ר יוסה לרבי חנניה אחוי דרב הושעיה נהיר את כד הוינן קיימין קומי חנותיה דרב הושעיה חביבך
אמר רבי יוסה לרבי חנייה אחוי דרב הושעיה נהיר את כד הוינן קיימין קומי חנותיה דרב הושעיה חביבך
dost thou remember when we were standing &c.?

findings.reasoning: Venice and Mechon-Mamre agree on אחוי ('his brother'). Mechon-Mamre spells the addressee חנייה. נהיר את = 'do you remember' (Jastrow).
findings.graph_effect: Record the printed epithet 'brother of Rav Hoshaya' as a textual reading only (see F5-F6 for why it should not become a sibling edge).

findings.claim: חביב has two lexical senses: 'beloved' and 'uncle, father's brother'. Every interpreter consulted takes the uncle sense here: Korban HaEdah and Ohr LaYesharim (דודך), Guggenheimer ('your uncle'), Schwab ('ton oncle').

evidence.exact_quote: uncle, father’s brother
beloved, dear, precious; favored, privileged.
זכור אתה כשהיינו עומדין לפני חנותו של ר"ה דודך
כאשר היינו עומדים לפני חנותו של רב הושעיה דודך
do you remember when we were standing in front of your uncle Rav Hoshaia’s store
devant la boutique de R. Oshia ton oncle

findings.reasoning: The 'beloved' sense is lexically possible, but none of the commentaries or translations I checked adopts it for this line. It stays a live lexical option with no interpretive support in the checked sources.
findings.graph_effect: Treat the 'uncle' reading as primary. Keep 'beloved' as a low-support alternative branch.

findings.claim: Two parallel Yerushalmi passages give Hananya's epithet as 'son of the brother of Rav Hoshaya'. JT Megillah 3:7:3 repeats almost the same remembered scene at Rav Hoshaya's shop and uses both בר אחוי and חביבך.

evidence.exact_quote: לְרִבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר אָחוֹי דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָה. נָהִיר אַתְּ כַּד דַּהֲוִינָן קַיָימִין קֳדָם חָנוּתָה דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָה חָבִיבָךְ
said to Rebbi Ḥanania the son of Rav Hoshaia’s brother, do you remember when we were standing in front of your uncle’s store
רבי חנניה בן אחוי דרב הושעיה אמר מתניתין בעמי הארץ
Rebbi Ḥananiah the son of Rav Hoshaia’s brother

findings.reasoning: In Megillah the full epithet and חביבך occur together without contradiction. That suggests the Taanit reading אחוי is short by one word (בר). In Megillah the speaker is printed as bare רבי (Guggenheimer n.150 cites Soferim 13:4 with a different speaker), and the sage who passes is R. Abba bar Zavda. So the Megillah scene is a parallel formula, not proof that the same event is meant.
findings.graph_effect: This supports a nephew relation through an unnamed parent. Do not merge the Megillah and Taanit scenes into one event.

findings.claim: Guggenheimer and Ohr LaYesharim both emend the Taanit text to 'son of Rav Hoshaya's brother'. On that reading Hananya is Rav Hoshaya's nephew, and the Hoshaya in his epithet and the shop owner are the same person. Read literally, 'brother of Rav Hoshaya' plus 'your uncle Rav Hoshaya' cannot both describe one Hoshaya. No source I checked proposes two different Hoshayas here. Schwab translates both phrases literally and does not comment.

evidence.exact_quote: From the following it is obvious that one has to read “son of Rav Hoshaia’s brother”
(צריך לומר: בר אחוי)
בן אחיו של רב הושעיה (אמורא בדור השלישי)
R. Yossé dit à R. Hanina, frère de R. Oshia: tu te souviens

findings.reasoning: The emendation rests on three things: the internal contradiction, the lexical sense 'father's brother', and the parallels in F5. It remains an emendation of the printed text.
findings.graph_effect: Replace the explicit sibling_of(Hananya, Rav Hoshaya) with: child_of(Hananya, unnamed parent) plus sibling_of(unnamed parent, Rav Hoshaya), both with basis = emendation/commentary. Make the two Rav Hoshaya mentions one entity under this branch. Keep the printed 'brother' as a rejected/variant reading, not as an asserted edge.

findings.claim: Lieberman identifies the shop owner as 'R. Hoshaya the second', who had a shop in Tiberias. He cites this passage and JT Megillah 3. JT Sanhedrin 10:1 has 'the Tiberians' measuring distance 'up to the shop of R. Hoshaya'. Ohr LaYesharim places Rav Hoshaya in the third Amoraic generation.

evidence.exact_quote: והוא ר' הושעיה השני שהיתה לו חנות בטבריא, כמפורש בירושלמי תענית פ"א ה"ב
טִיבֵּרִיאֵי אָמְרִין. מִן סִידְרָא רַבָּה עַד חָנוּתֵיהּ דְרִבִּי הוֹשַׁעְיָה
בן אחיו של רב הושעיה (אמורא בדור השלישי)

findings.reasoning: This is scholarly historical identification. The Sanhedrin passage spells the name רבי הושעיה, not רב, and gives no kinship. Placing the shop in Tiberias is an inference that joins passages, not a statement in Taanit. The same chapter (JT Taanit 1:3:2) also has a ruling 'in the name of R. Hoshaya' that should not be merged by name alone.
findings.graph_effect: At most, add an optional historical-identity hypothesis (shop owner = 'R. Hoshaya II', Tiberias) with basis = modern scholarship. Do not attach a place edge from Taanit alone. Do not merge with other Hoshaya mentions by name.

findings.claim: 'We' in the remembered scene (הוינן 'we were', שאלנן 'we asked') includes at least R. Yose, the speaker, and very likely R. Hananya: Yose asks him to remember the scene, and at the end speaks of Hananya's own action ('you ...'). The text does not say whether anyone else was present.

evidence.exact_quote: נהיר את כד הוינן קיימין
עבר רבי זעורה ושאלנן ליה ואמר עוד אנא היא צריכה לי עבר רבי יסא ושאלנן ליה ואמר עוד אנא היא צריכה לי
ושאלנו ליה ואמר גם לדידי קמיבעיא לי

findings.reasoning: Asking the addressee whether he remembers presupposes he was there. The plural verb does not limit the group to two. The whole scene is Yose's recollection inside the halakhah, so it has the status of reported speech.
findings.graph_effect: Participation edges for Yose (high) and Hananya (medium-high). Give them voice = R. Yose (reported recollection), not narrator. The unnamed parent and Rav Hoshaya are not participants, only the owner of the landmark.

findings.claim: R. Zeura and then R. Yasa each passed by, were asked, and replied 'עוד אנא היא צריכה לי'. Commentators read עוד two ways: 'still' (Penei Moshe, Guggenheimer) or 'I too' (Korban HaEdah, Ohr LaYesharim). Either way, each sage says he is himself unsure.

evidence.exact_quote: עדיין אני מסופק בדבר זה אם יש לחלק בין הזכרה לבין שאלה
גם לדידי קמיבעיא לי
this is still problematic for me

findings.reasoning: The 'I too' reading implies the questioners were also unsure. The 'still' reading implies an ongoing doubt. Neither changes who spoke.
findings.graph_effect: asks(Yose+Hananya → Zeura), asks(Yose+Hananya → Yasa), answers-with-doubt from each. These stay inside R. Yose's recollection.

findings.claim: Interpreters differ on what exactly the two sages were asked. Penei Moshe and Ohr LaYesharim say it was whether mentioning rain and asking for rain can be separated (the 'או נימר' question). Guggenheimer says it was the best date to start praying for rain.

evidence.exact_quote: אם יש לחלק בין הזכרה לבין שאלה
The date when best to start praying for rain.

findings.reasoning: The text only says 'we asked him'. The content has to be supplied from context. The two readings are close: Guggenheimer's n.113 connects the mention/request rule to the autumn start date.
findings.graph_effect: The content role of the asks edges should point to the mention-vs-request question, noting Guggenheimer's start-date reading as an alternative.

findings.claim: 'ובסופה את מציית ליה ואמר לא שנייא' is read in three ways. (a) 'At the end you made him listen / pressed him, and he said...': Jastrow, A Dictionary of the Talmud, Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah ('you cried out with him in argument'), Schwab. (b) 'At the end you heard from him': Guggenheimer. (c) Emend to one word אתמציית, 'at the end it became clear to him': Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael (R. Z. W. Rabinovitz), endorsed by Lieberman and followed by Ohr LaYesharim. On (a) and (b) Hananya takes part in the final exchange. On (c) he does not.

evidence.exact_quote: and finally thou madest him listen (to thee), and he said &c.
פַעל, גרם להקשבה ולציות
to cause to listen
שלחצת אותו לומר לך האמת
ולבסוף אתה צעקת עמו דרך פלפול
Ce n’est qu’après l’avoir poussé à bout et pressé, qu’il finit par s’écrier
But at the end you heard from him: there is no difference; where one mentions one asks.
פי' שזכר ונמצא לו דין זה, ומלת "אתמציית" נתחלקה לשתים
כלומר ובסוף נתמצתה לו [ההלכה] ואמר וכו'
ובסוף נמצאה לו (נודעה ונתבררה לרבי אסי שאלה זו), שידע להשיב עליה

findings.reasoning: Both printed Hebrew texts have two words, את מציית. Reading (c) is a conjectural emendation, though highly regarded (Lieberman calls it 'הגהתו היפה', 'his fine emendation'). Reading (b) is the most neutral translation and treats the clause as transmission. Reading (a) treats it as a pressured exchange.
findings.graph_effect: Branch the final exchange. (a) speech: Hananya presses the sage, and the sage answers; (b) transmission: Hananya hears the ruling from the sage; (c) the sage comes to know the ruling himself and states it (no Hananya edge). The earlier single heard_from edge is branch (b) only.

findings.claim: The pronoun 'him' (ליה), the one who finally says 'לא שנייא', is not named. The nearest antecedent is R. Yasa. Ohr LaYesharim names him outright ('R. Assi'), and Schwab's French continues from R. Yassa. No consulted source makes it R. Zeura.

evidence.exact_quote: ובסוף נמצאה לו (נודעה ונתבררה לרבי אסי שאלה זו)
עבר רבי יסא (רבי אסי, אמורא ארץ ישראלי בדור השלישי)
et la même question ayant été adressée à R. Yassa qui passa, il y répondit de même
ולרבי אסי היו דברי רבי יוחנן ברורים, ולרבי זירא היו הדברים מסופקים.
אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא לְרַבִּי אַסִּי: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי?

findings.reasoning: Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah, Guggenheimer and Jastrow leave 'him' unnamed. Ohr LaYesharim supports R. Yasa by linking to Bavli Taanit 4b, where R. Assi transmits R. Yohanan and R. Zeira questions him. That is cross-text support, and it depends on identifying Yerushalmi יסא with Bavli אסי, which is a commentator's identification, not something the text states.
findings.graph_effect: Resolve the final speaker to R. Yasa at medium confidence (basis: nearest antecedent plus one commentary). Zeura is a low-confidence alternative. Do not create a Yasa–Yohanan transmission edge from this Yerushalmi passage: Yasa is not said to cite Yohanan here.

findings.claim: R. Hiyya bar Ba came from Tyre and said the ruling in R. Yohanan's name. Ohr LaYesharim suggests, explicitly as a possibility, that he had heard it from R. Yohanan in Tyre.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי חייה בר בא אתא מן צור ואמר מן שמיה דרבי יוחנן
אפשר, שכשחזר רבי חייא בר אבא מצור, אמר משמו של רבי יוחנן מה ששמע ממנו בצור.

findings.reasoning: The travel and the attribution are textual. The claim that R. Yohanan was in Tyre, and that the ruling was heard there, is marked 'אפשר' ('it is possible') by the commentator. It is conjecture.
findings.graph_effect: reports_in_name_of(Hiyya bar Ba → Yohanan) and origin = Tyre stay explicit. Do not add co-location of Yohanan in Tyre.

findings.claim: R. Aha preached in the study house and R. Yirmeya in the 'כנישתא דבולי'. The ruling formula follows once, after both clauses. Ohr LaYesharim says both preached R. Yohanan's ruling. What בולי means is disputed: a place called Buli (Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah), 'importance' (Penei Moshe's alternative), the city council (Guggenheimer; Ohr LaYesharim, which conjectures Tiberias), or 'prob.' the senate building in Sepphoris (Jastrow).

evidence.exact_quote: רבי אחא דרש בבית מדרשא רבי ירמיה דרש בכנישתא דבולי הלכה מקום שמזכירין שואלין
שניהם דרשו כדברי רבי יוחנן
מקום הנקרא בולי. א"נ בולי לשון חשיבות הוא
בבית הכנסת של עיר בולי
prob. the assembly building of the Senate in Sepphoris
כנראה נערכו בבית הכנסת של הבולי בטבריה כינוסי מועצת העיר
נוּקְנִיקָה אִישְׁתַּכַּח בִּכְנִישְׁתָּא דְבוּלֵי. אֲתַא עוֹבְדָא קוֹמֵי רִבִּי יִרְמְיָה.

findings.reasoning: The two preachings are separate events in separate places. Saying they share the same content is a reasonable syntactic reading. JT Shekalim 7:2 connects a case in the same synagogue with R. Yirmeya, but that is a co-occurrence, not evidence of where the building was.
findings.graph_effect: Two public-teaching events. Content = the mention/request ruling (medium-high). The place 'כנישתא דבולי' has no fixed city: Sepphoris (Jastrow) and Tiberias (Ohr LaYesharim) are both hedged conjectures.

findings.claim: The competing dates come from the Mishnah (JT 1:3:1 / Mishnah Taanit 1:3). The anonymous first opinion asks for rain from the 3rd of Marheshvan. Rabban Gamliel says the 7th, fifteen days after the festival, so that the last Israelite pilgrim can reach the Euphrates. The Yerushalmi's own halakhah on that Mishnah (1:3:2) calls the anonymous opinion R. Meir's, and gives a ruling 'in the name of R. Hoshaya' that follows the 3rd.

evidence.exact_quote: בִּשְׁלשָׁה בְּמַרְחֶשְׁוָן שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים. רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר בְּשִׁבְעָה בוֹ חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר יוֹם אַחַר הֶחָג כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ הָאַחֲרוֹן שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לִנְהַר פְּרָת.
בִּשְׁלשָׁה בְמַרְחֶשְׁוָן שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים. רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר, בְּשִׁבְעָה בוֹ
מַתְנִיתָא דְרִבִּי מֵאִיר.
רִבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זְמִינָא רִבִּי לָעְזָר בְּשֵׁם רִבִּי הוֹשַׁעְיָה. הֲלָכָה כְמִי שֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר. בִּשְׁלשָׁה בְּמַרְחֶשְׁוָן שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים.
דזמן רביעה ראשונה בג' במרחשון וכר"מ וכדמפרש בגמרא

findings.reasoning: The anonymous Mishnah voice is not a person node. The Yerushalmi's 'this is R. Meir's Mishnah' is an attribution made by the Talmud, and the same line adds 'there are tannaim who switch' (אית תניי תני ומחלף). The Bavli has a different ruling (R. Elazar: halakhah like Rabban Gamliel, B. Taanit 4b), and Penei Moshe on 1:3:1 rules like Rabban Gamliel. So the halakhic outcome is disputed between sources.
findings.graph_effect: Add the missing claim: anonymous Mishnah (tanna kamma) holds_view 'ask from 3 Marheshvan', and Rabban Gamliel holds_view 'ask from 7 Marheshvan' (reason: pilgrims reach the Euphrates). Add an attribution claim: the Yerushalmi (stam) attributes the anonymous opinion to R. Meir. Add the ruling: R. Abba bar Zamina, R. La'zar in the name of R. Hoshaya, halakhah like the 3rd. Keep this R. Hoshaya separate from the shop owner.

findings.claim: In 1:2:4 the anonymous challenge ('והא תנינן') quotes that Mishnah against the rule 'where one mentions, one asks'. R. Tanhum bar Hiyya answers: 'בשעת המקדש שאני' ('Temple times are different'). Commentators explain the delay as time for pilgrims to get home. In Guggenheimer's edition the word 'בשלשה' in the challenge is a corrector's addition in brackets, and he writes that the scribe's shorter text may be correct.

evidence.exact_quote: והא תנינן בשלשה במרחשון שואלין את הגשמים אמר רבי תנחום בר חייה בשעת המקדש שאני
וְהָא תַנִּינָן. [בִּשְׁלשָׁה] בְּמַרְחֶשְׁוָן שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים.
It is possible that the scribe’s text correctly gives the argument.
דהוי עולי רגלים ואין מזכירין ושואלין עד ג' במרחשון שלא יטרדו בחזירתן מחמת הגשמים
דאיכא עולי רגלים לא היו שואלין עד ג' במרחשון אבל בזמן הזה הלכה במקום שמזכירין שואלין
בזמן שבית המקדש קיים שנו את דברי המשנה
בשעת מקדש שאני הכי משני ומסיק נמי בבבלי דף ד ע"ב
כָּאן בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים, כָּאן בִּזְמַן שֶׁאֵין בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים.

findings.reasoning: The challenger is the anonymous Talmud voice, not a person. Tanhum's answer limits the 3rd-of-Marheshvan rule to Temple times. Ohr LaYesharim notes the vocalized שַנֵי should read שָנוּ ('they taught'); the meaning is the same. The pilgrim explanation is commentary, though it follows the Mishnah's own Euphrates reason. Venice has 'בשלשה', so whether the challenge names the 3rd depends on the witness.

lessons: A kinship epithet in the printed text ('אחוי') can conflict with a kinship term in the same sentence ('חביבך'). The graph needs a way to store an explicit-but-emended reading without asserting it.
Parallel passages with the same framing formula (JT Taanit 1:2:4 and JT Megillah 3:7:3) are strong evidence for a text reading. They are not evidence that the same event is meant.

A verb's construal can decide whether a person takes part in an exchange at all (את מציית 'you pressed/heard' vs אתמציית 'it became clear to him'). Claims should be able to branch on the reading, not just on the referent.

Separate three kinds of voice: the anonymous Talmud voice (challenger), the anonymous Mishnah voice (the 3rd-of-Marheshvan opinion), and attributions the Talmud itself makes ('this is R. Meir's Mishnah'). None should become a person node by default.
A precedent spoken inside an attributed view ('שכן מצאנו ... בימי יואל') is an attributed exegetical claim. A biblical name used as a time anchor is not a relationship partner.
Commentators often mark conjectures with 'אפשר' or 'כנראה', and a lexicon may mark one with 'prob.'. Keep these hedges as a separate confidence basis from lexical or textual evidence.
Shared patronymics across Talmuds (Yehuda vs Yehoshua ben Betera) and shared names within one chapter (several R. Hoshaya and R. Yose mentions) must not merge automatically.
When commentary consensus resolves a pronoun (בעון קומוי → R. Yohanan), record the basis as commentary consensus plus internal evidence, distinct from 'explicit'.

findings.claim: The full rule set in scope concerns high priests. (a) Mishnah: an anointed priest and a priest invested by garments differ only in the bull for all the commandments. (b) Mishnah: a serving priest and a former priest differ only in the Yom Kippur bull and the tenth of an ephah. (c) Tanna: the anointed priest brings the bull and the garment-invested priest does not; Rabbi Meir disagrees. (d) Rabbi Yohanan: a former priest's tenth of an ephah brought anyway is valid. (e)-(h) are in 1:10:4-5: the backup priest, "one, not two", the first and second priest, and "valid if served".

findings.claim: Maimonides codifies the rules this way. A backup high priest is prepared. After Yom Kippur the first returns; the second passes out of service, bears all the high-priestly commandments, does not serve as high priest, has valid service if he served, and succeeds if the first dies. Two high priests are not appointed together.

lessons: A repeated legal term can name a role category ("fit for high priest") in one place and a person ("happened to the high priest") a few words later. An anchor needs an occurrence number checked against its governing verb, not just the string.

Eligibility rules need a claim type whose subject is a generic legal role (first/second priest) and whose object is a role category (high priest, ordinary priest). No person node should be created for the category.
When a story is cited to answer a legal question, link it with "illustrates" or "role-instantiation" edges marked as interpretation. Do not copy the rule's predicates onto the story persons.
A "ben X" name is not a filiation edge to a person X unless X appears or acts.
Parallel tellings give different names (Yosef ben Ilim/Elem; Yishmael and Yeshevav/Yosef ben Kimhit). They belong in identity packs as candidates, never as merges inside a passage graph.
Some attributes depend on the reading, such as "Arab" versus "eve", or valid versus invalid. They need branch labels, with the witness or editor that supports each.

Commentary disagreements (Penei Moshe versus Ohr LaYesharim on ownership; Korban HaEdah versus Guggenheimer on קרי) should be stored with the commentator as voice. They should not be collapsed into one gloss.

Keep candidate identity or narrative-variant links in an evidence pack rather than declaring that the parallels provide no identity evidence.

Rav is named nine times: twice in each of the two "Rav disagrees" sentences, and once each in the baraita challenge, "what does Rav do with it", the salt case, "Rav's view is reversed" and "what Rav practised". findings.claim: The baraita quoted against Rav gives four separate acquisition conditions for movables, by location. (1) In a public domain, or a courtyard belonging to neither party, movables are acquired by drawing (משיכה). (2) In the buyer's domain, the buyer acquires once the other party "accepted" the deal. (3) In the seller's domain, the buyer does not acquire until he lifts the goods, or draws them and removes everything from the owner's domain. (4) In the domain of a person holding the goods on deposit, the buyer does not acquire until that person transfers title to him, or rents him the goods' place.

findings.claim: Commentators explain the baraita's challenge to Rav in two ways. Penei Moshe argues a fortiori: a buyer does not acquire without lifting or removing the goods, so a gift recipient surely does not acquire by words alone. Why, then, does Rav say he never retracts? Sirilio argues that if Rav held a biblical prohibition on retracting, the baraita could not say "he has not acquired" in the seller's domain.

findings.claim: The answer "what does Rav do with it? Here when he stood him with him, there when he did not" is the anonymous Talmud reconstructing Rav's position. It is not something Rav is reported to say. Who "stood" whom is not stated, and commentators differ. Penei Moshe: in the baraita the seller did not have the buyer standing with him where the goods lay, while in Rav's case the giver had the recipient with him and showed him the gift. Sirilio: in Rav's case the seller stood the buyer with him to see the merchandise. The GRA's reading is "in the presence of both". Schwab: the promise was made formally, before the household.
