R. Jacob bar Zabdi ou R. Abahou dit au nom de R. Yohanan
Rebbi Jacob bar Zavdi, Rebbi Abbahu in the name of Rebbi Joḥanan

findings.reasoning: Only the Abbahu-to-Yohanan link carries an explicit "בשם" (in the name of). The unconnected juxtapositions can be read as a sequence (X from Y), as parallel tradents, or (following Schwab) as alternatives. Guggenheimer keeps a neutral comma. The Gittin "and" is one printed wording. Penei Moshe on Maaser Sheni shortens the chain to "R. Yose in the name of R. Yohanan", which is an interpretive summary, not a text.
findings.graph_effect: Keep "Abbahu reports in the name of Yohanan" as explicit. Keep the Yaakov bar Zavdi links (c11/c12) as alternative branches, and add a third branch: alternative attribution, following Schwab. Record the R. Yose-headed chain as a reading in other passages (MS 4:4, Shevuot 4:7, Gittin 6:1), not in Sheviit. No teacher-student relation is established.

findings.claim: The dialogue about "a just yes" also differs across parallels. In Sheviit, R. Yose "stood with" R. Yaakov bar Zavdi and objects, and the answer is introduced by a bare "he said". Maaser Sheni introduces the answer with a plural "they said". Gittin (Venice) has "he said to him". Guggenheimer says that in Gittin R. Yaakov bar Zavdi answers R. Yose. In Shevuot, R. Yaakov bar Zavdi is the one who asks, before R. Abbahu. Bava Metzia 4:2 in the Venice print has no question at all. Guggenheimer supplies a question from the Escorial manuscript in which R. Yaakov bar Zavdi asks R. Abbahu.

evidence.exact_quote: קָם רִבִּי יוֹסֵי עִם רִבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר זַבְדִּי אָמַר לֵיהּ הָהֵן לָאו צֶדֶק וְהִין צֶדֶק אָמַר בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר הִין שֶׁל צֶדֶק הָיָה
קם רבי יוסי עם רבי יעקב בר זבדי אמר ליה והינו הין צדק אמרין בשעה שאמר הין צדק הוה
קם רבי יוסי עם רבי יעקב בר זבדי אמר ליה והן הוא הין צדק אמר ליה בשעה שאמרו הין צדק היה
Rebbi Yose stood near Rebbi Jacob bar Zavdi and said to him
In the Giṭṭin text, it is R. Jacob bar Zavdi who gives the answer to R. Yose
רבי יעקב בר זבדי בעא קומי ר' אבהו ואהן הין לא בצדק הוא והין צדק אמר בשעה שאמ' הין של צדק הוה
חוזר אמ' בשעה שאמר צריך לומר בדעת גמורה
Text added from E. Since the answer is given in L, the question must have been in the original text.

findings.reasoning: The Sheviit answer has no named speaker. The nearest addressee of R. Yose's objection is R. Yaakov bar Zavdi, and the Gittin wording "אמר ליה" and Schwab's "répondit-il" point the same way. The Maaser Sheni "אמרין" instead makes the answer anonymous and plural. In Shevuot and Bava Metzia (Escorial), the questioner is R. Yaakov bar Zavdi and the implied answerer is R. Abbahu. The same exchange has different directions in different passages. The Guggenheimer Bava Metzia bracket is an editorial insertion from one manuscript (E), so it is a different kind of evidence from a printed reading.
findings.graph_effect: For Sheviit: Yose objects to Yaakov bar Zavdi (explicit). The answer is by Yaakov bar Zavdi (local coreference, medium), with an alternative branch of an anonymous or plural answer. Do not import "Yaakov bar Zavdi asks Abbahu" into Sheviit. Record it as the Shevuot and Bava Metzia (Escorial) reading.

findings.claim: Two textual interventions on the Sheviit dialogue exist, and they are later proposals, not variants. Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael emends "אמר ליה ההן" to "והיינו", matching Maaser Sheni. In the Beur HaGra (manuscript A of the commentary), R. Yaakov bar Zavdi himself states the "just hin" teaching, with "יהיה" ("should be") where the text has "היה" ("was").

evidence.exact_quote: א"ל ההן לאו צדק והין צדק. — צ"ל: והיינו
כתב יד א ר' יעקב בר זבדי אמר הין צדק יהיה לך שיהא הן שלך צדק ולאו שלך צדק בשעה שאומר הן של צדק יהיה

findings.reasoning: צ"ל ("one must read") marks an emendation. The GRA line may be a reconstruction or a paraphrase. It is not labelled "ה"ג" as other GRA entries are. It is saved as a proposed reading and is not treated as a manuscript witness.
findings.graph_effect: Record the GRA reading as a later proposal in which Yaakov bar Zavdi is the speaker of the hin teaching. Do not use it to settle F14.

findings.claim: Other passages tell a similar deposit-and-price-rise case with different named people. Bavli Bava Metzia 48b: buyers gave Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef money for salt, and he came before Rabbi Yohanan. Bavli Bava Metzia 49a: buyers gave Rav Kahana money for flax, and he came before Rav, who told him to deliver for what he received, since the rest was "words". JT Bava Metzia 4:2: Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef paid for salt, and a silk case came before Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef and Rabbi Yohanan.

evidence.exact_quote: דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף יְהַבוּ לֵיהּ זוּזֵי אַמִּלְחָא. לְסוֹף אִיַּיקַּר מִלְחָא. אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
רַב כָּהֲנָא יְהַבוּ לֵיהּ זוּזֵי אַכִּיתָּנָא, לְסוֹף אִיַּיקַּר כִּיתָּנָא. אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב
רבי חייה בר יוסף יהב דינר למלחא חזר ביה ההוא
In the Babli, Baba Meẓi‘a 48b, the story is told of R. Ḥiyya bar Josef, who appeared before R. Joḥanan.

findings.reasoning: These are similar cases in different passages, with different named participants and judges. A shared plot does not make the Sheviit "one person" identical to any named figure.
findings.graph_effect: Keep salt_client as an unnamed local person. Store the parallels as possible story parallels, not as identity links.

findings.claim: The Bava Metzia 4:2 parallel has a different version of Rav's practice, with a condition that Sheviit lacks. Rav instructed his attendant (שמשיה): if the recipient is poor, give at once; if rich, consult him again. Guggenheimer notes this contradicts Sheviit. The preceding line ("this applies to a poor ... but with a rich one it becomes a vow") is emended by Mareh HaPanim to reverse "poor" and "rich".

evidence.exact_quote: הדא דתימר בעני אבל בעשיר נעשה נדר רב מפקד לשמשיה אימת דנימר לך תתן מתנה לבר נש אין הוה מסכן הב ליה מיד ואין עתיר אימליך בי תניינות
This contradicts the statement in Ševi‘t 10:9 that Rav never changed his mind once he had promised a gift.
ויש לגרוס כאן הדא דתימר בעשיר אבל בעני נעשה נדר
רב. היה מצוה למשרתו כשאומר לך תן מתנה לעני תתן לו מיד ולא תשאל אותי עוד לפי שאיני יכול לחזור בו ואם הוא עשיר המלך בי שנית

findings.reasoning: Own translation of Bava Metzia: "Rav used to command his attendant: whenever I tell you, give a gift to someone, if he is poor, give it to him at once; if he is rich, consult me a second time." The addressee (attendant vs household) and the condition (poor vs rich) differ from Sheviit. Guggenheimer's "10:9" is his halakhah numbering, which corresponds to Sefaria's Sheviit 10:4 here.
findings.graph_effect: Record a separate version of Rav's practice in another passage, with an attendant addressee and a poor/rich condition. Do not merge the attendant with the Sheviit household. Keep the two versions as conflicting reports of Rav's practice.

findings.claim: The Bavli reverses the positions. There Rav holds that words have no aspect of breach of faith, and Rabbi Yohanan holds that they do. In the Yerushalmi it is Rav whose own practice is not to retract. Sirilio explicitly notes the reversal.

evidence.exact_quote: דְּבָרִים, רַב אָמַר: אֵין בָּהֶן מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה, וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: יֵשׁ בָּהֶם מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה
ובגמ' דילן פ' הזהב איפכא גרסינן דרב סבר דברים אין בהן משום מחוסרי אמנה ור' יוחנן אמר דברים יש בהן משום מחוסרי אמנה
הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ מַתָּנָה אֲנִי נוֹתֵן לָךְ – יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ

findings.reasoning: The two Talmuds attribute the stricter and more lenient positions differently. This is a difference in textual attribution. It does not show what either sage historically held.
findings.graph_effect: Store the Bavli positions as views attributed in another passage. Do not use them to overwrite the Sheviit reading.

findings.claim: The wider context: the halakhah comments on the Mishnah's last clause, "all movables are acquired by drawing, and whoever keeps his word, the Sages are pleased with him". Segment 10:4:6 is the last segment of the tractate: the Venice print closes the chapter and tractate after it.

evidence.exact_quote: כָּל הַמִּטַּלְטְלִין נִקְנִין בִּמְשִׁיכָה וְכָל הַמְקַיֵים אֶת דְּבָרָיו רוּחַ חֲכָמִים נוֹחָה הִימֶּינּוּ

findings.reasoning: No later Sheviit context exists to check. Context for the people comes from the parallels, not from following segments.
findings.graph_effect: The episode can be closed at 10:4:6. Context needed beyond the supplied segments is limited to the Mishnah (10:4:1) and the parallels.

findings.claim: In 10:4:5, the ring rule is carried by "R. Zeira, R. Abbahu in the name of R. Yohanan". The Bava Metzia 4:2 parallel attributes a similar ring statement to "R. Yaakov bar Idi, R. Abbahu in the name of R. Yohanan". Schwab again translates the Sheviit names as alternatives ("R. Zeira ou R. Abahou").

findings.graph_effect: Keep Zeira's links (c5/c6) as branches. Add a Schwab alternative branch. Record the Yaakov bar Idi chain as a reading in another passage.

findings.claim: Two small legal-wording points in 10:4:4 affect the condition in Rabbi Yohanan's teaching on verbal dealings. The Venice print reads "ומניין" where Guggenheimer, following manuscripts, reads "זמניין". Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael and the GRA would drop "אלא" ("only") from "one hands him over only to מי שפרע". Guggenheimer calls "only" a scribal error.

evidence.exact_quote: הנושא והנותן בדברים ומניין דאת אמר
צ"ל: אין מוסרין אותו למי שפרע
כתב יד א ה"ג מוסרים אותו למי שפרע
“Only” must be a scribal error since the curse by the court is more of a punishment than the displeasure of the Sages.

findings.reasoning: These are emendations and variants in a context segment. They are recorded because the question asks for missing legal conditions.
findings.graph_effect: None for people. Attach the wording variants to verbal_rule.

findings.claim: The translations differ materially on the salt case. Schwab renders "deposited earnest on salt" as "confier du sel en gage" (entrusting salt as a pledge). He renders "hand him over to מי שפרע" as "le livrer à qui l'a payé" (deliver it to the one who paid), not as the imprecation formula. Guggenheimer translates the formula as "Him who made pay".

evidence.exact_quote: il arriva à quelqu’un de confier du sel en gage à son prochain
ou l’on devra remettre à l’acquéreur toute la valeur du gage, ou le livrer à qui l’a payé
or he should be given up to “Him who made pay”

findings.reasoning: The two translations understand the ruling differently. The commentaries consulted (Penei Moshe, GRA) read מי שפרע as the imprecation formula. This supports Guggenheimer's reading here, but the disagreement is kept.
findings.graph_effect: None for the people. The ruling's content should follow the commentary reading, with Schwab's reading recorded as an alternative translation.

unresolved: Whether the Sheviit juxtaposition "R. Yaakov bar Zavdi, R. Abbahu" is sequential or parallel. The text gives no connector, and the parallels vary.

Whether the Sheviit answer to R. Yose is by R. Yaakov bar Zavdi or anonymous. The Sheviit text has only "אמר". No Sheviit manuscript was checked directly. The manuscript notes consulted are Guggenheimer's (Rome, Leiden, Escorial) and the GRA's.
Who "stood whom with him" (הֶעֱמִידוֹ עִמּוֹ): giver and recipient, or seller and buyer. The commentators differ.
Who came before Rav in the salt case: the depositor, as subject continuity suggests, or the seller. The Mechon-Mamre wording "אתא לגביה רב" was not traced to a manuscript.
Whether the Beur HaGra line giving R. Yaakov bar Zavdi the "just hin" teaching reflects a manuscript reading or the commentator's own reconstruction.

The identity of "R. Yose" here, compared with the "R. Yose" heading the chain in Maaser Sheni and Shevuot, and whether "Rav" is Rav (Abba Arikha). Both are historical identity questions and were not decided.

The commentaries checked were Penei Moshe, Sirilio, Beur HaGra, Mareh HaPanim and Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael on Sheviit, plus some commentary on the parallels. A Sefaria request for Korban HaEdah on Sheviit 10:4 and on Bava Metzia 4:2 returned 404. That shows only that the request failed, not that no commentary exists. Ridbaz (Chiddushei Ridbaz) was read only on Bava Metzia 4:2. Commentaries listed in the Sefaria link index but not fetched include Mishnat Eretz Yisrael, Noam Yerushalmi, Maharsham and Haamek Sheilah.

lessons: A dictum quoted several times in one argument (here Rav's household saying, three times) needs one statement node with several citation mentions. Each re-quotation is not a new observation.
Answers introduced by "what does X do with it?" (מה עבד לה X) are reconstructions the anonymous voice makes on X's behalf. The graph needs a voice type distinct from "X said".
Deictic references (תמן/כא, "there/here") can switch referent between question and answer. Store the resolved referent for each occurrence, not for each word.
Buyer, seller, owner and depositary in a baraita are hypothetical legal roles. They carry conditions, but are not people.
Implied counterparties (the salt seller) need a placeholder with basis "implied by the ruling". Otherwise the ruling has no object.
Parallel passages can reverse the direction of a dialogue (who asks whom) and add a head to a chain. Keep each passage's version as its own reading. Import nothing into the focal passage.
Translating juxtaposed names as "or" (Schwab) is an interpretive choice. It creates an alternative-attribution branch, not evidence that two people disagreed.

A final qualification that moves a view from law to piety changes the modality of an earlier disagreement. The claim "X disagrees with Y" should carry a discourse status such as "proposed, later narrowed".
Guggenheimer's Hebrew text and English translation are one editorial work, as are his manuscript insertions. They are not independent witnesses. Schwab is a separate translation.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications and quoted evidence. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

A difference involving whether someone stood with another can change the condition, even when described as minor wording. Retain the complete clauses and the edition-specific pairing of here and there before comparing the legal result.

findings.reason: Keep each step of the argument. The final distinction between law and personal piety may narrow a proposed disagreement. It does not delete the earlier textual claim.
A named speaker in one parallel cannot silently fill an anonymous speaker in another. Save competing local readings and compare them in a separate pack.

Compare like with like: law, personal practice and the stage of the argument may differ. Save the commentator’s reported reversal and each full source claim; do not treat the short reversal label as a settled historical contradiction.

cases.question: The actual one-versus-two peah rules were lost. Recover each rule, condition, negation, named opinion, challenge and reply. Distinguish legal scenario roles from historical people.

findings.claim: The Mishnah (3:3:1 in Sefaria's layout; Mishnah Peah 3:4) opens with an UNATTRIBUTED ruling that mother onions are liable for peah. Rabbi Yose disagrees and exempts them. The liable voice is the anonymous first voice of the Mishnah. The text does not call it 'the Sages' here.

evidence.exact_quote: האמהות של בצלים חייבות בפיאה ר' יוסי פוטר
הָאִמָּהוֹת שֶׁל בְּצָלִים חַיָּבוֹת בְּפֵאָה, וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי פּוֹטֵר
are subject to peah, Rebbi Yose frees.
וטעמ' דת"ק דמחייב

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'Mother onions are liable for peah; Rabbi Yose exempts.' Two rulings with opposite polarity. Penei Moshe names the liable voice ת"ק (the first, anonymous tanna). The earlier reading kept only Rabbi Yose's exemption.
findings.graph_effect: Add a statement 'mother onions are liable' held by an unnamed Mishnah voice, not the group חכמים. Rabbi Yose opposes it and holds 'exempt'. His exemption is a response, not a standalone rule.

findings.claim: The one-versus-many peah rule for onion beds: Rabbi Yose says peah must be given from each bed separately. The Sages say one peah, taken from one bed, covers all of them.

evidence.exact_quote: מלבנות הבצלי' שבין הירק ר' יוסי אומר פיאה מכל אחד ואחד וחכמים אומרים מאחד על הכל
Rectangles of onions among vegetables, Rebbi Yose says peah from each single one, but the Sages say from one for everything
וְכֵן מַלְבְּנוֹת הַבְּצָלִים שֶׁבֵּין הַיָּרָק נוֹתֵן פֵּאָה אַחַת לְכָל הַבְּצָלִים
וְאֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'Onion beds among vegetables: Rabbi Yose says peah from each and every one; the Sages say from one for all.' Condition: onion beds separated by vegetables. Count: Rabbi Yose, one peah per bed; the Sages, one peah in total. Maimonides codifies one peah for all. Bartenura says the law does not follow Rabbi Yose. Those are later rulings, not part of the Talmud text.
findings.graph_effect: Replace the vague labels 'separate' and 'together' with rule statements that carry a condition and a count. Rabbi Yose holds 'one peah per bed', the Sages hold 'one peah for all beds', with an opposes edge between them. The later codifications are rulings about the dispute, not new speakers inside the passage.

findings.claim: The chapter's first halakhah states Rabbi Yose's reason for separate peot. People do not usually plant onions among vegetables, so the vegetables divide the onion beds. The Talmud compares this with the House of Shammai. This reason comes from the wider chapter, not from 3:3:3.

evidence.exact_quote: כמה דר' יוסי אמר אין דרך בני אדם להיות מכניסין בצלי' בין הירק
Just as Rebbi Yose said that people do not usually introduce onions between vegetables
מפ' טעמא בריש פירקין משום דאין דרך בני אדם להכניס בין הירק בצלים ומשום הכי מפסיקי

findings.reasoning: My translation of the Venice line: 'just as Rabbi Yose said, people do not usually bring onions among vegetables.' Sirilio and Penei Moshe point readers back to this passage for the reason.
findings.graph_effect: Add a 'reason for' link from this statement to Rabbi Yose's separate-peah view. It is evidence from 3:1:4 and should be scoped to that segment. The anonymous Talmud voice reports the reason in Rabbi Yose's name. This is not a new speech act at 3:3.

findings.claim: Rav and Shmuel each give a word for 'mother onions': Rav says פורגרה and Shmuel says צומחתה. The spelling varies by edition. Commentators disagree on whether the two glosses really conflict.

evidence.exact_quote: רב אמר פורגרה ושמואל אמר צומחתה
רב אמר פורגדה ושמואל אמר צומחתה
והיינו הך ולא פליגי אלא בלישנא בעלמא
פודגרא. יש גורסין כן וכן גריס ר"י מסיפונטי ז"ל
ובהנהו מחייבי רבנן דבמאי דקאמר רב אפילו רבנן מודו
a sprouting bulb, seed-onion

findings.reasoning: Venice and the Guggenheimer Hebrew read פורגרה. Mechon-Mamre reads פורגדה. Sirilio reports the reading פודגרא from R. Yitzhak of Siponto. Penei Moshe and Ohr LaYesharim say the two names refer to the same thing. Sirilio treats them as different objects and says the Sages agree with Rav's case.
findings.graph_effect: Save two separate 'defines term' statements, one each for Rav and Shmuel. An 'opposes' edge between them is a commentary interpretation (Sirilio), not the text; Penei Moshe denies it. Keep the spelling variants as branches of the term, not as different speakers.

findings.claim: Rabbi Yaakov bar Bun, in the name of Rabbi Hanina, says Rabbi Yose exempted the mother onions only because they are ownerless (hefker). This explains Rabbi Yose's view and is transmitted by one named person from another.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי יעקב בר בון בשם רבי חנינא לא אמר רבי יוסי אלא משום הבקר
in the name of Rebbi Ḥanina: Rebbi Yose said only because of ownerless property
לא א"ר יוסי. לפוטרן אלא משום הפקר דהואיל ועושין כן במיעוט מהבצלים אינו מקפיד עליהן ומפקירן

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'Rabbi Yose said [it] only because of ownerlessness.' The transmission formula is בשם. It shows attribution, not that the two met. Beur HaGra reports a reading 'לא אמרו' (they said) instead of 'לא אמר רבי יוסי' (see F13).
findings.graph_effect: Keep c9 (Yaakov bar Bun reports in the name of Hanina) and c10 (Hanina explains Rabbi Yose's exemption, with ownerlessness as the content). Do not infer teacher and student from בשם alone.

findings.claim: Rabbi Bun bar Hiyya asks before Rabbi Mana: 'Is ownerless property liable for peah?' The commentators read this as a rhetorical objection. If the mother onions are ownerless, how could the first tanna make them liable?

evidence.exact_quote: רבי בון בר חייא בעי קומי רבי מנא והבקר חייב בפיאה
והבקר חייב בפאה. בתמיה ולטעמיה דר' יעקב אליבא דר' יוסי פריך דא"ה מ"ט דת"ק דמחייב וכי הפקר חייב בפאה
והפקר חייב בפאה. בתמיה כלומר ומ"ט דת"ק
הרי הפקר פטור מפאה לדעת הכול

findings.graph_effect: Speech edge: Bun bar Hiyya asks, with Rabbi Mana (as printed) as addressee. Add a discourse function 'challenge' aimed at the F5 statement, marked as commentary interpretation. For the addressee's identity see F11.

אָמַר לָהֶן בְּזָכָה בָהֶן אַחַת אַחַת
א"ל בזכה בהן אחת אחת

Ohr LaYesharim says so explicitly. The Rome reading reaches us only through Ohr LaYesharim; I did not see the manuscript. Mechon-Mamre's א"ל abbreviation is singular.

Merge the duplicate mentions m14 and m15 into one mention with several candidate referents.

findings.claim: Commentators disagree about the case in 'he acquired them one at a time'. Both the owner who acquires the onions and the process are legal scenario roles, not people in history.

evidence.exact_quote: הכא במאי עסקינן בזכה בהן אחת אחת אחר ששתלן וגלי דעתיה דלא הפקירן
דחוזר וזוכה בהן אחר התלישה רבנן סברי לא הפקירן מעולם וחייבות ור' יוסי סבר נמלך הוא וכבר נפטרו
If the owner reasserted his right to these onions after they sprouted new growth they are not abandoned property.
שלדעת התנא החלוק על רבי יוסי הן חייבות בפאה כיוון שחזר וזכה בהן, ולדעת רבי יוסי הן פטורות מפאה כיוון שלא חזר וזכה בכולן יחד
דזכה מעט מעט דהיא פי' אחת אחת והשאר הוי הפקר עדיין

findings.reasoning: Penei Moshe: after planting, he took them one by one, which shows he never abandoned them. Sirilio: he reclaims them after pulling. The Sages hold he never abandoned them; Rabbi Yose holds he changed his mind after they were already exempt. Guggenheimer: he reasserted ownership after regrowth. Ohr LaYesharim: he reclaimed them bit by bit after abandoning them. The Ridbaz, reading the Gra: he took a little and the rest stays ownerless, so he holds only a small amount.
findings.graph_effect: Save the reply content as one statement, with an interpretation branch for each commentator. The 'he' who acquires is a generic owner role. Do not create a person node for him.

findings.claim: The Talmud then cites a baraita (והתני): 'although they do not endure for him in a large quantity, they endure in a small one.' It concludes that the only reason is bringing the onions in for storage. On the reading most commentators give, this moves the dispute away from ownerlessness to whether a small amount stored counts as storage.

evidence.exact_quote: והתני אף על פי שאינן מתקיימות לו במרובה מתקיימות בממועט הוי לית טעמא דלא משום מכניסו לקייום
והתני אע"פ שאין מתקיימות לו במרובה מתקיימות לו במועט הוי לית טעמא דלא משום מכניסו לקיום
והתני. בברייתא אע"פ וכו' דברי חכמים הן שהשיבו לר' יוסי
ואין הטעם משום הפקר
The difference between Rebbi Yose and the Sages is a difference of opinion on matters of agricultural practice rather than on the theory of abandoned property.

findings.reasoning: My translation: 'But it was taught: although they do not keep for him in a large [harvest], they keep in a small one. So the reason is only that he brings it in for storage.' No named tanna speaks the baraita. Penei Moshe says its words are the Sages' reply to Rabbi Yose. Guggenheimer's note 76 says 'the reason' is the Sages' reason. Ohr LaYesharim calls it a challenge that rejects the ownerlessness explanation. Mechon-Mamre adds לו and reads במועט; Beur HaGra reads אלא for דלא (see F13).
findings.graph_effect: The unnamed argument voice cites a baraita from an unnamed tanna. The content 'storage of a small quantity makes them liable' is attributed, by commentary, to the Sages or first tanna answering Rabbi Yose. The anonymous Talmud voice concludes that the reason is storage. Retarget c14: the anonymous voice challenges the ownerlessness explanation (F5), not Rabbi Yose himself. See F10 for the dissent.

findings.claim: Commentators disagree on whether the baraita overturns or supports the ownerlessness explanation. Penei Moshe and Ohr LaYesharim read it as overturning. The Ridbaz, reading the Gra's Shenot Eliyahu, calls it 'support' and ties the dispute to Rabbi Yose's view on ownerlessness in Nedarim. Tosafot HaRid rejects another commentator's reading of the Gra.

evidence.exact_quote: וכתב בשנו"א ז"ל והא תניא סיוע הוי דלית טעמא אלא משום מכניסו לקיום
דאזיל לטעמי' במס' נדרים (מ"ד) דס"ל דאין הפקר יוצא מת"י הבעלים אלא בזכי'
ודבריו נפלאו האיך מפרש סיוע למי הוי סיוע
הכי מקשי רבנן לר' יוסי אלמא דטעמא דפליגי אי הוי לקיום מה שמתקיימין לו במיעוט או לא
Rabbi Yosei, who holds that rendering property ownerless is complete only when one takes possession of that property

findings.reasoning: In Beur HaGra the Sages challenge Rabbi Yose (מקשי רבנן לר' יוסי), and the dispute turns on whether storing a little counts as storage. The Ridbaz reads the Gra's Shenot Eliyahu as calling the baraita a 'support'. Tosafot HaRid disputes how Maayanei Yehoshua read the Gra. The Nedarim link is a commentator's cross-reference about a Rabbi Yose in another tractate. Treating him as the same Rabbi Yose is the commentators' assumption, and I have not checked it independently.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the discourse function of והתני as a branch: 'challenge to the ownerlessness explanation' (Penei Moshe, Ohr LaYesharim, Guggenheimer) or 'support' (the Ridbaz reading the Gra). No person edges change. Do not settle it.

findings.claim: The addressee 'Rabbi Mana' is printed in Venice, Guggenheimer and Mechon-Mamre. Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael proposes emending it to Rabbi Ami. The ground is chronology, not a manuscript: Rabbi Bun bar Hiyya died while Rabbi Zeira was alive, so he could not have asked the younger Rabbi Mana. Ohr LaYesharim keeps 'Mana' and identifies him as an earlier Mana.

evidence.exact_quote: ר' בון בר חייא בעי קומי ר' מנא. — ע' מ"ש בברכות רפ"ח (לעיל עמ' 18) שיש להגיה כאן: בעי קומי ר' אמי.
ועוד בפיאה פ"ג ה"ד [י"ז ע"ג] ר' בון בר חייא בעי קומי ר' מנא, ולעיל פ"ב ה"ח [ה' רע"ג] מפורש שרבב"ח נפטר בחיי ר' זעירא ור' זעירא הספידו וא"א שישאל מר' מנא הצעיר
כד דמך רבי בון בר רבי חייא על רבי זעירא ואפטר עילוי
שאל לפני רבי מנא (הראשון, אמורא ארץ ישראלי בדור הראשון)
בעא קומי רבי זעירא

findings.reasoning: This is a later proposed emendation based on historical inference. It is not a textual witness. The Berakhot eulogy names 'רבי בון בר רבי חייא' (with a second רבי). That it is the same person as our 'רבי בון בר חייא' is the emender's assumption. In the first 60 Yerushalmi search hits, R. Bun bar Hiyya often 'asks before' Rabbi Zeira. Peah 3:3:3 is the only hit where he asks before Rabbi Mana. This is a usage pattern, not proof.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the addressee node as 'Rabbi Mana (as printed at Peah 3:3:3)'. Add an emendation branch 'Rabbi Ami (proposed, Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael)' as a separate evidence type. Do not merge this Mana with the Mana son of R. Yonah or with a 'Mana I' without a separate identity decision.

findings.claim: Both patronymics give local parent placeholders: Yaakov's father Bun, and Bun's father Hiyya. Neither parent acts in the passage. Nothing in the passage identifies Yaakov's father Bun with Rabbi Bun bar Hiyya. The Guggenheimer translation spells both as 'Abun'.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי יעקב בר בון
רבי בון בר חייא
Rebbi Jacob bar Abun
Rebbi Abun bar Ḥiyya
A third generation Amora, student of R. Yose ben R. Ḥanina.

findings.reasoning: בר is read literally as 'son of'. I found no sign here that it is a title. The generation labels and identifications (Hanina = bar Hama; Yaakov bar Bun as student of R. Yose b. R. Hanina) are historical inferences by the translator and by Ohr LaYesharim, not claims of this text.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 and c2 (child of) with local father placeholders. Keep the two Bun nodes separate. Store the commentators' identifications and generations as proposals attributed to them, not accepted.

findings.claim: Beur HaGra proposes readings for 3:3:3. His first version reads 'they said [it] only because of ownerlessness'. It also emends 'the reason is only' from דלא to אלא.

evidence.exact_quote: כתב יד א ה"ג לא אמרו אלא משום הפקר

findings.claim: The halakhah's rule on partners (Sefaria 3:4:2). If partners harvested half a field jointly and then divided, 'he does not separate from his own, neither at the start nor at the end'. The second clause covers partners who joined again. In Venice it is NEGATED ('אינו מפריש'). The Guggenheimer Hebrew and Mechon-Mamre read it positively, and the Rome manuscript is reported to lack 'אינו'. Penei Moshe and Mareh HaPanim correct it; Maimonides codifies the positive rule.

findings.reasoning: Literal Venice: 'he does NOT separate from the end-portion for his fellow's end-portion, but not from his start-portion for his fellow's start-portion.' 'But not' after a negative is incoherent, which signals a textual problem. Penei Moshe adds אלא ('only'), and Mareh HaPanim says the result is the same. Guggenheimer Hebrew, Mechon-Mamre and the Rome MS (as reported) read the verb positively. The resulting rule: once they are partners again, one may give from one's own last-harvested portion for the partner's last-harvested portion, but not from a first-harvested portion for the partner's first-harvested portion. The editions and translations are not independent: each works from the Venice print and a few manuscripts.

lessons: Legal rules need a statement type with condition, action and count (for example 'divided brothers → two peot'). Generic 'event' or 'participates_in' records drop the actual rule.
Polarity can flip between editions (אינו מפריש versus מפריש). Polarity must be storable per reading branch, and an emendation must be a different evidence type from a variant reading.
An anonymous first Mishnah voice (תנא קמא) is not the same node as the named group חכמים, even when they end up on the same side.
A question used as a rhetorical objection (בתמיה) needs a discourse function (challenge) and a target statement. The target is often an explanation, not a person.
A name change made on chronological grounds (Mana→Ami) is a proposal that already assumes a historical identity. It should stay a branch until a separate identity decision is made.
Singular or plural addressee variants (להן / ליה) change the speech graph. Addressees need branch support.
Kinship inside a legal example (brothers dividing an inheritance) is scenario-internal and hypothetical. It is not a family relation between historical people.
Commentators' generation labels and identifications (bar Hama, ben Halafta, 'Mana I') are historical inferences and should be stored with who proposed them.

Editions that all derive from the Venice print with limited manuscript input are not independent witnesses. Agreement among Guggenheimer, Mechon-Mamre and the commentators' emendations is agreement among editors.

findings.reasoning: For linking them: the two sentences are adjacent, and 'recite in your teaching' suits a professional reciter, which is what Tsaydaniya does in 11:7:3. Against linking: the epithet is dropped; the Yevamot parallel spells the name יוסה, not יוסי; and in JT Shabbat 9:3:4 an unqualified R. Yose(h) receives the identical instruction 'recite in your Mishnah' from R. Zeira, so the phrase does not mark a professional reciter. None of the commentaries I read (Penei Moshe, Korban HaEdah, Sheyarei Korban, Noam Yerushalmi, Mareh HaPanim, Amudei Yerushalayim) and neither of Guggenheimer's translations identifies the two. Guggenheimer names them differently. The different spelling in Yevamot is suggestive, but I did not verify any spelling convention in this edition, so it proves nothing.

findings.claim: A competing reading takes Mana's answer as a statement: she eats, but her slaves (the melog slaves she brought into the marriage) do not. This is how Maimonides rules. Commentators tie that ruling to this Yerushalmi, and Guggenheimer's translation follows it.

Maaseh Rokeach and Yad Eitan split the slaves into two kinds: the husband-owned (tzon barzel) slaves obviously eat, and only her own melog slaves do not. That split is their reading; Mana's words do not make it. Guggenheimer's translation is declarative, and the accompanying note explains it by Maimonides and Radbaz.

lessons: A title embedded in an address formula ('X רבי אמר לי' = 'my teacher X said to me') is a first-person relationship claim. It should be recorded as explicit, with the variant witnesses that carry or lack the word attached to the edge.
'תני X קומי Y ופליג על Y' records that X recites a baraita before Y and the baraita contradicts Y. Model it as recites_before(X, Y) plus contradicts(baraita, Y's view), not as a personal dispute.
Restrictive rules (אין ... אלא) need a polarity or scope field. Otherwise a label silently turns 'only in these cases' into 'in these cases'.

The anonymous talmudic voice (והא תנינן / ומשני) needs its own node type, distinct from 'group of people'. Its challenge and answer steps should be claims, so that the argument around a named sage's rule is not flattened.
Rhetorical versus declarative readings (בתמיה / בניחותא) can reverse the legal content without changing the speech-act edges. Store them as branches on the content, with who-holds-what.
Commentary emendations (ה"ג, צ"ל) are a different evidence type from print or manuscript variants. A translation that silently follows an emendation should be tagged as such.
A parallel sugya (here JT Yevamot 9:4, Gittin 9:9) is a separate textual witness, but its translation by the same editor, reused for the focal passage, is not independent corroboration.
A variant name for the same speaking slot (Reuven / Abun) is one asks-edge with alternative subjects, not two edges.
An editor's cross-corpus identification (Yose Tsaydaniya = Rav Yosef Tsidoni) is a historical-identity proposal and must stay separate from local coreference.

findings.claim: Return rules in the baraita. One should not accept deposits from women, slaves or minors. If one did: from a woman, return it to her, or to her husband if she died. From a slave, return it to him, or to his master if he died. From a minor, return it to him, or to his father if he died, and invest it safely ('סגולה'). All of these are hypothetical roles. The person who accepted the deposit is an unnamed generic bailee.

findings.claim: The Bavli (Bava Batra 52a) tells a parallel story that differs in actors and outcome. The husband is Rabbah bar bar Hana. The dying wife says the rings belong to 'Marta and the sons of [the] daughter'. The case comes 'before Rav'. Rav gives a conditional answer (if you trust her, do as she said; if not, disregard it), and there is a second version of his answer. Rashbam explains Marta as a sage, the brother of Rabbi Hiyya.

lessons: Repeated mishnah cases with the same frame ('Where is my deposit? ...') are separate hypothetical scenarios. Roles need a scenario scope so the keeper of case 1 is not the keeper of case 2.

A legal consequence depends on a condition: the claim made (lost or stolen) and how the lie comes out (witnesses or self-admission). The contract needs a conditional-consequence claim, not only person-to-person relations.
A halakhah heading ('איכן פקדוני ... כו'') cites a mishnah unit. It is not a new speech event.
A story introduced by 'כהדא' ('like this case') illustrates a rule. Its named actors do not fill the rule's generic roles (woman, husband, bailee, So-and-so) unless the text maps them.
A parallel story in another Talmud with different names, beneficiaries and ruling is a separate episode. It is not corroboration of each detail and not a basis for merging actors.
An uncertain lexical gloss can create people or events that are not there (for example, a betrothal and a groom). Object labels should stay neutral when glosses disagree.
A patronymic of the form 'bar bar X' encodes a grandparent. Two name forms for one story can yield incompatible kinship edges, which is another reason not to merge on name similarity.
A translator's historical note is an identity or biography proposal from that translator. Store it with its authority, separate from the text's own evidence.

review.scope: Separate review of selected graph implications. Source hashes and quotation matches checked separately. Not human adjudication or exhaustive historical verification.

findings.reason: The wife and her daughter each need a local person even though neither is named. Her marriage and her statement my daughter do not by themselves prove that the husband fathered the daughter. Keep the proposed pronoun resolution attributed.
A case coming before Rav records adjudication. It does not identify who travelled, who attended, or whether the wife was alive when it reached him.
Keep the disputed ring or other item and its interpretations. Do not turn a possible betrothal-gift meaning into a narrated betrothal event.

Different names and beneficiaries require separate passage records. They do not prove either separate historical events or a single event. Keep the shared-story and identity hypotheses, including the commentator’s proposed match, for a later evidence pack.

Keep the two hypothetical deposit cases and their people separate from the narrated household. The hypothetical family roles are relationships inside the legal scenarios, not additions to the historical person graph.

The short claim says three people, but the daughter is also a person mentioned in the account, and Hana is a patronymic parent. If three counts only active story participants, label that explicitly. Keep every supported referent even when absent from the action.

findings.reasoning: A shared name is not identity. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak is also often called just 'Rav Nachman'. Still, when a son reports in the name of someone with his father's name, the Talmud's name conventions favour reading them as one person. Otherwise the sentence would usually add a distinguishing patronymic, such as 'Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak'. This is an inference from how the texts write names, not a statement in the text.
findings.graph_effect: Keep RN_patronymic and RN_quoted as separate local mentions, linked by a same-person candidate edge with status 'plausible, commentary-supported, not explicit'. Do not assert that they are two different men either.

lessons: One sentence can carry a relation built into a name (child_of) and a speech relation (reports_in_name_of) that point to two mentions with the same name. The schema needs separate mention ids, not one name-pair label.
Same-name coreference inside one sentence is its own decision (same_person_candidate), separate from both the kinship edge and global identity.

Later works quoting the Talmud (Rif, Yam shel Shelomoh, Tosafot Rid) should be saved as citation-form evidence, not treated as Talmud textual variants. A shortened quotation is not a witness that a clause is missing.
Parallel versions of one story (Sotah 10a and Sanhedrin 48b) count as one cross-passage observation.
A bare name resolved from earlier in the discussion (50a:4 'מר זוטרא') should take the local full name, not the registry's most frequent holder of that name.

review.scope: I checked every dossier quote against the saved bytes in sources/ and read Gittin 49b:9-50a:12 (Aramaic and English), Rashi, Steinsaltz, Rif, Rosh via Yam shel Shelomoh, Ramban, Rashba, Meiri, Tosafot Rid, Maggid Mishneh, Seder HaDorot, the Sefaria topic records, the Hebrew Wikipedia extract and the seven Bavli parallels; I fetched nothing new and did not check manuscripts, Hyman, Albeck or the Tosafot passage on which Rav Nachman an unqualified name means.

findings.reason: The one-local-person conclusion holds, but the graph effect lists Mar Zutra mentions at 49b:12 and 49b:14-15 that do not exist in the Aramaic. Those lines are 'אָמַר רָבָא: תָּא שְׁמַע', 'אָמַר אַבָּיֵי, תָּא שְׁמַע' and 'אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן'. They argue about his view without naming him. The name 'Mar Zutra' there appears only in the Davidson English ('against the opinion of Mar Zutra'). The Aramaic mentions are 49b:9, 50a:4 and 50a:5. At 49b:12-15 his teaching is the target of the arguments, but he is not a mention, and the English wording should be recorded as editorial evidence.

The dossier cites 'תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּמָר זוּטְרָא תְּיוּבְתָּא' as 'the refutation of Mar Zutra' but leaves out who speaks. The argument is Ravina's ('אָמַר רָבִינָא: תָּא שְׁמַע מֵעִיקָּרָא דְּתַקַּנְתִּין'), and the verdict is the anonymous Talmud voice. Record Ravina as the speaker, with Mar Zutra's 49b:9 teaching as the target. Record the verdict as unattributed. None of this is contact between Ravina and Mar Zutra, and it sets no birth order.

The same-person candidate between P2 and P3 at medium confidence is sound. One piece of the reasoning is unsourced, though: 'Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak is also often called just Rav Nachman'. The only saved source on this (S39) says the opposite, that he is 'המוזכר בדרך כלל יחד עם שם אביו' (usually mentioned together with his father's name). S39 reports the bar-Yitzchak reading only second-hand, as Tosafot's report of Rashi's view. The 'naming convention' support listed on the proposed edge is the reader's own inference, not evidence. Label it that way, or drop it from the support list.

The dossier says the Wikipedia sons list ('בניו של רב נחמן - הון, מר זוטרא, רבה...') has no cited source. But S39 was fetched with explaintext=1, which strips footnotes, so the saved bytes cannot show whether a citation exists. Say 'citation status unknown from the saved extract'. The low confidence and the external_biography label stay. The list also names a 'מר הונא בר רב נחמן', which is relevant to the open sibling question but does not create a sibling edge.

F10 uses S28 'אמר ליה מר זוטרא בריה דרב נחמן לרבא' to place Mar Zutra with Rava. S09, Seder HaDorot, indexes the same page differently: 'אמר לרב הונא ברי' דרב נחמן בכורות (נ"ד ב')'. The saved Aramaic has 'מתקיף לה רב הונא בריה דרב נחמן' just before, so who is addressed there is uncertain across sources. Note this as a disagreement about the addressee in a parallel passage. F10 is already low confidence and adds no edge at Gittin 50a:5, so it changes only the supporting note.

'Medieval codifiers rule in favour of Rav Nachman/Abaye against Rava' is too broad. Tosafot Rid (S16) rules the other way: 'והלכתא כרבא דקי"ל כל אביי ורבא הלכה כרבא'. Ramban (S15) also suggests Rava may have argued only against Abaye's proof: 'ולדחויי תדע דידיה ולאו למיפלג עליה דרב נחמן'. The local text supports Rava speaking to Abaye ('אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא'), with Abaye's proof as his target. In 50a:8 Rava goes on to argue against the ruling itself. Whether Rava disputes Rav Nachman's ruling, or only Abaye's proof, should stay a commentary question.

S01 50a:5 reads 'אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן, מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן'. This is one speaker with two separately written Rav Nachman mentions. The patronymic gives child_of P1->P2, and the father stays as a placeholder even though he does not act. משמיה gives reports_in_name_of P1->P3, with no meeting or teacher edge (F11). Splitting the single 'cites' label this way is correct. Ramban, Yam shel Shelomoh and Rashba are commentary on this passage, not extra text witnesses.

Yam shel Shelomoh introduces its 'רב נחמן ומר זוטרא בריה ואביי קיימי בחדא שיטתא' with 'וכתב הרא"ש מדברי הרי"ף'. The Rif line it reworks reads only 'כיון דאביי ורב נחמן קיימי בחדא שיטתא'. So 'בריה' is Yam shel Shelomoh's own wording, one later commentator's reading, and it rests on the same Rif-Rosh chain. Rif, Rosh and Yam shel Shelomoh therefore count as one line of transmission, not three votes. The dossier treats this correctly at medium confidence. Keep it as commentary support for the same-person candidate, not as text.

The ruling is a hypothetical legal case. Rashi glosses 'היוצא על היתומים - שלוה אביהם', so it involves a creditor, orphans and their dead father who took the loan. These are legal roles, not people, and must not become nodes. The orphans' 'father' in Rashi is especially easy to confuse with Mar Zutra's father P2. Add an explicit note to keep them out of the graph.

cases.question: Recover family relations, unnamed women, academic journeys, narrated chronology and the distinction between marriage mentioned by the passage and marriage inferred from other sources. Locate pronouns carefully.

findings.claim: Yehuda is literally the son of R. Hiyya. The patronymic בריה means 'his son'. Keep R. Hiyya as a local parent placeholder even though he does not act or speak in this segment.

evidence.exact_quote: יהודה בריה דרבי חייא חתניה דרבי ינאי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: יהודה בריה דר' חייא חתניה דר' ינאי
Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai

findings.reasoning: בריה is the ordinary Aramaic word for 'his son'. It is not a title here. The two Hebrew editions agree on the wording. The English is built on the same editorial work as the Davidson Aramaic, so it is not separate corroboration.
findings.graph_effect: Add child_of(P1 -> P2 'R. Hiyya', local). Evidence type: name-embedded kinship. Historical identity of P2 is decided separately (see F13).

findings.claim: Yehuda is R. Yannai's son-in-law. The marriage is stated by the passage through the kinship word חתניה, not narrated as an event. It implies an unnamed wife, a daughter of R. Yannai, who is never mentioned directly.

evidence.exact_quote: יהודה בריה דרבי חייא חתניה דרבי ינאי
ר' חייא, חתניה [חתנו] של ר' ינאי
יהודה בר חייה הוה יליף סליק ושאיל בשלמיה דרבי ינאי חמוה מערב שבת לערב שבת
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Yehuda bar Hiyya used to go up and greet Rabbi Yannai, his father-in-law, every Sabbath eve (translation_by_this_dossier)

findings.reasoning: חתן of a named man means the husband of his daughter. The Yerushalmi parallel uses the converse term חמוה ('his father-in-law'). That is a second compilation giving the same relation, but it tells the story differently (F8) and may come from a shared tradition. It is a parallel attestation, not proof of historical independence. Neither text names the daughter, says when they married or mentions children.
findings.graph_effect: Add one directed relation son_in_law_of(P1 -> P3). Displaying father_in_law_of(P3 -> P1) is the inverse, not a second observation. Add local P4 (unnamed daughter of P3, wife of P1) with child_of(P4 -> P3) and spouse(P1, P4), both marked 'implied by kinship term' rather than 'narrated marriage'.

findings.claim: The wife is also implied by 'his bed' and 'his conjugal time' (עונתו), which assume a wife waiting at home. The text does not say she is R. Yannai's daughter. That is the natural reading because R. Yannai watches for the homecoming, but it is inference.

evidence.exact_quote: כפו מטתו שאילמלי יהודה קיים לא ביטל עונתו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Overturn his bed, for if Yehuda were alive he would not have cancelled his conjugal time (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: עונה של תלמידי חכמים אימת אמר רב יהודה אמר שמואל מערב שבת לערב שבת
כ"ש שקיים זה עונה אחת לז"א כפו מטתו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: all the more so that this one would keep one conjugal time; therefore he said 'overturn his bed' (translation_by_this_dossier)

findings.reasoning: The preceding segment (62b:5) sets scholars' conjugal time as Friday night. R. Yannai's inference only works if Yehuda had a wife at home. The passage never uses a word for wife in 62b:6. Maharam Schiff explains R. Yannai's certainty: even when ill, David kept his conjugal obligation (Sanhedrin), so Yehuda would not have missed one; therefore he must be dead.
findings.graph_effect: Attach the conjugal-time evidence to spouse(P1, P4) as supporting context. Do not create a second unnamed wife. Mark 'wife = daughter of R. Yannai' as a reading with medium confidence, not text.

findings.claim: The academic journey is habitual and weekly. Yehuda 'would go and sit in the study house' and come home at twilight. The study house, its place and any teacher are not named, so no teacher edge follows.

evidence.exact_quote: הוה אזיל ויתיב בבי רב וכל בי שמשי הוה אתי לביתיה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: he would go and sit in the study house, and every twilight he would come to his house (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: וכל בי שמשי [בין השמשות] של ערב שבת
every Shabbat eve at twilight he would come to his house.

findings.reasoning: The Hebrew says only 'every twilight'. Steinsaltz (Hebrew) and the Davidson English (not in bold) both add 'of Shabbat eve', drawing on 62b:5. That is a strong contextual reading, but it is editorial. בי רב here is the generic 'study house', not 'the house of Rav'. The passage gives no distance and no city.
findings.graph_effect: Record a habitual scene: P1 studies at an unnamed study house; P1 travels home weekly (weekly = editorial reading from context). No teacher_of edge. No place node.

findings.claim: The grammar does not say who sees the pillar of fire. Davidson and Steinsaltz supply R. Yannai. Daf Shevui says 'the people saw'. Maharsha writes that the pillar signalled 'to them'.

evidence.exact_quote: וכי הוה אתי הוה קא חזי קמיה עמודא דנורא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and when he would come, [someone] would see before him a pillar of fire (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: When he would come, Rabbi Yannai would see a pillar of fire preceding him due to his sanctity.
<small>[וכאשר היה בא, היה רואה</small> ר' ינאי <small>לפניו עמוד של אש]</small> מפני קדושתו
When he would arrive the people saw a pillar of light going before him.
אפשר שהיה העמוד דנורא רומז להם על זמן קבלת שבת
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: perhaps the pillar of fire hinted to them the time of receiving Shabbat (translation_by_this_dossier)

findings.reasoning: חזי is a singular participle with no stated subject. The next clause (כיון דלא חזי ההוא סימנא אמר להו רבי ינאי) makes R. Yannai the one who fails to see the sign, which supports reading him as the habitual observer too. Davidson and Steinsaltz share editorial work, so they count as one line of interpretation. Daf Shevui's 'the people' and Maharsha's 'to them' keep a wider set of observers open. Daf Shevui also says 'light' where the Aramaic has fire (נורא).
findings.graph_effect: Scene 'sees pillar' has observer P3 in reading A and an unnamed group in reading B. Do not use it as evidence that P1 and P3 lived in the same house.

findings.claim: R. Yannai speaks to an unnamed group (להו, 'to them'). The group is not named. Translations fill it in as 'the family' or 'those around him'. The instruction is a mourning rite.

evidence.exact_quote: כיון דלא חזי ההוא סימנא אמר להו רבי ינאי כפו מטתו
אמר להו [להם] ר' ינאי חותנו לבני המשפחה
he said to the family: Turn his bed over,
R. Yannai said to those [around him]
כפו מטתו - כדת המתאבלים דחייבין בכפיית המטה:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Overturn his bed: according to the practice of mourners, who are obliged to overturn the bed (translation_by_this_dossier)

findings.reasoning: The speaker is named. The addressee is a plural pronoun only. 'The family' could include Yehuda's wife, but no source I checked says so. The Yerushalmi parallel has R. Yannai's students present (F8), a different setting.
findings.graph_effect: Speech edge P3 -> G1 (unnamed group). Do not create P3 -> P4 speech. Mourning instruction concerns P1.

findings.claim: The narrator treats R. Yannai's words as a ruler's mistaken decree that came true: Yehuda died. The death and its narrated cause are literary claims inside the Bavli story.

evidence.exact_quote: הואי כשגגה שיוצא מלפני השליט ונח נפשיה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: it became 'like an error that goes out from before the ruler' (Eccl. 10:5), and he died (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: ונח נפשיה [ונפטר] יהודה בר' חייא.
and Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya, died.
and he [Judah] died.
מפורש במסכת מ"ק דברית כרותה לשפתים
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: explained in tractate Moed Katan: a covenant is made with the lips (translation_by_this_dossier)

findings.reasoning: All three translations make Yehuda the one who died. The verse casts R. Yannai as 'the ruler' whose mistaken statement takes effect. Maharsha links this to the idea that spoken words can come true. The Yerushalmi parallel has no such cause (F8).
findings.graph_effect: Event: death of P1 (in the Bavli story). Narrative causal link: P3's utterance -> P1's death, labelled literary/narrated, not historical. Relative time: P1 dies within P3's lifetime in this story.

findings.claim: The Yerushalmi (Bikkurim 3:3) tells a different version. Yehuda goes up each Sabbath eve to greet his father-in-law R. Yannai. R. Yannai sits on a raised spot to see him coming and rise for him. His students object, and he answers that one does not sit before Sinai. Once Yehuda does not come, and R. Yannai concludes he has died. There is no study house, no conjugal time, no overturned bed and no ruler's error.

evidence.exact_quote: והוה יתיב ליה על אתר תלי בגין מיחמיניה ומקים לי' מן קומוי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and he would sit on a raised spot in order to see him and rise before him (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: אמרי' ליה תלמידוי לא כן אלפן ר' לזקן ד' אמו' אמר לון אין ישיבה לפני סיני
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: His students said to him: did not our master teach us, for an elder, four cubits? He said to them: there is no sitting before Sinai (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: חד זמן עני מסיק אמר לית איפשר דיהודה ברי משני מנהגיה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Once he was late coming up. He said: it is impossible that Yehuda my son would change his habit (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: Jehudah bar Ḥiyya used to go and greet his father-in-law Rebbi Yannai every Sabbath eve. He used to sit on a hilly place in order to see him and get up before him.
It is reasonable that we lost the great Jehudah.
והיה ר' ינאי יושב במקום אחד ותולה עיניו לראותו ולקום מפניו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and R. Yannai would sit in one place and lift his eyes to see him and rise before him (translation_by_this_dossier)

findings.reasoning: The journey's direction and purpose differ between the two versions. In the Bavli, Yehuda comes home from the study house. In the Yerushalmi, he goes up to greet R. Yannai. Both agree on the kinship, the weekly Sabbath-eve pattern, the one missed visit and R. Yannai inferring the death. This is a parallel tradition, not two historical events and not independent corroboration. The Yerushalmi adds R. Yannai's unnamed students and treats Yehuda as 'Sinai', a figure owed honour.
findings.graph_effect: Add a separate passage reading for Yerushalmi Bikkurim 3:3:13 linked as a parallel. Its own claims: son_in_law_of(P1, P3) again (same relation, different compilation); honour scene P3 rises for P1; P3 teacher of an unnamed student group (G2) who addresses P3. Do not merge the two scenes into one event.

findings.claim: In the Yerushalmi, R. Yannai calls Yehuda 'my son' (ברי). This is how a father-in-law addresses a son-in-law, not biological kinship.

evidence.exact_quote: לית איפשר דיהודה ברי משני מנהגיה
He said it is impossible that my son Jehudah should change his habits

findings.reasoning: The same segment calls R. Yannai Yehuda's חמוה (father-in-law), and the Bavli gives Yehuda's father as R. Hiyya. A form of address is not a patronymic.
findings.graph_effect: No child_of(P1 -> P3). Record 'addresses as my son' as an address form on the speech event only.

findings.claim: The Yerushalmi ends with יהודה ב"ר. It is unclear whether ב"ר is an honorific or 'son of Rabbi'. Guggenheimer vocalizes בְּרִיבִי and translates 'the great Jehudah'. Penei Moshe writes ברבי. The same form is used for Hizqiah at the start of the segment.

evidence.exact_quote: מסתברא שאין לנו יהודה ב"ר
מִסְתַּבְּרָא שֶׁאֵין לָנוּ יְהוּדָה בְּרִיבִי.
It is reasonable that we lost the great Jehudah.
דומה שאין לנו יהודה ברבי שנפטר
חִזְקִיָּה בְּרִיבִי

findings.reasoning: Read as a title, it adds no kinship. Read as 'son of Rabbi', it would at most repeat the known father (R. Hiyya is called Rabbi). It must not create a new parent. Penei Moshe elsewhere in the same comment writes בר' חייה, so its ברבי may mean the same father.
findings.graph_effect: Save ב"ר as a name-form alternative (title vs patronymic). Never add a second father from it.

findings.claim: Commentators on the Yerushalmi read it through the Bavli. Penei Moshe adds the 'error from the ruler' ending, and Sirilio cites the Bavli story. The Yerushalmi witnesses also differ slightly: Venice and Guggenheimer read עני, Sirilio's lemma reads שני, and Mechon-Mamre repeats a sentence.

evidence.exact_quote: שנפטר והיה כשגגה היוצא מלפני השליט:
חד זמן שני מסיק. פעם אחת שינה מלעלות על אותו מקום גבוה ובפ' אע"פ קאמר חד זמן משכא שמעתיה ואמר כפו מטתו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Once he changed [his habit] of going up to that high place; and in chapter Af al pi (Ketubot ch. 5) it says: once his study held him, and he said 'overturn his bed' (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: חד זמן עני מסיק
יהודה בר חייה הוה יליף סליק ושאל בשלמיה דרבי ינאי חמוי מערב שבת לערב שבת והוה יתיב ליה על אתר תלי בגין מיחמוניה ומיקם ליה מן קומיהון. יהודה בר חייה

findings.reasoning: The ruler's-error ending belongs to the Bavli. When Penei Moshe adds it, that is harmonizing commentary, not Yerushalmi text. The Mechon-Mamre repetition (and its plural מן קומיהון in the first copy) looks like a transmission or typing duplication. It must not be read as a second visit. The עני/שני variant changes the wording (late vs changed), not who the participants are.
findings.graph_effect: Keep commentary harmonization as commentary evidence. Save the variant as a source-variant evidence type. Do not add a second visit event.

findings.claim: Yehuda's brother Hizqiah does not appear in Ketubot 62b:6. He appears elsewhere. Bavli Sanhedrin 38a names 'Yehuda and Hizqiyya, sons of R. Hiyya' at Rabbi's meal. The Yerushalmi segment opens with a separate Hizqiah anecdote. Guggenheimer's note and Seder HaDorot call them twins.

evidence.exact_quote: יהודה וחזקיה בני רבי חייא הוו יתבי בסעודתא קמי רבי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Yehuda and Hizqiyya, sons of Rabbi Hiyya, were sitting at a meal before Rabbi (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: Ḥizqiah ben R. Ḥiyya the elder, twin brother of Jehudah ben Ḥiyya.
יהודה וחזקיה בני ר' חייא נולדו מטיפה אחת

findings.reasoning: Sanhedrin 38a states a sibling relation through a shared father. Linking that Yehuda to the Ketubot Yehuda rests on the matching name and father's name in the same corpus. That is plausible but it is an identity decision. The twin claim comes from later commentary and chronicle, not from these Talmud passages.
findings.graph_effect: No sibling edge from Ketubot 62b:6. If identity packs later accept P1 = Yehuda of Sanhedrin 38a, siblings(Yehuda, Hizqiyya) comes from Sanhedrin 38a. The twin claim stays chronicle/commentary evidence.

findings.claim: The passage does not say which R. Hiyya or which R. Yannai is meant. Seder HaDorot and Guggenheimer treat the father as R. Hiyya the elder, the associate of Rabbi. The next Bavli segment (62b:7) has Rabbi dealing with R. Hiyya's household, but adjacency is not identity.

evidence.exact_quote: Ḥizqiah ben R. Ḥiyya the elder
רבי איעסק ליה לבריה בי רבי חייא כי מטא למיכתב כתובה נח נפשה דרביתא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with the household of Rabbi Hiyya; when it came to writing the ketubah, the girl died (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: חתנו של ר' ינאי.

findings.reasoning: Shared names do not establish historical identity. The later identifications are reasonable scholarly positions and are saved here as commentary or chronicle evidence.
findings.graph_effect: Keep P2 and P3 as local persons. Proposing P2 = R. Hiyya the elder goes to an identity pack with this evidence, not to the text layer.

findings.claim: 62b:6 belongs to a chain of stories illustrating a warning. Rava says the Sages who relied on a lenient ruling about leaving home to study 'paid with their lives'. The Rav Rehumi story (62b:4) uses the same formula. The order of the chain is thematic, not chronological.

evidence.exact_quote: התלמידים יוצאין לתלמוד תורה שתים ושלש שנים שלא ברשות
אמר רבא סמכו רבנן אדרב אדא בר אהבה ועבדי עובדא בנפשייהו
בנפשייהו - והוא בא להם ליטול מהם נפשות שנענשים ומתים:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: with their lives: and it came to take lives from them, for they are punished and die (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: יומא חד משכתיה שמעתא הוה מסכיא דביתהו

findings.reasoning: The Rav Rehumi story is set before Rava in Mahoza, a later generation. It comes before the R. Yannai story, and Rabbi's family follows. So the order of segments cannot supply 'before' relations between the people. The shared formula יומא חד משכתיה שמעתא shows a literary template, which is a reason not to treat the details as independent reports.
findings.graph_effect: Do not derive temporal 'before/after' edges from segment order. Tag 62b:4 and 62b:6 as template-sharing illustrative stories under Rava's remark.

findings.claim: In the next segments, one marriage is only arranged and one is completed. Rabbi's match for his son with R. Hiyya's household ends when the girl dies at the ketubah stage. His son's match with R. Yosei b. Zimra's household leads to marriage: the son says 'I will marry and then go', and later the text speaks of 'his wife'. Neither woman is named.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי איעסק ליה לבריה בי רבי חייא כי מטא למיכתב כתובה נח נפשה דרביתא
איעסק לבריה - להשיא בתו של רבי חייא:
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: arranged for his son: to marry him to the daughter of Rabbi Hiyya (translation_by_this_dossier)

evidence.exact_quote: arranged for his son to marry a daughter of the household of Rabbi Ḥiyya.
אזיל איעסק ליה לבריה בי רבי יוסי בן זימרא פסקו ליה תרתי סרי שנין למיזל בבי רב
אמר להו איכניס והדר איזיל הוה קא מכסיף מאבוה אמר ליה בני דעת קונך יש בך
אזיל יתיב תרתי סרי שני בבי רב עד דאתא איעקרא דביתהו

findings.reasoning: The Hebrew says בי רבי חייא, 'R. Hiyya's household'. Rashi makes the girl R. Hiyya's daughter, which would make her Yehuda's sister. That sibling link would rest on Rashi's reading plus an identity decision, not on the text. The son of Rabbi is unnamed in these segments and in the commentaries checked. In 62b:8, 'they agreed for him' has an unstated subject. Rashi says it was 'before he marries'. In 'he was ashamed before his father' and 'he said to him: my son', the speaker is Rabbi and the addressee his son.
findings.graph_effect: Wider-context proposals (not 62b:6): arranged_match(son-of-Rabbi, girl of R. Hiyya's household) status=not completed, girl died. Married(son-of-Rabbi, woman of R. Yosei b. Zimra's household) status=completed (62b:10 דביתהו). The son's 12-year study journey after marriage. No sibling edge between P1 and the girl without an explicit decision.

findings.claim: The 62b:7 inquiry reports biblical descent for both families: Rabbi from Shefatya son of Avital (David's son), R. Hiyya from Shim'i, David's brother. Rashi and Maharsha disagree on what the 'disqualification' was.

unresolved: Whether Yehuda lived in R. Yannai's household or nearby. The Bavli says 'his house', and the Yerushalmi has him 'go up' to R. Yannai, which points to separate homes in that version. Not settled for the Bavli.
The name of R. Yannai's daughter, the date of the marriage and any children. None of the sources checked give these.
Where the study house was and who taught there. The Bavli gives only בי רב.
Which son of Rabbi is meant in 62b:7-10. He is unnamed in the text and in Rashi, Tosafot and Maharsha as checked. Other sources were not searched.
Whether the Bavli and Yerushalmi versions come from one tradition reshaped or from two traditions. This affects how much the shared kinship counts, not whether it is attested.
Bavli manuscript readings of 62b:6 were not checked (for example whether any witness names the observer of the pillar or the addressee).
Other linked commentaries (Yisrael Kedoshim, Tur Orach Chayim 280, Sha'arei Torat Eretz Yisrael, Tosefta Kifshutah) were listed by Sefaria but not read.

lessons: Kinship terms like חתן/חמוה state a marriage without narrating it. The graph needs a spouse-edge provenance value 'implied by kinship term', separate from 'narrated wedding' and from 'marriage inferred from another passage'.
An implied spouse needs a local placeholder even with zero mentions. The pronoun map should record the words that imply her (עונתו, מטתו) even though they refer to the husband.
Unstated subjects of participles (הוה קא חזי) should be stored as an observer slot with competing fillers and who supplies each, not resolved silently.
Forms of address (ברי 'my son', בניי 'my children') must be kept apart from kinship. Honorifics like בריבי must be kept apart from patronymics.
A parallel in another Talmud is a separate passage reading. It can re-attest a relation but not merge scenes. Commentaries that harmonize one version with the other are commentary evidence, not text.
Story chains ordered by theme (Rava's era before Rabbi's) must not generate before/after edges.
Shared narrative formulas (יומא חד משכתיה שמעתא) are a signal of literary shaping and should be tagged.
Arranged-but-unfinished matches (62b:7) need a status value distinct from marriage.

review.scope: I checked every exact_quote in dossier.json against its saved file (all 62 are present, at the occurrences claimed), reread Ketubot 62b:3-11 in the four saved versions, the Yerushalmi Bikkurim 3:3:13 witnesses with Penei Moshe, Sirilio and Seder HaDorot, and fetched Bavli Niddah 27a; I did not check Bavli manuscripts, the unread linked commentaries or any historical identity.

findings.target: F8 (Yerushalmi honour scene and student group) and reading.md 'The Yerushalmi tells it differently'
findings.reason: In Venice, 'והוה יתיב ליה על אתר תלי בגין מיחמיניה ומקים לי' מן קומוי' does not name the one who sits and rises. The next clauses, 'אמרי' ליה תלמידוי' and 'אמר לון אין ישיבה לפני סיני', do not name the teacher of 'his students' or say who is 'Sinai'. Only Penei Moshe names R. Yannai ('והיה ר' ינאי יושב במקום אחד'). Sirilio glosses only 'על מקום גבוה', and Guggenheimer writes only 'He used to sit'. So reading.md is wrong to credit Sirilio and Guggenheimer with R. Yannai as the sitter. Seder HaDorot's paraphrase keeps Yehuda as the running subject ('היה רגיל לשאול בשלום ר' ינאי חמיו ... והיה עומד במקום גבוה לראותו מרחוק כדי לעמוד לפניו אמרו לו תלמידיו'), which would reverse the direction of honour. Store 'rises for' and 'teacher of G2' as an unfilled sitter slot, with R. Yannai as Penei Moshe's filling (medium) and Yehuda as a possible alternative (low). Do not store them as settled edges P3 -> P1 and P3 -> G2.

findings.target: proposed_corrections 1-3 (son_in_law_of direction, child_of R. Hiyya, unnamed wife P4); F1, F2, F3
findings.reason: Both Bavli editions read 'יהודה בריה דרבי חייא חתניה דרבי ינאי' (Wikisource 'דר''), so the parent inside the name and the directed son-in-law relation are text. R. Hiyya stays as a local parent even though he never acts. The Yerushalmi 'דרבי ינאי חמוה' is a parallel telling of the same relation, not a second vote. The dossier rightly separates two claims. That Yehuda married a daughter of R. Yannai is implied by חתניה. That she is the wife behind 'מטתו ... עונתו' is inference, at medium confidence. Nothing in 62b:6 names her, dates the marriage or mentions children.

findings.target: F14 (tagging 62b:6 under Rava's remark) and reading.md 'The study journey and the order of events'
findings.reason: Only 62b:4 is tied to Rava's remark by a connecting formula: 'כי הא דרב רחומי'. Rashi's 'שנענשים ומתים' glosses 'בנפשייהו' in 62b:3. It does not comment on the Yehuda story. 62b:6 has no connecting formula. It follows 62b:5, 'עונה של תלמידי חכמים אימת ... מערב שבת לערב שבת', and turns on 'עונתו'. Yehuda also comes home at every twilight, so he is not a case of leaving home for two or three years without permission. Tag 62b:6 as illustrating the scholars' conjugal-time rule in a theme-ordered chain that shares the formula 'יומא חד משכתיה שמעתא' with 62b:4. Do not tag it as a case of Rava's warning. The ban on before/after edges from segment order stands.

findings.target: F15 (son of Rabbi in 62b:7-10) and unresolved item 4
findings.reason: 62b:7 says 'רבי איעסק ליה לבריה' and 62b:8 says 'אזיל איעסק ליה לבריה'. Each is an unnamed 'his son'. The text never says they are the same son, although that is the natural reading of 'he went and arranged' after the first match failed. Keep two local 'son of Rabbi' mentions, each with child_of -> Rabbi from 'בריה'. Record 'same son' as a reading (medium), not a merge. The arranged-but-not-completed status of the first match ('כי מטא למיכתב כתובה נח נפשה דרביתא') and the completed marriage in 62b:10 ('איעקרא דביתהו') are correct.

findings.target: F12 (Hizqiyya and the twin claim) and reading.md table row 'Yehuda's brother Hizqiah; twins'
findings.reason: The dossier traces the twin claim only to Guggenheimer's note and Seder HaDorot. Seder HaDorot does not say 'twins'. It says 'נולדו מטיפה אחת, ונתעכב לידתן זה אחר זה ג' חדשים' (born from one drop, their births three months apart). That report is in the Bavli itself, at Niddah 27a (saved in review-sources). There Rav Menahem, cited by R. Avin bar Rav Adda, tells of a second child born three months after the first. The anonymous question 'ומאן נינהו' then names them 'יהודה וחזקיה בני רבי חייא'. This is still not evidence from Ketubot 62b:6, so the ruling of no sibling edge from this segment stands. A sibling claim from Niddah 27a or Sanhedrin 38a belongs to those passages and waits on the identity decision.

findings.target: F8 and F17 (who concludes Yehuda has died in the Yerushalmi); A4
findings.reason: The Yerushalmi has a second, separately marked 'אמ' לית איפשר דלא יגיעון ייסורין בההוא גופא צדיק'' and then an unattributed 'מסתברא שאין לנו יהודה ב"ר'. The text names no speaker for either, although continuing with R. Yannai is the natural reading and Penei Moshe makes it explicit. Guggenheimer's English, 'it is impossible that sufferings should come over this holy body', drops the negation 'דלא' that his own Hebrew prints ('דְּלָא יְגִיעוּן'), and his note 50 builds on that translation. His Hebrew, English and notes are one editorial line, so F10 should not cite S12G and S12E as two witnesses. A4's 'suffering reached the righteous body' follows the printed text correctly.

findings.target: pronoun_map_62b6 'כיון דלא חזי' (confidence high) vs F5 (confidence medium)
findings.reason: In 'כיון דלא חזי ההוא סימנא אמר להו רבי ינאי' the subject of 'לא חזי' is no more stated than the subject of the earlier 'הוה קא חזי'. It is supplied from the main verb 'אמר ... רבי ינאי'. That is a strong reading, and Steinsaltz and Davidson (one editorial line) make it explicit. But the pronoun map should say 'supplied from the main clause', not 'text'. It is also inconsistent to rate the failed seeing high and the habitual seeing medium when the second is inferred from the first. Daf Shevui's 'When he did not see the sign, R. Yannai said' keeps the ambiguity.

findings.target: F6, F7, F9 and proposed_corrections 4-5 (speech to unnamed group, death, no child_of from ברי)
findings.reason: 'אמר להו רבי ינאי' names the speaker and marks only a plural addressee. 'the family' (Davidson; Steinsaltz 'לבני המשפחה') is editorial, so G1 stays an unnamed group and the wife is not made an addressee. Yehuda is the target of the speech ('שאילמלי יהודה קיים'), not its addressee. The link from utterance to death rests on 'הואי כשגגה שיוצא מלפני השליט ונח נפשיה', given by the anonymous narrator, and is rightly labelled literary. The Yerushalmi 'יהודה ברי' is a form of address in the same segment that calls R. Yannai 'חמוה', so no child_of -> R. Yannai.
