cases.question: Investigate branch-scoped teacher/student statements and participant identity. Preserve which relationship belongs to which reported version. Read wider context and commentary for exactly who is called a teacher.

findings.claim: In the first reported version (version A), Yirmeya bar Abba speaks in the first person: he asked his own teacher, and the text itself names that teacher as Rav.

evidence.exact_quote: אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא: שְׁאֵילִית אֶת רַבִּי בְּיִחוּד, וּמַנּוּ: רַב.
R. Jirmeja b. Abba sagte, er habe seinen Lehrer, das ist Rabh, besonders gefragt
אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא: שְׁאֵלִית אֶת רַבִּי בְּיִחוּד, וּמַנּוּ — רַב: מַאי פַּת עָבָה? פַּת מְרוּבָּה.

findings.translation: My translation: 'Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said: I asked my teacher [biyichud], and who is he? Rav.'
findings.reasoning: שאילית is first person singular, so the asker is the speaker named by אמר. רבי here is 'my teacher' (noun with first person suffix); ומנו ('and who is he?') resolves it inside the text to רב. The Beitzah parallel has the same wording.
findings.graph_effect: Version A only: Yirmeya bar Abba -asks-> Rav; Yirmeya bar Abba -calls my teacher-> Rav (explicit student-teacher statement by the student). Do not carry either edge into version B.

findings.claim: In the second version (introduced by 'some say'), Yirmeya bar Abba only transmits. The first-person asker is Rav, and Rav's teacher is named 'Rabbeinu HaKadosh' (our holy teacher).

evidence.exact_quote: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב: שְׁאֵילִית אֶת רַבִּי בְּיִחוּד, וּמַנּוּ: רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ.
ואיכא דאמרי - רב גופיה אמר שאלית את רבי ביחוד
ומנו - רבו דרב רבינו הקדוש
Rabh erzählte, er habe seinen Lehrer, das ist unser heiliger Meister, privatim gefragt

findings.translation: My translation of the Talmud: 'Some say: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said that Rav said: I asked my teacher [biyichud], and who is he? Our holy teacher.' My translation of Rashi on Beitzah: 'Some say: Rav himself said I asked my teacher privately. And who is he: Rav's teacher, Rabbeinu HaKadosh.'
findings.reasoning: The chain X אמר Y makes the following first-person speech Y's. Rashi on the Beitzah parallel says so explicitly (רב גופיה). Goldschmidt, an independent translation, also renders Rav as the narrator in Beitzah.
findings.graph_effect: Version B only: Yirmeya bar Abba -transmits in the name of-> Rav; Rav -asks-> the teacher called רבינו הקדוש; Rav -calls my teacher-> רבינו הקדוש. In version B, Yirmeya bar Abba is not the asker and no teacher relation between Yirmeya and Rav is stated.

findings.claim: The word רבי in 'I asked רבי' is a role word, 'my teacher'. It refers to a different person in each version: Rav in A and Rabbeinu HaKadosh in B. It is not, in this passage, the proper title 'Rabbi' used for Judah HaNasi.

evidence.exact_quote: רביה דר' ירמיה רב רביה דרב רבינו הקדוש
Pes. 37ᵃ שאילית את רבי בי׳ I asked my teacher privately.
er habe seinen Lehrer, das ist unser heiliger Meister, besonders gefragt

findings.translation: My translation of Rashi: 'The teacher of R. Yirmeya: Rav. The teacher of Rav: Rabbeinu HaKadosh.'
findings.reasoning: The resolution after ומנו differs between the versions, and Rashi assigns one teacher per speaker. Jastrow (a reference work) and Goldschmidt both translate רבי here as 'my teacher'. So the two occurrences of the same letters are two separate teacher slots.
findings.graph_effect: Create one local teacher-slot mention per branch. In A it corefers with the local Rav; in B it corefers with the local person named רבינו הקדוש. Never join the two רבי tokens with each other, and never read A's רבי as Judah HaNasi.

findings.claim: The printed Aramaic says only 'Rabbeinu HaKadosh'. The name 'Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi' is an editorial identification added by the Koren/Steinsaltz editions, not words of the source.

evidence.exact_quote: Rav said: I asked my special Rabbi, and who is this? Our holy Rabbi, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi:
ומנו [ומי הוא] רבינו הקדוש (ר' יהודה הנשיא)
It is our holy Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
ומנו רבינו הקדוש מאי פת עבה

findings.reasoning: In the William Davidson English, bold marks translated source words; 'Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi' is outside the bold. Steinsaltz puts it in round brackets as an explanation. These are one editorial family (Koren Noé / Steinsaltz), so they count as a single identification, not several witnesses. Rashi and Goldschmidt keep the epithet without naming anyone.
findings.graph_effect: Save רבינו הקדוש as the literal name of the local person in version B. Link to the global Judah HaNasi node only as a separate identity assertion, citing the Koren/Steinsaltz gloss as its source.

findings.claim: Both versions report the same question ('What is pat ava?') and the same short answer ('a large quantity of bread'). They differ only in who asked whom. In Pesachim the question and answer are written once, after version B. In the Beitzah parallel, version A has its own copy of the question and answer.

evidence.exact_quote: וּמַנּוּ: רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ. מַאי פַּת עָבָה? פַּת מְרוּבָּה.
אמר רב ירמיה בר אבא שאלית את רבי ביחוד ומנו רב מאי פת עבה פת מרובה

findings.reasoning: The Beitzah layout shows that version A has its own content. It is not just a heading. So the question and answer belong to both branches, each with its own asker and answerer.
findings.graph_effect: Attach the statement 'pat ava = pat merubah' to both branches. In A the answerer is Rav; in B it is רבינו הקדוש, reported by Rav and then by Yirmeya. The Beitzah passage is a parallel of the same tradition, not an independent second observation.

findings.claim: The Aramaic has no verb of answering. Saying that the teacher gave the answer is a reasonable reading, but it is supplied by the translators.

evidence.exact_quote: מאי [מה היא] פת עבה? אמר לו: פת מרובה
Rav explained that it means a large quantity of bread
und [dieser habe erwidert], viel Brot

findings.translation: Steinsaltz, my translation: 'What is pat ava? He said to him: pat merubah.' Goldschmidt, my translation: 'and [he replied], much bread' (the brackets are Goldschmidt's own).
findings.reasoning: Steinsaltz adds אמר לו, and Goldschmidt brackets his verb, so both mark the answerer as supplied. The reading is natural: the teacher was asked and the next words are the answer.
findings.graph_effect: Record 'teacher explains to student' edges (Rav to Yirmeya in A; רבינו הקדוש to Rav in B) as interpretive supplements. They are weaker than the explicit asks and my-teacher edges.

findings.claim: The explanations that follow ('Why call it pat ava? ... And if you wish, say ...') may be the anonymous Talmud's own discussion, not the teacher's words. Translators differ on this.

evidence.exact_quote: וְאַמַּאי קָרוּ לֵיהּ פַּת עָבָה? מִשּׁוּם דִּנְפִישָׁא בְּלִישָׁה. וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא
And he explained the matter as follows
– Weshalb nennt er es ‘dickes Brot’? – Weil [der Teig] beim Kneten dick ist.

findings.reasoning: 'And if you wish, say' (ואי בעית אימא) is a common formula of the anonymous Talmud when it offers alternative explanations; that is my interpretation of the formula. The Davidson English on Beitzah puts the explanations in the teacher's mouth. Goldschmidt sets them off with dashes as dialogue, which treats them as a separate exchange.
findings.graph_effect: Do not attach the two etymologies of pat ava to Rav or to רבינו הקדוש as their statements. At most, save them as an alternative attribution.

findings.claim: Commentaries disagree on what ביחוד means. Rashi says 'privately' or 'clearly'. The Pesachim Steinsaltz and Davidson English read 'my special/unique teacher'. The same editors on Beitzah say 'in private'.

evidence.exact_quote: ביחוד - בינו לביני
לישנא אחרינא בייחוד בברור
שאילית [שאלתי] את רבי ביחוד [המיוחד]
I asked my special Rabbi, and who is this? Rav.
שאלית [שאלתי] את רבי ביחוד (ביני לבינו)
Ich fragte meinen Lehrer, das ist Rabh, privatim

findings.translation: My translation of Rashi: 'Biyichud: between him and me. Another explanation: biyichud, clearly.' Steinsaltz on Pesachim: '[the unique one]'. Steinsaltz on Beitzah: '(between me and him)'.
findings.reasoning: Under Rashi's readings, ביחוד describes how the question was asked. Under the 'special teacher' reading, it describes the teacher, which might suggest a principal teacher. The Koren/Steinsaltz family gives both readings in the two parallels. The teacher relation already rests on רבי + ומנו, so this word should not be used to make the tie stronger.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the teacher edge at 'explicit my-teacher'. Save 'special/principal teacher' only as an alternative gloss attributed to the Pesachim Koren/Steinsaltz rendering. Optionally add a 'private question' setting attribute, following Rashi's first reading.

findings.claim: The title of the transmitter varies between witnesses. The Davidson vocalized text reads רב in both versions. Wikisource and the Pesachim Steinsaltz read ר' in version A and רב in version B. Beitzah reads רב throughout. Rashi on Pesachim writes ר' ירמיה.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר ר' ירמיה בר אבא שאילית את רבי ביחוד ומנו רב איכא דאמרי רב ירמיה בר אבא אמר רב
אמר ר' ירמיה בר אבא: שאילית
איכא דאמרי אמר רב ירמיה בר אבא אמר רב
בברכות גרסי' ברוב ספרים רב ירמי' ובקדושין ר' ירמיה

findings.reasoning: The איכא דאמרי presents two forms of one tradition from one named transmitter. The ר'/רב difference is an abbreviation or title variant, a kind Seder HaDorot also notes elsewhere. It is not a reason to split the passage's transmitter into two local people.
findings.graph_effect: One local person 'Yirmeya bar Abba' serves both branches, with the title variant saved on the mention. Matching him to other Talmudic occurrences is a separate identity decision (see F11).

findings.claim: The patronymic 'bar Abba' is name-embedded evidence that Yirmeya had a father called Abba. That parent does not appear in this passage.

evidence.exact_quote: רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא

findings.reasoning: Project rule: a relation embedded in a name is still evidence. Reading בר אבא as literal parentage is the ordinary reading, but it comes from the name form. Seder HaDorot's further remarks about this father are a later biographical claim and are not used here.
findings.graph_effect: Keep a local placeholder 'Abba (father of Yirmeya)'. Edge: Yirmeya -child of-> Abba, marked 'name-derived (patronymic)'. It is shared by both branches. Keep it even though Abba plays no role.

findings.claim: Later scholars disagree about who 'Rav Yirmeya bar Abba' is across the Talmud. Seder HaDorot calls him a student-colleague (תלמיד חבר) of Rav and cites this passage. Tosafot on Kiddushin sees a conflict with his being Rav Huna's student and suggests there were two men called Rav Yirmeya.

evidence.exact_quote: ר' ירמי' בר אבא תלמיד חבר לרב היה
שאלית את רבי ומנו רב פ' כל שעה (ל"ז א') ביצה (כ"ב ב')
משמע הכא דרב ירמיה תלמידיה דרב הונא הוה
ונראה דתרי רב ירמיה הוו

findings.translation: My translation: Seder HaDorot, 'R. Yirmeya bar Abba was a student-colleague of Rav'. Tosafot, 'It implies here that Rav Yirmeya was a student of Rav Huna ... it seems there were two Rav Yirmeyas.'
findings.reasoning: These are later identity and biography claims. Tosafot's evidence for 'student-colleague' is Berakhot 27b, not this passage. Seder HaDorot does list this passage. Neither changes the local reading. Both show that joining this Yirmeya bar Abba to every other occurrence of the name is not settled by the name alone.
findings.graph_effect: Save 'student-colleague of Rav' (Seder HaDorot) and 'possibly two Rav Yirmeyas' (Tosafot Kiddushin 46a) as later-scholarship assertions on the identity layer. Keep them separate from the version-A teacher edge, which rests on the text.

findings.claim: The Talmud does not choose between the two versions. The teacher relation in each version exists only inside that version.

evidence.exact_quote: Some say that Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said that Rav said
manche lesen, R. Jirmeja b.Abba im Namen Rabhs sagte

findings.reasoning: איכא דאמרי ('some say'; Goldschmidt: 'some read') introduces a different transmitted form, and the passage moves on without deciding. Both conversations could have happened. The text gives no basis for calling them mutually exclusive, nor for treating both as confirmed.
findings.graph_effect: Two branches of one group: A = {Yirmeya asks / calls teacher Rav}; B = {Yirmeya transmits from Rav; Rav asks / calls teacher רבינו הקדוש}. Shared across both: the Yirmeya mention, the Rav mention, the patronymic parent, and the question topic. Neither branch's teacher edge should count as confirmed by the other.

findings.claim: Ritva's 'two versions' (שתי לשונות) refers to the two explanations of why the bread is called pat ava, not to the two versions of who asked whom. The Rav that Ritva mentions is linked to a different ruling (Pesachim 48a), not to this question.

וכלישנא בתרא קיל"ן דקאי כרב

unresolved: Manuscript and early-print readings of Pesachim 37a and Beitzah 22b were not checked (e.g. Dikdukei Soferim, manuscript images). Whether any witness drops the איכא דאמרי, changes the resolving names, or reads ר'/רב differently is not established here.
Whether the 'why is it called pat ava' explanations belong to the teacher (version B) or to the anonymous Talmud: translators differ (F7, ALT2).
Identity of רבינו הקדוש with Judah HaNasi is an identity assertion from the Koren/Steinsaltz gloss and common usage. It is not decided in this dossier.
Whether this Yirmeya bar Abba is the same man as every other Rav/R. Yirmeya bar Abba in the Talmud: Tosafot on Kiddushin 46a raises the possibility of two. Not decided.

Other Sefaria-linked items on Pesachim 37a:4 (Tur, Shulchan Arukh, Mishneh Torah, Semag, Torat HaOlah, Arukh) were listed but not read for person claims beyond what is quoted. The Torat HaOlah and Arukh texts in the saved links file do not mention the teacher exchange.

Agree with its five claims and branch scopes. Add: (1) interpretive explains_to edges per branch (F6); (2) the patronymic parent placeholder Abba (F10); (3) the fact that the Judah HaNasi identification comes from one editorial family and is unbolded in the English (F4); (4) the Beitzah 22b:6-7 parallel and Rashi there ('רב גופיה אמר'), which state the version-B speaker explicitly (F2, F5); (5) later identity disputes about Yirmeya bar Abba (F11).

lessons: A 'role slot' mention type is needed. רבי meaning 'my teacher' is a pointer resolved inside the text (here by ומנו), not a name. Coreference of the slot is branch-local.
'Explicit self-declared teacher' (רבי + ומנו X) should be a relation separate from, and stronger than, 'asks'. It should carry who makes the declaration: the student speaks in A, Rav speaks in B.
Pairs formed from neighbouring names must be suppressed across an איכא דאמרי boundary. The last name of one version and the first name of the next are not related.
Nested report depth should be recorded: B is Yirmeya ⟶ Rav ⟶ (Rav's first-person account) ⟶ teacher. The one who asks is the innermost first-person speaker, not the outer 'said'.
An answerer supplied by a translator (no verb in the source) should be marked as an interpretive supplement, not as source text.
Editorial glosses outside the bold in the William Davidson English, and in round brackets in Steinsaltz, are identity assertions from one editorial family. They are not independent witnesses.

A parallel sugya (Beitzah 22b) that repeats the same tradition is a parallel of one observation, not a second observation. Differences in layout between the parallels are still useful evidence of structure.
Later chronographic labels such as 'student-colleague' (Seder HaDorot) and 'two men of the same name' (Tosafot) belong on the identity/biography layer, with their own provenance.

review.scope: I checked every finding, proposed correction and edge in the dossier's branch-scoped proposal against the saved sources (Pesachim 36b:16 and 37a:1-7 in Davidson Aramaic/English, Wikisource and Goldschmidt; the Beitzah 22b:6-8 parallel in the same three; Rashi, Steinsaltz and linked commentary on both; Seder HaDorot 2232; Tosafot Kiddushin 46a); I fetched nothing new and did not check manuscripts, Dikdukei Soferim or the identity of any person across the Talmud.

findings.target: F1, F3 and the calls_my_teacher edges (branch A and branch B)
findings.reason: The student's own first-person words are only שְׁאֵילִית אֶת רַבִּי בְּיִחוּד ('I asked my teacher'). The identification that follows, וּמַנּוּ: רַב / וּמַנּוּ: רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ ('and who is he?'), is third person and is not marked as the student's speech; Rashi on Beitzah glosses it as רבו דרב, speaking about Rav, and Steinsaltz on Beitzah 22b:6 resumes the first person only after it (ושאלתי היתה). So F1's 'explicit student-teacher statement by the student' overstates the basis: keep both edges, but record them as 'speaker calls the one he asked my teacher' plus 'an unmarked narrating voice (transmitter or anonymous Talmud) names that teacher'. In B this also means the epithet רבינו הקדוש is the narrator's label, not a word Rav is quoted as using; confidence in the printed identification stays high.

findings.target: F6 and F5 graph_effect; explains_to edges (Rav -> Yirmeya in A, רבינו הקדוש -> Rav in B)
findings.reason: The Aramaic has no verb of answering and no addressee: מַאי פַּת עָבָה? פַּת מְרוּבָּה. The dossier itself shows the answer verb is supplied (Steinsaltz אמר לו, Goldschmidt '[dieser habe erwidert]', Davidson 'He explained' outside the bold), yet F5 states flatly 'In A the answerer is Rav; in B it is רבינו הקדוש'. A separate person-to-person explains_to edge fills an addressee the text does not mark and restates, in reverse, the direction already stored by the asks edge. Attach 'pat ava = pat merubah' to each branch's teacher slot as an interpretive content attribution (medium, basis: question-answer sequence), with no addressee and no extra edge.

The focal segment also names an unnamed person: בְּאַתְרֵיהּ דְּהַאי תַּנָּא ('in the place of this tanna'). In context he is the tanna of the baraita at Pesachim 36b:16 (אֵין אוֹפִין פַּת עָבָה ... דִּבְרֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי), picked up again at 37a:6 (וְהַאי תַּנָּא בְּיוֹם טוֹב שֶׁל פֶּסַח קָאֵי). Add one local role mention 'this tanna' with a place-usage attribute only, spoken by the anonymous discussion; do not identify him with a named person or with the school of Beit Shammai, and do not link him to Yirmeya, Rav or רבינו הקדוש.

The pair joins the last word of branch A (וּמַנּוּ: רַב) with the first name of branch B (רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא) across אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי. No relation is stated between those two tokens; the real B-branch transmission is the next pair (…|59|79, 'רב ירמיה בר אבא אמר רב'). Deleting this pair does not lose any observation, and keeping it would store the Yirmeya-Rav direction twice.

Rashi on Pesachim 37a:4 assigns one teacher per speaker: 'רביה דר' ירמיה רב רביה דרב רבינו הקדוש'. So the two רבי tokens are two role slots, one per branch, and a global same-man between the title 'Rabbi' and Rav would be false here. Scoping |4|30 to A (object = A's slot, resolved to Rav) and |79|92 to B (object = B's slot, resolved to רבינו הקדוש) follows the grammar of שְׁאֵילִית after אָמַר רַב. Subject to the voice qualification in the first finding.

'רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב: שְׁאֵילִית' makes Rav the first-person asker in B and Yirmeya only the transmitter; Rashi on Beitzah says 'רב גופיה אמר שאלית את רבי ביחוד'. Keep transmits_in_name_of (Yirmeya -> Rav, B only) as one stored direction, with no student_of or meeting implied. F2 calls Goldschmidt 'an independent translation' supporting this; that is fine as a separate translation witness, but it translates the same printed text and should not be counted as an extra vote beyond the grammar and Rashi.

Confirmed: the Davidson English prints 'Our holy Rabbi, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi' with the name outside the bold, and Steinsaltz has '(ר' יהודה הנשיא)' in brackets; the Aramaic and Wikisource have only רבינו הקדוש. These are one editorial family and count once. Store רבינו הקדוש as the literal printed label (given by the narrating voice, see the first finding) and any Judah HaNasi link only as a separate provisional identity assertion.

findings.target: F7 and ALT2 (who speaks the pat ava etymologies)
findings.reason: The conclusion holds: do not attach 'מִשּׁוּם דִּנְפִישָׁא בְּלִישָׁה' or the local-usage explanation to Rav or רבינו הקדוש. Two narrowings: the formula argument (וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא) fits Pesachim only, because Beitzah 22b:7 has אִי נָמֵי instead; and the second explanation speaks of 'this tanna' in the third person, which fits the anonymous discussion of the baraita. In Beitzah the A-branch copy stops at פַּת מְרוּבָּה, so the etymologies are never in A's report; keep ALT2 as an alternative attribution for B only, from one editorial family.

Seder HaDorot's 'ר' ירמי' בר אבא תלמיד חבר לרב היה' rests on Berakhot 27b's form of address ('לכך אמר לרב מי בדלת ולא אמר מי בדל מר'); it lists 'שאלית את רבי ומנו רב פ' כל שעה' only later, among his occurrences. reading.md's 'calls him a student-colleague ... and cites this passage' can be read as this passage being the basis, which it is not. Tosafot Kiddushin 46a's 'ונראה דתרי רב ירמיה הוו' is itself an inference from that address form; both stay on the identity layer and must not strengthen or weaken the branch-A teacher edge.

findings.target: F9, F10 and F12 (one transmitter, patronymic parent, undecided branches)
findings.reason: Wikisource reads 'אמר ר' ירמיה בר אבא ... איכא דאמרי רב ירמיה בר אבא' and Davidson reads רב in both; a title variant inside one איכא דאמרי is not grounds for two local people. 'בַּר אַבָּא' keeps a local placeholder Abba with a name-derived child_of edge, shared by both branches, even though Abba never acts; Seder HaDorot's remark on the father ('אבא אביו היה') is rightly left out. The passage never chooses between A and B, so each teacher edge stays inside its branch and neither confirms the other.

quote_checks.note: Rashi on Pesachim 37a:4:1, inside the lemma ביחוד. Supports one teacher slot per branch.

quote_checks.note: Rashi on Beitzah 22b:7:1. Supports Rav as first-person asker in B. It is on the parallel, so it supports the reading of the wording, not extra participants here.

quote_checks.note: Rashi on Beitzah 22b:7:2. Matches F2; also shows the ומנו identification is phrased about Rav in the third person, which bears on the voice qualification.

cases.question: Investigate the packed teaching chains, using Guggenheimer translation and footnote 256 plus Ohr LaYesharim and other available commentaries. Identify where chain boundaries are explicit and where the commentators differ. Earlier Tanna Yirmeya versus later Amora changes chronology; do not settle identity without support. Explain the Hebrew carefully in plain English.

findings.claim: In the Hebrew as printed, the list names eight people in a row. The linking word בשם ('in the name of') appears four times: Shimon-Yohanan, Yohanan-Yirmeya, Hanina-Miasha and Hiyya-Simai. Three joins have no linking word at all: Helbo-Shimon, Yirmeya-Hanina and Miasha-Hiyya. No 'and', no new 'said', and no other marker shows where one chain ends and the next begins.

evidence.exact_quote: רִבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ רִבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּשֵׁם רִבִּי יוֹחָנָן בְּשֵׁם רִבִּי יִרְמְיָה רִבִּי חֲנִינָא בְשֵׁם רִבִּי מְיָישָׁא רִבִּי חִיָּיא בְשֵׁם רִבִּי סִימַאי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Translation by this dossier, word for word: 'Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Shimon, in the name of Rabbi Yohanan, in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya, Rabbi Hanina, in the name of Rabbi Miasha, Rabbi Hiyya, in the name of Rabbi Simai.'

findings.reasoning: Counted directly in the saved Guggenheimer Hebrew. Every chain boundary here is an editorial decision about bare juxtapositions. The printed text does not settle any of them.
findings.graph_effect: Only the four בשם joins are text-explicit 'cites' edges, and even two of those are disputed by commentary (see F4, F5). The three bare joins are 'juxtaposed' edges. Any 'cites' reading of them belongs to a named interpretive branch.

findings.claim: The framing sentence says that Rabbi Yose (spelled יֹסֵא) 'had not heard' the teaching. Penei Moshe reads these words as the Talmud's own surprised remark about Yose, not as Yose's speech. The chain list is therefore quoted by the narrator. It is not an exchange between Yose and Helbo.

evidence.exact_quote: אָמַר לוֹן מַהוּ דֵין לְחִישָׁה וְלֹא שְׁמִיעַ דָּמַר
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Translation by this dossier: 'He said to them: What is this whispering? And had he not heard what [X] said...'

evidence.exact_quote: ומתמה הש"ס ומה היא השאלה מהו דין לחישה וכי לא שמיע ליה מה דאמר ר' חלבו וכו' שנוהגין לומר כנוסחאות הללו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Translation by this dossier: 'The Talmud expresses surprise: what is the question "what is this whispering"? Had he not heard what R. Helbo etc. said, that one customarily says these formulas?'

evidence.exact_quote: ומעירים: ולא שמיע דמר – ולא שמע (רבי יסא שלא ידע מה הציבור אומרים בזמן ששליח הציבור אומר את ברכת ההודייה) שאמר
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Translation by this dossier: 'And they remark: had he not heard what was said - he did not hear (R. Yisa, who did not know what the congregation says while the prayer leader says the thanksgiving blessing) what was said by...'

findings.reasoning: The text marks this negatively: Yose did NOT hear the chain's teaching. Both commentaries give the words to the editorial voice.
findings.graph_effect: No speech, contact or teaching edge between Yose/Yisa and any chain member. Yose's own actions (came up, saw them bowing and whispering, asked) are a scene with the anonymous congregation.

findings.claim: Guggenheimer's English keeps the Hebrew order and punctuates the list into these groups: 'Rebbi Ḥelbo, Rebbi Simeon said in the name of Rebbi Yoḥanan, in the name of Rebbi Jeremiah', then 'Rebbi Ḥanina in the name of Rebbi Miasha', then 'Rebbi Ḥiyya in the name of Rebbi Simai'. On this reading Yohanan transmits in Jeremiah's name. Miasha and Hiyya are not linked. The English does not say whether Helbo reports from Simeon or the two report together.

evidence.exact_quote: Rebbi Ḥelbo, Rebbi Simeon said in the name of Rebbi Yoḥanan, in the name of Rebbi Jeremiah, Rebbi Ḥanina in the name of Rebbi Miasha, Rebbi Ḥiyya in the name of Rebbi Simai

findings.reasoning: The English groups the pairs by commas and 'in the name of', and it adds nothing to the three bare joins. The comma after Ḥelbo has two possible meanings, and the translation does not choose between them.

findings.claim: Guggenheimer identifies this Jeremiah as an early figure: 'A Tanna of the last generation, student of R. Yehudah ben Batyra' (footnote 256). findings.claim: Ohr LaYesharim divides the list differently, into three chains. (1) Helbo in the name of Shimon (bar Ba/Abba), in the name of Yohanan. (2) 'And likewise Rabbi Yirmeya [said in the name of] Rabbi Hanina.' (3) 'And likewise Rabbi Meisha in the name of Rabbi Hiyya [bar Ba], who said it in the name of Rabbi Simai.' It puts the printed בשם after Yohanan in parentheses, which reads as marking it for removal. It supplies unbolded 'בשם' between Helbo and Shimon and between Meisha and Hiyya. It identifies Yirmeya and Meisha as Palestinian Amoraim of the third and fourth generations. On those identities, 'Yohanan in the name of Yirmeya' would run backwards in time. That fits its decision to start a new chain at Yirmeya.

findings.claim: Ohr LaYesharim reports three kinds of evidence about the two contested בשם words. Each is a different type of evidence. (a) A manuscript variant: the Rome manuscript has בשם before Meisha. (b) A correction inside the base manuscript: a later hand ('מגיה') added that בשם 'in our transmitted text'. (c) A later proposed emendation: the editor abbreviated רז"פ deleted that word, and added בשם between Yirmeya and Hanina. So the בשם before Miasha in the printed Hebrew is not original to the first scribe of the base text, according to this commentary.

lessons: Packed attribution lists need a text-level edge for each join: an explicit בשם, or a bare juxtaposition. Commentator chains go on top as named branches. Never collapse to one chain without naming its source.
Segmentation and identity can depend on each other. A commentator who dates Yirmeya late will break the chain at Yirmeya. Chronology checks must state which identity branch they assume.
Keep four evidence types apart for a single connective word: the printed edition, a manuscript variant (Rome MS), an in-manuscript corrector, and a later scholarly emendation (RZ"P).
An alternative that swaps the reporter ('some say: the colleagues in the name of X') is an alternative-reporter relation. It is not a same-man link between the two mentions of X.
A narrator's 'had he not heard what A said' is an explicit NON-contact between the observer and A.
Patronymics with unstable father names (Inia/Mina/Ina/...) need a parent placeholder carrying all the variants, not a chosen name.
Footnote teacher claims ('student of Aha') are commentary-sourced proposals and must not upgrade a text-level 'in the name of' edge.

findings.claim: Yevamot 34b sets a ten-year rule beside a short exchange. First, Rabbi Yohanan's rule: a woman who waits ten years after her husband and then remarries no longer bears children. Rav Nahman limits it to a woman who did not intend to remarry. Then Rava tells 'the daughter of Rav Hisda' that the Rabbis are gossiping about her. She answers, 'My mind was on you.' The Talmud text here does not name a first husband or call her Rava's wife. Rashi supplies both: she is Rava's wife, and her first husband was Rami bar Hama, after whom she waited ten years.

findings.claim: Several other Bavli passages show Rava with 'the daughter of Rav Hisda' in a marital or household setting. Ketubot 65a is the most explicit: Rava goes home and asks the daughter of Rav Hisda for intercourse, and she then drives Homa out of Mehoza. Shabbat 129a is part of Rava's own statement: the daughter of Rav Hisda immersed away from her husband, caught cold, and her bier was carried after Rava to Pumbedita. Berakhot 56a: bar Hadaya tells Rava his wife will die, and Rava forgives him for everything except the daughter of Rav Hisda. Rashi there says Rava's wife was the daughter of Rav Hisda. Ketubot 39b, Berakhot 62a, Ketubot 85a and Chagigah 5a show the same pairing in household or court settings.

findings.claim: In the Talmud passages checked, no text states that Rami bar Hama married a daughter of Rav Hisda. That marriage appears in commentary and reference works. Rashi on Yevamot 34b names him as the first husband. Korban Netanel says Rami was Rav Hisda's son-in-law and that his wife married Rava after he died, 'as in Bava Batra 12'. Seder HaDorot calls Rav Hisda his father-in-law and teacher. Berakhot 47b does record, as text, that Rami bar Hama died while Rava was alive: Rava explains his death.

So the Rami bar Hama marriage rests on one commentary tradition: the forecast, read as fulfilled, plus Rashi. Later works repeating it are not independent. Berakhot 47b supports only the fact that Rami died before Rava, which fits the tradition without stating it.
findings.graph_effect: If a Rami bar Hama married_to (daughter of Rav Hisda) edge is kept, mark its evidence type as commentary identification (Rashi on Yevamot 34b), not Talmud text. Its modality is completed. Its status is provisional. Add a separate text-level fact: Rami bar Hama died during Rava's lifetime (Berakhot 47b). Do not count Korban Netanel or Seder HaDorot as extra independent observations.

findings.claim: Commentators disagree about how Rava's 'I will be last' works. Maharsha says it was not a curse that Rami would die, but that Rami would divorce her and Rava would then marry her. He explains why Rava, not Rami, said 'last': Rami would avoid marrying a divorcee. Ben Yehoyada objects to that reasoning and offers alternatives, including that Rami may have been a priest. Benayahu and Sha'arei Torat Bavel read Rava's remark in Berakhot 47b as clearing himself of blame for Rami's death, a blame that arose from 'ואנא בתרא'.

evidence.exact_quote: לא קללו שימות רמי בר חמא לפניו אלא שיגרשה רמי בר חמא ואח"כ ישא אותה רבא
וקשיא לי בדבריו
מפני דאפשר רמי בר חמא היה כהן
כדי שלא יאמרו על רבא שהוא גרם שיפטר רמי בר חמא

Do not make Rami a priest (Ben Yehoyada's conjecture). Link Berakhot 47b to this episode only as a commentary connection.

findings.claim: The Talmud shows that Rav Hisda had more than one daughter. It also shows a 'daughter of Rav Hisda' married to Rabba, not Rava, in Chullin 44b. There, both Hebrew texts checked read רבה, and the Davidson English calls her 'His wife'. Eruvin 65a has an unnamed daughter speaking to her father, Rav Hisda.

lessons: Relations need modality. 'Chooses as a prospective spouse' and 'forecasts marrying after X' are different edges from married_to. A later completed marriage must be a separate edge with its own evidence.

Explanatory sentences in translations, such as 'And this is what happened...', are editorial claims. They are not text. Davidson English and Steinsaltz Hebrew share an editorial lineage and count as one source family.

'Daughter of X' is a role descriptor. Each mention should be its own local person. Joining them into one woman is an identity decision made on sourced evidence, especially when the text shows X had several daughters.
Later works that cite a forecast passage as their source for a completed marriage are circular (Korban Netanel citing Bava Batra 12). They add no independent observation.
A commentary's identification (Rashi: 'the first husband was Rami bar Hama') needs its own evidence type, distinct from Talmud text and from a modern translation.

A later work's quotation form (Tosafot: 'תרווייהו קבעינא') is not a manuscript variant. A reported reading in another work (Halakhot Gedolot 'Rami bar Abba') is a variant claim that still needs checking.
An aggadic frame (prophecy given to children) is episode metadata. It neither confirms nor denies the scene.

review.scope: Checked every dossier quote against the saved sources (all 60 quoted strings found, hashes match) and reread the surroundings of the focal segment and of each cross-passage quote (Yevamot 34b, Ketubot 65a/39b/85a, Shabbat 129a/140b, Berakhot 47b/56a/62a, Chagigah 5a, Chullin 44b, Eruvin 65a, Beitzah 29b) plus the linked commentaries; I fetched nothing new and did not check manuscripts or the Jerusalem Talmud.

findings.reason: The dossier makes every cross-passage 'daughter of Rav Hisda' married_to Rava locally, calling all but Ketubot 65a 'strong context'. The Aramaic of Ketubot 85a only has her speaking in Rava's court ('הָהִיא אִיתְּתָא דְּאִיחַיַּיבָא שְׁבוּעָה בֵּי דִינָא דְּרָבָא. אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ בַּת רַב חִסְדָּא'), and Rava later says he trusts her, with no household or marriage word; 'her husband' is added by the Davidson English. Chagigah 5a ('וְהָא רָבָא מְשַׁגַּר! שָׁאנֵי בַּת רַב חִסְדָּא') names neither what is sent nor to whom, and Ketubot 39b sets her beside Abaye's informant 'אֵם' (his foster mother), so 'told me' is not a marriage marker by itself. Grade each passage separately: Ketubot 85a gets speaks_to and trusted_by Rava only, with no married_to; Chagigah 5a and Ketubot 39b get married_to as low-to-medium context; Berakhot 56a and 62a stay medium-to-strong context.

Ketubot 65a has 'קָם רָבָא, עָל לְבֵיתֵיהּ תַּבְעַהּ לְבַת רַב חִסְדָּא', followed by her asking who was in court and chasing Homa out. That is the strongest household and intimacy context in the set, but there is no word for wife or marriage. Label it 'strongest context', not 'explicit'. No passage checked states the marriage in so many words.

findings.target: F8 (Shabbat 129a) and reading.md 'Not checked' (same death as Berakhot 56a?)
findings.reason: The Aramaic is 'וְאַמְטְיוּהָא לְעַרְסַהּ בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְפוּמְבְּדִיתָא'. ערסה is literally 'her bed' or 'couch'. 'Funeral bier' and 'Rava's wife' come from the Davidson English, and saved Rashi has no gloss on the line. So the text shows illness and being carried after Rava. It shows her death only on the translation's reading, and the open question about 'the same death' in Berakhot 56a rests on that assumption. Also, the husband in 'שֶׁלֹּא בִּפְנֵי בַּעְלָהּ' is not named. The 'כִּי הָא' story may be the anonymous discussion illustrating Rava's rule rather than 'Rava's own statement', so keep the voice open.

findings.target: proposed_local_edges: P2 wishes_or_foretells_marrying [P3,P4]; P3 forecasts_order_as_later_spouse_after P4
findings.reason: The question is 'מַאן מִינַּיְיהוּ בָּעֵית' and the answer is 'תַּרְוַיְיהוּ'. The verb is 'want', and no marriage word appears. F3 itself says the marriage sense is contextual, so the edge label should not build marriage in: use 'chooses/wants both' with marriage_sense = contextual. Rava's 'וַאֲנָא בָּתְרָא' names nobody else. 'After Rami bar Hama' is inferred from there being two men, so the object P4 should be flagged as implicit. No addressee for Rava's line is marked, and none should be filled.

The pattern 'קמיה [A] ורמי בר [B]' filled B with the last word of the patronymic. The text reads 'הֲווֹ יָתְבִי קַמֵּיהּ רָבָא וְרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא', right after 'בְּכַנְפֵיהּ דַּאֲבוּהָ'. So 'before him' points back to her father, Rav Hisda, and both men sit before him side by side. Replace B with Rami bar Hama, keep a symmetric co-presence stored once, reject the first-pass 'before' between Rava and Hama, and add both sits_before Rav Hisda.

findings.reason: 'דְּבַת רַב חִסְדָּא' plus 'דַּאֲבוּהָ' makes the daughter's kinship literal, and she sits, is addressed and answers, so she needs her own local person. findings.reason: Benayahu does report that Rami married her first and died ('וכן הוה להו שנשאה רמי בר חמא תחלה ונפטר'). But he ends by allowing that 'אנא בתרא אינו מוכרח שימות רמי בר חמא, אלא יהיה לו סיבה שיגרשנה'. He should be listed as giving both readings of Rava's words, not only the death reading. findings.reason: Seder HaDorot says 'הרי רבא ורמי ב"ח הוו בני גילי' and supports it by comparing Abaye and Rava as small children before Rabbah ('הרי אביי ורבא היו קטנים ובני גילי'). So it does not contradict Benayahu's 'בעודם ילדים קטנים'; it simply puts the point differently. The main conclusion stands: the Talmud text gives no age or peer status, so no age or peer edge is added.

cases.question: Reconstruct the legal exchange and cited authorities across adjacent segments; distinguish a remembered practice, a live challenge, the response and alternative reported wording. Do not infer direct meetings from all citations.

findings.claim: The focal segment is the last of four moves in one narrated exchange that starts at 103a:5. First, Rava is shown performing a practice: at Rava's house he blesses the spices before the light, with Rav Huna bar Yehuda present. Second, Rav Huna bar Yehuda challenges him on the spot. Third, a source is supplied: the Mishnah, in which both schools put the candle first. Fourth, at 103a:7, Rava answers.

evidence.exact_quote: רַב הוּנָא בַּר יְהוּדָה אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רָבָא, אַיְיתוֹ לְקַמַּיְיהוּ מָאוֹר וּבְשָׂמִים. בָּרֵיךְ רָבָא אַבְּשָׂמִים בְּרֵישָׁא וַהֲדַר אַמָּאוֹר.
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rav Huna bar Yehuda happened to come to Rava's house. They brought before them light and spices. Rava blessed over the spices first and then over the light.'

evidence.exact_quote: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְהָא בֵּין בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵין בֵּית הִילֵּל — מָאוֹר בְּרֵישָׁא וַהֲדַר אַבְּשָׂמִים.
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'He said to him: But according to both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, light comes first and then spices!'

evidence.exact_quote: וּמַאי הִיא? דִּתְנַן, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: נֵר וּמָזוֹן, בְּשָׂמִים וְהַבְדָּלָה. וּבֵית הִילֵּל אוֹמְרִים: נֵר וּבְשָׂמִים, וּמָזוֹן וְהַבְדָּלָה.
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'And what is it? As we learned [in the Mishnah]: Beit Shammai say: candle and food [Grace], spices and havdala. Beit Hillel say: candle and spices, and food and havdala.'

evidence.exact_quote: עָנֵי רָבָא בָּתְרֵיהּ וְאָמַר: זוֹ דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rava answered after him and said: This is the statement of Rabbi Meir'

findings.reasoning: The words 'אמר ליה' in 103a:5 have no new subject, so the speaker is still Rav Huna bar Yehuda, the visitor just named, and the addressee is Rava. Rashbam states this outright (F02). 'בתריה' (after him) in 103a:7 points back to that challenger. So 103a:7 is Rava's reply inside a single narrated encounter, not a free-standing statement.
findings.graph_effect: Add a narrated encounter between Rava and Rav Huna bar Yehuda: a visit at Rava's house (103a:5). Add challenges: Rav Huna bar Yehuda -> Rava (103a:5). Add responds_to: Rava -> Rav Huna bar Yehuda (103a:7). Within 103a:5-8 this is the only narrated co-presence (103a:9 narrates a separate visit). Treat it as a literary narrative of a meeting, not an independently dated event.

findings.claim: Commentary (Rashbam) confirms that Rav Huna bar Yehuda is the challenger and Rava the addressee. Rashbam says the challenge came after Rava finished havdala, on the close of an ordinary Shabbat. He also records that he rejects a reading 'ולא פליגי' (and they do not disagree) in the challenge.

evidence.exact_quote: א"ל - רב הונא לרבא לאחר שגמר הבדלה והא בין ב"ש כו' ולא פליגי לא גרסינן:
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'He said to him: Rav Huna to Rava, after he finished havdala. "But both Beit Shammai..." We do not read "and they do not disagree".'

evidence.exact_quote: רב הונא בר יהודה איקלע לבי רבא - במוצאי שבת של חול:
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rav Huna bar Yehuda happened to come to Rava's house: on the close of a Shabbat followed by a weekday.'

findings.reasoning: This is a commentator's reading. It identifies the speaker and addressee and makes a textual choice. The rejected reading 'ולא פליגי' is a source-variant note: Rashbam knew texts with those words. That wording closely resembles the Berakhot 52b parallel's 'לא פליגי' (F07). That the rejected reading came from the Berakhot parallel is my inference, not something Rashbam says.
findings.graph_effect: This supports the direction of F01's challenge and response edges. Store 'ולא פליגי לא גרסינן' as a commentator's source-variant note on 103a:5. It does not change any person relation.

findings.claim: In 103a:7 Rava names two tannaim, but he meets neither. He labels the Mishnah's version of the Beit Shammai / Beit Hillel dispute as 'the words of Rabbi Meir', and he sets against it a version taught in Rabbi Yehuda's name. Rava attributes one text and quotes another. Neither act describes an encounter.

evidence.exact_quote: זוֹ דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר, אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: לֹא נֶחְלְקוּ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִילֵּל עַל הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁהוּא בַּתְּחִלָּה וְעַל הַבְדָּלָה שֶׁהִיא בַּסּוֹף,
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'This is the statement of Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yehuda says: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree over the food [Grace], which is first, or over havdala, which is last'

evidence.exact_quote: עני רבא בתריה ואמר זו דברי ר' מאיר אבל ר' יהודה אומר לא נחלקו בית שמאי ובית הילל על המזון שהוא בתחלה ועל הבדלה שהיא בסוף

findings.reasoning: 'זו' (this) refers to the Mishnah just quoted in 103a:6. 'זו דברי רבי מאיר' is therefore an amora assigning an anonymous tannaitic text to a named tanna. 'רבי יהודה אומר' introduces a tannaitic teaching, which the Tosefta preserves under Rabbi Yehuda's name (F06). The William Davidson and Wikisource texts agree word for word, apart from vocalisation and abbreviation. Both are printed-tradition digital texts, not independent manuscripts.
findings.graph_effect: Change the Rava -> Rabbi Meir pair from 'explains'/'disputes' to attributes_text_to: Rava says the anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir's version. Add cites_teaching: Rava -> Rabbi Yehuda. Add no meeting, teacher, or contemporaneity edge between Rava and either tanna.

findings.claim: Commentary (Rashbam) explains Rava's attribution by a general rule: an anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir. On this reading, the Mishnah is how Rabbi Meir taught the schools' dispute. So Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree about what the two schools disagreed about. This is a disagreement between two reports of an earlier dispute.

evidence.exact_quote: זו דברי ר"מ - דהכי הוו תני לפלוגתייהו דב"ש וב"ה דסתם מתני' ר"מ:
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'This is Rabbi Meir's statement: because this is how he taught the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, since an anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir.'

evidence.exact_quote: לֹא נֶחְלְקוּ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִילֵּל עַל הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁהוּא בַּתְּחִלָּה
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree over the food, which is first'

findings.reasoning: Rabbi Yehuda's 'לא נחלקו... על מה נחלקו' (they did not disagree about X; about what did they disagree?) is a form that corrects another report of a dispute. In the Tosefta, Rabbi Yehuda's sentence stands with no Rabbi Meir named (F06). The name Rabbi Meir therefore enters through Rava's attribution. Rashbam explains that attribution with the anonymous-Mishnah rule. The two tannaim are not shown talking to each other.
findings.graph_effect: Keep Rabbi Meir <-> Rabbi Yehuda as disputes, but subtype it as disagrees_on_report_of_earlier_dispute. Record the provenance: Rabbi Meir's side comes from Rava's attribution, which Rashbam explains by the anonymous-Mishnah rule. Do not add a direct-exchange edge between the two tannaim from this passage.

findings.claim: Rabbi Yehuda does not 'explain' Beit Shammai. He reports the positions of both schools and says where their dispute lies: over light and spices. In this report Beit Shammai put light first and Beit Hillel put spices first. The segment also contains a Beit Shammai vs Beit Hillel dispute, and it appears in both versions (Mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda).

evidence.exact_quote: עַל מָה נֶחְלְקוּ? עַל הַמָּאוֹר וְעַל הַבְּשָׂמִים. בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: מָאוֹר וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּשָׂמִים, וּבֵית הִילֵּל אוֹמְרִים: בְּשָׂמִים וְאַחַר כָּךְ מָאוֹר.
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'About what did they disagree? About light and spices. Beit Shammai say: light and afterwards spices; Beit Hillel say: spices and afterwards light.'

findings.reasoning: The input pair's pattern '[A] אומר לא נחלקו [B]' catches only the first-named school. Rabbi Yehuda's statement concerns both schools equally. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are collective schools, not individuals. The segment boundary falls mid-sentence: 103a:7 ends with a comma and 103a:8 continues the same statement.
findings.graph_effect: Replace 'Rabbi Yehuda explains Beit Shammai' with two edges: reports_position_of Rabbi Yehuda -> Beit Shammai and reports_position_of Rabbi Yehuda -> Beit Hillel. Add disputes Beit Shammai <-> Beit Hillel, stored once, with two version branches (the Mishnah per Rava's attribution to Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yehuda). Type both nodes as collective schools. Read 103a:7 together with 103a:8.

findings.claim: The Tosefta preserves Rabbi Yehuda's teaching on its own, with the same assignment of positions to the schools as the Bavli. Two editions on Sefaria were checked: Lieberman (codex Vienna) and the default text. Neither names Rabbi Meir in this sentence.

evidence.exact_quote: אמ' ר' יהודה לא נחלקו בית שמיי ובית הלל על ברכת המזון שהיא בתחלה ועל הבדלה שהיא בסוף, על מה נחלקו על המאור ועל הבשמים, שבית שמיי אומר מאור ואחר כך בשמים, ובית הלל או' בשמים ואחר כך מאור.
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rabbi Yehuda said: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree over Grace after Meals, which is first, or over havdala, which is last. About what did they disagree? About light and spices: Beit Shammai say light and then spices, Beit Hillel say spices and then light.'

evidence.exact_quote: א"ר יהודה לא נחלקו ב"ש וב"ה על ברהמ"ז שבתחלה ועל הבדלה שבסוף

findings.reasoning: Both Tosefta texts attribute the teaching to Rabbi Yehuda, which supports the Bavli's 'רבי יהודה אומר'. The Tosefta reads 'ברכת המזון' where the Bavli has 'המזון'. That is a small wording difference, not a change in who holds what. Sefaria's links index ties 103a:7-8 to several Tosefta numbers (5:25, 5:30, 5:31, Lieberman 5:30). The Rabbi Yehuda sentence appears at Lieberman 5:30 and default-text 5:31. Default-text 5:25 and 5:30 deal with other Beit Shammai / Beit Hillel meal disputes.
findings.graph_effect: Attach the Tosefta as a tannaitic witness for Rabbi Yehuda's reports_position_of edges (F05). Because the Tosefta names no Rabbi Meir here, the Rabbi Meir side of F04 remains an amoraic attribution.

findings.claim: The Bavli tells the same exchange at Berakhot 52b in different words. There, Rav Huna bar Yehuda saw Rava bless the spices first, and the Mishnah text sits inside his own challenge, introduced by 'דתניא'. Pesachim has a separate 'ומאי היא? דתנן' step. Berakhot also lacks 'ואמר' after 'עני רבא בתריה'.

evidence.exact_quote: רַב הוּנָא בַּר יְהוּדָה אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רָבָא. חַזְיֵיהּ לְרָבָא דְּבָרֵיךְ אַבְּשָׂמִים בְּרֵישָׁא. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מִכְּדִי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִלֵּל אַמָּאוֹר לָא פְּלִיגִי, דְּתַנְיָא
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rav Huna bar Yehuda happened to come to Rava's house. He saw Rava blessing over the spices first. He said to him: Now, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel do not disagree about the light, as it is taught...'

evidence.exact_quote: עָנֵי רָבָא בָּתְרֵיהּ: זוֹ דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rava answered after him: This is the statement of Rabbi Meir'

evidence.exact_quote: א"ל מכדי ב"ש וב"ה אמאור לא פליגי דתניא בש"א נר ומזון בשמים והבדלה
וּמַאי הִיא? דִּתְנַן,
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'And what is it? As we learned [in the Mishnah]'

findings.reasoning: In Berakhot the source citation is grammatically part of Rav Huna bar Yehuda's speech. In Pesachim, 'ומאי היא' can be read either as the anonymous Gemara stepping in to supply the source or as Rav Huna bar Yehuda continuing. The Berakhot wording favours the second, but the parallel does not settle Pesachim's own wording. Berakhot's 'דתניא' usually introduces a baraita, yet the text it introduces matches the Mishnah. The Berakhot English and Steinsaltz both render it as 'in our mishna' (S14, S17), and both come from one editorial project. This is a difference in reported wording of the same exchange. It is not a second encounter.
findings.graph_effect: Record the Berakhot 52b text as a parallel version of the same narrated encounter. Do not count it as an independent second meeting between Rava and Rav Huna bar Yehuda. Put the Mishnah citation inside Rav Huna bar Yehuda's speech in the Berakhot branch, and keep the speaker open in the Pesachim branch.

findings.claim: The Jerusalem Talmud reports Rabbi Yehuda's teaching with the schools reversed: Beit Shammai put spices first and Beit Hillel put light first. It then gives a ruling from Rabbi Ba and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the law follows whoever says spices first. All three Yerushalmi texts checked (Guggenheimer Hebrew, Venice, Mechon-Mamre) have this order.

evidence.exact_quote: תני אמר ר' יהודה לא נחלקו בית שמאי ובית הלל על המזון שהוא בתחילה ועל הבדלה שהיא בסוף ועל מה נחלקו על המאור ועל הבשמים שבית שמאי אומרי' בשמי' ומאור ובית הלל אומרי' מאור ובשמים
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'It was taught: Rabbi Yehuda said: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree over the food, which is first, or over havdala, which is last. About what did they disagree? About light and spices: Beit Shammai say spices and light, Beit Hillel say light and spices.'

evidence.exact_quote: רבי בא ורב יהודה בשם רב הלכה כדברי מי שאומר בשמים ואחר כך מאור
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'Rabbi Ba and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the law follows the words of whoever says spices and afterwards light.'

evidence.exact_quote: שֶׁבֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים בְּשָׂמִים וּמָאוֹר. וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים מָאוֹר וּבְשָׂמִים.
שבית שמאי אומרים בשמים ומאור. ובית הלל אומרים מאור ובשמים.

findings.reasoning: This is a real alternative report of what Rabbi Yehuda said. The practical order in the ruling (spices before light) matches Rava's practice and the Bavli's 'נהגו העם', but the school it is credited to is reversed. The Yerushalmi does not name the school in its ruling ('whoever says'). Its three texts may share one textual tradition, so they should not count as three independent witnesses. Guggenheimer's English (S25) renders the ruling as 'Rebbi Abba and Rav Yehudah: Practice follows...'. The English does not render 'בשם רב', although his Hebrew edition (S24) has it.
findings.graph_effect: Put the content of Rabbi Yehuda's reports_position_of edges on version branches: Bavli and Tosefta say Beit Hillel puts spices first, the Yerushalmi says Beit Shammai does. Do not merge the branches or treat either as the correction of the other. Rabbi Ba, Rav Yehuda and Rav belong to the Yerushalmi passage, not to Pesachim 103a:7. Their chain (Rabbi Ba and Rav Yehuda reporting in the name of Rav) is a separate observation in Yerushalmi Berakhot 8:5.

findings.claim: The segment right after the focal one adds a report of practice: Rabbi Yochanan says the people follow Beit Hillel according to Rabbi Yehuda's version. The Aramaic does not say that Rava quotes Rabbi Yochanan, and it does not say that Rava acted on this custom. The English sentence 'Rava acted as dictated by this custom' is the translator's addition. It follows Steinsaltz's 'וכך נהג רבא' and has no Aramaic counterpart.

evidence.exact_quote: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: נָהֲגוּ הָעָם כְּבֵית הִילֵּל וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.
evidence.translation_by_researcher: Researcher translation: 'And Rabbi Yochanan said: The people have adopted the practice of Beit Hillel, according to Rabbi Yehuda.'

evidence.exact_quote: Rava acted as dictated by this custom.
ואמר ר' יוחנן: נהגו העם כבית הילל ואליבא [ועל פי שיטת] ר' יהודה, וכך נהג רבא.

findings.reasoning: 'ואמר רבי יוחנן' can be read as part of Rava's reply (Rava citing Rabbi Yochanan) or as the anonymous Gemara adding a supporting statement. The words do not decide between these. The English and Steinsaltz belong to one editorial project, so their shared gloss is one interpretation, not two. Rava's action at 103a:5 does match the practice Rabbi Yochanan reports. Even so, the text does not state that Rava was following him.

findings.claim: Tosafot reads Rabbi Yochanan's statement as disagreeing with the anonymous Mishnah. Tosafot suggests that Rabbi Yochanan had learned the Mishnah as an individual's view, explicitly Rabbi Meir's. It adds that this 'נהגו' is not the weaker 'we do not instruct, but we do not stop them' kind found elsewhere. Rashi on Berakhot 52b confirms the reading 'ואמר רבי יוחנן', which implies he knew another reading.

findings.reasoning: Tosafot's harmonisation assumes that Rabbi Yochanan knew the Mishnah as Rabbi Meir's. That is a later commentator's reconstruction, not something the Talmud says. Rashi's 'גרסי'' marks a textual choice, but he does not state which alternative he rejects. It is not established here whether that alternative dropped the Rabbi Yochanan line or read a different name.
findings.graph_effect: Record Tosafot's view as commentary: Rabbi Yochanan's report presupposes that the Mishnah is Rabbi Meir's individual version. That supports the provenance note in F04, but it adds no Rabbi Yochanan-Rabbi Meir relation. Record Rashi's 'גרסי'' as a commentator's note that a textual variant existed, with the variant itself unknown.

findings.claim: Context only, a separate episode: in 103a:9-10 a different visitor, Rav Yaakov bar Abba, challenges Rava's practice of blessing twice over wine. This time Rava justifies himself by remembered practice: 'when we were at the Exilarch's house, this is what we did'. He then appeals to the students of Rav, and the text itself calls Rav Beruna and Rav Chananel students of Rav. This is where the passage has a remembered practice in the strict sense. The 103a:5-8 exchange rests instead on a text citation plus a report of popular custom.

At 103a:7 he defends himself by a tannaitic text. The student-of relation for Rav Beruna and Rav Chananel is stated by the text ('תלמידי דרב'). lessons: 'זו דברי X' after a quoted anonymous source is an attribution of a text, not a dispute with X or an explanation of X. It needs its own relation kind (attributes_text_to).
'X אומר לא נחלקו A ו-B' reports the dispute of both A and B. A name-pair extractor that pairs X only with the nearest name loses the second school and the A <-> B dispute.

The addressee of a response ('עני X בתריה') is often named only in an earlier segment. Pairs should be read across segment boundaries, because Sefaria segments can break mid-sentence (103a:7 ends with a comma).
Parallel tellings of one encounter (Pesachim 103a / Berakhot 52b) are version branches of one observation, not two meetings.
The same tanna's teaching can come down with reversed content (Bavli and Tosefta vs Yerushalmi). Edge content needs version branches, not a single value.

Translation glosses ('Rava acted as dictated by this custom') can add relations with no counterpart in the source. The English and Steinsaltz belong to one editorial project and are not independent corroboration.

Useful distinctions for practice-related edges: practice performed (Rava's blessing), live challenge (Rav Huna bar Yehuda), text-based response (Rava citing a baraita), reported popular custom (Rabbi Yochanan's 'נהגו העם'), and remembered personal practice ('כי הוינן בי ריש גלותא', 103a:9).

review.scope: I checked every person-, speaker- and relation-bearing finding (F01-F12), the four proposed corrections and the reading.md relations list against the saved sources (Pesachim 103a Aramaic, English and Wikisource; Berakhot 52b; Rashbam, Rashi, Tosafot and Steinsaltz; Tosefta; the three Yerushalmi texts; Mishnah Berakhot 8:5; Rif Pesachim 21a); I fetched nothing new and did not check manuscripts, the codes, or anyone's historical identity.

findings.reason: The dossier saved Rif Pesachim 21a (S28) but used it only to count votes for Rabbi Yehuda's order (A5). The Rif has no 'ומאי היא' step: it reads 'א"ל והא בין ב"ש ובין ב"ה מאור ואח"כ בשמים דתנן ב"ש אומרים...', so the Mishnah quotation runs straight on inside Rav Huna bar Yehuda's challenge, as in Berakhot 52b. The Rif also reads 'עני רבא בתריה זו דברי ר' מאיר' with no 'ואמר'. Record the Rif as a later-quotation witness for reading A2 (the challenger quotes the Mishnah) and for the shorter reply formula. Keep it separate from the printed Pesachim text. It does not settle who speaks 'ומאי היא' in the printed Pesachim, so the speaker there stays open.

The words 'אַיְיתוֹ לְקַמַּיְיהוּ מָאוֹר וּבְשָׂמִים' ('they brought before them light and spices', 103a:5) name unnamed people who carry the light and spices into the room where Rava and Rav Huna bar Yehuda sit. So F01's statement that the visit is 'the only narrated co-presence' should not read as if only two people were there. Add an unnamed plural local participant (people of the household or servers, bringing items) with low graph weight and no identity. They play no speaking or legal role. The Berakhot 52b telling and the Rif ('אייתו לקמיה') word this differently, so the participant belongs to the Pesachim wording branch.

'נָהֲגוּ הָעָם כְּבֵית הִילֵּל וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה' says the people follow Beit Hillel, as Rabbi Yehuda's version reports Beit Hillel's view. The dossier stores only 'the people follows_version_of Rabbi Yehuda'. That leaves out the main object of the practice, Beit Hillel. Store it as one observation: reporter Rabbi Yochanan; the people (a collective, not a person) follow Beit Hillel, qualified by 'according to Rabbi Yehuda'. The dossier rightly keeps 'Rava cites Rabbi Yochanan' provisional. Its refusal to add 'Rava follows the custom' also stands: that comes only from the English 'Rava acted as dictated by this custom' and Steinsaltz's 'וכך נהג רבא', and the Rif, a later quotation, also lacks it.

findings.target: F11 / proposed correction 4 (child_of Rav Huna bar Yehuda -> Yehuda)
findings.reason: Keep the child_of claim and the local parent placeholder from 'רַב הוּנָא בַּר יְהוּדָה', as the project rule requires. But the dossier marks it 'literal kinship' and calls it a 'literal patronymic'. The rule asks us to flag that such a form may work as a fixed name rather than tell us about a real parent. Mark it as name-embedded kinship, literal by default, possibly a fixed name. Also note that Rashbam calls the same local man simply 'רב הונא' ('א"ל - רב הונא לרבא'). That short form refers back to this visitor. It must not be used to link him to any other Rav Huna.

findings.target: F01 / proposed correction 4 (responds_to Rava -> Rav Huna bar Yehuda)
findings.reason: The challenge direction holds: 'אֲמַר לֵיהּ' in 103a:5 has no new subject, and Rashbam states 'רב הונא לרבא'. The reply in 103a:7 is marked only by 'עָנֵי רָבָא בָּתְרֵיהּ' ('Rava answered after him'). There is no 'ליה' marking an addressee. Steinsaltz glosses it 'כמשלים את דבריו' (as completing his words). Store it as Rava responding to Rav Huna bar Yehuda's challenge, with the target being the challenge. Mark the addressee as inferred from the sequence ('after him'), not as a marked 'said to him'.

findings.target: F04 / proposed correction 2 (Rabbi Meir <-> Rabbi Yehuda disputes)
findings.reason: The opposition exists only in Rava's words 'זוֹ דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר, אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר'. The Mishnah (S19) is anonymous, and the Tosefta (S20, S21) gives Rabbi Yehuda's sentence without naming Rabbi Meir. Rashbam's 'דסתם מתני' ר"מ' is a later explanation of Rava's attribution, not separate proof of it. The dossier's subtype and provenance note are right. The edge should carry the evidence type 'amoraic attribution, explained by commentary' and must never count as a tannaitic record of two men arguing. Medium confidence is appropriate.

findings.target: F03 / proposed correction 1 (Rava -> Rabbi Meir attributes_text_to; Rava -> Rabbi Yehuda cites_teaching)
findings.reason: 'זו' points back to the Mishnah just quoted in 103a:6 ('דִּתְנַן, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: נֵר וּמָזוֹן...'). So Rava is naming who taught that text, not arguing with or explaining Rabbi Meir. The Wikisource text, the Berakhot 52b parallel and the Rif all have 'זו דברי ר' מאיר' at this point. No meeting, teacher or same-time edge follows from either tanna being named, and the dossier adds none.

findings.target: F05 / proposed correction 3 (Rabbi Yehuda reports_position_of both schools)
findings.reason: 103a:8 continues Rabbi Yehuda's sentence: 'בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: מָאוֹר וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּשָׂמִים, וּבֵית הִילֵּל אוֹמְרִים: בְּשָׂמִים וְאַחַר כָּךְ מָאוֹר'. So he reports both schools, and the input pair caught only the first one. The Yerushalmi branch reversal (F08) checks out in all three saved texts ('שבית שמאי אומרים בשמים ומאור'). The dossier rightly keeps it as a separate branch rather than a correction. One small addition: in 103a:5 Rav Huna bar Yehuda also states both schools' shared position ('בֵּין בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵין בֵּית הִילֵּל — מָאוֹר בְּרֵישָׁא'), following the Mishnah's version. That can be stored as content of his challenge, not as a new relation to either school.

The student_of claims stand, because the text says 'רַב בְּרוֹנָא וְרַב חֲנַנְאֵל תַּלְמִידֵי דְרַב'. But 'אֲנָא עֲבַדִי כְּתַלְמִידֵי דְרַב' tells a story as precedent inside Rava's argument. It is not an event of this visit, and it gives no student_of or meeting link between Rava and Rav or his students. The remembered practice 'כִּי הֲוֵינַן בֵּי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא הָכִי עָבְדִינַן' is in the first person plural: a group practice Rava says he shared, at an unnamed Exilarch's house. Rashbam's lemma reads 'רבי יעקב בר אבא' where the printed text has 'רַב יַעֲקֹב'. Keep that as a commentary name variant, not a correction.

findings.target: F10 (Tosafot and Rashi on Rabbi Yochanan)
findings.reason: The Tosafot on Pesachim (S12) does say 'והאי נהגו לא הוי כהאי נהגו דבפרק בתרא דתענית'. The Tosafot on Berakhot (S18), cited next to it, answers differently: 'אבל הכא יכול להיות דאין כאן אלא נהגו גרידא'. These are two commentary positions and should not be merged into one 'Tosafot says'. Rashi's 'וא"ר יוחנן – גרסי'' shows a textual choice but does not identify the rejected reading, as the dossier says. Neither note adds or removes a person relation.

cases.question: In Sanhedrin 101a:6, what does the text say about Rav Huna's ruling on Rabbi Yosi, the danger explanation and the story of Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef and the cedar? Which graph claims are explicit, which rest on interpretation, and which alternatives must stay open?

findings.claim: Both readings of Rav Huna's line are attested, with and without the negation אין. The sources are of different kinds and should not be pooled. (a) Texts that quote the line without אין: Rif, Yad Ramah, the Vilna Rosh, and a Ramban responsum quoted in Beit Yosef. (b) Texts that quote it with אין: Bach's Gemara, and the Gemara in front of Be'er Sheva. Radbaz prints it in parentheses, as the Wikisource/Koren text does; whether that means 'read' or 'delete' is not stated. (c) Reports about other books: Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and its gloss, Bach and Be'er Sheva. (d) A later emendation: the Gra deletes the word, as reported in a Soncino footnote. (e) Modern translations: the William Davidson English and Steinsaltz omit it; Soncino keeps it.

findings.reasoning: The Ramban reading comes from Beit Yosef's quotation (S11, F1b), so it is second-hand. The William Davidson English and the Steinsaltz Hebrew come from one editorial project and count as one witness. So does the Koren Hebrew, which keeps the parentheses but whose English drops the word. Be'er Sheva's claim that 'most decisors' read without אין is his own report, not a count made here. The Semag gloss seems to say that 'not' was deleted to match Alfasi and Asheri while most old books had it, but the sentence is compressed. Bach reads it both ways across Semag copies. The parentheses in the Wikisource/Koren text match the word the Gra deletes. That they record his deletion specifically is an inference; the page does not say so.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c6 and c7 as a two-branch group; do not choose either. Record each branch's support by evidence type: medieval quoting texts, reports about books, a later emendation, modern translations. Do not count two William Davidson outputs as two witnesses.

findings.claim: Beit Yosef quotes a Ramban responsum that gives Rav Huna's ruling without אין.

evidence.exact_quote: ובתשובות הרמב"ן כתוב סימן רפ"ב

findings.reasoning: This is inside Beit Yosef's quotation of the Ramban's responsum. It is therefore a quotation within a quotation, not a direct witness to the Ramban's text.
findings.graph_effect: Adds one more quoted witness for the branch without the negation, marked as second-hand.

findings.claim: The Vilna Rosh attributes the ruling to Ulla (עולא), not Rav Huna. Radbaz, quoting the Rosh on the same point, has Rav Huna. Every other text checked has Rav Huna.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר עולא הלכה כרבי יוסי.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Ulla said: the halakha is like R. Yosi.

evidence.exact_quote: הביא הרא"ש ז"ל ראיה

evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rav Huna said: (not) the halakha is like R. Yosi.

findings.reasoning: There is one printed witness for Ulla, and another quotation of the same Rosh passage reads Rav Huna. That suggests a transmission variant inside the Rosh rather than a separate Talmudic tradition. This dossier cannot tell which way it ran.
findings.graph_effect: Add a source-variant branch for the speaker of c6/c7: Rav Huna (the Talmud text and most quoting witnesses) or Ulla (the Vilna Rosh only). Record it as a variant in a quoting work. Do not replace Rav Huna, and do not create an Ulla-Rabbi Yosi edge outside the branch.

findings.claim: The Vilna Rosh gives the story's subject as 'רבי יצחק ברבי יוסף', with the title Rabbi for both son and father. The Talmud texts, Radbaz, Yad Ramah and Seder HaDorot have 'רב יצחק בר יוסף'.

evidence.exact_quote: כי הא דרבי יצחק ברבי יוסף אבלע בארזא.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: as in the case of Rabbi Yitzhak son of Rabbi Yosef, who was swallowed in a cedar.

evidence.exact_quote: כי הא דרב יצחק בר יוסף דאיבלע בארזא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: as in the case of Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, who was swallowed in a cedar.

evidence.exact_quote: כי הא דרב יצחק בר יוסף שבא לשאול בשדים
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: as in the case of Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, who came to ask of demons.

findings.reasoning: In every version the patronymic names a father Yosef. Only the titles differ. A title variant is not identity evidence.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c8 (child_of Yosef) and the local placeholder for Yosef. Add the Rosh's form as a name variant on the local person, with 'Rabbi' as a variant title for the father. Do not merge with any other Yitzhak or Yosef on this basis.

findings.claim: The text does not say who speaks 'ואף רבי יוסי לא אמרה אלא משום סכנה'. The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz give it to the anonymous Gemara voice ('The Gemara notes', 'ומעירים'). Rif, Yad Ramah, the Rosh and Soncino run it straight on from the ruling with no new speaker, which leaves open that it continues Rav Huna's statement.

evidence.exact_quote: The Gemara notes:
ומעירים:
as R. Jose</font>, and even <font style= >he said it only on account of its danger</font>
אמר רב הונא הלכה כרבי יוסי ואף רבי יוסי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rav Huna said: the halakha is like R. Yosi, and even R. Yosi...

findings.reasoning: The Aramaic has no speech marker between the ruling and 'ואף'. Assigning it to the anonymous voice is an editorial choice in one translation project. The continuous layout in the medieval quotations shows that the text can be read either way; it does not prove Rav Huna said it.
findings.graph_effect: c5 should carry a speaker branch: anonymous Talmudic voice, or Rav Huna continuing. Do not create a Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yosi edge except inside that branch.

findings.claim: The Talmud text does not say that Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef consulted demons, and it names no demon. Rashi, Yad Ramah, the William Davidson English, Steinsaltz, the Soncino notes and Seder HaDorot all supply both.

evidence.exact_quote: היה שואל במעשה שדים ובקש השד להזיקו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: He used to ask by means of demon-craft, and the demon sought to harm him.

evidence.exact_quote: שבא לשאול בשדים ורצה השד להרגו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: who came to ask of demons, and the demon wanted to kill him.

evidence.exact_quote: consulted a demon and as a result
שנשאל בשד וגרם לו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: who inquired of a demon, and it caused him...

evidence.exact_quote: אלמא להדיא דשרי מעשה שדים מדרב יצחק דהיה שואל במעשה שדים
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: So clearly demon-craft is permitted, from Rav Yitzhak who used to ask by demon-craft.

findings.reasoning: The link comes from 'כי הא' ('as in this case'), which offers the story as an example of the danger. Commentators agree broadly, but it is still an interpretation. Bach even builds a legal inference on Rav Yitzhak's conduct, which shows how much weight the supplied detail can carry.
findings.graph_effect: Any 'Rav Yitzhak inquired of demons' action, and any demon participant, belongs in a commentary layer with basis interpretation, attributed to the commentators who say it. Keep it out of the explicit text layer. The demon is an unnamed non-human agent, not a person.

findings.claim: Commentators disagree about what swallowed him and what the miracle was. Rashi: the demon sought to harm him, and the miracle was that the cedar swallowed him. Rashash, Steinsaltz and the William Davidson English: the swallowing was the harm, and the miracle was that the cedar split and spat him out. Rashash calls this the plain sense. Seder HaDorot sets Rashi against the Gemara's wording. The Soncino note: the demon turned itself into a tree and swallowed him. Yad Ramah: the demon wanted to kill him, a miracle was done, and he was swallowed 'בארץ' (in the earth).

evidence.exact_quote: ונעשה לו נס ובלעו הארז
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and a miracle was done for him and the cedar swallowed him.

evidence.exact_quote: פשוטו משמע דהבלעת הארז היתה ע"י השד והנס הוא שפלטי'. ורש"י אולי רצה להשוות בליעת ארז זו להא דישעיה דבס"פ החולץ דהוה לאצולא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: The plain sense is that the swallowing by the cedar was done by the demon, and the miracle is that it spat him out. Rashi perhaps wanted to compare this cedar-swallowing to that of Isaiah at the end of Perek HaCholetz, which was to rescue him.

evidence.exact_quote: מלשון רש"י נראה דנס היה שבלעו הארז ומלשון הגמ' משמע דהנס היה שפקע הארז.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: From Rashi's wording the miracle was that the cedar swallowed him; from the Gemara's wording the miracle was that the cedar split.

evidence.exact_quote: and a miracle was performed for him and the cedar split and expelled him.
He consulted a demon, which turned itself into a tree and swallowed him</font>; it was only through a miracle that he escaped.
ונעשה לו נס ונבלע בארץ וכי תימא וליעקריה לשדא מיניה קב"ה הוא דבעא לאחיזי ליה ניסא רבא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: and a miracle was done for him and he was swallowed in the earth. And if you ask, let Him uproot the demon from him: the Holy One wanted to show him a great miracle.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר שם איבלע בארזא אתיוה לארזא ונסרוה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: He uttered a Name and was swallowed in a cedar; they brought the cedar and sawed it.

findings.reasoning: The text's sequence is: swallowed, miracle, cedar split, released. It leaves open whether 'ניסא' names the swallowing or the splitting, and who did the swallowing. Yad Ramah's 'בארץ' may be a different wording or a print error; this dossier cannot decide. Yevamot 49b is the story Rashash points to: Isaiah flees into a cedar by uttering a Name. It is a literary parallel, not evidence about Rav Yitzhak.
findings.graph_effect: The first reading's 'rescue' event ('The cedar split and released him in a miracle') follows the Rashash / plain-sense grouping. Split it into three nodes: swallowing (agent not stated), miracle (referent open) and split-and-release. Mark the miracle referent as an interpretation branch: Rashi, swallowing; Rashash / Steinsaltz / William Davidson / Seder HaDorot on the Gemara's wording, splitting. Keep 'cedar is the demon' (Soncino note) and 'earth' (Yad Ramah) as recorded alternatives, not defaults.

findings.claim: In the Tosefta parallel, Rabbi Yosi's prohibition concerns whispering (לוחשין) about demons, not asking (שואלין). In the Vienna codex he is ר' יוסה. Tosefta Kifshutah sets the Tosefta wording against the Bavli's.

evidence.exact_quote: יוסה | ד א ל יוסי.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Variant apparatus: 'Yosah' — three other witnesses (sigla ד, א, ל) read 'Yosi'.

evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: same, with the spelling R. Yosi.

findings.reasoning: This is a parallel source with different wording. The attribution to Rabbi Yosi is the same. It is not an independent second observation of the Bavli's teaching, and it has no Rav Huna and no story (chapter 7 in the Vienna text checked). Lieberman's apparatus shows only a spelling difference in the name (יוסה/יוסי).
