Tosafot on Sanhedrin 36a and other Rishonim (e.g. Ramah is covered; Ran, Rif and Rosh on Gittin not checked) were not examined for this line. The Sefaria links for 36a:5-7 list no Tosafot, but that does not show that none exists.
Whether Rav's report ('הוו מתחלי', they would begin) describes one vote or repeated practice. The Sanhedrin wording allows either.

corrections.change: Relabel the statement as 'Between Moses and Rabbi no one else combined Torah and greatness (praise of Rabbi)', and add Moses and Rabbi as 'about' roles.
corrections.why: The Gemara's objections and Rashi/Yad Ramah show that the claim is about the gap between Moses and Rabbi, both of whom did combine the two. The current label can be read as denying it to them (F7).

corrections.change: Add mentions of רבי in s2 ('דבי רבי') and s3 ('ועד רבי') linked to entity 'rabbi'.
corrections.why: The first reading anchored Rabbi only in s1 (F8).

corrections.change: Mark the two groups as a repeated, probably correlated alternation, so that downstream counting does not treat them as four independent combinations.
corrections.why: Both parallels repeat the identical pair after ואמר (F10). This agrees with the earlier review's minor finding.

corrections.change: Keep the practice only. Add any motive as a separate commentary claim with its author (Rashi on Sanhedrin / Yad Ramah / Tosafot on Gittin: humility; Rashi on Gittin: the verse; Steinsaltz and the William Davidson editors: deference to Rabbi's esteem).
corrections.why: The text states no reason, and the commentators disagree, including Rashi with himself (F6).

corrections.change: Add a candidate link to the Gittin 58b:15 sicarii court vote with basis 'parallel sugya + Rashi', not explicit.
Add a source-citation claim: the anonymous objection cites the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 4:1-2 / Bavli 32a).
Do not add 'Rav was the youngest judge' as a text claim. If recorded, store it as a disagreeing commentary view.
corrections.why: It appears only in commentary and editorial plain text, and Rashi records a 'middling' view (F5).

corrections.change: Attach the name-form variants וולס / ולס (Munich manuscript, reported by Jastrow) / וילס (Arukh ed. Kohut, reported by Jastrow) as a reported-variant attribute.
Note that the unit continues to 36a:13 with more persons and a cross-parallel attribution difference (Rav Adda bar Ahava vs Rav Acha son of Rava).
corrections.why: F11. The supplied excerpt ends inside the unit that the focal speaker opens.

lessons: A parallel sugya in another tractate is a second copy of the text, not an independent witness to what happened. Where the parallels differ (Rav Adda bar Ahava vs Rav Acha son of Rava), record a parallel-witness attribution difference.
A commentator can disagree with himself across locations (Rashi on Sanhedrin vs Rashi on Gittin). Commentary claims need the author and the exact location, not only the author.
A motive for a practice (humility, deference, a scriptural rule) is a separate claim with its own author. It must not be folded into the textual claim of the practice.
A repeated ואיתימא pair joined by ואמר needs a 'linked alternation' construct. Otherwise branch enumeration multiplies one doubt into independent combinations.
A comparison of the form 'from X until Y none...' creates 'about' relations and end-point roles, not interaction or contemporaneity.

Editorial glosses (William Davidson plain text, Steinsaltz) that add rank ('youngest'), identity ('Yehuda HaNasi') or motive must be typed as editorial commentary. They come from one editorial project, so they are one witness, not two.
When a commentary paraphrase leaves out a speaker's name (Rabbeinu Chananel's 'והן אמרו'), that is not a textual variant.
Spelling variants of a parent's name belong on the name-mention as reported readings. They do not create new persons.

review.scope: I checked every quotation in dossier.json against the saved files in sources/, and checked the findings and proposed corrections against Sanhedrin 36a:5-13, Gittin 58b:15-59a:9, Rashi, Tosafot, Yad Ramah, Steinsaltz, the William Davidson English, Jastrow, Seder HaDorot, Chatam Sofer, Arukh LaNer, Petach Einayim, Avodah Zarah 52b and Yerushalmi Kilayim 9:1; I fetched nothing new and did not check manuscripts, Dikdukei Soferim, or any history.

findings.reason: Replacing the old label is right, but the new wording, 'Between Moses and Rabbi no one else combined Torah and greatness', goes too far. The Gemara's answers ('הוה אלעזר', 'הוו זקנים', 'הוה שמואל') accept that Joshua, Saul and the others had both Torah and greatness. What they deny is that any of them stood alone, without an equal. Rashi on 36a:7 explains 'במקום אחד' as 'באדם אחד שאין כמותו בכל ישראל בתורה ובגדולה', one person with no equal in all Israel. The label should read something like 'From Moses until Rabbi, no single person was unrivalled in both Torah and greatness'. The narrower condition in 'כולהו שניה קאמרינן' (for all his years) comes from the anonymous Gemara's answers, not from the named speaker. That Moses and Rabbi themselves had both qualities stays a Rashi and Yad Ramah reading.

findings.target: mentions (rabba, rava, hillel, voles) in s3; claims c5, c6, c7, c8
findings.reason: Both names, each with its father's name inside it, appear a second time in 36a:7: 'ואמר רבה בריה דרבא ואיתימא רבי הלל בריה דר' וולס'. The first reading anchored all four name mentions (m3-m6) in s2 only. The dossier added the repeated 'רבי' in s3 (F8) but missed these names. c5 and c6 have speakers with no name mention in the segment that attributes to them. Add mentions in s3 for both sons and both fathers, and let c7 and c8 cite both places. In s3, Wikisource abbreviates the father's title as 'דר' וולס', where the William Davidson Aramaic has 'דרבי וולס'.

Rav's report in Gittin does not come 'directly after' 'רבי הושיב ב"ד ונמנו' (58b:15). Rav Ashi's comment on the baraita comes in between: 'אמר רב אשי כי תניא ההיא לאחר שבאו מעות לידו'. The speaker tag 'אמר רב' closes 58b:16, and his words go on in 59a:1. The dossier's S15 quote leaves that tag out, so Rav's role as speaker in Gittin should be anchored at the end of 58b:16. The candidate link to the sicarii vote can stay, with basis 'parallel placement plus Rashi (Sanhedrin 36a:5, Gittin 59a)', not 'directly after'.

findings.target: F11 (Huna bar Natan and Rav Ashi; 'I too say' speakers)
findings.reason: The line 'הונא בר נתן מיכף הוה כייף ליה לרב אשי' answers the anonymous objection 'ולא והא הוה הונא בר נתן'. Its voice is the anonymous Gemara, not Rav Adda bar Ahava, and in Gittin not Rav Acha son of Rava either ('שאני הונא בר נתן דמיכף...'). Store the relation once, in one direction: Huna bar Natan submitted to Rav Ashi. It is the voice of the discussion used to answer a challenge, not a reported event. I support keeping Rav Adda bar Ahava (Sanhedrin 36a:13) and Rav Acha son of Rava (Gittin 59a:9) as a difference between the two parallels, without merging them. Rabbi and Rav Ashi are end points of a comparison ('about' roles), not people in contact.

findings.target: F12 (presence and time of the two explainers)
findings.reason: I support the core decision: no presence, meeting or same-time edges. But the reasoning, 'The explainers comment on Rav's report after the fact', slips in an order in time. The text only places 'אמר רבה בריה דרבא ואיתימא...' as the answer to the anonymous objection 'והא אנן מתחילין מן הגדול תנן'. It does not say the explainer heard Rav, answered him, or lived after him. Word it as an arrangement of the discussion, not a sequence. It is not a claim about who spoke to whom, and no addressee is marked. For Avodah Zarah 52b:15 the saved text does have R. Hillel son of R. Volas alone. Seder HaDorot 1042 puts 'ואי תימא רבה בריה דרבא' next to that list of references, but this does not import the alternation into AZ.

Keep both parent placeholders and both child_of claims, as F2 proposes. Add the project's caution that 'בריה ד...' may work as a fixed name, and that the kinship holds only for the reading carrying the name. Seder HaDorot 3190, the dossier's own source, notes that for another passage one text seems to read 'רבא ברי' דרבה', with father and son reversed. So the direction of this pair can flip in transmission elsewhere, even though nothing here reverses it. Seder HaDorot's identification of the father with the well-known Rava is a later biographer's identification and does not come from this passage. F2 already says this.

findings.target: F5, F6, F8, A3, A4 (rank, motive, Rabbi = Yehuda HaNasi)
findings.reason: I support these. The saved Aramaic says only 'ומינאי דידי הוו מתחלי ברישא' and gives no motive. 'Youngest', 'junior', 'Yehuda HaNasi' and 'held in such high esteem' appear only in the plain, unbolded words of the William Davidson English and in Steinsaltz. Rashi on Gittin 59a keeps two views of Rav's rank: 'בינוני' (middling) and 'ואני שמעתי שקטן שבהם היה' (I heard he was the smallest of them). The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz come from one editorial project. In A3 and A4 they must count as one editorial witness, not two, as F8 already says.

Jastrow's parenthesis '(Ms. M. ולס, Ar. ed. Koh. וילס)' follows 'Snh. 36a', so it applies to this passage. It must be stored as a manuscript reading that Jastrow reports, not one this dossier checked. The Chatam Sofer's 'ובסנהדרין כתב כך שמו' reports a Rashi wording that the saved Vilna Rashi on 36a:7 does not have (it has only the heading 'בריה דרבי וולס:'). Keep it as a later quotation of Rashi, not as Rashi's text. None of these spellings creates a new person.

findings.target: F1, F10, A1, A2 (one explanation, two alternative speakers; repeated pair)
findings.reason: In both Sanhedrin and Gittin, 'ואיתימא' gives two alternative names for the same words. In each branch the son is the speaker. The alternative does not prove that only one of them historically said it. The second statement repeats the same pair after 'ואמר', so the dossier's choice to treat the two groups as one linked doubt is a fair modelling default, and it is labelled as not stated by the text. The Gittin copy is a parallel and does not count as a second observation.

quote_checks.exact_quote: אמר רבה בריה דרבא ואיתימא רבי הלל בריה דרבי וולס שאני מניינא דבי רבי דכולהו מנינייהו מן הצד הוו מתחלי
quote_checks.note: Sanhedrin 36a:6 exactly, one occurrence. Supports F1, F2 and the local parents in c7 and c8.

quote_checks.exact_quote: ואמר רבה בריה דרבא ואיתימא רבי הלל בריה דר' וולס מימות משה ועד רבי לא מצינו תורה וגדולה במקום אחד
quote_checks.note: 36a:7 exactly. The same names, fathers included, are repeated here, and the first reading gave them no mentions. Note the abbreviation 'דר''.

quote_checks.exact_quote: ולא הא הוה יהושע הוה אלעזר והא הוה פנחס הוו זקנים
quote_checks.note: 36a:8. The 'between Moses and Rabbi' reading holds, but these answers name a peer for each candidate. They do not deny that the candidate had both qualities, so the dossier's 'no one else combined' wording overreaches (see the F7 finding).

quote_checks.exact_quote: במקום אחד - תורתן וגדולתן של ישראל באדם אחד שאין כמותו בכל ישראל בתורה ובגדולה
quote_checks.note: Rashi on 36a:7: one person with no equal. This supports the narrower label I propose. The dossier quoted only the later clause, about Moses and Rabbi.

quote_checks.exact_quote: רבי הושיב ב"ד ונמנו שאם שהתה בפני סיקריקון שנים עשר חודש כל הקודם ליקח זכה
quote_checks.note: The quote is exact (Gittin 58b:15), but it does not support 'directly after'. Next comes 58b:16, 'אמר רב אשי כי תניא ההיא לאחר שבאו מעות לידו אמר רב', and only then Rav's words in 59a:1.

quote_checks.exact_quote: אמר רב אחא בריה דרבא אף אני אומר מימות רבי ועד רב אשי לא מצינו תורה וגדולה במקום אחד
quote_checks.note: Gittin 59a:9. Against Sanhedrin 36a:13 ('אמר רב אדא בר אהבה אף אני אומר'), this confirms the difference between the parallels. It also carries its own patronymic (Rava), kept apart from 36a:6.

quote_checks.exact_quote: הונא בר נתן מיכף הוה כייף ליה לרב אשי
quote_checks.note: The quote matches, but the voice is the anonymous Gemara answering 'ולא והא הוה הונא בר נתן', not Rav Adda bar Ahava. Record it that way.

quote_checks.exact_quote: Rabba, son of Rava, says, and some say that it was Rabbi Hillel, son of Rabbi Valles, who says:
quote_checks.note: This string occurs twice, in 36a:6 and 36a:7. F1 needs the first occurrence, but the dossier gives no occurrence or segment.

quote_checks.exact_quote: (Ms. M. ולס, Ar. ed. Koh. וילס)
quote_checks.note: It comes right after 'Snh. 36a', so it is about this passage. It is Jastrow's report of a manuscript reading, not a checked one.

quote_checks.exact_quote: ציין רש"י וולס ולא פי' כלום ובסנהדרין כתב כך שמו
quote_checks.note: Exact. The 'כך שמו' it credits to Rashi on Sanhedrin is not in the saved Vilna Rashi on 36a:7, which reads 'בריה דרבי וולס:', a heading with no comment.

quote_checks.exact_quote: רִבִּי הִלֵּל בֵּירִבִּי וַולֶס הָיָה לוֹ בֶגֶד בִּשְׁלֹשִׁים רִיבּוֹא דֵינָר (וִיהֲבֵיהּ לְרִבִּי)
quote_checks.note: It matches the saved text after Unicode NFC normalization; the only difference is the order of the vowel and dagesh marks on one letter. Only an identity lead, not evidence for this passage.

quote_checks.exact_quote: דִּינֵי הַטֻּמְאוֹת וְהַטָּהֳרוֹת מַתְחִילִין מִן הַגָּדוֹל, דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת מַתְחִילִין מִן הַצָּד
quote_checks.note: It matches after Unicode NFC normalization; the byte-level difference is only in the order of the vowel marks. Supports F9's point that the objection cites the Mishnah.

cases.question: In the story of the two mute men near Rabbi (Chagigah 3a:4-5), which people and relations are stated by the text, which rest on interpretation, and which alternatives must stay open? Focus: the short 'Rabbi Yohanan' in the 'some say' report, the plural 'before them', missed relations, speech turns and source attributions.

findings.claim: The first report gives the full name 'Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada'. The 'some say' report gives only 'Rabbi Yohanan'. In both checked Aramaic texts on Sefaria, the Aramaic of the second report has no patronymic.

evidence.exact_quote: בני ברתיה דרבי יוחנן בן גודגדא ואמרי לה בני אחתיה דרבי יוחנן דכל אימת
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sons of the daughter of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada, and some say: sons of the sister of Rabbi Yohanan, who every time...

evidence.exact_quote: בני ברתיה דרבי יוחנן בן גודגדא ואמרי לה בני אחתיה דרבי יוחנן דכל אימת

findings.reasoning: The two Aramaic texts agree word for word here. Both share the Vilna-type print tradition, so they are not independent witnesses. The short name follows immediately and is naturally read as the same man, but the words do not say so.
findings.graph_effect: Give the short 'Rabbi Yohanan' in the sister report its own mention. Link it to the Yohanan ben Gudgada entity only as a local coreference candidate (basis: local_coreference / interpretation), not as the same mention.

findings.claim: Translations and commentaries that expand the short name all make it ben Gudgada. In the William Davidson English and in Steinsaltz, 'ben Gudgeda' appears only as editor's text. Glick renders it as 'his sister'. The Community and Goldschmidt translations keep the bare name.

evidence.exact_quote: sons of the sister of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda
evidence.note: Bold = Aramaic; plain 'ben Gudgeda' = editor's addition.

evidence.exact_quote: בני אחתיה [אחותו] של ר' יוחנן בן גודגדא
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sons of his sister of R. Yohanan [unbolded:] ben Gudgada.

evidence.exact_quote: sons of the daughter of R. Jochanan b. Gudgada, and others say, sons of his sister
(and some say it was the sons of R. Yochanan's sister)
Schwesterssöhne R. Joḥanans
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sister's sons of R. Johanan.

evidence.exact_quote: בני בתו או בני אחותו היו אלמים ושומעים
evidence.location: Seder HaDorot 1818, entry R. Yohanan ben Gudgada
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: the sons of his daughter or the sons of his sister were mute and hearing.

findings.reasoning: The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz come from one editorial work, so they count as one interpretation. Glick and Seder HaDorot also read the pronoun as the same man. None of these is a textual witness for the patronymic in the second report.
findings.graph_effect: The coreference is well supported as an interpretation. Record who holds it (Steinsaltz/WD editor, Glick, Seder HaDorot). Never cite the plain 'ben Gudgeda' in the English as Talmud text.

findings.claim: Rav Sherira Gaon's Epistle, in the Oxford 1888 edition, quotes the story with the two reports reversed. The sister report comes first and the daughter report is 'some say'. The full name 'Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada' appears in both. The Sefaria Community translation of this passage mistranslates the 'some say' formula.

evidence.exact_quote: בני אחתיה דר' יוחנן בן גודגדא ואמרי ליה בני ברתיה דר' יוחנן בן גודגדא
evidence.location: Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon 1:38, Hebrew/Aramaic
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sons of the sister of R. Yohanan ben Gudgada, and some say: sons of the daughter of R. Yohanan ben Gudgada.

evidence.exact_quote: And the sons of the daughter of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada said that whenever Rabbi would enter the study hall
evidence.note: This translation turns ואמרי ליה ('and some say') into speech by the daughter's sons. The Aramaic does not support that.

findings.reasoning: This is a quotation in a later work, not a Bavli manuscript. It shows that at least one transmitted form of the story named ben Gudgada in both reports and ordered them the other way. So neither report is textually 'primary', and the short name in the printed Bavli is not the only transmitted form.
findings.graph_effect: The two kinship branches must stay symmetric. Neither should be labelled the main reading. Save the Sherira form as a separate quotation-witness variant, not as corroboration of the print. Ignore the Community translation's speech reading: it creates no speech turn.

findings.claim: In the Torat Emet text, Yalkut Shimoni quotes the story with only the daughter report. It has no 'some say' sister clause.

evidence.exact_quote: בְּנֵי בְּרַתֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן גּוּדְגְּדָא, דְּכָל אֵימַת
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sons of the daughter of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada, who every time...

findings.reasoning: An anthology may shorten what it quotes, so this does not prove that a Bavli text lacked the clause. It does show that the sister alternative is absent from one transmitted form.
findings.graph_effect: Record this as a variant that lacks the sister branch. Do not drop the sister branch, which the print, both Ein Yaakov editions and Sherira all have.

findings.claim: Witnesses differ on 'before them' (plural) and 'before him' (singular), and translators resolve the pronoun differently. Vilna/Wikisource and William Davidson read plural קמייהו. Ein Yaakov (both editions), Sherira and Yalkut read singular קמיה. The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz make it 'the Sages'. The Community and Goldschmidt translations make it 'him', meaning Rabbi.

evidence.exact_quote: הוו עיילי ויתבי קמייהו
הוו עיילי ויתבי קמיה
וְיַתְבֵי קַמֵּיהּ
הוו עיילין ויתבין קמיה
הֲווּ עָיְילֵי קַמֵּיהּ
enter and sit before the Sages
<small>[היו נכנסים ויושבים לפניהם,</small> לפני החכמים<small>]</small>
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: [they would enter and sit before them,] before the Sages.

evidence.exact_quote: they would enter and sit before him
sich vor ihn setzten
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sat down before him.

findings.reasoning: In the singular reading, the natural antecedent is Rabbi, who has just been named. In the plural reading, the text names no group; 'the Sages' is the editor's resolution. Community and Goldschmidt may translate a singular text or may be resolving the plural freely. Their base text was not stated in the saved files.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the first reading's coreference candidates [rabbi, listeners]. Attach the singular/plural variant, and attribute 'the Sages' to the William Davidson/Steinsaltz editor. A 'sat before Rabbi' edge is supported only under the singular variant or by interpretation.

findings.claim: The text states that the two men lived in Rabbi's neighbourhood. The first reading recorded no relation for this.

evidence.exact_quote: הנהו תרי אילמי דהוו בשבבותיה דרבי
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: those two mutes who were in the neighbourhood of Rabbi.

evidence.exact_quote: two mute people who were in the neighborhood of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi

findings.reasoning: שבבותא means neighbourhood. This is a stated relation between the pair and Rabbi, shared by both kinship branches. The sources quoting the story (Sherira, Ein Yaakov, Yalkut) all keep it.
findings.graph_effect: Add a shared claim: pair lives_near / neighbour_of rabbi (voice narrator, basis explicit). Do not upgrade it to a household, patron or teacher relation.

findings.claim: The text does not say that the two learned from Rabbi or were his students. It says they came into the study house whenever Rabbi did, sat, nodded and moved their lips, and were later found to know the material. Guggenheimer and Sherira read this as learning in Rabbi's study house.

evidence.exact_quote: דכל אימת דהוה עייל רבי לבי מדרשא הוו עיילי ויתבי קמייהו ומניידי ברישייהו ומרחשין שפוותייהו
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: whenever Rabbi entered the study house they would enter and sit before them, nod their heads and move their lips.

evidence.exact_quote: They went to the lectures of Rebbi and when Rebbi prayed that they should be healed, it turned out that they had learned the entire Mishnah and halakhic Midrashim from his lectures.
evidence.location: Guggenheimer, note 34 on Jerusalem Talmud Terumot 1:1

evidence.exact_quote: דביומיה דרבי איתרצן תוספתא ומתניין מן ההוא זימנא במדרשיה דר'. ומיתחזי האי סברא מההיא מימרא דמסכ' חגיגה
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: in the days of Rabbi the Tosefta was arranged and taught from that time in Rabbi's study house; and this view appears from that saying in tractate Chagigah.

findings.reasoning: Being present in the same study house is not the same as a teacher-student relation. Sherira uses the story as evidence about when the Tosefta was taught. That is his inference and depends on his reading of the list of works.
findings.graph_effect: Keep co-attendance as explicit. Any taught_by / student_of edge from the pair to Rabbi must be an interpretation claim attributed to Guggenheimer or Sherira, never an explicit claim.

findings.claim: Rabbi prays for the two, and they are healed. The text says Rabbi 'asked for mercy for them'. It does not name God or any healer; 'God' is the translator's addition.

evidence.exact_quote: ובעי רבי רחמי עלייהו ואיתסו
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: and Rabbi asked for mercy for them, and they were healed.

evidence.exact_quote: prayed for God to have mercy upon them, and they were healed.

findings.reasoning: The prayer and its beneficiaries are stated. That the prayer caused the healing comes from the order of the clauses joined by 'and'; it is not stated as cause. Rabbeinu Chananel paraphrases the result as 'ואתפתחו' ('they were opened').
findings.graph_effect: Keep c12 and c15. If a divine addressee is added, make it interpretation (editor's plain text), not a speaker or participant stated by the text.

findings.claim: Source attribution and speech turns. The exclusions come from an anonymous baraita introduced by 'and it was taught'. The objection is in the anonymous voice of the Gemara. In the wider text (3a:6), Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi answer the objection. Rashi says Rav Ashi's reading would hold even without the difficulty of the two mutes.

evidence.exact_quote: ותניא למען ישמעו פרט למדבר ואינו שומע ולמען ילמדו פרט לשומע ואינו מדבר
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: and it was taught [in a baraita]: 'that they may hear' excludes one who speaks but does not hear; 'and that they may learn' excludes one who hears but does not speak.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר מר זוטרא קרי ביה למען ילמדו רב אשי אמר ודאי למען ילמדו הוא
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: Mar Zutra said: read in it 'that they may teach'. Rav Ashi said: it certainly is 'that they may teach'.

evidence.exact_quote: בלאו קושיא דהנך תרי אילמי ליכא לאוקמי לדרשה דתנא דמעיט מהכא שומע ואינו מדבר אלא מלמען ילמדו
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: even without the difficulty of those two mutes, one cannot base the tanna's exclusion of one who hears but does not speak on anything other than 'that they may learn'.

findings.reasoning: The first reading kept the exclusion as a statement with no source voice. ותניא marks a tannaitic source, and no tanna is named. Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi fall outside the saved input window, but they are the named respondents to the objection that the story supports.
findings.graph_effect: Attach the exclusion statement to an unnamed 'baraita' source voice. When the window is widened to 3a:6, add speech claims: Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi each respond to the anonymous objection. No relation between Mar Zutra/Rav Ashi and the story's people follows from this.

findings.claim: The text calls the two 'sons' of one daughter (ברתיה) or one sister (אחתיה). They therefore share a mother in either report, and they are counted as two.

evidence.exact_quote: תרי אילמי
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: two mutes.

evidence.exact_quote: בני ברתיה
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sons of his daughter (singular).

evidence.exact_quote: בני אחתיה
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: sons of his sister (singular).

findings.reasoning: The singular mother noun supports the first reading's c8 (sibling_of) as a close inference. Whether they are full brothers is not stated. No father is named, so no father placeholder is required.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c4-c8. Label c8 as derived from a shared mother (maternal siblings at minimum). Do not add a father node. The grandchild relation to Yohanan is derived from c2+c4/c6 and is not a new observation.

findings.claim: The text calls him only 'Rabbi'. That he is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi comes from the editor's plain text in the William Davidson English and from commentators such as Ben Yehoyada ('רבינו הקדוש').

evidence.exact_quote: Whenever Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would enter the study hall
לכך רפואתם היתה על ידי רבינו הקדוש
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: therefore their healing came through our holy Rabbi.

findings.reasoning: This is the standard use of the bare title, but it is still an identification. It should be scored at the identity stage.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the local entity 'Rabbi'. Record the Yehuda HaNasi identification as an interpretation attributed to the editor and commentators.

findings.claim: The Tosefta and Yerushalmi (Terumot 1:1) contain a different report. There Rabbi Yehuda tells of the sons ('בניו') of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada, who were deaf, and says all the ritually pure food of Jerusalem was prepared under their supervision. Tosefta Kifshutah holds that these are his actual sons in Temple times, while the Bavli tells of his grandsons in Rabbi's time. It adds that Yuchasin tried to harmonise the two.

evidence.exact_quote: מעשה בבניו של ר' יוחנן בן גודגדה שהיו חרשים והיו כל הטהרות שבירושלים נעשות על גבם
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: it happened with the sons of R. Yohanan ben Gudgada, who were deaf, and all the purities in Jerusalem were prepared under their supervision.

evidence.exact_quote: מעשה בבניו של ר' יוחנן בן
מַעֲשֶׂה בְּבָנָיו שֶׁל רִבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן גּוּדְגָּדָא שֶׁהָיוּ כּוּלָּן חֱרֵשִׁים
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: it happened with the sons of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada, who were all deaf.

evidence.exact_quote: וכנראה שרצה להשוות את המעשה בבבלי עם מסורת התוספתא והירושלמי
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: apparently he [Yuchasin] wanted to equate the story in the Bavli with the tradition of the Tosefta and Yerushalmi.

evidence.exact_quote: ולא עוד אלא שכאן מדברים בבניו ממש שהיו בזמן הבית
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: moreover, here they speak of his actual sons, who lived in Temple times.

evidence.exact_quote: ובבבלי מסופר על נכדיו שהיו בזמנו של רבי
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: and in the Bavli the story is about his grandsons, who lived in Rabbi's time.

findings.reasoning: The Tosefta and Yerushalmi texts are textual. The claim that they describe different people from the Bavli pair is Tosefta Kifshutah's interpretation, and it opposes a harmonising earlier compiler. Tosefta Kifshutah's 'grandsons' also follows only the daughter report.
findings.graph_effect: Do not merge the Tosefta/Yerushalmi 'sons' (a plural group, number not stated) with the Bavli pair. If those passages enter the graph, they add a separate child_of claim to Yohanan ben Gudgada, reported by R. Yehuda, in their own passages. Any identity link to the Bavli pair is a separate, disputed identity decision.

findings.claim: Modern summaries simplify the passage in ways the texts do not support. Guggenheimer gives only the daughter report ('sons of his normal daughter'). Mishnat Eretz Yisrael says Yohanan ben Gudgada had 'two sons' who were deaf, but the saved Tosefta says only 'his sons' and the Yerushalmi says 'all of them'.

evidence.exact_quote: it is reported that his grandsons, the sons of his normal daughter, were ostensibly deaf-mutes
evidence.location: Guggenheimer, note 34 on Jerusalem Talmud Terumot 1:1

evidence.exact_quote: שני בניו היו חירשים
evidence.location: Mishnat Eretz Yisrael on Mishnah Terumot 1:1:48
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: his two sons were deaf.

findings.reasoning: A summary can fold a Bavli detail (two) into a Tosefta report, or drop an alternative. Neither summary is evidence for a count or for a single branch.
findings.graph_effect: Do not take a count of two for the Tosefta sons from Mishnat Eretz Yisrael. Do not collapse the Bavli kinship to the daughter branch on the strength of Guggenheimer.

findings.claim: A later kabbalistic tradition identifies the two mutes as reincarnations of Eldad and Medad. The Chida (Petach Einayim) cites it from the Rama of Fano, received from R. Israel Saruk, and Ben Yehoyada repeats it.

evidence.exact_quote: כתוב בגלגולי הנשמות שקבל הרמ"ע ממהר"י סרוק דהני אלמי היו גלגול אלדד ומידד
evidence.translation_mine: Researcher's translation: it is written in Gilgulei HaNeshamot, which the Rama received from R. Israel Saruk, that these mutes were a reincarnation of Eldad and Medad.

evidence.exact_quote: עיין פתח עינים שהיו גלגול אלדד ומידד

findings.reasoning: This is a mystical soul identification by later authors. It is not an identity of persons and not a historical claim about the two men.
findings.graph_effect: Do not link the pair to Eldad or Medad in the person graph. If kept at all, store it as a reception-history claim attributed to these authors, not eligible for the historical graph.

lessons: A short name inside a 'some say' alternative needs its own mention and a coreference candidate. Editor's plain-text expansions in translations (for example 'ben Gudgeda') are interpretation, not textual evidence.
Branch only the claims whose truth depends on the branch. A relation embedded in a name (a patronymic) rests on wording that appears in the text regardless of which alternative report is right.
The number of a pronoun suffix (קמייהו against קמיה) can differ between witnesses and change coreference, so coreference candidates should carry variant evidence.

Later works that quote a passage (a Geonic epistle, Yalkut, Ein Yaakov) are a distinct evidence type, a quotation witness. They can reorder or drop alternatives. They are neither translations nor independent Bavli manuscripts, and they may depend on each other.
Parallel stories about 'the sons of X' in other corpora must not be merged with a Bavli 'daughter's sons of X' without an explicit identity decision.
A mystical soul identification (gilgul) is a reception claim, never a person merge.
Being in the same study house does not make a teacher-student relation.
A neighbour/residence relation between persons is needed as a predicate.
Translation errors in secondary sources (for example 'ואמרי ליה' rendered as the daughter's sons 'said') must not create speech turns.

review.scope: I checked every dossier finding and proposed correction that touches a person, relation, speaker or branch against the saved pilot input, the first reading, the previous review and the saved files in sources/ (Wikisource and William Davidson 3a, 3a:6, Steinsaltz 3a:4-5, Rashi, Sherira, both Ein Yaakov editions, Yalkut 356:3, Tosefta, Lieberman, Yerushalmi with Guggenheimer, Tosefta Kifshutah, Mishnat Eretz Yisrael, Seder HaDorot, Jastrow, Ben Yehoyada), and fetched Yevamot 113a once to check a citation; I did not check Bavli manuscripts, Dikdukei Soferim or the printed Yuchasin, and no page images were involved.

findings.target: first reading entities hearing_no_speech / speech_no_hearing (m12, m13), not addressed by the dossier
findings.reason: The first reading types 'לשומע ואינו מדבר' and 'למדבר ואינו שומע' (3a:3) as kind 'person'. They are legal categories inside the baraita's exclusion ('פרט ל...'), not people. The dossier gives the exclusion a baraita voice (F09) but leaves these two as person entities, so they could become graph nodes. Retype them as legal roles or categories, attached to the baraita statement, and keep them out of the person graph.

findings.target: proposed_corrections c3 (new mention for the short 'רבי יוחנן')
findings.reason: I support a separate mention with a coreference candidate, but the correction gives no anchor. In s2, 'רבי יוחנן' occurs twice: occurrence 1 is inside 'דרבי יוחנן בן גודגדא' (already m2), and occurrence 2 is the sister-clause name. The new mention must anchor on occurrence 2, or on 'בני אחתיה דרבי יוחנן' occurrence 1. If it is anchored on occurrence 1, it silently re-merges it with m2. The candidate's support should list the interpretation holders (WD/Steinsaltz as one, Glick, Yuchasin/Seder HaDorot as one) and Sherira's quotation form as separate evidence types.

findings.target: proposed_corrections c1 (make Yohanan child_of Gudgada shared)
findings.reason: Making c1 shared is reasonable. The name 'רבי יוחנן בן גודגדא' stands in the passage whichever kinship report is right, and 'ואמרי לה' disputes only the mother's relation to Yohanan. But c1's evidence must stay the one printed occurrence in the daughter clause. Sherira's full name in both reports is a later quotation witness and must be recorded separately, not as print evidence for the sister clause. Do not derive 'sister child_of gudgada' from c1 plus c3: the text does not say whether she is a full or half sister, and her Yohanan is only a candidate.

findings.target: entity rabbi mentions (first reading m1 only), not addressed by the dossier
findings.reason: Rabbi is named three times: 'בשבבותיה דרבי' (s2; m1, occurrence 1 of 'דרבי', which is correct), 'דהוה עייל רבי לבי מדרשא' (s2), and 'ובעי רבי רחמי עלייהו' (s3). Only the first is a mention, although c9 and c12 rest on the other two. Add mentions for 'עייל רבי' (occurrence 1) and 'ובעי רבי' (s3, occurrence 1). All three stay one local entity 'Rabbi'. Yehuda HaNasi stays an attributed identification (F11).

findings.target: F09 / proposed correction on exclusion (Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi as respondents)
findings.reason: In 3a:6, 'אמר מר זוטרא קרי ביה למען ילמדו' answers the objection. Rav Ashi's 'ודאי למען ילמדו הוא דאי סלקא דעתך...' argues from the verse's own redundancy. The dossier's own Rashi quote says this holds 'בלאו קושיא דהנך תרי אילמי', even without the mutes' difficulty. So record Mar Zutra as answering the anonymous objection, and Rav Ashi as ruling on how the verse is read, supported by his own argument. Neither statement marks an addressee, and there is no relation between the two men or to the story's people.

I agree that no teacher edge is explicit. But the list of who holds the interpretation is incomplete and partly overstated. Sherira says the Tosefta 'איתרצן ... ומתניין ... במדרשיה דר'' and uses the story as proof. He implies, but does not state, that the pair learned it from Rabbi, and his proof needs the Tosefta variant. Yuchasin (quoted in Tosefta Kifshutah: 'היו בישיבת רבי') and Seder HaDorot ('והיו בישיבת רבי') also hold a study-house reading. Treat them as one line, and attribute any such edge to them as interpretation.

findings.target: F02 (holders of the ben Gudgada coreference)
findings.reason: Seder HaDorot's entry opens 'וכתב היוחסין' and repeats Yuchasin's 'בני בתו ... או בני אחותו' wording, which Tosefta Kifshutah quotes as 'ובני בתו של ר' יוחנן בן גודגדה או בני אחותו'. They are one line, not two. Glick's 'sons of his sister' is a translation choice. None of these is a textual witness for the patronymic in the printed sister clause. The dossier already treats WD and Steinsaltz as one; apply the same rule here.

findings.target: F05 / m9 coreference and claim c11
findings.reason: Ein Yaakov (Glick 'ויתבי קמיה', Daat 'וְיַתְבֵי קַמֵּיהּ') and Sherira ('ויתבין קמיה') do read singular 'sit before him'. Yalkut reads 'הֲווּ עָיְילֵי קַמֵּיהּ' with no 'sit' verb, so it supports 'entered before him', not 'sat before him'. Glick's English drops the sitting clause altogether. Also, c11 hard-codes object 'listeners', while m9 carries candidates [rabbi, listeners]. c11's object should follow the m9 candidates, not fix one of them.

findings.target: F06 / proposed shared claim pair neighbour_of rabbi
findings.reason: 'הנהו תרי אילמי דהוו בשבבותיה דרבי' states it, in the narrator's voice, before the kinship alternative, so it is shared by both branches. Sherira ('בשיבבותיה'), Ein Yaakov ('בשביבותיה') and Yalkut ('בְּשִׁיבְבוּתֵיהּ') keep it. Choose one predicate and store it once, in one direction (pair near Rabbi). It is residence only: not household, patronage or teaching.

findings.target: F12 / F13 (Tosefta and Yerushalmi sons; Mishnat Eretz Yisrael's 'two sons')
findings.reason: The Tosefta reads 'מעשה בבניו של ר' יוחנן בן גודגדה שהיו חרשים' and the Yerushalmi 'שֶׁהָיוּ כּוּלָּן חֱרֵשִׁים', reported by R. Yehuda, with no count. Mishnat Eretz Yisrael's 'שני בניו' cites 'תוס', פ"א ה"א; בבלי, יבמות קיג ע"א'. I checked Yevamot 113a: it has only Yohanan ben Gudgada's testimony about a deaf woman, not his sons. So neither of its citations supplies 'two'. Its footnote 17 separately calls the Bavli pair his 'נכדיו' in Rabbi's days, citing Yalkut, the one witness that lacks the sister report. Keep them unmerged, as the dossier says.

cases.question: Who speaks, acts, is named or is cited in Menachot 29b:3 (with its continuation 29b:4-5)? Which graph claims are explicit, which rest on interpretation, and which alternatives must stay open when the first reading is checked against wider context, translations, commentaries, a manuscript and an early print?

findings.claim: The whole story is one report: Rav Yehuda states it in Rav's name. Every event and speech inside it is part of what Rav is reported to have said. Neither Rav Yehuda nor Rav appears as a participant in the scenes.

אמר רב יהודה אמר רב לא נצרכה אלא לקוצה של יוד

findings.reasoning: The chain opens the story and is never resumed, so it governs 29b:3-5. The same chain is used just before, at 29a:17, for a ruling about the thorn (קוץ) of a yod; the story's 'each and every thorn' picks up that word. That placement is a literary link inside the sugya. It gives no evidence that Rav Yehuda heard Rav tell this particular story on a particular occasion, and it says nothing about when either of them lived.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 (reports_in_name_of Rav Yehuda to Rav) as the only link between the two amoraim. Do not add direct hearing, co-presence or life order. All story claims carry voice = Rav, as transmitted by Rav Yehuda.

findings.reasoning: The Hebrew הלכה למשה מסיני literally means 'a law to Moses from Sinai'. This names Moses as the one who received it at Sinai, and each translator fills in the role differently. So there is no meeting, no hearing and no teaching link between Moses and Akiva.

The Community Translation renders the phrase itself as 'flaying his flesh with [iron] combs', which is Rashi's gloss rather than the words of the text.

findings.claim: The first reading captured all twelve speech turns in 29b:3-5: five from Moses to God, five from God to Moses, one from the students to the teacher and one from the teacher back. The first reading attaches Moses's weakness to Moses only through the pronoun in 'his strength'; Munich 95, in my reading, may add 'of Moses' here, but I could not read it with confidence.

unresolved: The Munich 95 readings ('eighteen rows'; a possible explicit 'Moses' at the calming, and possibly 'of Moses' after 'his strength failed') are my visual readings and need to be checked against a transcription or variant apparatus.

Other manuscripts of Menachot (for example the Vatican and Florence manuscripts) and the Hachi Garsinan apparatus were not checked. So the spread of 'eight' versus 'eighteen' and of singular versus plural 'reached' is unknown beyond the witnesses listed.

The Ein Yaakov edition Ben Yehoyada relied on is not identified. The Daat Ein Yaakov puts 'עשרה' in parentheses and the Glick Ein Yaakov Hebrew lacks it; what the Daat parentheses mean was not checked.
The text never says which 'one matter' the students asked about.
Identifying 'Akiva son of Yosef' with the tanna Rabbi Akiva is a separate identity decision. It is supported by commentary and by the story's intent, not by an explicit statement here.
Academic studies of this story (Rubenstein 2010; Yadin-Israel 2014, cited by Wikipedia) were not read; any claims they make about the story's composition or its links to the sugya are unchecked.
The steinsaltz.org page was fetched, but its static HTML contained no article text, so it was not used.

corrections.change: Add a variant note: 'eighteen rows' (Munich 95 visual reading; reported for Ein Yaakov by Ben Yehoyada; Seder HaDorot). Leave the claim's participants unchanged.
Add a note that the teacher is unnamed in 29b:4. The link to Akiva is story coreference, and 'Rabbi Akiva' in the English is editorial. Scope the student relation to the depicted scene.
Same note as c12. If the 'reaching' action is ever modelled, add a branch for the Bomberg plural reading.
Same note as c12 on the unnamed teacher.

Rephrase as citing the Sinai tradition, with Moses as the recipient named in the formula. Add Rashi's 'ומשמו אומר' as commentary. Record that translations differ on whether Moses received or delivered it. Keep the note denying hearing.

Add Rashi 29b:4:2 as commentary evidence that the calmed mind is Moses's. Add the Munich 95 wording as a separate manuscript-variant evidence item (visual reading). Keep the basis as local coreference for the printed text.
Keep the bracket in the quote, and note that 'לאחורך' is absent from the William Davidson Aramaic but present in both Ein Yaakov texts and, by visual reading, in Munich 95.
Add a note that no agent is named in the Hebrew. The Romans and the killing come from the editors' plain text. The link to Berakhot 61b is Rashi's.
Keep 'weighers' as an unnamed group. Do not relabel them as Romans.
Keep as explicit literal kinship inside a divine prediction. Add a note that identifying him with the tanna Rabbi Akiva is a separate pending decision.
Add mentions for Moses inside 'הלכה למשה מסיני' (s2) and for the descriptions and pronouns referring to Akiva ('אדם אחד', 'אדם כזה', 'הראהו', 'תורתו', 'שכרו').
Previous review: its passes stand. It did not note the unnamed teacher, the source variants, or that the Roman agent is editorial only; add those points.

lessons: A scene someone is shown inside a story (vision, heavenly ascent) needs its own modality. Relations inside it, such as students of the teacher, must be scoped to that scene and must never produce historical co-presence or cross-era teaching edges.
'הלכה למשה מסיני' is a formula naming a legal category and where it comes from. Model it as a source attribution with Moses as the named recipient, not as a speech turn or a hearing.
Agents added in editorial plain text (here 'the Romans') must not become entities. The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz Hebrew are one editorial voice.
A translation can take in a commentator's gloss (the Community Translation's 'iron combs' comes from Rashi). Treat a translation's wording as that translator's reading, not as a text variant.
Kabbalistic spark or soul-root identifications are not kinship and not historical identity. Keep them outside the person graph.
The same stock opening told by a different sage in another tractate (Shabbat 89a, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) is a parallel story, not an alternative attribution of this one.
The contract needs a way to type God as a speaker without typing God as a human person, as the earlier review noted.
Store manuscript and print variants (eight or eighteen; שהגיע or שהגיעו) as a source-variant evidence type, separate from later emendations and from translation choices.

review.scope: I checked every dossier quotation against its saved file in sources/ (all text quotes were found), re-read the Munich 95 and Bomberg images myself for the five visual readings, and read the context around Menachot 29a:15-29b:8, Maharsha, Ben Yehoyada, both Ein Yaakov texts and the Community Translation; I did not consult other manuscripts, variant apparatus or academic studies, and I fetched nothing new.

findings.target: A2 / F6 / proposed correction c13 (who 'reached one matter')
findings.reason: Maharsha should not be listed as support for the 'class reached' branch. In his gloss the plural 'כיון שהגיעו לדבר אחד דהיינו מסופן לראשן עד הא'' has the letters of his alphabet allegory as its subject: the reading runs backwards until it reaches alef. It is not the students or the class. He also does not quote this as a heading, which the dossier itself notes. So the plural branch rests on Bomberg alone among the witnesses checked. Keep the branch, but drop Maharsha from its supporters, or list him only as commentary wording.

The singular 'שהגיע' has more support than the dossier lists. The Glick Ein Yaakov Hebrew has it ('תשש כחו כיון שהגיע לדבר אחד'). By my own reading of the image, Munich 95 line 5 also has 'שהגיע', ending in ayin with no final vav, before 'לדבר'. The Glick English has 'until they reached', but that is the translator's choice and not a text variant. The singular branch should list men29b, Daat Ein Yaakov, Glick Hebrew and Munich 95 (visual). The plural branch should list Bomberg (visual) only.

findings.target: c11 (Moses's strength waned) / F14 / unresolved item 1
findings.reason: The dossier left 'of Moses' after 'תשש כחו' in Munich 95 as unreadable and proposed no change to c11. In the zoomed image I read line 5 as 'תשש כחו של משה כיון שהגיע'. The words 'של משה' are fairly clear, though the join of 'כחו' and 'של' is cramped. So c11 should get the same treatment the dossier gives c16: printed text basis = coreference (the pronoun in 'כחו'), plus a separate evidence item typed as a visual manuscript reading that names Moses. Confidence is medium, since this is one visual reading and not a transcription.

'ראה ששוקלין בשרו במקולין' uses a plural participle with no subject. In Hebrew this can be an impersonal 'his flesh was being weighed', and Glick in fact renders it as a passive: 'his flesh is being marketed'. The dossier is right to forbid a Roman agent, but it keeps c23 as a group taking part in the scene with basis 'explicit'. The text states the weighing, not a group of people. Keep 'weighers' only as an unnamed grammatical subject that may be impersonal. It should not become a group entity with identity or membership.

F3 says 'Rabbi Akiva' appears only in the William Davidson English and Steinsaltz. The saved files show two more editorial insertions. The Community Translation adds '[of students in Rabbi Akiva's Beit Midrash]' in 29b:4, and Glick adds '(R. Akiba and his associates)' and 'replied R. Akiba'. The conclusion still holds, since the Hebrew of 29b:3-5 never gives the title and the teacher of 29b:4 is unnamed. But the list should name all four translation layers, typed as translation, not text.

The 'eighteen' column should not be read as three votes. Ben Yehoyada's words are 'כן הגירסא בעין יעקב', a report of the Ein Yaakov, and the Daat Ein Yaakov's '(עֶשְׂרֵה)' comes from the same Ein Yaakov line. Seder HaDorot is a later paraphrase whose source is not stated. Munich 95 is the only manuscript, and I confirm its reading 'שמונה עשר שורות'. Ben Yehoyada then builds a letter count on this reading (ayin is the nineteenth letter, with eighteen before it). His report counts as a reported edition reading, not as support for his own interpretation. No person or edge changes.

findings.target: F12 (what kind of scene the classroom is)
findings.reason: The graph effect is right: no co-presence, and no Moses–Akiva teaching edge. But the wording 'God says turn back' is not what marks the scene as a showing. The marking words are Moses's request 'הראהו לי' and his later 'הראיתני תורתו הראני שכרו'. 'חזור לאחורך' is only a spatial instruction. The only time statement in the passage is God's 'בסוף כמה דורות'. It should stay a relative time claim inside a prediction voiced by God in Rav's report, never a date. 'All three readings agree they do not share a historical time' describes the commentators. It is not something the passage states.

findings.target: F14 / proposed correction on added mentions
findings.reason: The twelve-turn speech count is correct: c5, c8, c18, c20 and c24 are Moses to God; c6, c9, c19, c21 and c25 are God to Moses; c13 and c14 are the classroom exchange. The added mentions are right. The list should also include 'ע"י' (Moses), which F14's reasoning names but the correction leaves out, and 'שמו' (Akiva). It should include the vocative 'רבי' as the students' address to the unnamed teacher, a title of address and not part of a name. It should also include 'לי' and 'הראיתני/הראני' for Moses, and 'ידך' and 'לפני' for God.

findings.target: F1, F2, F4, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F13, F15 and proposed corrections c2, c10, c12, c14, c15, c16, c21, c22
findings.reason: These hold on the sources. The chain 'אמר רב יהודה אמר רב' governs 29b:3-5. The 29a:17 quote points at the first of the three chain uses in that segment, the thorn-of-yod ruling, although 29a:18-29b:2 comes in between, so 'just before' is loose. Yosef stays as a local parent in 'ועקיבא בן יוסף שמו'. 'הלכה למשה מסיני' is a source attribution, and Rashi's 'ומשמו אומר' is citation, not hearing. The Romans are editorial. Shabbat 89a (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) and Berakhot 61b (the angels) are separate tellings whose speakers are not imported. The soul-root claims are not kinship.

quote_checks.exact_quote: אמר רב יהודה אמר רב בשעה שעלה משה למרום
quote_checks.note: Wikisource 29b:3 opens the story with this chain; 29b:6 moves on to Rava, so the chain governs 29b:3-5.

quote_checks.exact_quote: אדם אחד יש שעתיד להיות בסוף כמה דורות ועקיבא בן יוסף שמו
quote_checks.note: Patronymic present inside God's answer; no title 'Rabbi'. Supports c2 as literal kinship scoped to this prediction, with Yosef as local placeholder.

quote_checks.exact_quote: כיון שהגיע לדבר אחד אמרו לו תלמידיו רבי מנין לך אמר להן הלכה למשה מסיני נתיישבה דעתו
quote_checks.note: Wikisource 29b:4: the teacher is unnamed; 'דעתו' has no stated owner. Supports F4 and F7 as coreference-based.

quote_checks.exact_quote: נתיישבה דעתו - של משה הואיל ומשמו אומר אע"פ שעדיין לא קיבלה:
quote_checks.note: Rashi 29b:4:2 resolves 'his mind' to Moses and frames the answer as citation in his name; commentary evidence type only.

quote_checks.exact_quote: כיון שהגיעו לדבר אחד דהיינו מסופן לראשן עד הא' שהוא מורה על אחד
quote_checks.note: The quote is exact, but in context the plural subject is the backward reading of the letters in Maharsha's allegory ('ח' שורות א"ב ... למפרע'). It is not the class. It does not support the 'class reached' branch in A2.

quote_checks.exact_quote: תשש כחו כיון שהגיע לדבר אחד אמרו לו תלמידיו רבי מניין לך
quote_checks.note: Found by the reviewer in the saved Glick Hebrew. It is a singular witness that the dossier's A2 omits.

quote_checks.exact_quote: הָלַךְ וְיָשַׁב לְסוֹף שְׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה שׁוּרוֹת. כן הגירסא בעין יעקב.
quote_checks.note: A report of an Ein Yaakov reading, followed at once by his own count of letters. It is not an independent witness from the Daat Ein Yaakov line.

quote_checks.note: researcher_visual_reading_of_page_image. CONFIRMED by my own reading of the crop: 'רב יהודה' is written with רב, and 'א' רב בשעה שעל' follows.

quote_checks.note: researcher_visual_reading_of_page_image. CONFIRMED: line 5 clearly begins 'שמונה עשר שורות ולא היה יודע'.

quote_checks.note: researcher_visual_reading_of_page_image. PARTLY CONFIRMED: 'כיון' ends line 5, and line 6 reads '...שמע משה כך נתישבה דעתו'. The first letters of 'ששמע' are cramped. Moses is named.

quote_checks.exact_quote: תשש כחו כיון שהגיעו לדבר אחד אמרו לו תלמידיו רבי מנין לך

cases.question: Check the first reading of Sanhedrin 97a:6 (with 97a:7) against wider context, published translations and relevant commentaries. Focus on the unresolved questions in the saved reading and independent review. Identify which graph claims are explicit, which depend on interpretation, and which alternatives must stay open. Recover any missed person, family relation, speech turn or source attribution.

findings.claim: Rava is the outer speaker. In the Vilna-based text a sage speaks to Rava in person ('said to me'), and the story is the sage's own first-person report to Rava. Rashi says so directly: 'and he told me this: one time I happened to...'.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר רבא מריש הוה אמינא ליכא קושטא בעלמא אמר לי ההוא מרבנן
זימנא חדא איקלעי לההוא אתרא וקושטא שמיה
לשקר ואישתעי לי הכי זימנא חדא אקלעי לההוא אתרא וקושטא שמיה
וסיפר לי: זימנא חדא איקלעי לההוא אתרא ו"קושטא" שמיה

findings.reasoning: אמר לי plus the first-person verbs איקלעי, נסיבי, הוו לי make the sage the narrator of the story and Rava its hearer. Rashi (researcher translation: 'and he told me this') and Steinsaltz ('and he told me') confirm it. Only Rava's report records this meeting.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c2/c14: Rava heard this from the sage whose name depends on the branch. This is a speech turn Rava reports. Treat story claims in the sage's first person as spoken by that sage and passed on by Rava, not as statements by an unknown narrator.

findings.claim: Witnesses differ on whether the verb is 'said to me' or 'said to him'. Chokhmat Shlomo saw 'אמר ליה' and corrected it to 'אמר לי'. The Bomberg 1523 page looks to me like it reads 'אמר ליה'. Maharal quotes the line both ways and builds his allegory on 'אמר ליה'. Munich 95 appears to use the abbreviation א"ל, which can be expanded either way.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר ליה ההוא כו' צ"ל אמר לי
אמר רבא מריש הו"א ליכא קושטא בעלמא אמר לי ההוא מרבנן
ומה שאמר דאמר ליה ההוא מדרבנן דבר זה נקרא שאמר ליה
ליכא קושטא בעלמא אמר ליה ההוא מרבנן ורב
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of the Bomberg page image; not machine-checked.

evidence.exact_quote: מריש הו"א ליכא קושטא בעלמ' א"ל ההו' מרבנן ורב
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of a cursive hand; the abbreviation and the letters are uncertain.

findings.reasoning: Chokhmat Shlomo's note (researcher translation: 'said to him ... should read said to me') shows that an earlier printed text read 'said to him'. This is a correction, not a manuscript. An abbreviated א"ל would explain how both readings arose. That is my guess and is not attested. Under 'said to him' the hearer is most naturally still Rava, but the words no longer mark the report as first person.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c2/c14 as explicit in the Vilna/Wikisource text. Add a textual-variant note that 'אמר לי' against 'אמר ליה' changes how explicitly the speech is marked as addressed to Rava. Do not raise the confidence of a Rava–sage meeting beyond this one reported telling.

findings.claim: The sentence about refusing all the world's wealth is Rava's description of the sage. It is a hypothetical, not an event, and not the sage speaking. Translations put 'He said to me' / 'and he told me' after it.

evidence.exact_quote: who was so honest that if they were to give him the entire world, he would not deviate from the truth in his statement. He said to me:
who, even if he were given all the treasures of the world, would not lie, told me that he once came to a place called Kushta
אם אמר למכור דבר זה בסך מה ואח"ך בא אחר ונותן לו יותר

findings.reasoning: The third-person ליה / בדבוריה inside Rava's sentence marks it as Rava's words. דאי הוו יהבי is counterfactual ('if they were to give'). Commentators such as Iyun Yaakov (quoted by Petach Einayim) read it as a trait: he kept his word in sales even when offered more. The imagined givers are not real participants.
findings.graph_effect: c3/c15 should not be 'scenes/participates_in' with an 'offerers' group. Recode them as a character claim in Rava's voice, marked counterfactual. Drop 'offerers' as a participant group, or mark it hypothetical and non-referring.

findings.claim: Witnesses disagree on the person of 97a:7. Vilna/Wikisource has third person (סבר, אמר לה). A Vilna margin note records 'סברי . אמרי' (I thought, I said). The Koren vocalized text prints סְבַרִי / אֲמַרִי לַהּ. Bomberg (as I read it) mixes סבר with אמרי לה and אמרי להו. Munich 95 appears to keep first person throughout. Ein Yaakov (Glick Hebrew) mixes the persons, and Maharal quotes it all in third person.

evidence.exact_quote: סבר לאו אורח ארעא אמר לה ליתא הכא שכיבו ליה תרתין בנין אתו אינשי דאתרא לקמיה
סְבַרִי: לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא. אֲמַרִי לַהּ: לֵיתַהּ הָכָא. שְׁכִיבוּ לֵיהּ תְּרֵין בְּנֵיה
י"ג סברי . אמרי
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of the Vilna outer-margin note beside the asterisked words *סבר and *אמר לה.

evidence.exact_quote: אדשא סבר לאו אורח ארעא אמרי לה ליתה הכא שכיבו ליה תרתי' בניה
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of the Bomberg page image.

evidence.exact_quote: מאי האי אמרי להו הכי הוה מעשה
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of the Bomberg page image.

evidence.exact_quote: לאו אורח ארעא אמרי לה ליתה הכא
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of Munich 95; the words before לאו look like a first-person 'I thought' (אמינא), but that is uncertain.

evidence.exact_quote: אמינא להו הכי הוה מעשה אמרו לי במטות' מינך פוק מאתרין
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of Munich 95; low legibility.

evidence.exact_quote: סבר לאו אורח ארעא אמר לה לימא הכא שכיבי ליה תרתין בנין
נסיב אתתא מנהון והוי ליה תרתין בנין יומא חד יתבה דביתהו

findings.reasoning: Every witness keeps דביתהו ('his wife') and several keep ליה / לקמיה, so no witness is purely first person in the forms I could check. Even so, the first-person forms in 97a:7 in Koren, Bomberg, Munich and the variant the Vilna margin records show that the story was often passed on as the sage's own continuing report. The third person in Vilna therefore need not be a new narrator. Mixed person inside a quoted story is common in Talmudic Aramaic. The page-image readings are mine and unchecked.
findings.graph_effect: For c7, c10, c19, c22 and the shared claims c26-c31, replace voice 'unknown' with 'the branch-selected teller, as reported by Rava'. Keep an alternative in which the anonymous Talmudic narrator retells the story in the third person. The actors do not change under either reading: the husband is the sage.

findings.claim: The woman who knocks is 'her neighbour' (שיבבתה): a female neighbour of the wife. The first reading kept the neighbour as a person but lost the relation to the wife.

evidence.exact_quote: אתאי שיבבתה טרפא אדשא
Her neighbor came and knocked on the door.
[באה שכנתה</small> ו<small>דפקה בדלת]</small> להכנס
neighbor

findings.reasoning: The suffix ־ה on שיבבתה ('her neighbour') refers back to דביתהו. אתאי and טרפא are feminine, and the husband answers her with לה. Davidson ('Her neighbor') and Steinsaltz (שכנתה) agree.
findings.graph_effect: Add neighbor_of(neighbor, wife), explicit. Add a speech claim: the husband speaks to the neighbour, and his words concern the wife. The neighbour is the addressee and the wife is who the words are about.

findings.claim: Commentators give different reasons for the knock. Rashi says the neighbour was asking for the wife. Steinsaltz says she knocked to come in. Rashi's lemma reads אבבא ('at the gate') where the printed text has אדשא ('at the door').

evidence.exact_quote: טרפא אבבא - שהיתה שואלת אותה
טרפא אדשא [באה שכנתה ודפקה בדלת] להכנס
a female neighbor came to ask for her

findings.reasoning: Researcher translation of Rashi: 'she was asking for her'. Glick's English follows Rashi. The Aramaic says only that she came and knocked. The purpose comes from the commentators.
findings.graph_effect: Record the neighbour's purpose as commentary (Rashi: seeking the wife; Steinsaltz: wanting to enter), not as text. Do not add a 'neighbour asks for the wife' speech turn as explicit.

findings.claim: A missed turn: the husband thinks before he speaks ('he thought / I thought: it is not proper'). This private reason explains the false answer 'she is not here'. Commentators differ on what exactly was improper.

evidence.exact_quote: סבר לאו אורח ארעא אמר לה ליתא הכא
לאו אורח ארעא - לומר היכן היא הואיל וחייפ' רישה
זה לספר לה שאשתו רוחצת עצמה
He thought: It is not proper conduct to tell the neighbor that his wife is bathing.

findings.reasoning: סבר is explicit. What the impropriety consists of is commentary. Rashi (researcher translation): 'to say where she is, since she was washing her head'. Steinsaltz: 'to tell her that his wife is washing herself'. Davidson's plain words 'to tell the neighbor that his wife is bathing' are editorial.
findings.graph_effect: Add a views/thought claim for the teller: 'not proper conduct', stated, with the content left open. c7/c19: the denial ליתא הכא is spoken to the neighbour and is false within the story. It is not a statement that the wife was absent.

findings.claim: The Aramaic does not state that the lie caused the sons' deaths. It places the deaths right after the lie, and the residents' plea 'do not provoke death upon these people' implies the link. The words 'Since he deviated from the truth' (Davidson plain text), 'וכיון ששינה בדיבורו' (Steinsaltz) and '[As a punishment for this]' (Soncino, bracketed) are all editorial.

evidence.exact_quote: He said to her: She is not here. Since he deviated from the truth his two sons died.
וכיון ששינה בדיבורו שכיבו ליה תרתין בנין
[As a punishment for this] his two sons died.
ולא תגרי בהו מותנא בהנך אינשי
שהשקר מביא מיתה בלא זמן

findings.reasoning: In Davidson only the bold words translate the Aramaic. The causal clause is plain text. The link is strongly implied inside the story: the town where no one dies early, the residents' question and plea, and Maharsha's explanation (researcher translation: 'falsehood brings untimely death'). The Aramaic still does not state it.
findings.graph_effect: Any 'deaths caused by the lie' edge must be basis=interpretation with the editorial source named. It must not be basis=explicit.

findings.claim: The sons' parents are both stated. 'I had two sons from her' makes the teller their father and the wife their mother. The two sons who die in 97a:7 are naturally the same two, and the Koren text says 'his two sons'.

evidence.exact_quote: נסיבי איתתא מינהון והוו לי תרתין בנין מינה
שְׁכִיבוּ לֵיהּ תְּרֵין בְּנֵיה
שכיבו ליה תרתין בנין

findings.reasoning: מינה ('from her') states the mother, and לי ('to me') the father. The first reading marked c12/c13/c24/c25 (father) and c26/c27 (mother) as basis 'interpretation' and gave c26/c27 voice 'unknown'. Both are explicit in the teller's words. The sibling claim c28 is derived from the shared parents and is not a separate observation.
findings.graph_effect: Change the basis of c12, c13, c24, c25, c26 and c27 to explicit and their voice to the teller. Mark c28 as derived. Link the dying sons (c31) to the same 'sons' group, basis local coreference, supported by Koren's בְּנֵיהּ.

findings.claim: The wife is 'a woman from among them', one of the townspeople. That puts her in the residents' group, which the first reading did not record. The plea 'leave our place' also shows the teller was living there.

evidence.exact_quote: נסיבי איתתא מינהון
במטותא מינך פוק מאתרין
I married a woman from among them,

findings.reasoning: מינהון refers back to the people of the place who do not change their words. 'Leave our place' (researcher translation) assumes he lived there. That is a reasonable inference; the text does not say where he lived.
findings.graph_effect: Add member_of(wife, residents), explicit. Add resided_in(teller, town), interpretation. The residents' request to leave stays a request. No departure or expulsion is reported.

findings.claim: The residents speak three times. They come to him and ask 'What is this?'. He answers only 'this is how it happened'; no further words are quoted. Then they plead with him to leave. Witnesses differ between the singular abbreviation א"ל and plural אמרו ליה, and Munich appears to read 'they said to me'.

evidence.exact_quote: אמרו ליה מאי האי אמר להו הכי הוה מעשה א"ל במטותא מינך
אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: בְּמָטוּתָא מִינָּך
מעשה ששיניתי בדיבורי מפני הנימוס
So he related to them what had happened.

findings.reasoning: The content of the answer is not given. Steinsaltz supplies it in the first person (researcher translation: 'that I changed my words for the sake of manners'). That is his explanation, not the text. The speaker of the plea is the group. א"ל is an abbreviation that the Koren text prints as a plural.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c9/c21, c10/c22 and c11/c23. The content of c10/c22 is 'this is how it happened' with no further words; do not add a confession as quoted speech. The speaker of c11/c23 is the residents' group, whether the verb is singular or plural.

findings.claim: Some later authors retell the story beyond the text. Reshit Chokhmah names the teller as Rav Tavyomi and says the townspeople expelled him (וגירשוהו). The Talmud reports only a plea to leave.

evidence.exact_quote: רב טביומי שמו, ומפני ששינה בדיבורו בדבר קל כמו שנתבאר שם בגמרא, קבר ב' בניו, וגירשוהו מביניהם
על רב טביומי דאילו הוו יהבי ליה כל חללי דעלמא
ולכן אמר כאן על רב טביומי

findings.reasoning: Researcher translation of Reshit Chokhmah: 'Rav Tavyomi by name ... buried two sons, and they expelled him from among them'. These later works each pick one of the two names and simplify the story. They are secondary retellings, not independent witnesses to the story or to the name.
findings.graph_effect: Do not add an expulsion or departure event. Do not resolve the name branch from later quotations that give only one name.

findings.claim: The two names are given as alternatives ('Rav Tavut is his name, and some say Rav Tavyomi is his name'). The Vilna, Koren, Munich (as I read it) and Ein Yaakov texts all carry both. Maharal treats them as a disagreement between tradents and reads both names symbolically, and also as a possible allegory of Moses. That is homiletic, not an identification.

evidence.exact_quote: ורב טבות שמיה ואמרי לה רב טביומי שמיה
ורב טבות שמו ואמרי לה רב טביומי שמיה
טבות שמי' ואמרי לה רב טביומי שמי'
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of Munich 95.

evidence.exact_quote: ואם יש לך להבין מחלוקת זה מר אמר רב טבות שמיה ומר אמר רב טביומי שמיה
אמנם נ"ל כי המאמר הזה נאמר על משרע"ה
his name was R. Tabuth, some say, R. Tabyomi

findings.reasoning: ואמרי לה is the standard formula for a reported alternative. Maharal (researcher translation: 'one master says his name is Rav Tavut and another says Rav Tavyomi') confirms the tradition-dispute reading. His symbolic and Moses readings are later interpretation. The Bomberg spelling of the first name was hard for me to read (it could look like טבורת) and I do not count it as a variant.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the reading group: two branches, one teller. Neither branch establishes whether Rav Tavut and Rav Tavyomi are the same or different people historically.

findings.claim: Bava Metzia 49a has a close parallel with a different chain and a different alternative name. Rav Pappi says that Ravina told him that 'one of the Sages, Rav Tavut, and some say Rav Shmuel bar Zutra', who would not change his word for all the world, told him a different story (about sesame). Vilna Sanhedrin cross-references it in the margin.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר רב פפי אמר לי רבינא לדידי אמר לי ההוא מרבנן ורב טבות שמיה ואמרי לה רב שמואל בר זוטרא שמיה דאי הוו יהבי ליה כל חללא דעלמא
Rav Pappi said that Ravina said to me: One of the Sages, and Rav Tavot is his name, and some say Rav Shmuel bar Zutra is his name,
[ב"מ מט. ע"ש]
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading of the Vilna margin reference beside אמר לי *ההוא מרבנן.

findings.reasoning: The same description and the same first name appear with a different hearer (Ravina, not Rava) and a different alternative name. This may be a shared literary pattern for 'the truthful sage'. A shared name does not show that the two passages are about one person.
findings.graph_effect: Record a coreference candidate between the Sanhedrin Rav Tavut branch and the Bava Metzia Rav Tavut. Leave it unmerged. Do not add Ravina or Rav Shmuel bar Zutra to this passage's graph.

findings.claim: Be'er Sheva proposes that 'Rav Shmuel bar Zutra' in Bava Metzia is a scribal error and should read 'Rav Tavyomi' as in Sanhedrin. Gilyon HaShas repeats this. Seder HaDorot adds a chronological argument about which Ravina is meant. These are later emendations and inferences, not variants.

evidence.exact_quote: נראה לי שיש טעות סופר וצריך להגיה ואמרי לה רב טביומי שמיה דאי כו' דהכי גרסינן בפרק חלק דף צ"ז ע"א ושם עיקר מקומו
כ' הבאר שבע סי' יג דצ"ל רב טביומי שמיה דהכי אית' בסנהדרין
וצ"ל דרבינא הנ"ל הוא הקדמון כי בין שמואל לרבינא האחרון זמן רב ביניהם, או שהאריך רב טבות כ"כ ימים

findings.reasoning: Be'er Sheva (researcher translation): 'it seems to me there is a scribal error and one should emend ... for so we read in Perek Helek 97a, and that is its main place'. The emendation assumes the two passages are one tradition. Seder HaDorot's dating is historical inference from biographies. Jastrow also notes a manuscript spelling טאבות for Bava Metzia, which I did not verify.
findings.graph_effect: Store Be'er Sheva/Gilyon HaShas as 'proposed emendation' evidence, separate from source variants. They do not change the Sanhedrin branches. Any historical merge needs its own decision.

findings.claim: The story is placed as an illustration of 'truth will be lacking' (Isaiah 59:15) in the baraita about the generation of the Messiah. The segment's opening 'Concerning the lack of truth' is Davidson's plain text. Rava states his former view. The implied change of mind is never stated.

evidence.exact_quote: § Concerning the lack of truth, Rava says: Initially I would say
כיון שדובר בהעדר האמת, מביאים דברים ש<b>אמר רבא
ליכא קושטא בעלמא - אין אדם בעולם שידבר אמת תמיד
והאמת נעדרת שנאמר (ישעיהו נט, טו) ותהי האמת נעדרת

findings.reasoning: The placement is editorial. It links no people in the story to the baraita's speakers (R. Yehuda, the house of Rav, the house of R. Sheila). Rashi (researcher translation): 'there is no one in the world who always speaks truth'.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 limited to the former view. Add no claim that Rava now holds a revised view, and no edges from Rava to the baraita's speakers.

findings.claim: Translations differ in ways that matter for the graph. Glick has Raba 'met' the rabbi and turns the story into third person. Soncino renders it as indirect speech ('told me that he once came'). Davidson keeps it as direct first person.

evidence.exact_quote: However, I consequently met a certain Rabbi named Tabuth, according to others, R. Tibumi
It happened once, that he came to a city named Kushta
told me that he once came to a place called Kushta,
He said to me: One time I happened to come

findings.reasoning: 'Met' is Glick's word. The Aramaic has אמר לי. These are free translations, and none is an independent witness to the Aramaic.
findings.graph_effect: Do not use translation wording such as 'met' to create a scene or meeting edge beyond the reported speech.

findings.claim: The place is called Kushta ('Truth'). Maharal notes that no such place is known and reads it symbolically. Where it was, or whether it was real, is not established.

evidence.exact_quote: לההוא אתרא וקושטא שמיה
גם לא מצאנו המקום הזה
Lit., 'truth'.

findings.reasoning: Researcher translation of Maharal: 'also we have not found this place'. The name is also the theme of the story.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the town as a local place node labelled Kushta, with no geographic identification and a note that it may be literary.
