The review calls 'unknown' voice acceptable. The witnesses show that the teller is the more likely voice, so this is a correctable gap, not just a limit of the contract.

lessons: A nested first-person report needs a voice value such as 'teller of branch X, reported by Y'. 'unknown' loses evidence the witnesses provide.
When grammatical person shifts inside a story, check the variants before concluding that the narrator changed. Abbreviations such as א"ל can be expanded as 'said to me' or 'said to him'.
A possessive on a relational noun (שיבבתה, 'her neighbour') is an explicit social relation, just as a patronymic is a family relation.
A counterfactual used as praise ('if they gave him the whole world') is a character claim, not an event with participants.
In the Davidson English, causal glue ('Since he deviated from the truth') is often in plain text. Check bold against plain before setting basis=explicit.
Later retellings (expulsion, choosing one name) and emendations (Be'er Sheva) are separate evidence types from source variants. They do not resolve branches.
A stock description attached to the same name in another tractate is a coreference candidate, not a merge.

review.scope: I checked every dossier finding and proposed correction against the saved sources in sources/ (all text quotes found verbatim) and read the Vilna, Bomberg 1523 and Munich 95 page images myself; I did not check other manuscripts, Dikdukei Soferim or any source not already saved, and fetched nothing new.

findings.target: f04 / proposed correction 'c7, c10, c19, c22, c26-c31 (voice)' / alt_narrator_person
findings.reason: The alternative to the teller's first person is misnamed. The whole unit sits under 'אמר רבא', and nothing in the printed third-person wording 'סבר ... אמר לה ... אמר להו' marks a switch to the anonymous Talmudic voice. So the printed reading is most naturally Rava retelling in the third person, which is how Soncino ('told me that he once came') and Glick ('It happened once, that he came') render it. The first-person evidence is also thinner than the finding says. The Vilna margin note 'י"ג סברי . אמרי' (I confirmed it on the image) covers only the two asterisked words. Koren prints 'סְבַרִי ... אֲמַרִי לַהּ' but then 'בְּנֵיהּ' and 'אֲמַר לְהוּ', and the Davidson English of the same edition has 'He thought ... He said to her' throughout. Koren, Davidson and Steinsaltz are one editorial work, not three votes. Record the voice as 'Rava, reporting the branch-selected teller' under both readings. Keep a reading group for first against third person, with the printed Vilna reading kept as printed. An anonymous-narrator voice should be at most a low-confidence note.

findings.target: proposed_corrections voice list (c8, c9, c11, c20, c21, c23, c32, c33)
findings.reason: The voice correction leaves out claims that also carry voice 'unknown' in the first reading. c32 and c33 rest on 'ולא הוו משני בדיבורייהו ולא הוה מיית איניש מהתם בלא זימניה'. That sentence is in 97a:6, right after the first-person 'איקלעי' and before 'נסיבי', so in every witness it is the teller speaking, as reported by Rava. It is the strongest case for fixing the voice, and it was missed. c8/c20 (the residents come 'לקמיה'), c9/c21 (the question 'מאי האי') and c11/c23 (the plea) are in 97a:7 like c7 and c10. They should get the same voice treatment as the other 97a:7 claims.

findings.target: f09 (parenthood c12, c13, c24-c27; c28 derived; c31 coreference)
findings.reason: Support: in the printed text 'והוו לי תרתין בנין מינה' states the father ('לי') and the mother ('מינה'). Bomberg has the same (I read 'והוו לי תרתין בני מינה'). But on the Munich 95 image I read 'נסיבי איתתא מינייהו והוו לי תרי בני יומ' חד', with no 'מינה'. That is my own visual reading and it is uncertain. So scope c26/c27 (mother) as explicit in the printed reading. In a Munich-type reading the mother is inferred from the marriage just before. The father link is repeated in 97a:7 by 'שכיבו ליה' ('died to him'). That supports tying c31's dying sons to the same group by local coreference. c28 as derived is correct.

findings.target: f05 (neighbor_of neighbour, wife; addressee and person the words are about)
findings.reason: 'אתאי שיבבתה טרפא אדשא' has the feminine verbs אתאי/טרפא and the possessive ־ה ('her neighbour'), which points back to 'דביתהו'. The husband's 'אמר לה ליתא הכא' marks the neighbour as addressee with 'לה'. 'She is not here' is about the wife. Keep the addressee (neighbour) and the person spoken about (wife) as separate roles, as proposed. Do not add any spoken request by the neighbour. Rashi's 'שהיתה שואלת אותה' is commentary (f06).

findings.target: f07 (new thought claim before the denial)
findings.reason: 'סבר לאו אורח ארעא' is an explicit thought turn by the husband before 'אמר לה'. Its content is only 'not proper conduct'. What was improper comes from Rashi ('לומר היכן היא הואיל וחייפ' רישה') and from Steinsaltz/Davidson plain text ('to tell the neighbor that his wife is bathing'). Those are one editorial line and one commentary, not the text. Its grammatical person follows the same reading group as f04.

'דאי הוו יהבי ליה כל חללי דעלמא לא הוה משני בדבוריה' is a counterfactual ('if they were to give him') about the sage, in third person ('ליה', 'בדבוריה'). It sits inside Rava's framing sentence. It describes a trait. No offer ever takes place, so the imagined givers do not refer to anyone and should not be a participant group. Iyun Yaakov's sales example (via Petach Einayim) is commentary on the trait. It does not create an event.

findings.target: f14, f15 and the Bava Metzia coreference candidate
findings.reason: Support the unmerged candidate. Also record that Be'er Sheva's emendation is based on this very passage ('דהכי גרסינן בפרק חלק דף צ"ז ע"א ושם עיקר מקומו'), so it cannot count as evidence that the two passages share a person. Doing so would be circular. Seder HaDorot's 'או שהאריך רב טבות כ"כ ימים' already assumes that identity, so it cannot support it either. The printed Bava Metzia reading 'רב שמואל בר זוטרא' stays as printed, and any emendation must not erase it. If that branch is ever recorded, its embedded parent (child_of Zutra) belongs to the Bava Metzia reading only. The Bava Metzia chain ('אמר רב פפי אמר לי רבינא לדידי אמר לי ההוא מרבנן') is one direction per link. None of it enters this passage.

findings.target: f10 (member_of wife, residents; resided_in teller, town)
findings.reason: 'נסיבי איתתא מינהון' explicitly makes the wife one of 'them'. 'Them' is the implied subject of 'לא הוו משני בדיבורייהו', the people of Kushta. The residents group in the first reading, however, is anchored at 'אינשי דאתרא' in 97a:7. So linking the wife to that group entity is local coreference, not explicit. resided_in(teller, town) as interpretation from 'פוק מאתרין' is fine. No departure is reported.

findings.target: f02 (אמר לי / אמר ליה on c2, c14)
findings.reason: I confirmed on the image that Bomberg reads 'ליכא קושטא בעלמא אמר / ליה ההוא מרבנן'. I confirmed that Munich reads 'א"ל ההו' מרבנן', which can be expanded either way. Chokhmat Shlomo's 'אמר ליה ההוא כו' צ"ל אמר לי' is a correction, and Maharal's 'אמר ליה' comes inside his Moses allegory. Keep c2/c14 as in the Vilna text with a variant note. Under 'ליה' the addressee is a pronoun whose nearest antecedent is Rava; the words do not name him. So the addressee is Rava at medium confidence in that reading. Neither reading makes this a meeting beyond the one reported telling. Glick's 'met' (f17) is translation wording.

findings.target: f08, f11, f12 (cause of deaths, answer content, expulsion)
findings.reason: The Aramaic gives only 'אמר לה ליתא הכא שכיבו ליה תרתין בנין' in sequence. 'Since he deviated from the truth' is Davidson plain text, 'וכיון ששינה בדיבורו' is Steinsaltz, and '[As a punishment for this]' is a Soncino bracket, so any causal edge is interpretation. The answer is only 'הכי הוה מעשה'. The residents ask him to leave ('במטותא מינך פוק מאתרין'), but no leaving is reported. Reshit Chokhmah's 'וגירשוהו' is a later retelling and adds no event.

cases.question: Who are the people in Berakhot 5b:10, what relations and speech turns does the text itself state, and does the wider sugya, the textual witnesses, the translations or the commentaries change any saved claim in the first reading or its review?

findings.claim: The text names two people who act, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yohanan, plus a father named Abba through the patronymic. It names the sick man and the visitor. After that, the four speech and action turns use only 'said to him' and 'gave him'. Nobody is named again. Speakers are assigned by turn-taking, as the first reading did.

evidence.exact_quote: רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא חֲלַשׁ. עָל לְגַבֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲבִיבִין עָלֶיךָ יִסּוּרִין? אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֹא הֵן וְלֹא שְׂכָרָן. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַב לִי יְדָךְ. יְהַב לֵיהּ יְדֵיהּ, וְאוֹקְמֵיהּ.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba fell ill. Rabbi Yohanan went in to him [and] said to him: Are sufferings dear to you? He said to him: Neither they nor their reward. He said to him: Give me your hand. He gave him his hand, and he raised him.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי חייא בר אבא חלש על לגביה ר' יוחנן א"ל חביבין עליך יסורין א"ל לא הן ולא שכרן א"ל הב לי ידך יהב ליה ידיה ואוקמיה.
He gave him his hand and R. Johanan raised him.

findings.reasoning: The Wikisource (Vilna-based) and William Davidson Aramaic agree word for word, apart from abbreviations and vowels. The alternation is the only way to read the turns: the visitor asks, the sick man answers, the visitor asks for the hand, the sick man gives it, the visitor raises him. The Cohen and William Davidson English supply the name of the raiser. That is the translators' resolution, not extra wording in the Aramaic.
findings.graph_effect: Confirms c1-c8 roles and directions. Their basis stays local_coreference, except c3's subject, which is named.

findings.claim: This scene is not self-contained in the sugya. Next, Rabbi Yohanan falls ill and Rabbi Hanina raises him the same way (5b:11). The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Yohanan did not raise himself, and answers that a prisoner cannot free himself (5b:12-13). The question takes for granted that Rabbi Yohanan could raise a sick person. The only earlier case of him doing so in the sugya is 5b:10.

evidence.exact_quote: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן חֲלַשׁ. עָל לְגַבֵּיהּ רַבִּי חֲנִינָא.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rabbi Yohanan fell ill. Rabbi Hanina went in to him.

evidence.exact_quote: אַמַּאי, לוֹקִים רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ?
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Why? Let Rabbi Yohanan raise himself!

evidence.exact_quote: אָמְרִי: אֵין חָבוּשׁ מַתִּיר עַצְמוֹ מִבֵּית הָאֲסוּרִים.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: They say: a prisoner does not free himself from prison.

evidence.exact_quote: כדמוכח בעובדא דר' חייא ב"א לעיל דיהיב ליה ידיה גם שראה בו שקם
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Maharsha) as is shown by the earlier story of R. Hiyya b. Abba, where he gave him his hand and he saw that he rose.

findings.reasoning: The text does not say which earlier case the question means, but Maharsha makes the link explicitly. Maharsha also explains why the Gemara does not ask the same question about Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba. The first reading's job held only 5b:10, so it could not see this dependency.
findings.graph_effect: The raising event (c7/c8) is the presupposed premise of the anonymous question in 5b:12. Add a cross-segment context link, and list 5b:11-13 in episode.needed_context.

findings.claim: The witnesses arrange this story differently. In the Vilna-based text and the William Davidson edition, it is a stand-alone scene before Rabbi Yohanan's own illness. The Ein Yaakov text in the Glick edition (1916) puts Rabbi Yohanan's illness first. It then cites the Hiyya bar Abba story inside the Gemara's question, introduced by 'for' (דהא), as proof that Rabbi Yohanan could raise others. My visual reading of Munich Cod. hebr. 95 seems to show the same arrangement.

evidence.exact_quote: ואמאי לוקים ר׳ יוחנן לנפשיה דהא רבי חייא בר אבא חלש ועל לגביה רבי יוחנן ואמר ליה חביבין עליך יסורין אמר ליה לא הן ולא שכרן אמר ליה הב לי ידך יהב ליה ידא ואוקמיה וליקום איהו לנפשיה אמרי אין חבוש מתיר את עצמו מבית האסורין
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: And why did R. Yohanan not raise himself, for R. Hiyya bar Abba fell ill and R. Yohanan went in to him and said to him: Are sufferings dear to you? He said to him: Neither they nor their reward. He said to him: Give me your hand. He gave him the hand and he raised him. So let him raise himself! They say: a prisoner does not free himself from prison.

evidence.exact_quote: Why did not R. Jochanan make himself well without the aid of R. Chanina? [Did it not happen that] when R. Chiya b. Abba once became sick, he was visited by R. Jochanan
א"ל הב לי ידך יהב ליה ידיה ואוקמיה. ואמאי ליקום ר' יוחנן לנפשיה.
evidence.note: Researcher's visual transcription of the Munich 95 page image, not machine-checked. The words end the Rabbi Hanina / Rabbi Yohanan story and begin the question.

evidence.exact_quote: [?]הא ר' חייא בר [word not securely read]
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading, not machine-checked. On the same line, right after the question, a name beginning 'R. Hiyya' appears. I could not read the introductory letter or the patronymic with confidence.

evidence.exact_quote: חלש על לגביה ר' יוחנן לשיולי ביה א"ל חביבין עליך יסורין
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading, not machine-checked. The next line starts the embedded story: 'fell ill; R. Yohanan went in to him to ask after him; he said to him: Are sufferings dear to you'.

evidence.exact_quote: אין חבוש מתיר עצמו מבית האסורין
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading, not machine-checked. The prisoner answer follows the embedded story directly.

findings.reasoning: In the Ein Yaakov arrangement, the anonymous Talmud voice recalls the story to build its question. The narrator does not present it as a scene of its own. The people, the turns and the directions are the same in both arrangements. What changes is the voice and discourse status of claims c2-c8. I have not checked whether the Glick Hebrew follows an early Ein Yaakov print or a manuscript. A shared arrangement in Ein Yaakov and Munich 95 does not prove that the two are independent. Glick's bracketed English words are the translator's framing.
findings.graph_effect: Add a reading group on discourse framing. Branch A: a narrator-stated scene before 5b:11 (Vilna/Wikisource, William Davidson). Branch B: a precedent the anonymous Talmud cites inside the question of 5b:12 (Ein Yaakov Glick; Munich 95 by visual reading). Participants and roles are shared across the branches. Do not count this as a second occurrence of the event.

findings.claim: In the Munich 95 image, the embedded Hiyya story seems to differ from the printed text in two small ways. It adds 'to ask after him' (לשיולי ביה) to the visit. It also seems to go straight from the refusal to the hand-giving, without 'He said to him: Give me your hand'. This is a tentative visual reading.

evidence.exact_quote: א"ל לא הן ולא שכרן הב ליה ידיה ואוקמיה
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading, not machine-checked. I did not see 'א"ל הב לי ידך' between the refusal and the hand-giving. The word I read as הב may be a compressed יהב.

evidence.exact_quote: לשיולי ביה א"ל חביבין עליך יסורין א"ל לא הן ולא שכ
evidence.note: Researcher's visual reading, not machine-checked. The same 'to ask after him' seems to appear in the Rabbi Hanina story on the line above.

findings.reasoning: These readings come from enlarged crops of one manuscript page. The hand is small and my reading is not verified. They should be checked against a published transcription before any claim is changed.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c6 in branch A. In branch B, c6 is attested in Ein Yaakov (S6) but may be missing from Munich 95. Mark it as witness-dependent. Do not delete it.

findings.claim: ואוקמיה literally says Rabbi Yohanan 'raised / stood him up'. That he was healed is the translators' and commentators' interpretation, backed by the sugya's own question (F2). The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz state the recovery in their explanatory, non-bold words. Cohen translates 'raised him' and gives 'cured' only in a footnote. Glick renders it 'made him well'.

evidence.exact_quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan stood him up and restored him to health.
ר' יוחנן על רגליו ממטת חוליו, וחזר ר' חייא בר אבא לבריאותו.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Steinsaltz, explanatory words) R. Yohanan [stood him] on his feet from his sickbed, and R. Hiyya bar Abba returned to health.

evidence.exact_quote: Cured him of his ailment by the healing touch.
R. Jochanan asked for his hand and made him well.

findings.reasoning: The William Davidson English and Steinsaltz come from one editorial project and count as one interpretive witness. In both, the recovery wording is outside the bold translation. The first reading's note ('a separate medical outcome is not added') is correct at the text level. The healing sense can be added only as a separate interpretation-level claim.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c8 as 'raises', stated by the narrator. Optionally add an interpretation claim, 'the raising cures the illness', with basis translation/commentary plus sugya context (5b:12). Do not upgrade it to explicit.

findings.claim: The Aramaic of 5b:10 states no teacher-student relation between Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba. The William Davidson English adds 'Rabbi Yoḥanan’s student' in plain, non-bold words, and Steinsaltz adds 'who was his student' and 'his teacher'. Seder HaDorot calls Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba a close student of Rabbi Yohanan, citing other passages. That is prosopography, not this text.

evidence.exact_quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan’s student, Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, fell ill.
ר' חייא בר אבא שהיה תלמידו של ר' יוחנן חלש
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Steinsaltz) R. Hiyya bar Abba, who was R. Yohanan's student, fell ill.

evidence.exact_quote: ר' יוחנן רבו לביקור חולים
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Steinsaltz) R. Yohanan, his teacher, [entered] to visit the sick.

evidence.exact_quote: If he was able to heal his student, let Rabbi Yoḥanan stand himself up.
תלמיד מובהק של ר' יוחנן ועלה מבבל
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Seder HaDorot) a distinguished student of R. Yohanan, who came up from Babylonia.

findings.reasoning: Every 'student' word here is outside the Talmud's own wording. Seder HaDorot cites passages elsewhere (e.g. Hullin 86b, Berakhot 38b), which I did not check. Any teacher relation needs its own evidence pack from those passages. The later identification of this Hiyya bar Abba with the student figure is a historical-identity decision.
findings.graph_effect: Do not add teacher_of or student_of from 5b:10. The first reading's note ('No kinship or teacher relationship ... is stated') is correct and should stay. Flag the William Davidson plain text as a known source of relation leakage.

findings.claim: The patronymic 'bar Abba' is the passage's only kinship evidence. It supports child_of(Hiyya, Abba) as a name-embedded relation, with a local placeholder for Abba. Seder HaDorot's heading adds the priestly epithet 'ha-Kohen', which this passage lacks. Elsewhere, Seder HaDorot worries that the name was confused with Rav Hiyya bar Adda. So the name alone does not fix a historical person.

evidence.exact_quote: רבי חייא בר אבא חלש.
ר' חייא בר אבא הכהן,
ולולא דמסתפינא אמינא דט"ס וצ"ל רב חייא בר אדא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Seder HaDorot, on Ketubot 8b) Were I not afraid, I would say it is a scribal error and one should read Rav Hiyya bar Adda.

findings.reasoning: By the project rule, c1 and the Abba placeholder stay. The 'ha-Kohen' epithet and any merge with other 'Hiyya bar Abba' passages belong to the identity stage. I could not securely read the patronymic in Munich 95 (F3), so this witness neither supports nor challenges 'bar Abba'.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 as it is, with the abba placeholder. Add no priestly title or identity link from this passage.

findings.claim: Commentators explain why the sick man turns down both the suffering and its reward. Maharsha says these illnesses were so severe that they stopped Torah study. Etz Yosef explains the parallel refusal in Shir HaShirim Rabbah the same way and refers to Berakhot 5b. Marit HaAyin gives a symbolic reading of the hand. These are motives that commentators infer. The text does not state them.

evidence.exact_quote: אבל כל הנהו עובדי דהכא משמע דהוו חלישי כ"כ שהיה ביסורים שלהם ביטול תורה כדאמר דהיו צריכים להקים אותן ולכך קאמרי דלא הן ולא שכרן
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Maharsha) But all these stories here imply they were so weak that their suffering involved neglect of Torah, as it says they had to be raised; therefore they said 'neither they nor their reward'.

evidence.exact_quote: אין אני חפץ בהם ולא בשכרם, שלפי שהיה היסורים קשים עליו עד שביטל מחמתם לימוד תורה
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Etz Yosef) I want neither them nor their reward, since the suffering was so hard on him that he stopped Torah study because of it.

evidence.exact_quote: וכשא"ל לא הן ולא שכרן ש"מ דאין לו חטא והיסורין לשכר
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Marit HaAyin, citing Eretz HaChayim) When he said 'neither they nor their reward', this shows he had no sin and the suffering was for reward.

findings.reasoning: These are separate commentary layers. None changes who speaks or who acts.
findings.graph_effect: At most, attach commentary notes to the 'rejection' statement entity. Make no new claim.

findings.claim: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:16 tells a related tradition with a different cast. Rabbi Yohanan is ill and Rabbi Hanina helps him with a word. Later Rabbi Hanina is ill and Rabbi Yohanan visits. There Rabbi Hanina says 'I want neither them nor their reward', and explains that one inside cannot vouch for himself. The same refusal also recurs in the Bavli with Rabbi Yohanan (5b:11) and Rabbi Elazar (5b:16) as the patients.

evidence.exact_quote: לְבָתַר יוֹמִין אִתְּשַׁשׁ רַבִּי חֲנִינָא סְלַק רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לִמְבַקְּרֵיהּ
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: After some days R. Hanina fell ill; R. Yohanan went up to visit him.

evidence.exact_quote: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לָא אֲנָא בָּעֵי לְהוֹן וְלָא לְאַגְרֵיהוֹן.
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: He said to him: I want neither them nor their reward.

evidence.exact_quote: [Rabbi Ḥanina] said to him: ‘I want neither them nor their reward.’
והוא כמו שאמרו במס' ברכות דף הנזכר לעיל אין חבוש מתיר עצמו מבית האסורים
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Etz Yosef) And this is like what they said in tractate Berakhot, on the page mentioned above: a prisoner does not free himself from prison.

evidence.exact_quote: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר חֲלַשׁ. עַל לְגַבֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן.

findings.reasoning: In the Midrash the refusal is spoken by the patient, just as in 5b:10, but the patient is Rabbi Hanina. This is a parallel tradition with different participants, not another witness to the 5b:10 scene. The recurring formula shows a literary pattern. It cannot establish that any of these visits happened.
findings.graph_effect: Record Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:16 as a separate episode, linked as a parallel. Do not merge its events with 5b:10, 5b:11 or 5b:16. Do not use it to reassign any speaker in 5b:10.

findings.claim: Ben Yehoyada's commentary on the dark-room scene calls the weeping patient 'Rabbi Hiyya'. Sefaria links that comment to 5b:14, where the Talmud names Rabbi Elazar. His comment on the hand-giving, which Sefaria links to 5b:10, talks about Rabbi Yohanan's and Rabbi Hiyya's hands. The commentary may conflate the stories, or may be a slip. It is not evidence of another Hiyya-Yohanan scene.

evidence.exact_quote: ושאל אותו אמאי קא בכית? והשיב על האי שופרא דבלי, פירוש כי רבי חייא היה מחשב ומצייר אותה שעה בדעתו
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Ben Yehoyada) He asked him, why are you weeping? He answered, over this beauty that will decay; meaning that R. Hiyya was contemplating at that moment...

evidence.exact_quote: הרי נעשה שמאל רבי יוחנן בימין של רבי חייא
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: (Ben Yehoyada) thus R. Yohanan's left was placed in R. Hiyya's right.

evidence.exact_quote: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְהַאי שׁוּפְרָא דְּבָלֵי בְּעַפְרָא קָא בָּכֵינָא.

findings.reasoning: The saved text of 5b:14-15 names Rabbi Elazar (S1). The comment-to-segment mapping comes from Sefaria's link data (S16). Ben Yehoyada quotes the formula with the punctuation of 5b:16 in the Sefaria edition, so which segment he meant is uncertain.
findings.graph_effect: Do not add a weeping or beauty scene between Hiyya bar Abba and Yohanan on the strength of this commentary.

findings.claim: The earlier review's one finding is wrong. It says pronoun mentions m4-m10 are not attached to either participant. The first reading attaches m4, m5, m7, m9 and m10 to hiyya, and m6 and m8 to yohanan. Counting the four occurrences of ליה in the saved text confirms the pattern Hiyya, Yohanan, Hiyya, Yohanan. The real gaps are smaller. עליך and ידך (Hiyya) and לי (Yohanan) are not inventoried. m10 (ואוקמיה) is linked only to its object, Hiyya, although its unexpressed subject is Yohanan.

evidence.exact_quote: The standalone pronoun mentions m4–m10 are not attached to either participant’s mention_ids or resolved through a mention map.
Rabbi Hiyya son of Abba
אמר ליה: חביבין עליך יסורין? אמר ליה: לא הן ולא שכרן. אמר ליה: הב לי ידך. יהב ליה ידיה, ואוקמיה.

lessons: A story in a series can be a narrator's scene in one witness and a cited precedent inside a question in another. Discourse status and voice need branches of their own, independent of the event and its roles.
A later anonymous question can depend on an earlier scene (5b:12 on 5b:10). The contract needs a cross-segment 'presupposes' link, so single-segment jobs flag the dependency.

A recurring formula (Bavli 5b:10, 5b:11, 5b:16; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:16) is a literary pattern. Parallels with different casts are separate episodes. They are not extra witnesses to one event and do not justify reassigning speakers.

Prosopographic works (Seder HaDorot) use narrative details for chronology and teacher lists. Store those uses as historical inference, apart from text claims.

That is the same name, Hiyya bar Abba, passing on a teaching of Rabbi Yohanan, reported by his own son, Rabbi Abba. The dossier checked only 5b:8-16 and never mentions it, even though the Maharsha motive in F8 ('ביטול תורה') answers the 5a:16 teaching. Record it as a same-name coreference candidate and as its own transmission chain (son reports father, father reports Yohanan, each direction stored once). Do not merge people, and do not add student_of: 'in the name of' is not discipleship. Also keep the father-placeholder 'abba' in c1 apart from this son, Rabbi Abba. They are different people who share a name.

findings.target: F3 / reading group g1 (branch B, Munich 95)
findings.reason: I read the Munich 95 image myself and confirm the order. After the children discussion ('דין גרמא דעשיראה ביר ... לא קשיא'), the line goes straight to 'ר' יוחנן חלש על לגביה ר' חנינא לשיולי ביה'. There is no separate Hiyya scene before it. The Hiyya story follows 'ליקום ר' יוחנן לנפשיה' and runs straight into 'אין חבוש מתיר עצמו מבית האסורין'. The two-branch framing and the shared roles are right. Glick's English (S7) translates the Glick Hebrew (S6), so branch B has two textual witnesses (Ein Yaakov, Munich), not three. Do not count S7 as a vote.

My reading agrees that the embedded Munich story goes from 'לא הן ולא שכרן' directly to '[י]הב ליה ידיה ואוקמיה', with no 'א"ל הב לי ידך'. So in Munich, c6 (Yohanan asks for the hand) is not merely doubtful: on my reading it is absent. The hand-giving (c7) and the raising (c8) remain. Mark c6 as absent in Munich 95 by two independent visual readings, still low confidence until a published transcription is checked. Do not delete c6 from the printed-text branch.

I could not securely read the word after 'ר' חייא' either. I see 'דה[א/וו] ר' חייא' and then a cramped cluster at the line end that I cannot resolve into 'בר אבא'. The dossier is right that Munich neither supports nor challenges the patronymic. c1 (child_of Abba) stays, scoped to the printed text and Ein Yaakov, which both read 'רבי חייא בר אבא'. It may be a fixed name rather than literal kinship, but the name is still evidence.

The link is sound. Maharsha writes 'כדמוכח בעובדא דר' חייא ב"א לעיל דיהיב ליה ידיה גם שראה בו שקם'. But the word 'presupposes' fits only branch A, where 5b:10 is a separate earlier scene. In branch B (Ein Yaakov, Munich) the question itself contains the story ('דהא רבי חייא בר אבא חלש'), so nothing earlier is presupposed. Word the cross-segment link per branch: 'presupposed by 5b:12' in A, 'cited inside 5b:12' in B.

The quote 'He gave him his hand and R. Johanan raised him.' appears twice in the saved Cohen text: at segment 10 (Hiyya) and again at segment 16 (Elazar). The dossier gives no occurrence. It must point at segment 10, the first occurrence, or it could be read as support from the Elazar scene. The conclusion (the English supplies the raiser's name, the Aramaic does not) is unchanged.

In the first reading, entity 'hiyya' lists m1, m4, m5, m7, m9, m10 and 'yohanan' lists m3, m6, m8. The four ליה in 'אמר ליה ... אמר ליה ... אמר ליה ... יהב ליה' do alternate Hiyya, Yohanan, Hiyya, Yohanan. So the earlier review's omission finding is wrong. The narrower gaps are real: עליך and ידך refer to Hiyya, לי refers to Yohanan, and Yohanan is the unstated subject of ואוקמיה.

Checked and correct. 'student' appears only in the William Davidson English plain words and in Steinsaltz ('שהיה תלמידו של ר' יוחנן', 'רבו'), one editorial project. Healing is interpretation over literal 'ואוקמיה'. Shir HaShirim Rabbah has the sick Rabbi Hanina say 'לא אנא בעי להון ולא לאגריהון', a separate episode. Seder HaDorot's 'הרי מפורש שר' יוחנן אוקמי'' is a death-order inference. One small addition for F10: the saved Wikisource text names the 5b:14 patient 'רבי אליעזר', while William Davidson has 'רבי אלעזר'. That is a name variant outside the focal passage, to note and not resolve here.

findings.claim: Rav Yehuda is described as brother (אחוה) of Rav Sala Hasida. The same description recurs in other Bavli passages, where it identifies the speaker or actor, so it works as a distinguishing label as well as a stated kinship.

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'Rav Yehuda, brother of Rav Sala the Pious'; Seder HaDorot: 'Rav Sala Hasida - Rav Yehuda his brother. Rav Yosef his son.'
findings.reasoning: The plain sense of אחוה is 'his brother'. Its repetition as a fixed epithet shows it is used to tell this Rav Yehuda apart from others; that is a function of the label, not evidence against literal kinship. The Davidson Aramaic at Berakhot 29b lacks the ד ('אחוה רב סלא'); the meaning is unchanged. Seder HaDorot is a later compilation and is not an independent witness to the kinship; it restates the Talmud's epithets. Whether the Rav Yehuda of all these passages is one historical person is a separate identity decision not made here.

וכשאמר להם מי חשידנא בעינייכו דעבידנא מילתא דלאו דינא השיבוהו ומי חשיד קודשא בריך הוא דעביד מילתא דלא דינא

findings.translation: Researcher translation: Wikisource notes that 'manuscript מ' adds' to 'Am I suspect in your eyes' the words 'that I do a thing without justice'; and before 'if anyone has heard something against me, let him say it' adds 'Have the rabbis heard a thing that I did without justice?'. Meiri paraphrases: 'when he said to them, am I suspect in your eyes that I do a thing that is not just, they answered, is the Holy One suspect of doing a thing that is not just'.
findings.reasoning: These are reports of variants on a community-edited page whose template says the notes come mainly from Dikdukei Soferim or the Hachi Garsinan project; the manuscript sigla are not expanded in the saved page. Meiri's paraphrase has the fuller wording, which fits such a text but is a paraphrase, not a witness to exact words. The extra line does not add a person: it is Huna asking whether the rabbis heard something. It is a speech turn only in that text form.
findings.graph_effect: Optionally record a variant speech turn (Huna asks the rabbis whether they heard of an unjust act) as a text-variant alternative, evidence type 'secondary report of manuscript variant'. It must not be counted as an independent observation of the printed turn c10.

findings.claim: Huna's promise: printed text 'I undertake that I will give him' (object unstated). A reported manuscript reading adds 'all of them' (לכולהו); the annotator explains that by the printed text he undertook to give the sharecropper his share, by that manuscript to give him everything.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר להו: קבילנא עלי דיהיבנא ליה.
קבילנא עלי דיהיבנא ליה!{{דקס|בכת"י מ'|לכולהו}}{{הערה|והיינו דלפי נוסחתנו, קיבל עליו ליתן לו חלקו, למחצה לשליש ולרביע; ולפי כת"י מ', ליתן לו הכל.}}
He said to them,  "I undertake to give him what is due."

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'I take upon myself that I will give [it] to him' ; variant note: 'manuscript מ': all of them'; annotator: 'that is, by our text he undertook to give him his share, a half, a third or a quarter; by manuscript מ', to give him everything.' Cohen renders 'what is due', which supplies an object.
findings.reasoning: The recipient (ליה) is the sharecropper by local coreference with Huna's defense and the visitors' charge. The object of the gift is unstated in print; 'his share' (Davidson, Steinsaltz) and 'what is due' (Cohen) are translators' completions. A promise is not a narrated transfer.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c16 as an undertaking, with the promise object open between 'his share' (print, as completed by translators) and 'all of them' (reported manuscript variant). Anchor the recipient to the second ליה in s4 (C04).

findings.claim: The visitors report hearsay without a named informant ('thus we have heard'). Tosafot and Tosafot HaRosh interpret that they already knew about the vine-shoots and meant to hint; the Davidson English puts this into plain (editorial) text citing Tosafot.

evidence.exact_quote: הכי שמיע לן
הרבה צדיקים יש שלוקין בגופם ובממונם אלא הם היו יודעים שלא היה נותן שבישא לאריסיה והיו רוצים לרמוז לו שלא יעשה עוד
אבל הם היו יודעים דלא יהיב שבשתא לאריסיה והיו רוצין לומר לו שלא יעשה עוד
The Sages were aware of a flaw in Rav Huna’s conduct, to which they alluded (Tosafot).

findings.translation: Researcher translation of Tosafot: 'Many righteous people are afflicted in body and property; rather, they knew that he was not giving the vine-shoots to his sharecropper and wanted to hint to him that he should not do so again.'
findings.reasoning: The Talmud text states only that the visitors say they heard it. That they knew beforehand, and that their first two lines were a hint, is commentary. The Davidson sentence is in plain type, so it is editorial explanation, not the Talmud's words.
findings.graph_effect: Record 'visitors report hearing an accusation' (voice: visitors, discourse: reported hearsay, informant unknown). A 'visitors knew beforehand' claim, if kept, is commentary-sourced (Tosafot), not textual.

findings.claim: The accusation is that Huna does not give his sharecropper the vine-shoots (שבישא). Aramaic has one sharecropper (לאריסיה, singular); the Davidson English bold text says 'tenant farmers' (plural). Rashi explains שבישא as the sharecropper's portion of pruned vine-shoots.

evidence.exact_quote: דלא יהיב מר שבישא לאריסיה
does not give a share of his grapevines to his tenant farmers.
that our master has not given the vine-tendrils to his labourer.
שבישא – חלקו בזמורות הגפן שחותכין מהן בשעת הזמיר

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'that the master does not give the vine-shoots to his sharecropper'; Rashi: 'שבישא: his share in the vine-branches that are cut off at pruning time'.
findings.reasoning: The singular suffix and the singular verbs that follow (גניב, 'he steals') support one sharecropper. The plural in the Davidson English is a translation choice; Cohen keeps the singular.
findings.graph_effect: Keep a single local 'sharecropper' person (entity farmer). Do not create several tenant farmers from the English.

findings.claim: Huna's counter-charge that the sharecropper 'steals it all' is Huna's own claim. Rashi softens it to 'steals from me much more than his share'; Maharsha says that by Huna's own view he was taking what was his, and that the proverb fits only as the visitors heard it.

evidence.exact_quote: הא קא גניב ליה כוליה!
וכי אינו חשוד בעיניכם שהוא גונב לי הרבה יותר מחלקו
מי שביק כו' שהוא גנב לי כו' כצ"ל
גם שאין המשל הזה דומה ממש לעובדא דרב הונא שהוא נוטל את שלו לפי דעתו מ"מ לפי מאי דשמיע להו ולא היה חשוד להם הוה קצת בדומה

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'Why, he steals it all!'; Rashi: 'Is he not suspect in your eyes of stealing from me much more than his share?'; Maharsha: 'although this proverb does not exactly match Rav Huna's case, since by his own opinion he was taking what was his, still, according to what they had heard, and he was not suspect to them, it is somewhat similar.'
findings.reasoning: Neither theft (the sharecropper's, alleged by Huna; Huna's, implied by the visitors' proverb) is narrated as fact. Chokhmat Shlomo is a wording correction to Rashi's gloss, not a new reading of the Talmud.
findings.graph_effect: c13 stays in Huna's voice as an allegation. No 'Huna stole from the sharecropper' fact edge; the proverb applies theft language in the visitors' voice only.

findings.claim: The proverb is attributed to 'people' (אינשי) generally; its thief and the one who steals after him are figures of the saying, not persons in the story.

evidence.exact_quote: היינו דאמרי אינשי: ״בתר גנבא גנוב, וטעמא טעים״.
הגונב מן הגנב אף הוא טועם טעם גנבה
To rob even a thief is also stealing.

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'This is what people say: steal after a thief and you taste [the taste of theft].' Rashi: 'one who steals from a thief also tastes the taste of theft.'
findings.reasoning: The visitors apply the saying to Huna and the sharecropper, but the saying's figures are generic.
findings.graph_effect: Type entities 'thief' and 'retaliator' as generic figures of a quoted saying, excluded from the person network (C05). Keep 'people' as the anonymous source group of the proverb (c15).

findings.claim: Two anonymous reports of the outcome ('some say ... and some say'). The text does not state that the outcome was caused by Huna's promise; causal wording ('thereupon', 'as a result of Rav Huna's repentance') is supplied by translators.

evidence.exact_quote: איכא דאמרי: הדר חלא והוה חמרא. ואיכא דאמרי: אייקר חלא, ואיזדבן בדמי דחמרא.
Thereupon, as a result of Rav Huna’s repentance, God restored his loss.
Some declare  that thereupon the vinegar turned back into wine,  but others say  that vinegar became very dear and was sold at the price of wine.

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'Some say: the vinegar turned back and became wine. And some say: vinegar became dear and was sold at the price of wine.'
findings.reasoning: The Davidson sentence is entirely plain type (editorial). The juxtaposition invites a causal reading, and commentators read it that way, but the text itself only narrates the sequence. The seller in 'was sold' is not named; Huna as owner is a local inference.
findings.graph_effect: Keep the outcomes group with two branches, independent of the visitor branches. Mark c17/c18 as the owner's benefit by local inference, with no explicit causal link to c16. Optionally add a transmission note: each outcome is reported by an anonymous 'some say' group.

findings.claim: Commentators differ on what the two outcome reports represent: Petach Einayim suggests they disagree on whether Huna's promise covered the past; Ben Yehoyada suggests both groups heard the same report of the sale at wine's price and reasoned differently about how the miracle happened.

evidence.exact_quote: אפשר דהני תרי לישני פליגי בפירוש דברי רב הונא שאמר קבילנא דיהיבנא ליה
ששני כתות אלה שניהם שמעו דרב הונא מכר החבית

findings.translation: Researcher translation: Petach Einayim: 'Possibly these two versions disagree over the meaning of Rav Huna's words "I undertake to give him"'. Ben Yehoyada: 'that these two groups both heard that Rav Huna sold the barrel'.
findings.reasoning: Both are explicitly offered as possibilities ('אפשר', 'נראה לי'). They do not add people. Ben Yehoyada makes Huna the seller, which is his reading, not the text's.
findings.graph_effect: No new edges. Keep the two outcome branches open; record these as commentary interpretations of the branches if the graph stores interpretations.

findings.claim: The visitors' advice echoes the teaching two folios earlier, 'if a person sees suffering come upon him, let him examine his deeds'. In print that teaching is by 'Rava, and some say Rav Hisda'; the Wikisource annotation reports that manuscripts read 'Rava said Rav Sechora said Rav Huna said'; Petach Einayim says Ein Yaakov also gives it as Rav Huna's; Ben Yehoyada builds on that to explain the visitors' phrasing.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר רבא ואיתימא רב חסדא אם רואה אדם שיסורין באין עליו יפשפש במעשיו
אמר רבא ואיתימא רב חסדא{{דקס|בכתה"י|אמר רבא אמר רב סחורה אמר רב הונא}}
ומ"ש הרב ישרש יעקב דלעיל היא מימרת רב הונא הא דאם רואה שיסורין באים עליו. כן הוא גירסת עין יעקב אך בש"ס דקמן הגירסא אמר רבא ואי תימא רב חסדא
ונראה לי בס"ד כי מאמר יְפַשְׁפֵּשׁ בְּמַעֲשָׂיו דלעיל אתמר משמיה דרב הונא עצמו, ולכן משום שורת דרך ארץ לא אמרו לו יְפַשְׁפֵּשׁ בְּמַעֲשָׂיו, אלא אמרו לו לִיעַיֵּין מַר בְּמִילֵיהּ
evidence.note: Quotation filled in from the saved source after the first reader left it blank. See mechanical-corrections.json. The separate review checks it.

evidence.exact_quote: אמר רבא אמר רב סחורה אמר רב הונא כל שהקדוש ברוך הוא חפץ בו מדכאו ביסורין

findings.translation: Researcher translation: print: 'Rava said, and some say Rav Hisda: if a person sees suffering coming on him, let him examine his deeds'; Wikisource note: 'in the manuscripts: Rava said Rav Sechora said Rav Huna said'; Petach Einayim: 'what the author of Yashresh Yaakov wrote, that the earlier statement is Rav Huna's, is the Ein Yaakov reading, but in our Talmud the reading is "Rava said, and some say Rav Hisda"'; Ben Yehoyada: 'the dictum "let him examine his deeds" was said in Rav Huna's own name, so out of courtesy they did not say to him "let him examine his deeds" but "let the master look into his affairs"'.
findings.reasoning: This is a source attribution question for Berakhot 5a, not for 5b:17. The link between that teaching and the visitors' words is an interpretation (Ben Yehoyada), not stated in the story. The printed text does have a separate Rava - Rav Sechora - Rav Huna chain on suffering at 5a:11, which may be why commentators connect the two. The Ein Yaakov claim is reported by Petach Einayim; the Ein Yaakov text of 5a was not read here.
findings.graph_effect: For the 5a job: keep attribution alternatives open (Rava / Rav Hisda in print; Rava from Rav Sechora from Rav Huna reported for manuscripts and Ein Yaakov), with evidence types kept apart. For 5b:17: no 'visitors quote Huna' edge; at most an interpretation note citing Ben Yehoyada.

findings.claim: Ein Yaakov witnesses differ in small ways: Glick's text calls the visitor 'ר׳ יהודה' and keeps the Rav Adda alternative; the Daat text prints the Rav Adda alternative in square brackets and replaces a parenthesized opening with the Bavli wording.

evidence.exact_quote: על לגביה ר׳ יהודה אחוה דרב סלא חסידא ורבנן. ואמרי לה רב אדא בר אהבה ורבנן
[וְאַמְרֵי לָהּ: רַב אַדָא בַּר אַהֲבָה וְרַבָּנָן]
evidence.note: Quotation filled in from the saved source after the first reader left it blank. See mechanical-corrections.json. The separate review checks it.

evidence.exact_quote: R. Juda, brother of R. Sala the pions, accompanied by Rabbis, or as some say, R. Ada b. Ahaba, accompanied by Rabbis, came to visit him.

findings.translation: Researcher translation of Daat: 'Rav Huna (had four hundred barrels of wine; it soured) [four hundred barrels of wine soured on him]. Rav Yehuda brother of Rav Sala Hasida and rabbis came in to him. [And some say: Rav Adda bar Ahava and rabbis]'.
findings.reasoning: The Daat edition's bracket convention is not stated in the saved file. It may mean the Rav Adda alternative was absent from an Ein Yaakov base text and restored from the Bavli, but that is not established here. The title ר׳ vs רב in Glick is a single-letter abbreviation difference and does not create a different person.
findings.graph_effect: No change to branches. Note that the Rav Adda alternative may be missing in some Ein Yaakov text form, pending a check of the Daat edition's conventions or a printed Ein Yaakov.

findings.claim: The names in the passage have no variant flagged in the Wikisource variant notes that were read, and all Bavli texts checked (Davidson, Wikisource Bavli, Ein Yaakov) have Rav Huna, Rav Yehuda brother of Rav Sala Hasida and Rav Adda bar Ahava. Steinsaltz's lemma reads ואמרי ליה where the Davidson Aramaic has ואמרי לה; he still glosses it 'and some say'.

evidence.exact_quote: על לגביה רב יהודה אחוה דרב סלא חסידא ורבנן, {{ב|ואמרי לה|ויש אומרים שהיו אלו}} רב אדא בר אהבה ורבנן
על לגביה רב יהודה אחוה דרב סלא חסידא ורבנן ואמרי לה  רב אדא בר אהבה ורבנן
ואמרי ליה [ויש אומרים] שהיו אלה רב אדא בר אהבה ורבנן

findings.translation: Researcher translation of Steinsaltz: 'and some say [ויש אומרים] that these were Rav Adda bar Ahava and rabbis'.
findings.reasoning: Absence of a name variant note on one community page is not proof that manuscripts agree on the names; no manuscript was read directly. Steinsaltz and Davidson are one editorial family, so the לה/ליה difference is internal to that family and its gloss shows the same meaning.
findings.graph_effect: No change. Names stay as in print; a direct manuscript check remains open.

findings.claim: Identity is not settled by the passage. 'Rav Huna' has no patronymic here. Seder HaDorot files this story under the Rav Huna it describes as Rav's disciple. Taanit 20b tells another wine story joining a Rav Huna and a Rav Adda bar Ahava. Shabbat 112a has Rav Yehuda brother of Rav Sala Hasida bringing a question to Abaye.

evidence.exact_quote: ו) רב הונא היה תלמיד מובהק לרב
פ"ק דברכות <small>(ה' ב')</small> ר"ה ה"ל ת' דני דחמרא איתקוף עאל לגביה רב יהודה אחוה דרב סלא חסידא ורבנן
רב הונא הוה ליה ההוא חמרא בההוא ביתא רעיעא ובעי לפנוייה עייליה לרב אדא בר אהבה להתם
זמנין דנפיק ביה איהו זימנין נפיק ביה ינוקיה אתא לקמיה דאביי

findings.translation: Researcher translation: Seder HaDorot: 'Rav Huna was a principal disciple of Rav'; its paraphrase of our story names only Rav Yehuda brother of Rav Sala Hasida (no Rav Adda alternative). Taanit: 'Rav Huna had some wine in a dilapidated house and wanted to clear it; he brought Rav Adda bar Ahava in there.' Shabbat: 'sometimes he went out in them, sometimes his child went out in them; he came before Abaye.'
findings.reasoning: Seder HaDorot's identification and its shortened paraphrase are a later compiler's decisions. Taanit 20b shows the same two names together elsewhere; that is a co-occurrence of names, not proof that they are the same two people. Shabbat 112a raises a chronology question if one Rav Yehuda is meant throughout; it is not resolved here, and citation or consultation direction does not establish relative age.
findings.graph_effect: Keep local persons (huna, yehuda, ada, sala, ahava) unlinked to global identities. Record Seder HaDorot's Rav Huna identification as a proposal from a later compilation. Note that Seder HaDorot's paraphrase dropping the Rav Adda branch is a summary, not a text witness.

findings.claim: Rav Adda bar Ahava's patronymic gives a father named Ahava; he never appears and says nothing. The first reading keeps him as a placeholder with child_of(ada, ahava), in the Rav Adda branch only.

evidence.exact_quote: רב אדא בר אהבה
Rab Adda b. Ahaba

findings.translation: Researcher translation: 'Rav Adda son of Ahava'.
findings.reasoning: Under project rules a patronymic is kinship evidence and the parent is kept as a local placeholder. The relation holds only if the Rav Adda branch is chosen.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c2 and entity ahava as they are, branch ada_visits.

lessons: Single-word or two-letter quotes (מר, ליה) need occurrence checks against compiled spans, or longer quotes; short substrings occur inside other words (דחמרא, אמר).
When an alternative ('ואמרי לה') repeats a companion phrase (ורבנן), each repetition is a separate mention belonging to its own branch.
A group speaker needs explicit, branch-scoped membership edges so a named member does not become an individual speaker.
Kinship epithets that also serve as disambiguating labels (אחוה דרב סלא חסידא) remain kinship evidence; record the label function as a note, not as a reason to drop the relation.
Keep evidence types apart: printed text, secondary report of a manuscript variant, commentator's paraphrase (Meiri), later compilation heading (Seder HaDorot), and translator's plain-text additions.
Figures inside a quoted proverb are generic and should not count as persons.
An outcome narrated after an act is not a stated causal link; translators often add the cause.

A teaching's attribution variant in nearby context (Berakhot 5a) can affect how commentators read a story's dialogue; store it with the teaching's own passage, and link it to the story only as interpretation.

review.scope: I checked every finding and proposed correction that touches persons, branches, speakers, addressees, kinship or attributions against the saved sources and the frozen input and compiled record, both filled-in quotations, and the Ein Yaakov text of Berakhot 5a (fetched). I did not read manuscripts, Dikdukei Soferim, the unread responsa and Musar works, or anything bearing on historical identity or dates.

findings.reason: The dossier says the chain 'Rava from Rav Sechora from Rav Huna' is reported 'for manuscripts and Ein Yaakov'. Petach Einayim only reports the Yashresh Yaakov reading 'א"ר הונא' as the Ein Yaakov reading, and the Daat Ein Yaakov at 5a (fetched by this review) prints 'אָמַר רָבָא (אמר רב הונא) [וְאִיתֵימָא רַב חִסְדָּא]', i.e. a base text 'Rava said Rav Huna said' with no Rav Sechora, while the Glick Ein Yaakov reads the printed 'אמר רבא ואיתימא רב חסדא'. For the 5a job keep four separate evidence items: print (Rava, or Rav Hisda), Wikisource's report of manuscripts (Rava from Rav Sechora from Rav Huna), the Daat Ein Yaakov base wording (Rava from Rav Huna, removed by its editors), and the Glick Ein Yaakov (same as print). ALT5's 'relying on the Ein Yaakov attribution' is the reader's inference: Ben Yehoyada's words 'אתמר משמיה דרב הונא עצמו' name no source.

findings.target: F15 and unresolved item 3 (Daat bracket convention)
findings.reason: The filled quotation '[וְאַמְרֵי לָהּ: רַב אַדָא בַּר אַהֲבָה וְרַבָּנָן]' is in the saved Daat text and supports the bracket claim. The same edition at 5a puts a replaced base wording in round brackets and the Bavli wording in square brackets ('(אמר רב הונא) [וְאִיתֵימָא רַב חִסְדָּא]'), and at 1:28 it does the same to the opening ('(הוו ליה ארבע מאות דני דחמרא, איתקוף) [תְּקִיפוּ לֵיהּ...]'). So the square-bracketed Rav Adda line was most likely added from the Bavli, meaning the Daat base text lacked it (medium confidence: inferred from the edition's own pattern; the version notes do not state the convention). This is one later anthology witness and not a vote against the Bavli's two-branch reading; the Glick Ein Yaakov keeps the alternative, so ALT1 stays as it is.

The dossier says Seder HaDorot's paraphrase drops the Rav Adda branch. That holds only for the Rav Huna entry 958:7. The Rav Yehuda entry 1695:1, which the dossier already quotes for F03, keeps it in small print: 'ואמרי לה רב אדא בר אהבה ברכות (ה' ב')'. The same entry recasts the Talmud's 'על לגביה' (went in to him) as 'נכנס לפני רב הונא' (entered before Rav Huna). That is a compiler's wording and must not produce any rank or teacher/student edge. Whether the small-print 'צ"ל אחוה' correction is by the author or by the Warsaw editors is not shown in the saved text, so say 'a small-print correction in the same entry'. The conclusion 'no father-in-law edge' stands.

F01 rightly says the two 'ורבנן' are stated separately in each branch and are 'not shown to be the same set of people'. C02 then allows 'one group entity with two anchors', and C01 puts member_of(sages, visitors) 'in both branches'. A single shared sages entity would quietly assert the sameness F01 denies. Prefer one sages mention and group per branch (occurrence 1 at chars 75-80 for yehuda_visits, occurrence 2 at chars 106-111 for ada_visits), each with its own branch-scoped membership. Keep the named visitor tied to the plural 'ואמרו ליה' only as a group member (F05).

Checked against the frozen s1, s2 and s4 texts and the compiled spans. 'מר' in s1 occurs at 33 (inside דחמרא), 84, 115, 130 ('לעיין מר'), 142 and 172, so m14 needs occurrence 4. In s2 it occurs at 1 (inside אמר), 45 and 76 ('יהיב מר'), so m15 needs occurrence 3. 'ליה' in s4 occurs at 5 ('אמרו ליה', addressed to Huna) and 86 ('דיהיבנא ליה'), so m16 needs occurrence 2. As saved, m16 wrongly ties the sharecropper to a pronoun for Huna. The second 'ורבנן' at 106 is unanchored. The longer-quote suggestion is right.

Ben Yehoyada's words say the 'יְפַשְׁפֵּשׁ בְּמַעֲשָׂיו' teaching 'was said in Rav Huna's own name', so out of courtesy the visitors said 'לִיעַיֵּין מַר בְּמִילֵיהּ'. findings.target: F14 claim wording ('two folios earlier') and the interpretive link
findings.reason: The teaching 'אם רואה אדם שיסורין באין עליו יפשפש במעשיו' is at Berakhot 5a:8, the facing side of the same folio, not 'two folios earlier'. Also, Ben Yehoyada is not the first to link the visitors' words to it. Petach Einayim reports the Yashresh Yaakov (answering the Zahav Sheva) reading 'ותירץ הרב דלעיל א"ר הונא אם רואה אדם שיסורין באים עליו יפשפש', and Petach Einayim argues against that reading. That makes it a disputed commentary interpretation, not a settled one. No 'visitors quote Huna' edge is added, as the dossier already says.

The reported manuscript line 'שמעו רבנן מילתא דעבדי בלא דינא?' uses 'רבנן' as a polite third-person address to the visitors. If this variant turn is stored, its addressee is the visiting group, marked by that word. It is not a new or different group of rabbis, and it is not a second mention of the accompanying sages as actors. It stays a secondary report of a manuscript variant, separate from printed turn c10, as the dossier says.

'רב יהודה אחוה דרב סלא חסידא' keeps sibling_of(yehuda, sala) in the Yehuda branch, and 'רב אדא בר אהבה' keeps child_of(ada, ahava) with Ahava as a local placeholder in the Adda branch. This follows the rule that name-embedded kinship is evidence even when the relative never acts. The note that the recurring epithet also works as a fixed distinguishing label is right, and so is keeping the relation anyway. Seder HaDorot 2801:1 restates the epithet and is not an independent witness.

findings.claim: The first prayer is told with a continuous form, הוה קא בעי ('was praying / was seeking'). The Davidson English and Cohen translate it as a finished prayer ('prayed'; 'Once R. findings.reasoning: This is a separate work with its own passage record. It shares the named pair, the neighbourhood and the verse, which makes it a parallel telling. But the antagonist differs: one min against the Bavli's plural troublemakers. So does the relation word (אתתיה against דביתהו), and so does the ending. Neither text says the two antagonists are the same people. In Midrash Tehillim the '103 psalms without Halleluya' teaching is given to Rabbi Shmuel bar Abba. Berakhot 9b gives a similar teaching to Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi. That is a difference in attribution between works. It does not show that only one of them said it. alternatives.reading: חטאים = 'sins', against the vowels (Cohen, Tosafot HaRosh, Ya'avetz). Or the written form carries both senses (Maharsha). Keep. Add progressive aspect (הוה קא בעי: was praying / was seeking) to the modality, and an alternative branch 'begun or intended, not completed'. Keep the note that no deaths occur.
Keep. Add the implicit-subject mention of בעא → Meir as its basis. Do not add an explicit 'Meir accepts Berurya's view' edge; 'saw that Berurya was correct' is Davidson's plain text.
Keep as time order only. Do not upgrade it to an explicit cause.
Add an explicit claim: troublemakers located in Meir's neighbourhood (בשבבותיה דרבי מאיר), voice narrator, basis explicit.
Add mentions: דעתך → Meir; the addressee of שפיל/בעי → Meir; the subject of בעא → Meir; the subjects of דלימותו/דלהדרו/והדרו → troublemakers.
Relabel the entity 'reading': Berurya reads חטאים as 'sins' rather than 'sinners' (against the vowels, according to Cohen, Tosafot HaRosh and Ya'avetz).

Episode note: the story has no named teller. It is not part of Rabbi Yoḥanan's statement in 10a:1. It is set editorially beside R. Yehuda b. R. Shimon b. Pazi's reading of Psalms 104:35 (9b:29); treat that as a link between statements, not between persons.

Earlier review: its passes stand. It should add these findings: speaker attribution in 10a:3 by continuity; progressive aspect in c3; the missing neighbourhood relation and mentions; the Midrash Tehillim parallel with a different antagonist.

lessons: Speech that continues across segments without a new speaker marker needs its own basis value, such as speech_continuation. It is neither explicit nor ordinary coreference.
Aramaic progressive forms (הוה קא + participle) need a modality or aspect value (ongoing / attempted) separate from completed action. Translations routinely flatten it.
A possessive relation noun (דביתהו, אתתיה) is an explicit kinship term with a possessor resolved from context. Store both parts.
Editorial juxtaposition of two readings of one verse is a link between statements in the editor's voice. It is not an interaction between the people.
A parallel in another work is its own passage record. When the antagonist differs (a group of troublemakers against one min), cross-work story identity is a separate decision.
Community translations can reverse the source (Midrash Tehillim 104:22). Check a translation against the Hebrew before using it as evidence.
A reason one speaker attributes to another as a question ('What is your thinking? Because...?') is not that person's asserted view.
Plain-text additions in the Davidson English ('Rabbi Meir saw that Berurya was correct', 'the Gemara relates', the link to R. Yehuda b. R. Shimon b. Pazi) are editorial commentary, not text.

review.scope: I checked every text quote in dossier.json against its saved file in sources/, reread Berakhot 9b:26-31 and 10a:1-7 and all the saved commentaries, Ein Yaakov texts and the Midrash Tehillim parallel around each quote, and read the Munich 95 crops myself; I did not fetch new sources, check other manuscripts, or judge who Berurya was historically.

findings.reason: The proposed label 'Berurya reads חטאים as sins rather than sinners' takes one side of an open question. Two saved commentaries give a different reading that keeps the vowels. Chokhmat Shlomo goes on to say 'חטאים היינו כמו חוטאים אלא קרי חטאים בדרך מפעיל', meaning 'those who make others sin'. Ben Yehoyada's last answer reads 'חטאים כתיב, שהוא פועל יוצא לאחרים שהם מחטיאים אחרים'. So F8's summary of Chokhmat Shlomo is incomplete, and A3 is wrong to call this line of reading 'tertiary and unattributed'. Keep a neutral label ('the verse writes חטאים, not חוטאים') with separate branches: 'sins' (Cohen, Tosafot HaRosh, Ya'avetz), 'those who cause others to sin' (Chokhmat Shlomo, Ben Yehoyada), and both senses at once (Maharsha). None of this changes a person or an edge.

F5 says Meir's agreement 'appears only in editors' words: Davidson's plain text ... and Steinsaltz'. That misstates the saved sources. The Tzelach, which the dossier quotes in F3, says 'ברוריא הביאה הוכחה לדברי' ור"מ שמע וקיבל דברי''. Ben Yehoyada reports 'הרי"ף' as saying 'דלמסקנא הודה ר' מאיר לברוריה'. The conclusion still holds, because the Aramaic 'בעא רחמי עלויהו' names no one and says nothing of agreement. But the evidence list for any 'accepts view of' edge should include these as commentary voices, kept apart from Davidson and Steinsaltz (one editorial project) and never marked as stated in the text.

findings.target: F6 / c3 alternative branch 'begun or intended, not completed'
findings.reason: The progressive form 'הֲוָה קָא בָּעֵי' is really in the text, so adding that aspect to c3 is right. But in the saved sources nobody holds the 'not completed' reading. It comes from a two-sided question that Ben Yehoyada reports from 'ספר חסידים' ('אם כבר ר"מ בקש ... ואם לא בקש עדיין'). Ben Yehoyada then answers 'דלעולם בקש' (he did pray). Tosafot HaRosh also treats the prayer as made and defends it ('שמא היו מצערין אותו יותר מדאי'). Record the branch as a question raised in a reported commentary, with low confidence. Do not present it as an alternative reading someone holds.

'הנהו בריוני דהוו בשבבותיה דרבי מאיר' says outright, in the narrator's voice, that the group lived in Meir's neighbourhood. The pilot saved this only in a label. Add it as an explicit claim, with the group left unnamed and uncounted. Keep Rashi's 'פריצים' and Tosafot HaRosh's 'לסטים ישראל' as commentary glosses, not attributes of the group. Record the Midrash Tehillim 'ההוא מינא בשיבבותיה' separately, and do not merge it into this claim.

findings.target: F4 / c6, c7 speaker and addressee of 10a:3
findings.reason: 10a:3 names no new speaker. 'ועוד' continues Berurya's speech from 10a:2 ('אמרה ליה ברוריא דביתהו'), and the second-person masculine imperatives 'שפיל' and 'בעי' mark Meir as the addressee. So the addressee is marked by the text, while the speaker is known only because the speech continues. A basis like 'speech continuation', rather than bare local_coreference, is accurate. One small point: Cohen turns the 'כיון ...' clause into a statement ('i.e. when sins will cease, then the wicked will be no more'), while Davidson and the dossier read it as a rhetorical question. That affects only the content label of 'ending'.

I checked the pilot's anchors. m5 is the 'ליה' in 'מצערו ליה' and m6 is the 'ליה' in 'אמרה ליה', and both mean Meir. m7-m9 are the 'עלויהו' in s1-s3, and all mean the troublemakers. The mentions without a pronoun word (the suffix in 'דעתך', the addressee of 'שפיל/בעי', the unnamed subject of 'בעא', and the subjects of 'דלימותו', 'דלהדרו' and 'והדרו') are exactly what c7 and c8 rest on. Adding them creates no new person or edge.

findings.target: F2 / narrator of the story (and 10a:1 transmitter)
findings.reason: The main conclusion holds. The chain at 9b:31 (Davidson: 'דאמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יוחנן') introduces only 10a:1, and the story at 10a:2 opens a new unit with no teller. The dossier quotes the right occurrence (9b:31, not the 'דאמר' at 9b:29). However, the dossier's own saved Glick Ein Yaakov reads 'דאמר (דף י) רשב״ג אמר רבי יוחנן' at that point. This is a witness variant in the name of the 10a:1 transmitter. Record it for the 10a:1 statement without resolving it (it may be a print confusion), and still attach no chain to the story.

I read the crops myself (see quote_checks). I confirm, in broad terms, the margin note beside story line 3 ('כיון דיתמו ח... / ורשעים עוד אינם', with a small insertion mark), the main-line 'ועוד שפיל לסיפיה דקרא ורשעים עוד אינם', and 'אמרה ליה ברורי[?] דביתהו'. I cannot tell whether the name ends in א or ה. Like the dossier, I could not read the main-line words of the first prayer clause under the small interlinear writing. These stay visual readings, kept apart from printed text, and they cannot settle the wording of c3.

findings.target: F9, F13 / parallels and cross-passage joins
findings.reason: Midrash Tehillim 104:22 has one 'מינא', the wife called 'ברוריה אתתיה', 'הוה בעי עליה דלימות', and no repentance. The Community Translation does reverse her argument. So the parallel needs its own record and must not import a min into the Bavli. Avodah Zarah 18a ('ברוריא דביתהו דר' מאיר ברתיה דר' חנינא בן תרדיון הואי') gives a father and a sister only in that passage, and a join stays a proposal. A further note: the saved Glick Ein Yaakov goes straight from 'והדרי בתשובה' to 'א״ל ההוא צדוקי לר׳ אבהו'. That text has no 10a:5 challenge to Berurya at this point, so an extractor must not attach that tzeduki to Berurya.

cases.question: In Berakhot 10a:21-25, who are the people and how are they related? Who arranges aggadah before R. Yehoshua ben Levi, who asks and who answers, and which speech turns and attributions are explicit, interpreted or variant?

findings.claim: The printed Aramaic names a regular attendee in two reported forms, Rav Shimi bar Ukva or 'Mar Ukva', introduced by ואמרי לה ('and some say'). It says he was regularly before Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi. The verb is הוה שכיח קמיה ('was regularly present before'). Neither the verb nor its context names a formal teacher-student bond. The word 'study' in the William Davidson English, and ללמוד in its Hebrew version, are plain-text additions by the editors.

evidence.exact_quote: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר עוּקְבָא וְאָמְרִי לַהּ מָר עוּקְבָא, הֲוָה שְׁכִיחַ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי
evidence.translation_by_this_dossier: Rav Shimi bar Ukva, and some say Mar Ukva, was regularly before Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi

evidence.exact_quote: רב שימי בר עוקבא ואמרי לה מר עוקבא הוה שכיח קמיה דר' שמעון בן פזי
Rav Shimi bar Ukva, and some say Mar Ukva, would regularly study before Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi,
הוה שכיח קמיה [היה מצוי, ללמוד לפני]
was frequently in the company of R. Simeon b. Pazzi

findings.reasoning: ואמרי לה introduces a second name for one role. It does not put two people in the scene. In the English, 'study' is outside the bold text, so it is the editors' explanation. In the Steinsaltz Hebrew, ללמוד sits outside the bracketed gloss of the Aramaic. Cohen 1921 has only 'in the company of'. Frequent presence is a scene relation, not a teacher or student edge.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c5 and c6 as a two-branch group on one role. Keep the predicate as attendance or presence, with no student_of edge. The earlier reading already does this.

findings.claim: The Hebrew Wikisource explained edition gives manuscript variants for the name line. Its template page says the variants come mainly from Dikdukei Soferim or the Hachi Garsinan project. As this dossier parses the note, it reports three variants. (a) One manuscript, marked א, reads 'bar Akaviah' for 'bar Ukva'. (b) The manuscripts lack the words ואמרי לה מר עוקבא ('and some say Mar Ukva'). (c) The manuscripts marked מ' and פ' add בשמעתתא, giving 'was regularly present at the discourses' before R. Shimon ben Pazi.

unresolved: No manuscript image or transcription was viewed. Every manuscript reading here is secondhand, from the Wikisource explained edition (mainly Dikdukei Soferim or Hachi Garsinan), Cohen 1921 or Soncino, and these may share one origin.

The Wikisource page does not expand its sigla (מ', פ', א', בו', ס"פ). Reading מ' as Munich rests on agreement with Cohen's 'M.' and Soncino's 'MS.M.'. Which manuscripts 'the manuscripts' covers was not established.

lessons: One editorial project can contradict itself on who speaks (William Davidson English 10a:21 against 10a:24 and its Hebrew). Store translator-supplied speaker names as interpretations, check them for consistency, and never pool them with the same project's other outputs.

Manuscript readings reported by later works (Dikdukei Soferim through a wiki page, Cohen's 'M.', Soncino's 'MS.M.') are their own evidence type. They may share one origin and should not be counted as independent witnesses.
A reported-alternative name (ואמרי לה X) can itself be a printed-edition element that manuscripts lack. Branch groups need witness-type metadata, not only branch labels.
Variants can change the speech act, not only the speaker: 'I was saying to you' against 'I heard thus'. Speech claims need a speech-act field that can branch.
A manuscript can attribute a line that the print leaves anonymous, as here, or can give a closing line to a scriptural figure. Attribution should be branchable per witness.
Generic comparison figures ('flesh and blood', 'the soul') are not persons and should be kept out of person nodes.
A modern editor's conjecture is its own evidence type, below a commentary and far below the text.

Shimon ben Pazi answers' option in A5 is scoped to the printed text (and to the one editorial project that supplies 'he answered him').

findings.target: F6 and proposed correction for c10, c11, c15 (attendee asks, Shimon answers, attendee clarifies)
findings.reason: F6 leans on Rashi's 'הוא סבר דהכי בעי מאי שנא קרבים דנקט' (the answerer thought the question was about 'inward parts') to show that the answerer misread the question, so the 10a:24 clarifier must be the original asker. The Wikisource footnote on that very answer reports 'ובכתה"י השאלה היא "מאי דכתיב וכל קרבי"': in the manuscripts the question itself asks about 'and all my inward parts'. In that branch the first answer does not misread anything, so Rashi's logic does not carry over. Keep the asker/answerer/clarifier interpretation claims, but scope them to the printed text, and record the reported question wording as a separate variant that weakens the clarifier-equals-asker inference.

findings.target: F6 evidence and reading.md 'Who asked and who answered'
findings.reason: Most of the translator names F6 cites sit at 10a:24, not 10a:21. Cohen footnote 15 ('Rab Shimi to R. Simeon b. Pazzi. What follows is an alternative explanation...') and Soncino note 29 ('R. Shimi to R. Simeon b. Pazzi.') are attached to 'He said to him' before 'I tell thee as follows'. At 10a:21, Soncino note 26 names only the asker, in both forms ('R. Shimi or Mar 'Ukba.'), with no addressee. Cohen names no one there ('He asked him'). Only the Steinsaltz Hebrew names R. Shimon ben Pazi as the 10a:21 addressee. So the claim that the attendee asked R. Shimon ben Pazi at 10a:21 is inferred backwards from the 10a:24 notes. Store it that way, and do not present it as 'most sources' naming both parties at 10a:21.

findings.reason: Cohen note 14 glosses the arranging as a lecture-hall practice: 'the lecturer used to give the gist of his discourse to the Amora who then expounded it in fuller detail to the disciples.' That would turn 'מסדר אגדתא קמיה דר' יהושע בן לוי' into a formal expounder-for-a-master role. The Aramaic says only 'arranged aggadah before'. If the note is recorded, record it as a translator's interpretation. The predicate should stay 'arranged aggadah before', with no student_of, meturgeman or teacher edge.

The William Davidson English does put 'Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi' as the 10a:21 asker and 'Rav Shimi bar Ukva said to Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: Come and see' in plain text. Its own 10a:24 says 'This did not satisfy Rav Shimi bar Ukva', which contradicts that, so F5 is right to set it aside. Soncino has 'before R. Johanan' against every Hebrew text, as F13 says. The Midrash Tehillim quotes in F14 are exact and rightly kept out of this scene. 'Generic human artist' appears as an entity in the pilot output and should be retyped as a class, not a person.

cases.question: Who are the people in Ketubot 65a:9-10 (Homa, Abaye/Nahmani, Rava, Rav Hisda's daughter, Rav Hisda, the 'three' and 'another'), which of their family relations and speech turns does the text state, and which depend on commentary, parallels or editorial explanation?

findings.claim: Homa is Abaye's wife, stated twice: once by the narrator and once by Rava. The segment itself does not say that Abaye is dead. That she is his widow comes from the maintenance claim, from editors and commentators, and from Yevamot 64b.

findings.reasoning: The spouse relation rests on the construct דביתהו דאביי, and the narrator and Rava both use it. Rava's repetition is a second statement of the same relation in another voice inside the same story. It is not an independent observation. 'After Abaye died' is plain text in the William Davidson English, so it is the editor's explanation. The widowhood is supported by commentary and by the Yevamot narrator's ושכיב. The Ketubot sentence does not state it.
findings.graph_effect: Keep c1 (Homa spouse_of Abaye, explicit, narrator). Add time_scope 'marriage ended by Abaye's death' only as interpretation, citing Rashi mahadura kama and Yevamot 64b. Do not treat the plain-text English as Talmud wording. Record Rava's repetition (c14 content) as a voice of the same relation, not as a second edge.

findings.claim: Inside the passage, 'Nahmani' is Rava's name for Abaye. Rava answers the widow's wine claim with what he knows about Nahmani. Other passages make the alias explicit in context: in Shabbat 33a Rava says 'I know about Nahmani' right after the report that Abaye fell ill, and in Pesachim 112b a demon tells Abaye that Heaven announced 'beware of Nahmani'.

unresolved: Whether the Ketubot Homa is the Yevamot 64b Homa is supported by commentary and by the shared husband Abaye. The Ketubot text does not state it, so it stays a cross-passage decision.

Whether 'Rav Hisda's daughter' in Ketubot 65a is the same woman as in Yevamot 34b and Bava Batra 12b is not stated in any of these texts. Rav Hisda may have had more than one daughter; this was not checked here.
Whether Abaye drank wine is disputed inside the story (Rava versus Homa's oath) and is not settled by the narrator.

The Munich 95 and Vilna marginal readings are researcher visual readings. The Munich script was read only for the spelling of Homa's name, tentatively, and the rest of its wording was not transcribed.
Rashi at the end of Horayot (the 'disparaging' explanation of Nahmani) and the Arukh were not fetched directly. They are known here only as reported by Seder HaDorot.
The Moed Katan proof text cited by the Rosh was not fetched. Petach Einayim's claim that it concerns Rabbah bar Nahmani is unverified here.
